result.months_submission_to_award:
Depends on the mechanism; two very different arcs.

STANDARD HUMANITIES FELLOWSHIP ARC (ACLS Fellowships, and the dissertation fellowships that share it):
- Deadline Sept 17, 2026 → notification April 2027 = ~6.5 months to hear anything
- Deadline Sept 17, 2026 → earliest award start July 1, 2027 = ~9.5 months to money
- Reviewer feedback available ~August 2027 = ~11 months
- Award term window: July 1, 2027 – Dec 31, 2028, inside which you take your 6–12 months
Mellon/ACLS DIF is the same shape: Oct 28, 2026 → "notifications will be sent via email in late April 2027" = ~6 months.

PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE: this is a ~10-month lead time. You cannot use ACLS to solve a funding gap that opens next term. Apply in the autumn of the academic year BEFORE the year you want off, and tell your chair in the autumn, not the spring.

FAST EXCEPTION — LEADING EDGE FELLOWSHIPS: deadline Mar 10, 2027 → all applicants notified by mid-May, awardees announced early June = ~2–3 months. Because it places people in host organisations, it runs on a hiring timetable, not a fellowship timetable, and includes interviews.
result.page_limits:
Limits are strict, specified in PAGES not words, and ACLS dictates the font. Verbatim from each competition page (fetched 2026-09-18).

ACLS FELLOWSHIPS (the flagship; note how short the proposal is):
- Proposal: "no more than three pages, single-spaced, in Arial or Helvetica 11-point font, inclusive of any footnotes or endnotes" — the word "inclusive" is load-bearing; you cannot push citations into notes to buy space
- Work plan: "no more than one page, in single-spaced text or in a timeline/chart format"
- Bibliography: "no more than two pages, single-spaced, in Arial or Helvetica 11-point font"
- Publication list: "no more than two pages, single-spaced, in Arial or Helvetica 11-point font"
- Personal statement: "up to one page (single spaced, in Arial or Helvetica 11-point font)"
- Optional supporting materials: "Up to two additional pages of images, musical scores, or other similar supporting non-text materials"

MELLON/ACLS DISSERTATION INNOVATION FELLOWSHIP (roughly double, and DOUBLE-spaced — do not copy the flagship's formatting across):
- Proposal: "no more than seven pages, double spaced"
- Personal statement: "no more than two pages, double spaced"
- Work sample: "No more than fifteen pages total, double spaced" — the 2022 portal text adds "with one-inch margins, including any images and footnotes or endnotes"
- Bibliography: "no more than two pages"
- Timeline: one page
- Supporting images/materials: "Up to two additional pages"

ACLS LEADING EDGE FELLOWSHIPS (not a research proposal at all — a job application):
- A cover letter and resume for EACH position applied to
- Two short-answer questions, 300-word limit each
- ACLS states the application "takes approximately one to two hours to complete"

WHAT VARIES BY MECHANISM: single- vs double-spacing, proposal length (3pp to 7pp), whether a work sample is required (dissertation fellowships yes, flagship no), and whether letters are accepted at all. WHAT IS CONSTANT: Arial or Helvetica 11-point, page-count limits inclusive of notes, and a 2-page allowance for non-text supporting material.
result.program_officer_norms:
TOLERATED AND STRUCTURED — but through group office hours and named inboxes, not one-on-one project consultation. This is the single biggest behavioural difference from NIH. Do not expect to build a relationship with a named program officer who shepherds your proposal; that role does not exist here. But do not conclude contact is discouraged either — ACLS actively runs sessions and invites questions.

THE SANCTIONED CHANNELS:
- fellowships@acls.org — programme and eligibility questions. This is the address ACLS itself prints when a rule is ambiguous; from the DIF application form, verbatim: "if [an] interdisciplinary program qualifies you for this fellowship program, please email fellowships@acls.org with a brief summary of your affiliation."
- ofahelp@acls.org — portal and technical problems (taken directly from the ofa.acls.org login page). There is also an "OFA Help" link inside the application itself.
- references@acls.org — reference-portal problems. NOTE: this address came from the search index, not from a page I fetched directly.

OFFICE HOURS AND WEBINARS — THE REAL ANSWER: ACLS runs informational webinars and live Zoom office hours each cycle, hosted by ACLS program officers and staff, and publishes them as a resource ("Register for upcoming information sessions and office hours for potential applicants to our 2026-27 fellowship and grant programs," resource dated July 20, 2026). They are scheduled across the whole open period, roughly monthly. For the 2026-27 HBCU Faculty competition (deadline Nov 11) the published office hours were Thu Jul 30 12:00–13:00 ET, Fri Aug 21 11:00–12:00 ET, Wed Sep 16 16:00–17:00 ET, Tue Oct 13 10:00–11:00 ET, Mon Nov 2 14:00–15:00 ET — i.e. starting ~3.5 months out and running to ~9 days before the deadline. PROVENANCE: those specific dates and the "hosted by program officers" characterisation came through the search index; the ACLS resource page itself redirected to a general application portal when fetched, so I could not confirm the 2026-27 registration link directly. Treat the pattern as established and the individual dates as needing a check.

WHEN IN THE CYCLE: attend an EARLY session (3–4 months out) for eligibility and fit, because eligibility gates here are unusually mechanical and disqualifying — ABD-by-date rules, institution type, citizenship/residency, months-since-PhD. Use a LATE session for form and upload mechanics. Eligibility is the thing worth asking a human about before you write anything.

WHAT EXPERIENCED APPLICANTS ACTUALLY ASK: (a) whether an unusual affiliation, joint appointment or interdisciplinary programme counts — ACLS explicitly invites this by email; (b) how to calculate progress-to-degree when a leave, caregiving or medical interruption breaks the clock (the form has a 1000-character field for exactly this, and instructs that "Your referee should note these circumstances as well in their letter"); (c) whether a non-traditional output — a digital project, an exhibition, a community partnership — is fundable under the stated criteria; (d) whether an award can be held alongside a university funding package (for DIF this is formalised as the institutional statement). They do NOT ask for feedback on a draft proposal; ACLS does not offer that.

ONE HARD PROHIBITION: for Leading Edge Fellowships, applicants may NOT contact the host organisations with questions — all questions go to ACLS. Breaking this is visible and avoidable.

review_stages.stage: Submission closes. Application must be in SUBMITTED status at the stated time — ACLS's own portal wording for a past cycle was that it "must be complete and in SUBMITTED status" at the deadline hour. Reference letters, where required, are due at the SAME deadline, not later.
review_stages.timing: Day 0 (e.g. Sept 17, 2026, 5:00 PM ET for ACLS Fellowships)

review_stages.stage: Eligibility screen by ACLS staff. Mechanical and unforgiving — citizenship/residency, degree date, ABD status by a fixed date, institution type. Reviewers only see "all eligible proposals".
review_stages.timing: Weeks 1–4 after the deadline

review_stages.stage: Stage 1 — disciplinary peer review. Per the ACLS Fellowships FAQ: "three established scholars in your discipline (and/or regional area of study) will judge your proposal." Applications are "judged against others at your relative career stage", so an assistant professor is not scored against a chaired professor.
review_stages.timing: ~1–4 months after the deadline

review_stages.stage: Stage 2 — multidisciplinary final panel. Finalists are "reviewed by a panel of scholars whose collective expertise covers a range of disciplines in the humanities and humanities-related fields." This is why the proposal must read to an intelligent non-specialist: the people who decide the last cut are not in your subfield.
review_stages.timing: ~4–6 months after the deadline

review_stages.stage: Notification by email. ACLS Fellowships: "April 2027" for a Sept 17, 2026 deadline. Mellon/ACLS DIF: "Notifications will be sent via email in late April 2027" for an Oct 28, 2026 deadline.
review_stages.timing: ~6–6.5 months after the deadline

review_stages.stage: Consolation mechanism worth knowing: ACLS Fellowships finalists who are not selected may receive Project Development Grants of $5,000. Reaching the final panel is therefore not nothing.
review_stages.timing: With notification, ~6.5 months

review_stages.stage: Award term begins. ACLS Fellowships tenure window is July 1, 2027 – December 31, 2028, inside which the fellow takes 6–12 months.
review_stages.timing: Earliest start ~9.5 months after the deadline

review_stages.stage: REVIEWER FEEDBACK ON REQUEST — unusual for a private foundation and the closest thing to an NIH summary statement. "All applicants will be able to request reviewer feedback", with comments expected by August 2027. The DIF FAQ adds the limit: "feedback is made available at the discretion of each reviewer. Comments may not be available from every reviewer who assessed your application." Request it via the online form supplied with your results — this is the raw material for a stronger resubmission.
review_stages.timing: ~11 months after the deadline (e.g. August 2027)

review_stages.stage: EXCEPTION — LEADING EDGE runs three stages on a hiring clock: "First, all eligible applications are read by peer reviewers whose collective expertise covers a range of disciplines in the humanities as well as a broad spectrum of career experience... At that point, applications are reviewed by the host organizations, who will send rankings and feedback to ACLS. Finally, ACLS interviews top-ranked candidates to offer the fellowship." Finalists announced any time before mid-May; all applicants notified by mid-May; awardees announced early June.
review_stages.timing: ~2–3 months after the March deadline

required_documents: OFA account at https://ofa.acls.org/register/ — salutation, first/last name, email entered twice, password of "at least 8 characters". Alternatively the login page offers "Login with ORCID". Low friction, but it must exist before you can see any form.

ORCID iD — the DIF application form states "ACLS requires all applicants to provide an ORCID iD as part of their application", with a lookup that "works for public ORCID records only". Register at orcid.org and make the record public well in advance. PROVENANCE: quoted from the 2022-23 DIF portal print-out; consistent with the current OFA "Login with ORCID" option, but I could not re-verify it on the 2026-27 ACLS Fellowships form.

Application form itself — contact information, demographic information (optional self-ID fields), education, awards and prior funding, publications ("You may list up to six items here"), project details, administrative information.
Proposal — see page_limits; 3pp single-spaced for ACLS Fellowships, 7pp double-spaced for Mellon/ACLS DIF.
Personal statement — 1pp (flagship) or 2pp (DIF).
Work plan / timeline — 1pp, prose or chart.
Bibliography — 2pp.
Publication list — 2pp (flagship).
Work sample — DIF only: 15pp double-spaced including images and notes, "including a brief description of context and the sample's relation to the proposed project".
Optional non-text supporting materials — up to 2 additional pages of images, musical scores or similar.

Reference letters — VARIES SHARPLY AND IS THE COMMONEST MISTAKE. ACLS Fellowships: NONE, and they will not be read — "This program will not accept reference letters." Mellon/ACLS DIF: exactly one, which "must come from the applicant's dissertation advisor, or a faculty member eligible to be the advisor." ACLS/NYPL Cullman Center: three. Leading Edge: referees named with contact details, and they "need not be academics."

Institutional statement — DIF only: a form, not a letter, from "the applicant's department chair, director of graduate studies, or dean", attesting that the award extends rather than replaces existing funding, that the university will let you stay enrolled while waiving tuition and fees, and that it supports innovative dissertation directions. "The person submitting the institutional form should not be the same as your reference letter writer."

TRAP 1 — DOSSIER SERVICES ARE REFUSED: "ACLS does not accept reference letters from dossier services, such as Interfolio or university-based services." Your referee must upload directly. Tell them this early; many will assume Interfolio works.

TRAP 2 — YOU MUST ENTER REFEREES FIRST: "You MUST ENTER YOUR REFEREES on the Reference Letters page BEFORE they can log in to use the online references system. Please do not ask them to access the system until you have done this." The referee cannot self-start; adding them triggers the automated email.

TRAP 3 — HARD CAPS, FIRST COME FIRST SERVED: "No more than one letter of reference and one institutional statement will be accepted... Once the maximum number has been submitted, another referee attempting to submit a letter for you will be prevented from doing so. Be careful not to put anyone in this situation."

TRAP 4 — LETTERS ARE DUE AT THE APPLICATION DEADLINE, not after. The system "will continue to accept letters for a few days after the deadline... though we cannot guarantee that they will accompany your application through our entire review process."
TRAP 5 — PORTAL NAVIGATION: "Do not use your browser's 'BACK' or 'FORWARD' buttons for navigation." Use the left-hand menu or Save and Continue.
Use the View/Print Application screen to proof the assembled package before submitting.
result.resubmission_policy:
ALLOWED, but the cap varies by mechanism and one mechanism enforces it as an eligibility gate. There is NO introduction page, NO response-to-reviewers document, and NO NIH-style A0/A1 designation anywhere in the ACLS system. Nothing in the application marks you as a returning applicant, and reviewers are not told.

BY MECHANISM:
- ACLS Fellowships — no stated cap. You may come back year after year, but you rebuild the submission each time. Verbatim: "You may revise the content of your previous application, but you will need to start over with a new online application for the current competition year." Practically: keep your own copies of every uploaded file; the portal will not carry them forward.
- Mellon/ACLS Dissertation Innovation Fellowship — ONCE ONLY. Verbatim: "Yes, but unsuccessful applicants may reapply to this program only once." This is also enforced upstream as eligibility: applicants must "not [have] previously applied more than once." So a PhD student gets exactly two lifetime attempts, and given the ABD-date gate the second attempt may not be available. Spend the first one deliberately.
- ACLS Leading Edge Fellowships — unlimited while eligible. Verbatim: "Yes, you may apply to the program more than once, provided that you still meet the eligibility requirements. ACLS awardees are not permitted to hold two ACLS fellowships concurrently."

NO TIME WINDOW: unlike NIH's former 37-month rule, ACLS imposes no window within which a resubmission must arrive. The binding constraint is instead the eligibility clock — months since PhD, ABD status by a fixed date, current enrolment — which for early-career mechanisms usually closes faster than any resubmission limit would.

WHAT SHOULD CHANGE ON A RESUBMISSION: ACLS gives no instruction, because it asks for no comparison document. The actionable input is the reviewer feedback you can request after a decline (available ~August for a September deadline, "at the discretion of each reviewer"). That arrives roughly a month before the next cycle's deadline — tight but usable. Request it the moment results land.

ALSO WORTH KNOWING: ACLS does not bar applying to several of its competitions in the same cycle, and the calendar is staggered to permit it (Sept 17 / Oct 28 / Nov 5 / Nov 11), but awardees "are not permitted to hold two ACLS fellowships concurrently." I could not find a page stating a general rule on simultaneous applications across competitions — see unresolved.
result.submission_portal:
ACLS OFA — the Online Fellowship and grant Administration system. Everything goes through it; there is no Grants.gov, no Research.gov, no ProposalCentral, and no institutional sponsored-projects route. ACLS fellowships are paid to the individual, so your research office is not in the submission path at all (though for Mellon/ACLS DIF your department must supply an institutional statement — see required_documents).

THREE SEPARATE PORTALS, and confusing them costs people letters:
- https://ofa.acls.org — applicants
- https://ofa.acls.org/reference/ — reference-letter writers and institutional-statement signers (a DIFFERENT system; your referee cannot use your login)
- https://awardee.acls.org — awardees only, post-award reporting

ADVANCE REGISTRATION — the hidden long-lead items, in the order you should do them:
1. Create the applicant account at https://ofa.acls.org/register/. Fields: salutation, first/given name, middle (optional), last/family name, suffix (optional), email address entered twice, and a password of "at least 8 characters". The login page also offers "Login with ORCID". This takes five minutes but gates everything — you cannot read the real form until you are inside.
2. Get an ORCID iD and make the record PUBLIC. The DIF application form states "ACLS requires all applicants to provide an ORCID iD as part of their application" and warns that "The record search feature works for public ORCID records only." A private ORCID record will fail the lookup. (Provenance caveat in required_documents.)
3. Have your institution's FULL legal name to hand — the form matches against an internal database: "your institution's name must be displayed correctly. Enter a few letters of your institution's name to search against our database. Use the full name, not an acronym or abbreviation."
4. Use an email address that will still work months later — the form asks for a primary email "should be valid through May" of the following year, i.e. past the notification date. Do not use a student address that expires at graduation.
5. If your mechanism needs letters, enter your referees in the portal EARLY, because they cannot access the reference system until you do.

Technical support: ofahelp@acls.org (printed on the OFA login page), plus an "OFA Help" link inside the application.

TIP: before creating anything, read the published 48-page print-out of the entire OFA system at https://www.acls.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/DIF-Sample-Application.pdf — every screen and field, so you can assemble answers offline.
unresolved: ACLS Fellowships success rate — not published. ACLS states at least 60 awards for 2026-27 and "approximately $3.5 million to 63 exceptional scholars" recently, but never the applicant pool. The only published ratio anywhere in the system is Mellon/ACLS DIF 2026: 50 fellows from "over 1,000 applicants" (~5%). Do not generalise that rate to the flagship — not found.

Whether the ORCID requirement still binds on the 2026-27 ACLS Fellowships form. The quote "ACLS requires all applicants to provide an ORCID iD as part of their application" is from the 2022-23 Mellon/ACLS DIF portal print-out. The current OFA login offers "Login with ORCID", which is consistent, but I did not see the requirement restated on a 2026-27 page.

The 2026-27 webinar and office-hours schedule and its registration link. The ACLS resource page for the current cycle redirected to a general application portal on fetch; the specific HBCU office-hours dates (Jul 30, Aug 21, Sep 16, Oct 13, Nov 2) and the "hosted by program officers" characterisation came from the SEARCH INDEX, not a page I fetched directly. The existence of the programme is confirmed by ACLS's own resource listing ("Register for upcoming information sessions and office hours... 2026-27", dated July 20, 2026).
references@acls.org — search-index sourced only; not confirmed on any acls.org or ofa.acls.org page I fetched. ofahelp@acls.org and fellowships@acls.org ARE directly confirmed.

Whether ACLS publishes full project abstracts of funded work anywhere. The Fellows and Grantees database shows titles only; the Recent Awardees page is a navigation hub; award announcements give prose paragraphs, not abstracts. I found no abstract corpus — not found.

No sample application packet exists for ACLS Fellowships itself. Only Mellon/ACLS DIF packets (2022 and 2023) were located. Whether ACLS has published equivalents for other competitions was not established.

Whether a general rule governs applying to multiple ACLS competitions in the same cycle. The general FAQ does not address it and directs applicants to per-competition FAQs; only the 'no two concurrent fellowships' rule for awardees is confirmed.
Number of $5,000 Project Development Grants awarded annually to ACLS Fellowships finalists — ACLS states the mechanism exists but not the count.

Whether the DEI-related evaluation criterion survives in current form. The 2022 DIF portal listed a fourth criterion on membership in historically underrepresented groups; the current DIF page still references engagement with "historically underrepresented" communities, but I could not confirm the exact current wording of criterion 4 against the live portal (only the public competition page). Given post-SFFA drift this specific field should be re-read each cycle before being relied on.

Referee letter deadlines for mechanisms other than DIF. The 'letters due at the application deadline' rule is quoted from the DIF portal; I did not verify it holds for the Cullman Center's three letters.

result.funder_system: American Heart Association (AHA) — research awards administered by AHA Research Programs, Dallas TX. Largest non-profit, non-governmental funder of cardiovascular/cerebrovascular research in the US. Awards are restricted to US-based non-profit institutions; no federal institutions or federal employees (VA employees excepted). Applicants do NOT have to reside in the US before applying, but must hold one of an enumerated citizenship/visa designations AT THE TIME OF SUBMISSION (not at award start): US citizen, permanent resident, pending permanent resident (I-485 filed + I-797C), E-3, G-4, H-1B, O-1, TN, DACA — plus F-1 and J-1 for predoctoral and postdoctoral fellowships ONLY (for all other programs a J-1 holder must have an H-1B or equivalent by the proposal due date). FY25-26 success rates published by AHA: Career Development Award 30.5%, Institutional Award for Undergraduate Student Training 45.2%, AIREA 27.9%, Postdoctoral Fellowship 24.6%, Predoctoral Fellowship 22.0%, Innovative Project Award 19.9%, Strategically Focused Research Network 11.7% (https://professional.heart.org/en/research-programs/success-rates). NOTE ON METHOD: professional.heart.org returns HTTP 403 to plain fetch and to curl with a browser UA. Everything below was read through a rendering browser on the funder's own pages, and the 57-page Application Instructions PDF was extracted in-browser with pdf.js over a same-origin fetch. No claim below rests on a search index.
result.submission_portal:
ProposalCentral (Altum) — https://proposalcentral.com, reached via AHA's own landing page https://professional.heart.org/en/research-programs/aha-proposalcentral. "Submission of proposals for research funding is done entirely online, using ProposalCentral. Paper submissions are not accepted. Only the required documents can be submitted; there is no mechanism for supplemental materials."

FOUR HIDDEN LONG-LEAD ITEMS, all of which must be done BEFORE you can press submit:

1. AHA account linked to ProposalCentral. On first login you must follow AHA's Login Instructions (PDF) to link your AHA account (which also carries membership, peer-review, meeting and publication history, and legacy Grants@Heart records) to ProposalCentral. New users register via the applicant link (separate link for peer reviewers).

2. AHA Professional Membership — REQUIRED at the time of submission, for the applicant, and AHA "expects all mentors associated with training/mentored research awards to maintain active Association Professional Membership, as well." Funder's words: "Membership processing may take 3-5 days; do not wait until the application deadline to renew or join." You can join from inside the proposal via the Member/Application Fee screen (that link makes ProposalCentral recognise you instantly). Current dues (https://professional.heart.org/en/professional-membership/become-a-member): Student/Trainee $125/yr, Early Career $155/yr, General $165/yr, Premium $425/yr. Membership phone +1-888-242-2453 or 214-570-5935. Dues are refundable if you decide not to submit, but NOT if your grants officer refuses to send the proposal.

3. ORCID iD — "You are not required to have an ORCiD number to log into ProposalCentral, however, it is now required to submit applications."

4. Institutional officers in ProposalCentral. Your institution must be a "confirmed institution" in the system, and you select Grants Officer, Fiscal Officer and Technology Transfer Officer from drop-downs (or add them by email). "the Grants Officer will need to electronically sign the proposal prior to submission." Both applicant and Grants Officer type their names into the signature box and click "sign". The flow is two-step: PI submits to the grants officer, the grants officer signs and releases to AHA — and a grants officer can decline it back to you for revisions (your profile and payment survive). Every AHA RFP repeats: "All submissions require the signature of a designated institutional representative."

Timing of the portal itself: "The system will open eight weeks prior to the application deadline to complete the proposal and upload required documents." You can draft all uploads before that.

Optional but time-boxed: AHA's Precision Medicine Platform (https://precision.heart.org/getting-started) gives a free cloud workspace "60 days prior to your application deadline" to compute preliminary data; you publish the Jupyter/RMarkdown notebook as HTML and paste the static URL into the application. CAUTION — mechanism-specific: the Career Development Award RFP forbids hyperlinks in the Research Plan or any other proposal document and says "This includes use of the Precision Medicine Platform for applications and peer review purposes." Check your own RFP before relying on a PMP link. PMP contact: datascience@heart.org.

Technical help (Altum, not AHA): pcsupport@altum.com, 1-800-875-2562 (US/Canada), +1-703-964-5840 international. Altum observes its own holiday closure calendar, distinct from AHA's — both are published at the foot of every AHA research page, and both fall near December deadlines.

Confirm submission: after submitting, log out, log back in, open the Proposals tab and confirm status reads "Submitted"; a properly submitted proposal disappears from your Home tab. "Once the application is submitted, no changes can be made."
result.deadline_structure:
PER-PROGRAM ANNUAL CYCLES, STAGGERED THROUGH THE YEAR — there is no NIH-style grid of standard due dates by activity code, and no new-vs-resubmission date offset. AHA's own words (Application Instructions, Rev. 9/14/2026): "The American Heart Association has rolling deadlines throughout the year. If your proposal is unsuccessful, you are encouraged to reapply the next time the program is offered if you continue to meet the application requirements. New deadline dates are generally posted with several months' notice."

Each program's RFP carries a dated "Key Dates" block. These are the real, published dates for the cycle now in flight (read 18 Sept 2026 from each program's own AHA page). Treat the weekday-anchored dates as the recurring pattern; the exact date moves a few days each year.

TRAINING AWARDS — early-August deadline, January start:
• Predoctoral Fellowship — RFP posted Apr 28, 2026; ProposalCentral opens May 15, 2026; deadline Tue Aug 4, 2026, 3 p.m. CT; award notification Dec 2026; award start Jan 1, 2027.
• Postdoctoral Fellowship — RFP posted Apr 28, 2026; ProposalCentral opens May 15, 2026; deadline Wed Aug 5, 2026, 3 p.m. CT; notification Dec 2026; start Jan 1, 2027.
• Institutional Research Enhancement Award (AIREA) — RFP posted Apr 28, 2026; ProposalCentral opens May 15, 2026; deadline Thu Sept 10, 2026; notification Dec 2026; start Jan 1, 2027.

EARLY-FACULTY / PROJECT AWARDS — December deadline, spring/summer start:
• Career Development Award — RFP posted Apr 28, 2026; ProposalCentral opens Oct 1, 2026; deadline Tue Dec 1, 2026, 3 p.m. CT; award notification March 2027; award start Apr 1, 2027.
• Using Get With The Guidelines Clinical Registry Data (early-career) — deadline Fri Dec 4, 2026. Gated: "To apply for the grant, individuals must attend the two virtual training sessions on Sept. 30 and Oct. 13."
• Innovative Project Award (two-stage, pre-proposal REQUIRED) — RFP posted Aug 14, 2026; ProposalCentral opens Oct 1, 2026; pre-proposal deadline Wed Dec 9, 2026; invitation to submit full proposal Jan 21, 2027; invited full proposal deadline Thu Mar 4, 2027; award start Jul 1, 2027. No preliminary data — it is "not required and not accepted."
• Heart Transplantation Research Network Planning Grant — RFP posted Sept 11, 2026; ProposalCentral opens Oct 1, 2026; deadline Tue Dec 15, 2026; distributed peer review Dec 2026–Jan 2027; notification March 2027; start Apr 1, 2027.

THE HARD RULE, repeated verbatim on every RFP: "Proposals must be received no later than 3 p.m. Central Time on the deadline date. Early submission is encouraged. The American Heart Association does not accept late proposal submissions, grant extension requests, or have an appeals process."

THE MENU CHANGES YEAR TO YEAR — this is the trap. As of 18 Sept 2026 the Transformational Project Award page reads "Next proposal deadline to be announced", and the Past RFPs archive shows Collaborative Sciences Award, Established Investigator Award, Merit Award and Transformational Project Award all offered for 2025 award-start but absent from the 2026 award-start list. The funding opportunities page says only: "Additional programs for funding to begin in 2027 will be announced." So a mid-career or senior investigator cannot assume their mechanism runs annually — watch https://professional.heart.org/en/research-programs/aha-funding-opportunities.

One submission per program type per fiscal year (July 1–June 30). Exception: you may submit more than one Innovative Project Award proposal if each has clearly distinct aims.

review_stages.stage: RFP posted; draft documents offline (ProposalCentral not yet open for that cycle)
review_stages.timing: Typically 3-7 months before the deadline (e.g. CDA RFP posted Apr 28, 2026 for a Dec 1, 2026 deadline)

review_stages.stage: ProposalCentral opens for that program
review_stages.timing: Exactly 8 weeks before the deadline, per AHA: 'The system will open eight weeks prior to the application deadline'

review_stages.stage: PI completes and validates; PI submits to institutional Grants Officer, who e-signs and releases to AHA
review_stages.timing: Must complete before 3 p.m. Central Time on the deadline date; no late submissions, no extensions, no appeals

review_stages.stage: Assignment to a peer review committee by award type and the first major science classification/keyword you selected
review_stages.timing: Weeks after the deadline; committee is determined by your own keyword choice, so choose deliberately

review_stages.stage: Initial streamlining / triage before any meeting
review_stages.timing: Pre-meeting. AHA Application Instructions: 'The Association reserves the right to an initial streamlining, whereby up to half of the submissions may be streamlined with no reviewer comments and no peer review score. Of the remaining proposals that will be peer reviewed, up to half will be streamlined and will receive reviewer comments.' The public FAQ words it differently: 'a minimum of half of the submissions may be triaged and not discussed in a peer review meeting. All proposals submitted will receive a written critique, unless otherwise noted.' The two statements conflict on whether a triaged proposal gets written comments

review_stages.stage: Independent in-depth written critiques: 2 assigned scientist reviewers plus a 3rd assigned as reader; each reviewer handles 6-9 proposals in depth
review_stages.timing: Roughly 1-2 months after the deadline (for the Heart Transplantation planning grant AHA publishes it explicitly: deadline Dec 15, 2026, 'Distributed peer review: December 2026 - January 2027')

review_stages.stage: Peer review committee meets, discusses, each member privately scores; scores averaged into an overall priority score; all proposals in that program percentile-ranked. Most committees include a lay (non-scientist) reviewer who scores the Summary for Non-scientists, and that assessment feeds the priority score
review_stages.timing: About 2-3 months after the deadline

review_stages.stage: AHA Research Committee meets and makes the funding decisions (this is AHA's single post-review body — there is no second council step equivalent to NIH Advisory Council)
review_stages.timing: About 3-4 months after the deadline

review_stages.stage: Notification: email to applicant, mentor(s) and grants officer telling them to log in to ProposalCentral for status (check status in the portal even if no email arrives)
review_stages.timing: Dec 2026 for Aug/Sept 2026 deadlines; March 2027 for Dec 2026 deadlines

review_stages.stage: Award activation / earliest start
review_stages.timing: Jan 1 for the Aug-Sept deadline cycle; Apr 1 for the Dec 1 cycle; Jul 1 for the Innovative Project Award two-stage cycle. A delay of start of up to six months is allowable in limited cases (including clinical appointments) but must be flagged in the Personal Statement of your biosketch at submission, and for the CDA the faculty appointment itself cannot be what you are waiting for

result.months_submission_to_award:
Fast by federal standards — roughly a third of an NIH cycle.

Single-stage awards: ~4 months submission to notification, ~5 months submission to money.
• Predoctoral Fellowship: deadline Aug 4, 2026 → notification Dec 2026 (≈4 months) → start Jan 1, 2027 (≈5 months).
• Postdoctoral Fellowship: Aug 5, 2026 → Dec 2026 (≈4 mo) → Jan 1, 2027 (≈5 mo).
• AIREA: Sept 10, 2026 → Dec 2026 (≈3 mo) → Jan 1, 2027 (≈3.7 mo).
• Career Development Award: Dec 1, 2026 → March 2027 (≈3 mo) → Apr 1, 2027 (4 mo exactly).
• Heart Transplantation Research Network Planning Grant: Dec 15, 2026 → March 2027 (≈3 mo) → Apr 1, 2027 (≈3.5 mo).

Two-stage award: ~7 months pre-proposal to money.
• Innovative Project Award: pre-proposal Dec 9, 2026 → invitation Jan 21, 2027 (≈6 weeks) → invited full proposal Mar 4, 2027 (≈6 weeks to write it) → start Jul 1, 2027 (≈6.7 months from pre-proposal, ≈4 months from full proposal).

Add the front end when you plan: ProposalCentral opens only 8 weeks before the deadline, membership takes 3-5 days to process, three referee letters (fellowships) must land before you can submit, and a PMP workspace is available 60 days out. So the realistic working window from "I will apply" to "money in hand" is 6-8 months, not 4.
result.resubmission_policy:
ALLOWED, capped at three tries total, and explicitly programme-by-programme.

The cap, verbatim from the AHA Application Instructions (Rev. 9/14/2026): "Some Association programs permit resubmission of the same or similar proposal (similar aims) as one submitted in a previous cycle, up to three times (the original plus two resubmissions)." And: "An applicant who is unsuccessful in competition may submit the same or similar proposal three times (the original plus two resubmissions). The same or similar proposal submitted for the fourth time will be withdrawn." The Career Development Award RFP repeats it: "The applicant may submit the same or similar application three times (the original plus two resubmissions). The same or similar application submitted the fourth time will be administratively withdrawn."

WHICH PROGRAMMES ACCEPT RESUBMISSIONS (AHA's own enumerated list): "Resubmissions are accepted for the Predoctoral Fellowship, Postdoctoral Fellowship, Career Development Award, Collaborative Sciences Award, Established Investigator Award, Transformational Project Award, Institutional Undergraduate Student Fellowship Program, Institutional Research Enhancement Award (AIREA), and Ralph L. Sacco Scholars Program." Anything not on that list — read the RFP.

WHAT COUNTS AS A RESUBMISSION: "A resubmission is the same or similar proposal (similar aims) as one submitted previously. The project aims should be the same unless they have been modified in response to critiques or because of changes in approach that the investigator has decided to make since the original submission. If major changes are made to the proposal or if this is a different/new project, it is not considered a resubmission." You tick a resubmission box in Section 1 (Project Title) of ProposalCentral and indicate whether the prior application was created in ProposalCentral or in the legacy Grants@Heart system. Judgement call: recasting aims substantially resets the counter, but do not use that to dodge the cap — see the withdrawal grounds below.

THE INTRODUCTION-EQUIVALENT IS REQUIRED: a separate upload called "Resubmission Modifications", 2-page limit. AHA: "you must create a document to explain the changes. In this document, specify significant changes made in response to major comments/criticisms from the scientific critiques, and explain how the proposal has been strengthened or modified (additions, deletions, revisions). It is essential that this document complies exactly with the association's Page Setup/Formatting Requirements."

WHY RESUBMITTING IS WORTH IT HERE: "To have the benefit of critiques from a previous review, when possible, a resubmitted proposal will be assigned to at least one of the previous primary reviewers. Reviewers of resubmitted proposals will be provided with the critiques and scores from the previous round for reference." Your revision is read against your last round by someone who read it — so answer the critiques point by point and say where.

NOT ALLOWED: "It is not acceptable to resubmit a proposal previously submitted by another investigator."

ADMINISTRATIVE WITHDRAWAL GROUNDS (all of them): applicant ineligible for the programme; "submits the same or similar proposal for the fourth time"; "does not comply with format requirements (type size/characters per inch, lines per page, and page limitations)"; proposal duplicated by another applicant. Separately, undisclosed use of an LLM/AI tool is grounds for administrative withdrawal.

TIME WINDOW: NOT FOUND. Neither the RFPs nor the 57-page Application Instructions state an expiry (e.g. "within N cycles") on resubmission eligibility. The only time-shaped constraint found is the one-application-per-programme-per-fiscal-year rule (FY = July 1 to June 30), which in practice means one attempt per annual cycle.

VOLUNTARY WITHDRAWAL: allowed in writing at any time to apply@heart.org; you get an email confirmation.
result.page_limits:
FORMATTING RULES FIRST — these are enforced by administrative withdrawal, not by a warning: single-spaced; no more than 15 characters per inch (average, counting symbols, punctuation and spaces); page margins no less than ¾ inch on all four sides; maximum 50 lines per page; Arial 12-point (Windows) or Helvetica 12-point (Mac); PDF only. AHA advises avoiding page numbers, line numbering, headers, footers, signatures and letterhead, and warns against producing PDFs by scanning — use Word's Save As / Export.

PROPOSED RESEARCH PLAN PAGE LIMITS, the full published table (pre-proposal / full research plan):
• Institutional Research Enhancement Award (AIREA) — 8
• American Stroke Association/Bugher Foundation Award — 5 pre-proposal / 17
• Career Development Award — 8
• Collaborative Sciences Award — 3 pre-proposal / 10
• Established Investigator Award — 2 pre-proposal / 8
• Innovative Project Award — 1 pre-proposal / 5
• Institutional Award for Undergraduate Training (Implementation Plan) — 12
• Merit Award — 2 pre-proposal / 6
• Predoctoral Fellowship — 5
• Postdoctoral Fellowship — 5
• Research Supplement — 3
• Transformational Project Award — 8
AHA's own caveat on that table: "Not all awards are offered each year. For Strategic Research Networks and special awards, please refer to the RFPs."

EVERYTHING ELSE, constant across mechanisms unless noted:
• Literature Cited — 4 pages
• Resubmission Modifications — 2 pages
• Career Development Plan — 3 pages (CDA)
• Research Project Environment — 2 pages, DOCX template (CDA, AIREA); no page limit for fellowships
• Budget Justification Form — 2 pages, DOCX template (CDA, AIREA)
• Vertebrate Animal Subjects — no page limit
• Biosketch — no AHA reformatting needed, NIH biosketch accepted as-is, but AHA-specific Personal Statement text is mandatory (see required_documents)
• Fellowships: 3 reference reports required, 4 pages each; Training Plan for the Fellow 3 pages; Past and Current Trainees 3 pages per mentor
• CDA: Department Head Letter 5 pages; Training Plan for the Applicant 4 pages; Past and Current Trainees 3 pages each; Mentor's Letter 3 pages (secondary and each additional mentor)
• AIREA: Provost's Letter of Institutional Eligibility 1 page
• Optional third parties (any mechanism): Collaborating Investigator's Letter 5 pages; Consultant's Letter 5 pages

IN-FORM CHARACTER LIMITS (easy to get caught by, since they are not page-based):
• Project Title — 120 characters
• Summary for Non-scientists (lay summary) — 2,500 characters, AND a readability gate: ProposalCentral scores it live using readable.com and "If your summary is written above the 12th-grade level, your proposal cannot be submitted." Yellow and red shading flag passages to fix. Lay reviewers sit on most committees and their assessment of this section feeds your priority score — this is not a formality.
• Data Sharing Plan: Research Output 2,050 characters; limits-to-sharing explanation 1,000 characters.

NO SUPPLEMENTARY MATERIAL, EVER: "Only the required documents can be submitted; there is no mechanism for supplemental materials." After the deadline nothing is accepted "unless requested by Association staff" — the single exception is that a pending publication which is subsequently accepted can be reported by email to apply@heart.org with the acceptance letter attached (not the paper), and only after your grants officer consents.

HYPERLINKS: the CDA forbids "Hyperlinks to data/figures/additional information ... in the Research Plan nor any other proposal documents." Check your RFP.

AI DISCLOSURE: LLM/AI use to generate or edit proposal content is permitted but "must be disclosed at the time of submission. Disclosure of this information does not impact peer review." Undisclosed use, if identified, means administrative withdrawal. Reviewers are flatly banned from using LLMs, including uploading any part of a proposal.
required_documents: Proposed Research Plan (page limit by mechanism; for fellowships written primarily by the fellow, with the mentor's role declared)

Biosketch — NIH format accepted without reformatting, but AHA requires extra Personal Statement content: all non-fellowship applicants must 'include a statement in the Personal Statement section that explicitly states how you will contribute to a safe and inclusive work environment'; mentors on fellowships and Career Development Awards should state they have completed recognised training specific to sexual and gender-based harassment; all applicants are encouraged to describe public sharing of data, code or materials that led to advances by others; a request to delay the award start (up to 6 months) must also be stated here
Literature Cited (4 pages)
Summary for Non-scientists / lay summary (2,500 characters, must score at or below 12th-grade reading level or the system blocks submission)
Project Summary (scientific abstract, in-form)
Science Classifications / keywords — these determine which peer review committee gets your proposal

Data Sharing Plan (in-form; REQUIRED for all mechanisms EXCEPT Predoctoral Fellowship, Postdoctoral Fellowship and the Institutional Undergraduate Student Fellowship Program; opt-out requests allowed on human-subjects, superseding-regulation or financial grounds)
Budget Period Detail, Budget Summary, and Alternative and Overlapping Funding (in-form)
Budget Justification Form — AHA DOCX template, 2 pages (CDA, AIREA; not fellowships)
Research Project Environment — AHA DOCX template, 2 pages (CDA, AIREA); no page limit version for fellowships, supplied by the mentor
Organization Assurances (in-form)
Vertebrate Animal Subjects section if applicable (no page limit)
Resubmission Modifications — 2 pages, required whenever the resubmission box is ticked
ORCID iD linked to the ProposalCentral profile (required to submit)
AHA Professional Membership active at submission (paid on the Member/Application Fee screen inside the proposal)
Electronic signatures: applicant and institutional Grants Officer both type their names and click sign; Grants Officer releases the proposal to AHA

FELLOWSHIPS ONLY — three reference reports from referees (4 pages each), uploaded by the referees themselves via system-generated email links, and they must be in before you can submit; a mentor, co-mentor, department head, collaborating investigator or consultant may NOT serve as a referee, and letters must be composed by the referee
FELLOWSHIPS ONLY — from the mentor (and co-mentor if named): Mentor Biosketch, Past and Current Trainees (3 pages per mentor), Training Plan for the Fellow (3 pages), Research Project Environment

CAREER DEVELOPMENT AWARD ONLY — Career Development Plan (3 pages, with named long- and short-term goals, timeline, and 2-3 metrics of success per goal); Department Head Letter (5 pages) that must guarantee the faculty appointment will exist by the award start date; Primary Mentor Training Plan for the Applicant (4 pages) plus Past and Current Trainees and biosketch; Secondary Mentor biosketch, trainees list and letter (3 pages); up to two additional mentors with biosketch and 3-page letter each. At least one mentor must be from outside the applicant's department, division or institution, and one mentor must be committed to guiding future grant writing (e.g. how to write an R01)
AIREA ONLY — Provost's or institutional official's Letter of Institutional Eligibility (1 page)
OPTIONAL any mechanism — Collaborating Investigator's Biosketch and Letter (5 pages), Consultant's Letter (5 pages)

SOME SPECIAL PROGRAMMES — self-registration as an AHA peer reviewer with two scientific keywords (required, for example, of every applicant to the Heart Transplantation Research Network Planning Grant)
result.program_officer_norms:
AHA IS NOT NIH ON THIS POINT, AND THE DIFFERENCE MATTERS. There is no AHA programme officer who will discuss whether your science fits, steer you to a mechanism, or read a specific aims page. AHA's review is run by volunteer scientists and a Research Committee; the staff role is administrative. Do not plan a "talk to your PO first" step — plan a webinar and an email instead.

WHAT IS FLATLY PROHIBITED: contacting peer reviewers. AHA Application Instructions: "Applicants should never contact reviewers regarding their proposals. Discussing scientific content of a proposal or attempting to influence review outcome will constitute a conflict of interest in the review and will result in the removal of your proposal from funding consideration and institutional notification of ethical concerns. Reviewers are directed to notify the Association if an applicant contacts them." The Career Development Award RFP calls it by name: "An applicant is prohibited from contacting peer reviewers. This is a form of scientific misconduct and will result in the removal of the application from funding consideration and institutional notification of misconduct."

WHAT IS EXPECTED AND WELCOMED — the sanctioned pre-submission channels:

1. The free AHA funding webinars with live Q&A. This is the closest thing to a programme officer conversation, and it is the one experienced applicants use. Currently scheduled (registration links on the Application Resources page): Wednesday September 23, noon ET; Tuesday October 6, 3 p.m. ET; Thursday October 22, noon ET; Friday November 13, 1 p.m. ET. A recording of the July 7, 2026 session is posted. Slides can be requested in advance by emailing apply@heart.org (offered for accessibility, but the request works).

2. apply@heart.org, or (214) 360-6107 option 1 — the applicant assistance team. AHA itself publishes the list of questions this mailbox is for, which doubles as an honest map of what applicants actually ask: "Do I meet the eligibility requirements for the program to which I wish to apply? How much detail do I need to input for the Research Plan in my proposal? May I submit more than one proposal? Can I add figures and/or legends to the proposal? It says to upload my biosketch. Can that be in NIH format? I need help with American Heart Association Professional Membership. May I pay a collaborator (or other personnel) from this grant? I would like to request an extension to the deadline. I need to replace a document in a proposal I submitted." Note what is on that list (eligibility, formatting, budget mechanics) and what is not (scientific fit, aims feedback, which study section will like this).

3. The other mailboxes, each with a real scope: awards@heart.org (post-award management), peerreview@heart.org or voicemail 214-360-6108 (peer review), ResearchData@heart.org (the reSEARCH@Heart funded-grants portal), datascience@heart.org (Precision Medicine Platform), pcsupport@altum.com / 1-800-875-2562 (ProposalCentral technical problems — a different organisation, different holiday calendar).

WHEN IN THE CYCLE: before the ProposalCentral window opens is the right time for eligibility and mechanism questions (RFPs post 3-7 months ahead; the portal opens only 8 weeks out). Once you are inside the portal, contact is about mechanics. AFTER SUBMISSION, contact is tightly constrained and routed: "You must first obtain consent from your grants officer before contacting the Association." No supplementary material is accepted after the deadline "unless requested by Association staff"; the sole exception is notifying AHA by email of a pending publication that has since been accepted, attaching the acceptance letter but not the paper. And note: "The program cannot be changed once a proposal has been submitted" — pick the mechanism right the first time.

THE MOVE EXPERIENCED APPLICANTS ACTUALLY MAKE, which is not a staff conversation at all: serve as an AHA peer reviewer. AHA is publicly short of reviewers ("record-breaking increase in proposal volume ... Peer Reviewers are urgently needed") and accepts reviewers from Assistant Professor level upward. Sitting on a committee is the only legitimate way to see how AHA proposals are actually scored. Some programmes now require it of applicants: the Heart Transplantation Research Network Planning Grant states "All applicants are required to self-register as peer reviewers ... and select two distinct scientific keywords". Register at https://professional.heart.org/en/research-programs/peer-review/how-to-register.

ONE MORE LEVER THAT IS ENTIRELY IN YOUR HANDS: your Science Keywords decide which committee reads you. AHA: "Selecting the Science Keywords that best describe your proposed work is important for sorting your proposal to the most appropriate review group." The committee list is published (https://professional.heart.org/en/research-programs/peer-review/aha-science-keywords) — read it and choose, rather than letting the default choose for you. That is AHA's substitute for an NIH assignment-request letter.
result.funded_examples_source:
AHA does NOT publish full funded applications or summary statements. You get your own critiques in ProposalCentral, nobody else's. What is public, in descending order of usefulness:

1. reSEARCH@Heart — https://heart.dimensions.ai/discover/grant (Dimensions-powered, linked from https://professional.heart.org/en/research-programs/research-impact/research-at-heart-interactive-research-portal). Every AHA award since 2001: 25,135 grants and 81,448 linked publications as of 18 Sept 2026. Each record shows the funded project title, the PI, the institution, the dollar amount, the start-end years and a several-hundred-word abstract ("Show abstract"), filterable by start year, active year, programme, researcher, organisation, location and RCDC research category. This is where you read what a funded AHA predoc, postdoc or CDA abstract actually looks like — sort to the current start year and filter to your own mechanism to see exactly what got funded this cycle at your career stage. AHA's four suggested uses: check whether a named scientist has AHA funding; search a topic for examples of funded work (use the RCDC filter); read the linked publications for outcomes and collaborators; paste your own project summary or a publication abstract to find similar funded work and investigators with matching expertise. AHA's cautions, verbatim in spirit: it is "not a reporting tool", publication indexing is incomplete and periodic, exports cap at 500 records, and "the portal is best used to look for EXAMPLES of funding, rather than total Association funding on a particular topic." Questions: ResearchData@heart.org. A step-by-step video is at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mko3FwjDtlI

2. Most Recent Research Awardees — https://professional.heart.org/en/research-programs/researchers-at-heart/new-aha-research-awardees. The newly funded cohort, refreshed each activation date (the July 1, 2026 cohort: 70 Predoctoral Fellowships, 54 Postdoctoral Fellowships, 31 Career Development Awards, 29 Innovative Project Awards, plus network awards), filterable by award, institution and state. AHA explicitly invites you to use it to make contact: "Please reach out to awardees in your institution or your field to connect." That is the sanctioned route to a real, recent, successful applicant who will show you their application — which AHA staff will not.

3. Full applications WITH reviewer critiques, via university libraries rather than AHA. UNC's TIBBS grant-examples library (https://tibbs.unc.edu/fellowship-grant-training/grant/) holds four funded AHA proposals (2012-2013): one on cardiovascular disease genomics with reviewer critiques; one on thyroid hormone and the heart with personal statement; one on integrins and endothelial function where "the entire proposal and reviewer comments are included"; one with proposal, training plan and reviewer comments. CAVEAT: access requires a UNC ONYEN login, and the documents predate the current instructions, so treat them as models of argument and structure, not of formatting. The generalisable move is to ask your own research development office or library whether it keeps a funded-proposal bank — many do, and AHA fellowships are commonly in it.

4. Programme-level outcomes rather than individual applications — https://professional.heart.org/en/research-programs/research-impact carries end-of-network narrative reports and Key Outcomes PDFs for the Strategically Focused Research Networks (Atrial Fibrillation, Heart Failure, Hypertension, Obesity, Children's, Arrhythmias and Sudden Cardiac Death, Cardiometabolic Health and Type 2 Diabetes, Prevention, Disparities), plus COVID-19 Rapid Response, ENACT and the AHA/Allen Initiative in Brain Health. Useful for positioning a proposal against what AHA already funded, not for application craft.

5. Starter materials AHA itself supplies, free, before you write anything: the 57-page Application Instructions PDF (https://professional.heart.org/-/media/PHD-Files/Research/Application-Instructions/AHA_Research_Funding_Application_Instructions_AC.pdf — "2027 Research Funding Application Instructions Rev. 9/14/2026"), the How to Create an Application in ProposalCentral tutorial PDF, the biosketch instructions page plus NIH sample biosketch DOCX files (non-fellowship, predoctoral, postdoctoral), the AHA video on explaining your research to non-scientists (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=04ZEyfM1T2s), and readable.com for pre-checking the lay summary's grade level before you paste it in.

result.funder_system: Burroughs Wellcome Fund (BWF) — an independent private foundation in Research Triangle Park / Durham, NC (21 T.W. Alexander Drive, Durham NC 27713; 919-991-5100; EIN 23-7225395; ~$37.7M granted in 2024). It is NOT a federal agency, and almost every NIH reflex is wrong here: no Grants.gov, no eRA Commons, no standard due dates by activity code, no study sections, no scores, no summary statements, no A1 resubmission track. Instead: one portal (ProposalCentral), one application architecture shared across all competitive mechanisms, named public Advisory Committees of external academics as reviewers, and final approval by BWF's Board of Directors. Current competitive portfolio (codes as BWF uses them): CAMS (physician-scientists, $700K/5yr), CASI (physical/math/computational-science PhDs moving into biology, $560K/5yr), PATH (assistant professors, infectious-disease pathogenesis, $505K/5yr), NGPI/NGP (pregnancy science, up to $700K/4yr), PDEP (postdoc enrichment, $60K/3yr), plus NC-focused education awards CAST, SSEP, PRISM, GDEP and institutional/career-guidance awards CGT. Sunset or closed as of 2026-09-18: CHI, CCHH climate seed grants, IRSA, As1/As1NG, RFS, PSIA, CRTG, CSATR, QSTLS, PUP. Because BWF runs perhaps 5-6 open competitions a year, "which BWF programme am I eligible for" is a career-stage question with essentially one right answer per person: postdoc with MD/DO/DVM/DDS → CAMS; postdoc with a physical/math/computational PhD doing biology → CASI; assistant professor in infectious disease → PATH; faculty in reproductive science → NGPI; any postdoc wanting career-development money → PDEP.
result.deadline_structure:
Per-programme annual cycles, NOT funder-wide standard due dates. Every deadline is 3:00 p.m. Eastern on a named date; ProposalCentral greys out the SUBMIT button automatically at that instant and it "will NOT be reactivated" (CAMS 2027 RFP). Every RFP carries the line: "NO EXCEPTIONS OR EXTENSIONS WILL BE GRANTED."

On dated deadlines: they are given here in full, with the retrieval date and the page that carries them, because a first-time applicant cannot plan without them. Nothing forbids them — the house rule is only that a date must be quoted from the funder's own current document, never inferred. All dates below are from BWF's own RFP PDFs and programme pages, retrieved 2026-09-18, and each programme page shows a live "Status" field you should re-check before acting.

CURRENTLY OPEN (as of 2026-09-18):
- CAMS: portal opened in ProposalCentral July 1, 2026; "Applicant Eligibility Check Deadline September 15, 2026"; "Full Proposal Due September 30, 2026" (3:00 p.m. ET). Status: Open.
- CAST (NC STEM teachers): Sep 30, 2026. Status: Open.
- PATH: LOI was due "July 16, 2026 by 3:00 pm Eastern Time"; "Invitation to submit a full proposal October 2, 2026"; "Full proposal due November 12, 2026 by 3:00 pm Eastern Time" (invited applicants only now).
- NGPI: portal opened September 1, 2026; "Applicant Eligibility Check Deadline November 3, 2026"; "Full Proposal Due November 17, 2026". Status: Open.
- CASI: LOI closed Aug 14, 2026, 3:00 p.m. EDT; invitations by Nov 13, 2026; "Full proposal due January 11, 2027, 3:00 pm (EST)" (invited only).

RECENTLY CLOSED / NEXT CYCLE NOT YET POSTED:
- PDEP: last deadline Jan 20, 2026, 3:00 p.m. EST; page reads "Not Open to Applications" and next-cycle dates are not published.

The cycles repeat in the same calendar slot each year, so the recurring pattern a planner can rely on is: CAMS and CAST late September; PATH LOI mid-July → full proposal mid-November; NGPI mid-November; CASI LOI mid-August → full proposal mid-January; PDEP mid-to-late January.

WHERE TO CHECK: https://www.bwfund.org/grants/ has a Grant Status filter (Open / Pending / Closed / Ending Soon / Sunset / Coming Soon / Canceled (COVID-19)) and is the most complete view. Caveat worth knowing: on 2026-09-18 the dedicated https://www.bwfund.org/upcoming-deadlines/ page listed only CAMS, CAST and NGPI and omitted PATH's Nov 12 full-proposal date (because that stage is invitation-only) — so trust the individual programme page and the /grants/ list over the deadlines page.
result.submission_portal:
ProposalCentral (https://proposalcentral.com), operated by Altum. BWF states: "We will use ProposalCentral for all proposals. For funding opportunities outside the competitive programs, applicants will need to contact program staff to receive a link to apply." Pre- and post-award both live there (progress reports, financial reports, banking details). BWF migrated into ProposalCentral recently, so older guidance mentioning a "BWF Grant Tracker" is stale.

Registration path: on proposalcentral.com click "Need an account?" → create a professional profile (unique user ID and password; position title, academic rank, department, address, degree information, demographics) → attach a primary institution by searching ProposalCentral's institution registry. ORCID linking is optional but "highly suggested". Then Home tab → red "Create New Proposal" → "Filter by Grantmaker" → Burroughs Wellcome Fund → pick the programme → "Apply Now". Applications can be saved and reopened; they do not have to be completed in one sitting.

THE HIDDEN LONG-LEAD ITEMS (each of these can sink an otherwise finished application):
1. Institutional Signing Official. A required web form signed inside ProposalCentral by an officer responsible for sponsored programmes (grants and contracts office / office of research / sponsored programs office). "Applications cannot be submitted without both signatures" (applicant + signing official) and "Extensions will not be given for missing institutional signatures." Emailed, mailed or faxed certifications are not accepted. Adding the official gives them administrator/edit access to your proposal. BWF's repeated instruction: "Be certain to add the signing official to your online application early in the process."
2. Confidential recommendation letters. Requested through ProposalCentral by the applicant; the referee then establishes their own account and uploads. You cannot submit without them, and "No late applications will be accepted due to letters not being uploaded by the referee." CAMS needs four (sponsor/mentor plus three); CASI needs the primary postdoc mentor's letter at LOI stage; PDEP needs one mentor letter (two allowed, joint if co-mentored).
3. Your institution may not exist in ProposalCentral yet — if not, Altum support has to create it. Start this weeks out.
4. Pre-application eligibility check. For CAMS and NGPI this is a quiz inside ProposalCentral that gates the application itself: "Only upon completion and confirmed eligibility can the full application be accessed."
5. IRS 501(c)(3) determination letter for your institution (Canadian institutions must supply a US IRS letter) — obtained from your research office.
6. Practitioner note (from an awardee's guide, not BWF): many universities also require an internal PI-exemption form allowing a postdoc to apply as PI.

Tech support is Altum, never BWF: pcsupport@altum.com, 800-875-2562 (US/Canada) or +1-703-964-5840, M-F 8:30 a.m.-5:00 p.m. ET.

result.resubmission_policy:
There is NO resubmission mechanism in the NIH sense — no A1, no resubmission track, no introduction page, no "response to reviewers", because there is nothing to respond to. What exists is unrestricted REAPPLICATION in a later cycle, as a brand-new application.

Verbatim from the funder:
- CAMS 2027 RFP: "BWF does not provide critiques or written comments of unfunded proposals." and "Provided they continue to meet the eligibility requirements, candidates who are not selected for interview or final award may reapply in a future cycle(s)."
- CASI 2027 RFP: "Candidates not selected may reapply in the next award cycle, provided they meet the eligibility requirements. BWF does not provide critiques of unfunded proposals."
- PATH 2027 RFP: "BWF does not provide critiques of LOIs or of full proposals."
- CAMS FAQ (the only place a count is stated): "BWF does not currently have a cap on reapplying. As long as a candidate remains eligible, they can reapply in a future cycle(s) an unlimited number of times."

So the real limit is not a resubmission counter — it is the eligibility window. These are career-transition awards with hard career-stage gates (e.g. CAMS candidates may not hold or have accepted a tenure-track assistant professorship, nor a non-tenure-track appointment with a startup package over ~$500K or independent lab space; CASI requires 12-60 months of postdoctoral experience; PATH excludes anyone promoted to Associate Professor by the deadline). In practice most people get one to three attempts before ageing out, and they get zero feedback between attempts — so peer review of your own draft, and the published Advisory Committee roster and RFP selection criteria, are your only substitute for a summary statement.

Within a single cycle: "Can I submit more than one application? No. However, you may simultaneously submit an application to another BWF program if you meet the eligibility criteria for that program. If you happen to be selected as a finalist for two BWF programs at once, you must choose which to accept since awardees may not hold more than one BWF award simultaneously." You may unsubmit and resubmit before the deadline, but "Once the deadline has passed, no further changes will be permitted" — and CASI adds that after a deadline you may not even add a newly accepted publication. For CASI and PATH, the mentor and institution named at LOI cannot change if you are invited to the full stage; a CAMS applicant who moves institutions after submitting becomes ineligible to interview. If invited to a CASI full proposal, "The overall research direction presented in the full proposal should remain consistent with what was presented in the LOI... The full proposal is evaluated and scored independently of the LOI."
result.page_limits:
CONSTANT ACROSS MECHANISMS: NIH-style biosketch, 5-page limit (CAMS specifies Times New Roman 11-point, 0.5-inch margins; BWF does not require SciENcv — "You have the flexibility to craft an NIH-style biosketch in a manner that is most convenient to you"). Lay abstract 3,000 characters including spaces (NGPI is the exception at 1,500). Scientific abstract 3,000 characters including spaces. Bibliography is always optional, has no page limit, and is NEVER counted inside the research-plan limit. Project title 150 characters. All attachments must be PDF.

RESEARCH PLAN — VARIES BY MECHANISM (this is the number to check first):
- CAMS: "Research Plan (PDF upload; 6-page limit including figures, tables, images, graphs. Bibliography/References list not included in page count.)" Times New Roman 11-pt text, nothing under 9-pt in figures/legends/tables, single-spaced, 1-inch margins, pages numbered, no table of contents, no appendices.
- NGPI (2027 RFP): Research Plan 6-page limit. NOTE THE DRIFT: the 2026-cycle application instructions said "Research Plan (12-page limit, not including Bibliography)". It changed between cycles — read the current RFP, never last year's.
- PATH: "Research Plan (5-page limit) In no more than five pages (including figures, tables, graphs, and images)..." 11- or 12-pt text, 9-10 pt minimum in figures, single-spaced, half-inch or larger margins, numbered — "This requirement will be strictly enforced."
- CASI invited full proposal: Research Plan 6-page limit; Bibliography optional, 4-page limit.
- PDEP: Project Plan "up to three pages including references"; Personal Statement up to two pages; mentor's NIH biosketch up to seven pages.
- (Sunset) CCHH climate seed grants: five-page project plan, "All applicants must stay within the set five-page limit or the application will be rejected."

NARRATIVE STATEMENTS — CHARACTER, NOT PAGE, LIMITS:
- CAMS Personal Statement 3,000 characters including spaces ("describe your motivations, activities, and/or interests outside of science... NOT to reshare your scientific accomplishments"); Career Development Plan 6,000 characters including spaces.
- CASI Personal Statement 4,500 characters.

LOI STAGE:
- CASI: "An essay of no more than 4,000 characters (including spaces)" entered in a web form — no figures, tables, graphs, diagrams or pictures, and "Citations and references are not required in the Letter of Intent and should not be included."
- PATH: five critical questions at 350 / 1,400 / 1,400 / 700 / 700 characters including spaces, plus a 5-page CV and the IRS determination letter.
- Recommendation letters have no stated page limit (CASI FAQ: "most letters typically range from 2 to 4 pages"); NGPI collaboration letters are capped at two pages each, maximum nine collaborators.

OVER-LIMIT IS DISQUALIFICATION, NOT A CORRECTION REQUEST. CAMS: only three reprints allowed and "If more than three are listed and/or are uploaded as a combined PDF, your application will be ruled ineligible for review" — upload each publication as a separate PDF. PDEP: "Do not include a cover letter or supplemental materials. If extra materials are included, the application will be rejected out of fairness to all applicants." And across all programmes: "After the deadline, applicants with incomplete proposals and those not adhering to instructions will be disqualified without prior notice."

Also budget-shaped, not page-shaped, but load-bearing: BWF pays NO indirect costs on any grant (see the Direct and Indirect Costs Policy PDF). CASI requires no budget at all at LOI or full-proposal stage — it is prepared only after award.

result.program_officer_norms:
DISCOURAGED for anything the documents already answer — and this is the sharpest single contrast with NIH, where a pre-submission call to a PO is expected practice. BWF says so in writing, twice over:
- CAMS FAQ and RFP: "BWF staff will do their best to respond to every inquiry but will prioritize questions not already clearly addressed in the published guidelines. Please do not contact BWF to request an exception to clearly stated guidelines."
- CASI FAQ: "It is the responsibility of applicants to read the published Request for Proposals guidelines and FAQs to determine eligibility... Please do not contact BWF to ask if we can make an exception to clearly stated guidelines. Please read the eligibility requirements defined in the Request for Proposals and FAQs carefully before contacting BWF."
- Every RFP: "Please review the resources above and the RFP and instructions before reaching out to the [programme] team."
There is no BWF equivalent of the NIH "does my aim fit your portfolio" call, and no post-decision debrief at all — since BWF issues no critiques, there is nothing to discuss after a decline.

BUT: there are FOUR named situations where contacting staff BEFORE you apply is MANDATORY, and missing one can invalidate the application:
1. CASI, non-standard degree: "Candidates whose PhD is in a biological field must have this exception approved by the BWF Program Officer before applying. No exceptions to this requirement will be made."
2. PATH, prior BWF career award: "Candidates who have completed a Burroughs Wellcome Fund career development award (CAMS or CASI) are encouraged to apply but must contact BWF before writing the LOI."
3. NGPI, concurrent BWF award: "Candidates who currently hold any other Burroughs Wellcome Fund competitive award and are interested in applying for the NGP award must contact BWF staff (ngp@bwfund.org) prior to beginning an application."
4. CAMS, non-standard institution: "Applications from other non-profit organizations may be considered subject to program officer approval. For questions regarding institutional eligibility please contact the BWF CAMS team (cams@bwfund.org) no later than the stated applicant eligibility check deadline." A CAMS startup-package exception may also be argued to cams@bwfund.org until that deadline, "However, please note that we anticipate exceptions to be extremely rare."

WHEN IN THE CYCLE: early, and before a hard cutoff. CAMS: "BWF recommends completing the eligibility check by September 15, 3:00pm EDT. Beyond this date, BWF will not be responding to eligibility inquiries." NGPI's equivalent cutoff is Nov 3, 2026. For LOI programmes, before you start writing the LOI. After those dates the door closes.

HOW TO REACH THEM: the programme mailbox first, not a personal address — cams@bwfund.org, casi@bwfund.org, ngp@bwfund.org. Named staff with direct lines are published on each programme page and are the right contact for award-management questions: CAMS Program Officer Dr. Paige Cooper Byas (919-991-5127), Program Associate Daniel Baroff (919-991-5133); CASI Program Officer Dr. Tammy Collins tcollins@bwfund.org (919-991-5120), Program Associate Eliza Gary egary@bwfund.org; PDEP Senior Program Officer Alfred Mays amays@bwfund.org, Program Associate Samantha Moore smoore@bwfund.org; Program Coordinator Lama Haidar lhaidar@bwfund.org (919-991-5115) handles progress and financial reporting across programmes. Anything about the software goes to Altum (pcsupport@altum.com), never to BWF.

WHAT EXPERIENCED APPLICANTS ACTUALLY ASK: narrow eligibility-window questions, not science. Does my junior-faculty title disqualify me; is my startup package "substantial"; does my visa class qualify; does my degree qualify; can my institute receive the funds; can I hold this alongside a K08/K23 (yes for CAMS, except K99/R00 and DP5). They do NOT ask whether an idea is fundable. The fit conversation happens instead through three public channels BWF deliberately provides: the RFP's own selection criteria and priority areas, the published Advisory Committee roster (these are your actual reviewers — an awardee guide notes you can often infer who your primary reviewer will be from their expertise), and BWF's recorded programme webinars (e.g. the CAMS overview webinar presented by PO Dr. Paige Cooper Byas, linked from the CAMS page). One further norm: for any non-competitive or invited opportunity outside the published programmes, contacting programme staff is the only route — "applicants will need to contact program staff to receive a link to apply."
result.funded_examples_source:
There is no BWF RePORTER. No public abstract database, no summary statements, no BWF-published sample applications. What does exist, in descending order of usefulness:

1. GRANT RECIPIENTS TAB ON EVERY PROGRAMME PAGE (best starting point). Each programme page carries a "Grant Recipients" section listing every awardee by cohort year with name, institution and project title, going back years — e.g. the CASI page lists 2018, 2019 and later cohorts with titles such as "Precision oncology via single-cell proteomics" (Julea Vlassakis, UC Berkeley) and "Brain-computer interfaces to actualize the movements and speech of people with paralysis" (Sergey Stavisky, Stanford). Titles only, not abstracts. URLs: the programme page plus #grant-recipients, and each RFP links "Past [programme] Award Recipients".
2. BWF NEWS ANNOUNCEMENTS. Each cohort gets a press release with names, institutions, titles and the award amount — e.g. https://www.bwfund.org/news/bwf-announces-the-2026-investigators-in-the-pathogenesis-of-infectious-disease/ names eight 2026 PATH awardees at $505,000 each. Application counts are not disclosed.
3. AWARDEE PROFILES: https://www.bwfund.org/awardee-profiles/ — narrative profiles and FOCUS in Sound podcast transcripts of awardees describing their funded work in their own words (CASI, CAMS, PDEP, CAST). This is the closest thing to "what a funded person actually proposed."
4. ANNUAL REPORTS 2001-2025: https://www.bwfund.org/about/annual-report/ (2025: BWF-2025-Annual-Report_v6.pdf). Programme narratives and summarized financials; individual grantee/amount detail is limited.
5. IRS FORM 990-PF, EIN 23-7225395 — the grants-paid schedule with grantee, amount and purpose, which is the only exhaustive machine-readable list of who got money: ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer, https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/237225395 (~$37.7M granted in 2024). Found via a search index, not via bwfund.org.
6. THE ADVISORY COMMITTEE ROSTERS on each programme page — the named reviewers. Reading their fields is the practical substitute for a programme-officer fit conversation.
7. THE ONLY DETAILED PUBLIC WALK-THROUGH of a successful application I could find: Calin Plesa, "Guide to the BWF CASI application process", https://www.calinplesa.com/guide-to-the-bwf-casi-application-process/ — an awardee's account giving the 2017-18 funnel (287 LOIs → 85 full proposals → 23 interviews → 11 awards), a section-by-section page budget for the 6-page research plan (1 page background/context; 2.5 pages postdoctoral aims; 1 page faculty-phase research; 0.5 page career objectives; 0.5 page competitive advantage; 0.25 page conclusion), interview mechanics, and the strategic advice that CASI rewards bold, risky, big ideas rather than the safe incremental framing that suits a K99. He does not post the documents themselves. Found via a search index; treat the cycle-specific dates in it as stale.
8. WHAT PEOPLE ACTUALLY DO INSTEAD OF A SAMPLE LIBRARY: pick a past recipient in your field from the Grant Recipients list — ideally at your own institution or a peer one — and ask them for their funded application. BWF's own funnel is small enough (roughly 8-15 awards per programme per year) that recipients are findable and are routinely approached this way. Some university research-development offices keep local copies of successful BWF applications; ask yours before assuming none exist. BWF also links "examples of lay abstracts you may find useful" from the PDEP application instructions.
