ProposalCentral advance-registration lead time: the portal publishes no recommended lead time, and I did not open docs.proposalcentral.com/FAQ-Applicant.pdf. The binding lead time in practice is the referee-letter gate, which is a Damon Runyon rule, not a ProposalCentral one.
result.confidence: high — every substantive claim above is from damonrunyon.org's own guidelines pages, fetched directly (the site serves plain fetches; no search-index substitution was needed, and the one search-index-only item, the MGH internal-nomination example, is labelled as such and is from an earlier cycle). Two internal inconsistencies on the funder's own site are flagged rather than smoothed over. Lower confidence on: success rates (not established), Stage 2 / continuation mechanics (not located), and 2027 dates for three programs (not yet posted). All dates verified 2026-09-18.

result.funder_system:
Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) — a DoD agency that funds R&D almost entirely through Broad Agency Announcements (BAAs) and Research Announcements (RAs) under FAR 6.102(d)(2), FAR 35.016 and 2 CFR 200.203, not through a grant-cycle model. Six technical offices as of Sept 2026: BTO (Biological Technologies), DSO (Defense Sciences), IPTO (Information Processing Techniques), MXO (Multi X), STO (Strategic Technology), TTO (Tactical Technology).

DRIFT FINDING, verified this pass: the Information Innovation Office (I2O) no longer appears on darpa.mil/about/offices — its office-wide BAA HR001126S0001 (posted 28 Nov 2025, "Information Innovation Office (I2O) Office-Wide") has been replaced by HR001126S0011 "Information Processing Techniques Office Office-Wide" (posted 22 June 2026). Any guide that tells a user to look for "I2O" is now stale. This is the single most common way DARPA advice rots.

Two structural facts that determine everything else, both from DARPA's own text:
(1) BAA proposals are NOT scored against each other. DARPA BAA Guide (Dec 2023), Ch.2 §3.A.2: "Proposals need not be evaluated against one another since they are not submitted in accordance with a common work statement." There is no study section, no percentile, no score. A Government Reviewer marks each proposal Selectable or Not Selectable against the BAA's own published criteria.
(2) There are three routes, and which one you are on is set by the award instrument: procurement contract / OT → DARPA's own BAAT portal; grant or cooperative agreement → Grants.gov; SBIR/STTR → DSIP. A single BAA can offer all of them.

Award instruments offered on a typical office-wide BAA: Procurement Contract, Grant, Cooperative Agreement, OT for Prototype, OT for Research.

WHAT AN EARLY-CAREER ACADEMIC CAN ACTUALLY APPLY TO (the entry points that matter for PhD students / postdocs / ECRs):
- Young Faculty Award (YFA) — the one DARPA mechanism built for ECRs and the only one with a genuine annual dated cycle. Tenure-track/tenured at time of FULL PROPOSAL submission, within 3 years of tenure date (or equivalent at a non-profit research institution within 12 years of doctorate). Single PI only. Ineligible if you have already received >$500k from DARPA or >$1.25M from all DoD sources as prime or subawardee. FY2026 structure: $500k / 24-month base + $500k / 12-month Director's Fellowship option + up to $350k US-Person Graduate Student option running concurrent with the base = $1.35M max (DARPARA2502 Administrative FAQs, 31 Dec 2025, FAQ 85).
- DARPA Riser (nomination, not application) — graduate student, postdoc, or assistant professor not more than 5 years from highest degree, who has not yet been PI on a competitively awarded federal grant or contract. This is the genuine PhD-student/postdoc-level on-ramp; it is a nomination route through your institution, not a proposal.
- Office-wide BAAs — open to any responsible source including universities and non-US organisations; the realistic route for a postdoc is as named personnel on a PI's team, not as prime.
- SBIR/STTR — small business only (STTR requires a small-business prime partnered with a research institution; that is the route by which an academic lab gets in via a company partner).

Fetch-tooling notes (facts about my tools, not about DARPA): SAM.gov opportunity pages and USAspending.gov are single-page apps and return an empty body to a plain fetch, so individual office-wide BAA SAM pages could not be read directly; sbir.gov/awards returns 403 to curl but renders fine via a rendering fetch. The BAA PDFs below were read in full from DARPA-issued files (via darpa.mil directly, or via verbatim institutional mirrors at defencescienceinstitute.com and Tel Aviv University's research authority where SAM.gov blocked the fetch) and parsed locally with pypdf.
result.submission_portal:
FOUR SYSTEMS, AND YOU MAY NEED THREE OF THEM. The account setup is the hidden long-lead item — budget four weeks before you need it.

1. BAAT — DARPA Broad Agency Announcement Tool, https://baa.darpa.mil/ (verified live, HTTP 200, 18 Sept 2026). The default destination for all UNCLASSIFIED abstracts, executive summaries and (for contract/OT proposals) full proposals. Registration is a two-step process most first-timers do not anticipate: create a DARPA Extranet account via "Create New Account", then WAIT for two separate emails carrying username and temporary password, then register in BAAT via the "Register your Organization" link. DARPA's Proposer Instructions state: "Each user submitting a proposal must create their own Organization Registration." Accounts deactivate after 30 days of inactivity — so do not create it "early and forget it"; if you are unsure when you last logged in, make a new one. Uploads must be zip archives (.zip/.zipx), "no greater than 100 MB in size". "Email submissions will not be accepted." Technical support is business hours only, "Monday – Friday, 9 a.m. – 5 p.m. ET" — which is why DARPA warns that "proposers using the DARPA Broad Agency Announcement Tool (BAAT) may encounter heavy traffic on the submission deadline date."

2. Grants.gov — for grants and cooperative agreements, which is the instrument most university proposals land on. DARPA's own Grants/Cooperative Agreements page gives the registration chain and the lead time: entity identifier → SAM registration → Grants.gov registration, and states "These processes can take up to four weeks." Grants.gov itself recommends submitting 24–48 hours before the deadline so validation errors can be fixed. You get three emails from Grants.gov: receipt, validation-or-rejection, and a final confirmation once DARPA retrieves the proposal — treat the third as the only real proof of submission. Note the split that catches YFA applicants: the YFA executive summary goes to BAAT, the YFA FULL PROPOSAL goes to Grants.gov (DARPARA2502 FAQ 81: "Full proposals must be submitted through Grants.gov"), with budget justification as Section L of the SF-424 Research & Related Budget form.

3. SAM.gov — not a submission portal but a prerequisite for award. DARPA: "All proposers must be registered in SAM unless exempt per FAR 4.1102...and have a valid Unique Entity ID to receive an award," and must "maintain an active and current SAM registration at all times throughout the award process." Registration commonly takes up to ~10 business days (UEI validation 1–2 business days; government/CAGE validation ~7–10; longer if TIN or name/address mismatches trigger manual review). Universities already have this; a new small business or a spin-out does not. DARPA's SBIR contracting FAQ adds a trap: "If at all possible, please do not update your SAM registration after your proposal has been selected. If this is done, it may result in a delay in award."

4. DSIP — DoD SBIR/STTR Innovation Portal, https://www.dodsbirsttr.mil/submissions/login. All DARPA SBIR and STTR proposals go here, not to BAAT. Register as soon as you identify a topic. Post-selection, DARPA also runs its own SSIP (DARPA SBIR/STTR Information Portal, https://sbir.darpa.mil) via the Extranet — mandatory for retrieving the decision notice and technical evaluation narratives.

Also required before award: WAWF registration for electronic invoicing ("Registration in WAWF is required prior to any award"), an Organizational Conflicts of Interest disclosure with mitigation plan, and an affirmation regarding SETA/A&AS support to DARPA offices.

Classified submissions never go through these systems — they follow the separate Classified Submission Requirements, Instructions and Procedures attachment carried on each BAA, and a DD Form 254 is attached to the BAA itself.

Do not mix routes: "Proposers must submit all parts of their submission package using the same method; submissions cannot be sent in part by one method and in part by another method nor should duplicate submissions be sent by multiple methods." Failure "may result in the submission being deemed non-conforming and withdrawn from consideration."
result.deadline_structure:
There are no DARPA-wide standard due dates. Nothing resembles NIH's Feb 5 / Jun 5 / Oct 5 grid. But "per-solicitation" is an incomplete answer and it is the wrong answer to give an early-career researcher, because DARPA's deadline behaviour is genuinely three different regimes and one of them IS annual and dated. The dates below are real, quoted from the solicitations, and true as of 18 September 2026 — they are worked examples of the pattern, not a calendar to plan FY2028 against.

REGIME 1 — OFFICE-WIDE BAAs: rolling, inside an annually reissued window. Each of the six offices keeps a standing "office-wide" BAA open roughly a year, and you submit whenever you are ready. Governing rules from the DARPA BAA Guide (Dec 2023): "Office-wide BAAs may be open indefinitely but must be re-advertised at least annually" and "Office-wide BAAs are reissued annually unless extenuating circumstances exist." Verified examples:
- IPTO Office-Wide, HR001126S0011, posted 22 June 2026: "Abstract Due Date: June 22, 2027 at 2:00 PM" (ET), and "Proposal Due Date: By Invitation Only, a due date will be provided in the Invitation to Proceed." Twelve months of rolling abstracts; the proposal clock only starts when DARPA invites you.
- I2O Office-Wide, HR001126S0001, posted 28 Nov 2025 (now superseded by the above): "Abstracts may be submitted on a rolling basis until November 1, 2026, at 5:00 PM"; "Proposals may be submitted on a rolling basis until November 30, 2026, at 5:00 PM."
- DSO Office-Wide, HR001125S0013 (Amendment 1, 16 Sept 2025): executive summaries, abstracts AND proposals all "on a rolling basis until June 2, 2026, at 4:00 PM", with "Question Submittal Closing Date: May 8, 2026, at 4:00 PM".
Practical reading: the posted close date is a backstop, not a target. Money is committed as abstracts come in. Submitting in month 11 of a 12-month window is submitting into an emptier pot.

REGIME 2 — PROGRAM-SPECIFIC BAAs: single hard date, short fuse, unpredictable arrival. These are the named programmes (PINPOINT, Firefox, Hubble, BEAMERS…). Two floor rules protect you: "Per Subpart 5.203(e) of the FAR, BAAs must allow a response time of at least 45 calendar days between the date of the [publication and the proposal due date]", and critically "Having an abstract phase does not change the requirement for a minimum response time of 45 calendar days for proposal submission." Ceiling rules: "Program-specific BAAs will be posted for no longer than 180 calendar days from the date they are published at www.SAM.gov", and any that accept late submissions "must include a submission 'cut-off' date that is within six (6) months of the date of issuance." So: 45 days minimum, 180 days maximum, and you cannot know in advance when one will drop. The only way to see them coming is the Proposers Day announcement, which is why DARPA publishes them as Special Notices weeks ahead. Watch https://www.darpa.mil/rss/opportunities.xml — verified live, 10 items when checked, mixing Proposers Days, Industry Days, RFIs, new programmes and STTR topics.

REGIME 3 — ANNUAL DATED CYCLE: the Young Faculty Award, and this is the one an ECR should put in a calendar. DARPA's own YFA page states the recurrence: "The annual research announcement seeking YFA applications is typically posted to the grants.gov and sam.gov websites between September and October." The FY2026 cycle (DARPARA2502) ran: executive summary due 15 October 2025, 4:00 p.m.; full proposal due 20 January 2026, 4:00 p.m.; question submittal closed 9 January 2026. So the shape that recurs is: RA posts Sept/Oct → executive summary ~mid-Oct → full proposal ~mid-to-late Jan. An ECR who wants the next cycle should be talking to a PM the spring before, and have a concept ready in August.

Two further timing facts worth surfacing to a first-time applicant:
- "There is no minimum required response time for proposers to submit an abstract" — DARPA can set an abstract deadline with very little notice.
- Every deadline is stated in Eastern Time, and the hour varies by solicitation (2:00 PM, 4:00 PM and 5:00 PM ET all appear in the four solicitations read this pass). Do not assume 5 p.m.

review_stages.stage: Pre-submission contact with the Program Manager (the real first stage)
review_stages.timing: Any time while the BAA is open, and ideally months before. IPTO HR001126S0011 §5 states it outright: 'Potential proposers are strongly encouraged to reach out to DARPA Program Managers (PM) to gauge their interest in a technical approach prior to submitting a formal abstract.'

review_stages.stage: Proposers Day / Industry Day (where one is held)
review_stages.timing: Before or shortly after the BAA is published, announced by Special Notice on SAM.gov/Grants.gov. May include registered one-on-one PM meetings and teaming pitches. Briefing charts must be publicly released afterwards, so non-attendees can still get the material.

review_stages.stage: Executive summary (offered on DSO office-wide and YFA; optional)
review_stages.timing: Rolling. Reply is a bare encourage/discourage: DSO HR001125S0013 says responses 'will generally be limited to a statement of interest (or lack thereof), rather than providing detailed feedback.'

review_stages.stage: Abstract (required on IPTO office-wide; strongly encouraged on DSO; the key checkpoint everywhere)
review_stages.timing: PM response capped by DARPA policy: the PM 'should attempt to reply to the abstracts within a reasonable timeframe to allow feedback to be incorporated in a proposal submission, but no longer than 30 calendar days of receipt' (DARPA BAA Guide Ch.2 §3.A.1). Every conforming abstract gets a written answer with rationale.

review_stages.stage: Abstract outcome letter — three possible results on IPTO 2026
review_stages.timing: Non-Conforming (not reviewed at all), Invited to Proceed (with written feedback on the evaluation), or Non-Selection ('they will not be permitted to submit a full proposal', with feedback). On DSO and YFA the equivalent letter is advisory, not a gate.

review_stages.stage: Full proposal submitted
review_stages.timing: Minimum 45 calendar days between BAA publication and the proposal due date (FAR 5.203(e)); on IPTO office-wide the due date arrives inside the Invitation to Proceed.

review_stages.stage: Conformance determination by the Contracting Officer
review_stages.timing: Immediately on receipt, before any science is read. 'Only conforming abstracts will be reviewed, and only conforming proposals will be reviewed and considered for award.' IPTO 2026 formalises this as 'Step 1: Mandatory Technical Conformance', which explicitly fails 'generic, boilerplate, or broadly aggregated content lacking mission-specific synthesis'.

review_stages.stage: Scientific review by Government Reviewers (+ non-government SMEs on assigned sections)
review_stages.timing: DARPA's internal target schedule, from the BAA Guide's own template: conflict-of-interest review complete at X+3 days and individual scientific reviews complete at X+18 days, where X = receipt of proposals. Reviewers must be Government personnel; each writes a narrative of strengths and weaknesses per criterion and marks Selectable / Not Selectable.

review_stages.stage: PM review and recommendation for funding
review_stages.timing: X+25 days on the same internal target schedule. The PM may override a Reviewer's determination but must document the rationale in writing.

review_stages.stage: Selecting Review Official (SRO) concurrence — DARPA's only council-equivalent step
review_stages.timing: X+28 days target. The SRO can approve, require re-evaluation, substitute their own selection for the PM's, direct that the BAA be cancelled and reissued, or withdraw funding. The signed SRO independent review memorandum is the point at which funds are confirmed available. For office-wide BAAs 'the SRO briefings may be ad hoc as proposals come in' — which is why rolling office-wide submissions can move fast.

review_stages.stage: Notification letters (selection / non-selection / non-conforming), signed by the PM
review_stages.timing: After the SRO decision. For SBIR/STTR DARPA commits to notifying firms 'within 90 days of the closing date of the BAA'. No comparable published commitment exists for BAA/RA proposals.

review_stages.stage: Informal feedback session with the PM — offered to SELECTED AND NON-SELECTED proposers on request
review_stages.timing: After notification. This is DARPA's substitute for an NIH summary statement and it is under-used. 'If requested, PMs will hold informal feedback sessions with prime proposers after the proposers have been notified.' Not a FAR Part 15 debriefing. You must supply an attendee list first; if you bring legal counsel, DARPA General Counsel and the CO must attend. The PM may discuss only your proposal, never anyone else's.

review_stages.stage: Contracting Officer / contracting agent assigned; negotiation begins
review_stages.timing: DARPA SBIR/STTR Contracting FAQ: 'Please allow up to 4-6 weeks after receiving your selection letter from DARPA to be contacted by a Contracting Agent.' DARPA often uses Air Force, Army, Navy, DOI or NASA contracting shops rather than its own CMO.

review_stages.stage: Award executed — work may begin
review_stages.timing: Negotiation length depends almost entirely on how fast the proposer returns cost substantiation. Cost proposals are treated as valid for 180 days from submission, which is the practical planning horizon.

result.months_submission_to_award:
DARPA publishes no official submission-to-award figure. The number below is assembled from DARPA's own component durations, each sourced; I have marked it as an assembly rather than presenting it as a DARPA statement.

Sourced components:
- Abstract → written response: ≤30 calendar days (DARPA BAA Guide policy cap).
- Proposal receipt → SRO concurrence: ~28 days as DARPA's INTERNAL TARGET (X+3 COI / X+18 reviews / X+25 PM recommendation / X+28 SRO concurrence, from the BAA Guide's own Proposed Scientific Review Schedule template). Treat this as the floor, not the expectation — the Proposer Instructions hedge it: "DARPA's intent is to review proposals as soon as possible after they arrive; however, proposals may be reviewed periodically for administrative reasons."
- SBIR/STTR notification: within 90 days of BAA close.
- Selection letter → contracting agent makes contact: 4–6 weeks (DARPA's own words).
- Negotiation → executed award: not published; cost proposals held valid 180 days.

Assembled realistic planning figures:
- Abstract to abstract-decision: 1 month.
- Full proposal to selection decision: ~1–3 months (1 month if the office is running ad-hoc SRO briefings on a rolling office-wide BAA; longer if reviews are batched).
- Selection to executed award: ~2–4 months (4–6 weeks to be contacted, then negotiation, SAM/CAGE/NIST-800-171 checks, model-agreement redlines).
- END TO END, first PM email to money in hand: 6–12 months on an office-wide BAA, and that assumes the abstract is invited on the first attempt.
- YFA specifically, as a dated example: executive summary 15 Oct 2025 → full proposal 20 Jan 2026 → award start in the second half of calendar 2026. Roughly 9–12 months from first submission to start of work.

Two levers that genuinely compress this, both DARPA-provided:
(1) The DSO office-wide BAA carries an Accelerated Award Option — Attachment I, an "Accelerated Award Option Election and Attestation Form", plus pre-accepted accelerated model contracts for large business, small business, OT Prototype and OT Research (Attachments J–N). Electing it and accepting the model terms removes most of the negotiation delay.
(2) Redlining the model contract/cooperative agreement/OT agreement AT PROPOSAL TIME. Both IPTO and I2O office-wide BAAs "strongly encourage" it: submit track-changed edits with comment boxes explaining each requested change. Proposers who skip this discover their legal office's objections only after selection, which is where months disappear.
result.resubmission_policy:
DARPA has NO resubmission mechanism in the NIH sense. There is no A1, no resubmission application type, no Introduction to Resubmission page, no requirement to respond to prior reviewers, and no limit on how many times you may come back. There is also no appeal. What exists instead is four distinct rules that a first-time applicant conflates at their peril.

1. AFTER A DISCOURAGING ABSTRACT RESPONSE, YOU MAY USUALLY STILL SUBMIT THE FULL PROPOSAL. This is the most commonly misunderstood point and DARPA states it twice. BAA Guide Ch.2 §3.A.1: "Even though a PM may indicate that DARPA has no interest in the proposer's ideas, the proposer is not subsequently precluded from submitting a proposal, and the PM should remind the proposer of this in the written response." DSO HR001125S0013 repeats it: "Regardless of DARPA's response to an abstract, proposers may submit a full proposal. DARPA will review all conforming full proposals using the published evaluation criteria and without regard to any comments resulting from the review of an abstract." Same for YFA executive summaries (DARPARA2502 FAQ 82).

2. EXCEPT WHERE THE ABSTRACT IS A HARD GATE — AND ON IPTO IT NOW IS. The Guide permits a technical office to make the abstract "a hard decision point that does preclude a proposer from submitting a proposal", in which case "the BAA should clearly describe this process." IPTO HR001126S0011 does exactly that: "Proposals are by invitation only," and the Non-Selection outcome means "they will not be permitted to submit a full proposal." The superseded I2O BAA was the same: "A proposal will not be reviewed if it is submitted without: 1. Submitting an abstract, and 2. Receiving an invitation to submit a Proposal." So whether you get a second bite depends entirely on which office you are in — READ THE BAA'S OVERVIEW SECTION, do not generalise from another office.

3. THE REAL "RESUBMISSION" IS THE ANNUAL REISSUE. Because "Office-wide BAAs are reissued annually," a rejected concept can be resubmitted under next year's BAA number with no penalty, no marking, no introduction page, and no disclosure that it was submitted before. Nothing carries over — the new BAA is a fresh evaluation against its own criteria. Likewise YFA recurs annually. The practical constraint is not policy, it is eligibility drift: a YFA applicant's 3-year-post-tenure window closes, and the >$500k DARPA / >$1.25M DoD funding ceiling can make a successful year disqualifying for the next.

4. WHAT TO CHANGE, AND WHERE TO LEARN IT. Since there is no summary statement, the mechanism for finding out why you lost is the informal feedback session — request one from the PM after your notification letter, whether you were selected or not. That conversation is the DARPA equivalent of a critique and it is the single highest-value action a rejected applicant can take. Note the hard boundary on it: the PM "may discuss only the strengths and weaknesses of the proposal that is the subject of the feedback session" and may not reveal anything about competing proposals.

ONE-WAY DOOR TO KNOW ABOUT: the moment your proposal is received, the friendly pre-submission dialogue ends. BAA Guide Ch.2 §2.I, "Interactions After the Receipt of Proposals (Restricted Interactions)": "After receipt of proposals, all interactions with proposers must go through the CO regardless of communication method (email, in person, telephonic, etc.)." And: "the PM or CO cannot advise or direct a proposer on how to revise their proposal." Clarification requests do "not include giving a proposer a chance to provide substantive information that, per the BAA, should have been included in the proposal at the time of submission." You cannot fix a weak proposal after filing it.

PARTIAL SELECTION — the one place DARPA formally asks for a revised proposal: if the SRO selects a proposal for partial funding, the Contracting Officer issues a signed notice of partial selection "and a request for revised proposal" with a stated return date, and the reduced-scope revision must be in hand before funds are committed. This is a negotiation step, not a competitive resubmission.

NON-CONFORMING IS NOT REJECTION-ON-MERIT: a non-conforming submission gets "a sufficiently detailed letter... explaining why the submission is nonconforming and that it will receive no further consideration." It was never scientifically read. Formatting and completeness errors are therefore the cheapest possible way to lose, and the most avoidable.
result.page_limits:
DARPA does not publish agency-wide page limits. Three layers apply, and the crucial structural fact is that for office-wide BAAs the full-proposal page limits are NOT in the BAA at all — they arrive with the invitation.

LAYER 1 — DARPA-WIDE FORMATTING FLOOR (Proposer Instructions: General Terms and Conditions, applies to every submission):
- "All submissions...must be written in English with type not smaller than 12-point font"; "Smaller font may be used for figures, tables, and charts."
- Upload as a zip archive, "no greater than 100 MB in size".
- Every document "clearly labeled with the DARPA BAA number, proposer organization, and proposal title/proposal short title."
- Proprietary material: the cover page and every page containing it must be marked "Proprietary" or "Company Proprietary". Do NOT mark it "Confidential" — that is a national-security classification marking, and DARPA calls this out explicitly.
- All monetary references in U.S. Dollars.

LAYER 2 — ABSTRACT / EXECUTIVE SUMMARY LIMITS (published, and the only page limits you can see before you commit):
- I2O/IPTO office-wide abstract: 5 pages. Verbatim from the HR001126S0001 conformance checklist: "Is your submission 5 pages or less? Page limit does not include the coversheet, table of contents, optional bibliography, security plan, and/or optional technical papers." Format: "written in English on 8.5" by 11" pages with 1" margins, using 12-point Times New Roman font? 8 or 10-point font may be used for figures, tables, and charts." The abstract must map to named sections — Goals and Impact, Technical Approach, Capabilities/Management Plan, Cost and Schedule — and to a declared thrust area and a revolutionary-vs-evolutionary self-classification.
- YFA executive summary: 1 page. "Executive Summaries shall not exceed a maximum of 1 page, excluding the Cover Sheet. Items 1 through 4 (to include any figures, tables, and charts) will count toward the page limit. The Executive Summary should not include any references." (DARPARA2502 FAQ 60.) One page, figures inside the page, no bibliography — this is far tighter than most academics expect and is where ECR applications are most often lost.
- Public-release abstract for any GRANT award: "a maximum one (1) page abstract that may be publicly posted and explains the program or project to the public", signed by the proposer (required by the Consolidated Appropriations Act 2015, Pub. L. 113-235).
- Classified work: the security plan is excluded from the abstract page limit.

LAYER 3 — FULL PROPOSAL LIMITS (mechanism-dependent, and often invisible until invited):
- Office-wide BAAs: the limits live in the attachment templates, not the BAA. IPTO HR001126S0011 §6.2: "Instructions for proposal submissions, including content and formatting requirements, are contained within the required IPTO Office Wide Proposal Templates zip file." I2O HR001126S0001 §4.2: "After receipt and evaluation of an abstract, offerors invited to propose will be provided with additional instructions for proposal submissions, including content and formatting requirements." PLAN FOR THIS: you cannot scope your writing effort until DARPA invites you, so the abstract is the only artefact you can prepare with certainty.
- Program-specific BAAs: limits ARE stated in the BAA itself, per Volume, and vary widely by programme. There is no typical number to quote responsibly.
- Both IPTO and I2O add a hard content rule that functions like a page limit: "Information not explicitly requested will not be reviewed." Appendices are not a way around the limit.
- SBIR/STTR: limits are set per release in the DARPA component instructions on DSIP (commonly cited as ~20 pages for a Phase I technical volume and ~45 for Phase II including a 5-page commercialization strategy) — I did NOT verify these against a release PDF in this pass and they change between releases; verify in the specific release document. Flagged as unresolved.
required_documents: ABSTRACT or EXECUTIVE SUMMARY on the office's own required template — the single most important document, because it is the gate. Submitted via BAAT. Required on IPTO office-wide; strongly encouraged on DSO office-wide and YFA.
Volume I — Technical and Management (full proposal), on the office's template
Volume II — Cost (full proposal), on the office's template

Proposal Summary Slide — a single briefing slide, required on both IPTO and DSO office-wide. Also an Abstract Summary Slide on DSO (Attachment B). Academics routinely underestimate this: DARPA runs on quad charts and slides.

DARPA Standard Cost Proposal Spreadsheet — 'strongly encouraged but not required' on IPTO/I2O; REQUIRED on DSO (Attachment G). IPTO warns that if you use an alternative format 'the burden is entirely on the proposer to ensure the format provides the necessary fidelity, detail, and formula transparency required for a comprehensive Government evaluation.'

Redlined Model Contract / Model Cooperative Agreement / Model OT Agreement — track-changed edits WITH a comment box explaining the context for each change, submitted alongside the proposal. 'Strongly encouraged' on both IPTO and I2O. This is the main lever on time-to-award.

Common Disclosure Forms for the Fundamental Research Risk-Based Security Review (FRRBS) — required for any fundamental-research submission requesting a Grant, Cooperative Agreement or OT. IPTO: 'Proposal submissions that require the common form submission but failed to provide the common forms may not be reviewed.'
Organizational Conflicts of Interest (OCI) disclosure with a mitigation plan
Affirmation regarding SETA / A&AS support to DARPA offices — you cannot concurrently be a DARPA support contractor and a performer without a written Deputy Director waiver
Unique Entity ID from an active SAM.gov registration
One-page publicly postable abstract, signed — required for any grant award
Statement of Work, and (post-selection) an editable Word version of it
SF-424 Research & Related family via Grants.gov for grants/cooperative agreements, with budget justification as Section L of the R&R Budget form (YFA route)

Statement of whether you believe the work is fundamental or non-fundamental research — DARPA decides, but you must state your view; and where a subaward differs from the prime, you must explain which tasks are which

Citizenship / immigration documentation for team members where required (YFA: USCIS Form I-797 emailed to the programme address no later than the full proposal due date, or the proposal is removed from consideration)

DSO office-wide extras: Attachment A Executive Summary Template; Attachment B Abstract Summary Slide; Attachment C Abstract Instructions and Template; Attachment D Proposal Summary Slide; Attachment E Volume I Template; Attachment F Volume II Template; Attachment G DARPA Cost Proposal Spreadsheet; Attachment I Accelerated Award Option Election and Attestation Form (if electing accelerated award); Attachment O DSO CUI Guide compliance

Classified route only: DD Form 254 (attached to the BAA by DARPA) and a security plan per the Classified Submission Requirements attachment — the security plan does not count against the abstract page limit

SBIR/STTR pre-negotiation set (after selection): active SAM registration with Representations and Certifications; CAGE code on the DSIP firm profile; foreign-citizen documentation; current NIST SP 800-171 self-assessment in SPRS; Schedule of Milestones and Payments; STTR intellectual-property allocation agreement between company and research institution; SF1408 accounting-system checklist for Phase II
result.program_officer_norms:
EXPECTED — more strongly than at NIH, and it is the defining feature of applying to DARPA. At NIH the programme officer is a route to advice; at DARPA the Program Manager IS the programme. PMs are term-limited outsiders (typically 3–5 years) who conceive, fund, and run their own programmes and personally decide what to recommend for funding. There is no standing study section whose taste you can study. The PM's current interest is the variable, and it is only knowable by asking.

DARPA says so in its own solicitations, not just in folklore. IPTO HR001126S0011 §5: "Potential proposers are strongly encouraged to reach out to DARPA Program Managers (PM) to gauge their interest in a technical approach prior to submitting a formal abstract. Early coordination ensures alignment with IPTO mission priorities and minimizes the expenditure of resources on concepts that may not meet current technical or strategic office requirements." DSO HR001125S0013: "Contacting DSO program managers to discuss their research interests is strongly encouraged."

It is also mandated internally. The BAA Guide directs that "The PM is encouraged to maintain an open dialogue with proposers after release of a BAA and prior to the receipt of proposals," and the DARPA Proposer Communications Plan inverts the usual default: a PM who does NOT intend to interact with proposers must obtain a written waiver from the Deputy Director of DARPA before the BAA is released, with a written rationale. Silence is the exception that requires justification.

WHEN, precisely — there is a one-way door:
- BEFORE the abstract: open dialogue. This is the window and it is wide.
- Proposers Day (before or just after BAA release): often includes registered one-on-one PM meetings and teaming introductions. If no Proposers Day is scheduled, email the PM directly. Briefings are cleared for public release afterwards, so you can get the material even if you missed it.
- AFTER the proposal is received: the door shuts hard. "After receipt of proposals, all interactions with proposers must go through the CO regardless of communication method (email, in person, telephonic, etc.)." And "the PM or CO cannot advise or direct a proposer on how to revise their proposal."
- AFTER notification: request an informal feedback session — available to selected AND non-selected proposers.

WHAT EXPERIENCED APPLICANTS ACTUALLY DO: send a short, specific email with a one-page concept or a quad chart attached, and ask (a) is this in scope for your current thrust, (b) is anyone already funded to do this, (c) is the scale and cost realistic for your budget, (d) what would make this revolutionary rather than evolutionary. They frame the concept against the Heilmeier Catechism before the first email, because that is the frame the PM will answer in. They do NOT ask the PM to review a draft or to tell them how to write it.

WHAT THE PM CANNOT DO, so do not ask: "The PM cannot attempt to replace the proposer's original ideas with their own"; "The PM cannot share ideas or technical solutions that were provided to them by a competing proposer"; and any substantive answer given to you must be given to everyone, typically via the public Q&A document or a BAA amendment. So a question that reveals your approach may end up paraphrased into a public Q&A. Ask about DARPA's interests, not about your secret sauce.

TWO IMPORTANT EXCEPTIONS:
- HIGH-VOLUME SOLICITATIONS THROTTLE CONTACT. YFA is the clearest case, and it matters because YFA is the ECR mechanism. DARPARA2502 FAQ 82: "Due to the high volume of responses to the YFA Research Announcement (RA), we are unable to accommodate such telecoms/meetings to provide additional feedback for Executive Summary submissions." For YFA, questions go to the solicitation mailbox (YFA2026@darpa.mil) and answers appear in the public FAQ. The pre-solicitation conversation with a PM is still worth having; the post-executive-summary one is not on offer.
- FFRDCs, UARCs AND GOVERNMENT LABS MUST contact the PM before proposing — this is a requirement, not a courtesy, and the PM may steer them onto the Government team rather than the performer side.

CONTACT MECHANICS: every BAA carries a BAA Coordinator mailbox named for the solicitation number (e.g. HR001126S0011@darpa.mil, HR001125S0013@darpa.mil, YFA2026@darpa.mil) for administrative/technical questions; PM names and interests are listed on each office's page at darpa.mil/about/offices; general enquiries via contact.darpa.mil. Every solicitation also publishes a question-submittal closing date that is EARLIER than the proposal deadline (DSO: questions closed 8 May 2026 against a 2 June 2026 close; YFA: 9 Jan 2026 against a 20 Jan 2026 close) — so the window for asking anything officially shuts roughly two weeks before you submit.
result.funded_examples_source:
DARPA publishes NO funded proposals, no summary statements, and no equivalent of NIH RePORTER's abstract library. There is no DARPA sample-proposal page, and I could not find a university research office hosting a genuine funded DARPA proposal (marked unresolved). What exists is five partial sources; a first-time applicant needs to know which gives what, because they are unequal.

1. DARPA'S OWN PROGRAMME PAGES — the best free proxy for "what a funded DARPA effort looks like", and the one DARPA itself points proposers to. https://www.darpa.mil/research/programs, filterable by research topic, by office, and by Current vs Completed, with keyword search. Each page gives the problem framing, goals and the responsible office. Read these before writing anything: they show you the register, the ambition level, and what is already funded (proposing a duplicate is an explicit non-conformance risk — DSO tells proposers to review current DSO programmes "to avoid proposals that duplicate existing activities").

2. DoD SBIR/STTR AWARD ABSTRACTS — the only place with real, readable, scientific award abstracts at scale. SBA's https://www.sbir.gov/awards covers all agencies and lists "Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency" as a filterable sub-agency (6,662 awards when checked); fields include company, topic code, phase, year, agency, title and abstract; results are downloadable for ≤10,000 records and the dataset refreshes monthly. Also https://www.dodsbirsttr.mil. DARPA's own SBIR instructions confirm the pipeline: "final approved versions of proposal titles, abstracts, anticipated benefits, and keywords may appear on the DoD SBIR/STTR awards website and/or the SBA's SBIR/STTR award website" — and confirm the limit: "Abstracts contained in grant proposals that are not selected for award will not be publicly posted." Note this is small-business work, so it reads differently from a university BAA proposal.

3. DTIC DoD GRANT AWARDS SEARCH — https://discover.dtic.mil/grant/. The right tool for university-side DARPA grants: publicly searchable DoD research and non-research grants awarded since December 2014, "containing detailed project abstracts". CAVEAT, verified 18 Sept 2026: the search interface is currently offline — the page states it "is offline while we fine-tune the user experience." The URL resolves (HTTP 200) but the search is unavailable, so I could not confirm its DARPA filter or exact field set. This is a tooling/availability fact, not evidence the resource is gone; check it again.

4. USAspending.gov — verified live via its API this pass. DARPA is a SUB-TIER agency under Department of Defense (toptier code 097; sub-tier "Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency"), so in Advanced Search set Awarding Agency = Department of Defense and Sub-Agency = Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency. A live query returned real DARPA cooperative agreements to Georgia Tech Research Corp, Duke, Harvard, Delaware and UC Riverside with amounts and contract numbers (e.g. HR0011-19-2-0008). HONEST LIMIT: the description fields are administrative one-liners such as "THE PURPOSE OF THIS AGREEMENT IS TO FUND RESEARCH IN SUPPORT OF BTO" — this tells you WHO is funded, for HOW MUCH, under which office and contract number. It is not an abstract. Its real use is different and underrated: find which labs at which universities hold DARPA money in your area, then email those PIs — they are the people who will actually tell you how the process went.

5. SAM.gov contract award data — https://sam.gov/fpds. DRIFT WARNING: FPDS.gov was decommissioned on 24 February 2026 and all public contract-award search moved into SAM.gov; fpds.gov now redirects. Any guide still pointing at FPDS ezSearch is out of date. Contract-level records, no scientific content.

THE SOURCE THAT ACTUALLY SUBSTITUTES FOR A SUMMARY STATEMENT: the informal feedback session. DARPA offers these on request to non-selected as well as selected proposers, and they are where you learn the specific strengths and weaknesses the Reviewers recorded against your proposal. For SBIR/STTR, technical evaluation narratives are retrievable directly through the SSIP portal at https://sbir.darpa.mil.

MATERIALS TO GET STARTED, in the order a newcomer should use them:
(a) The Heilmeier Catechism, https://www.darpa.mil/about/heilmeier-catechism — eight questions DARPA uses "to assess and think through every proposed research program": what are you trying to do (no jargon); how is it done today and what are the limits of current practice; what is new in your approach and why will it succeed; who cares and what difference will it make; what are the risks; how much will it cost; how long will it take; what are the mid-term and final "exams" for success. Answer all eight in one page before contacting anyone. This is the highest-value single artefact for a first-time applicant.
(b) The office-wide BAA abstract template for your office — it is a free, published, structured outline of exactly what DARPA wants said and in what order.
(c) Proposer Instructions: General Terms and Conditions — the invisible half of the solicitation, incorporated by reference into every BAA.
(d) The RSS feed, https://www.darpa.mil/rss/opportunities.xml — the cheapest way to see Proposers Days coming.
(e) DARPAConnect, https://www.darpaconnect.us — DARPA's outreach programme for organisations new to national security, offering events, workshops, coaching, "Ask-Me-Anything" sessions and "DARPA Open Mic". Its resource library sits behind a free registration; the public /learning-resources URL currently 302-redirects to a broken third-party page, so the module list could not be enumerated (unresolved).

Full-proposal page limits for the CURRENT office-wide BAAs could not be established, because they are structurally not published: IPTO HR001126S0011 puts them inside the 'IPTO Office Wide Proposal Templates zip file' and I2O HR001126S0001 releases them only with the invitation to propose. The attachment zips are hosted on SAM.gov, which returns an empty body to a plain fetch.

DARPA SBIR/STTR technical volume page limits (commonly cited as ~20pp Phase I, ~45pp Phase II including a 5-page commercialization strategy) came from a search-index summary of DARPA component instructions, NOT from a release PDF I read. They change between releases. Verify in the specific DARPA release document on DSIP before relying on them.

Current status and dates of four of the six office-wide BAAs (BTO, MXO, STO, TTO) were not individually verified — their SAM.gov pages could not be fetched. Only IPTO HR001126S0011 (current), I2O HR001126S0001 (superseded) and DSO HR001125S0013 (closed 2 June 2026) were read in full.

Whether DSO has reissued its office-wide BAA under an HR001126S number after HR001125S0013 closed on 2 June 2026 could not be confirmed. The BAA Guide says office-wide BAAs are reissued annually, so a successor is expected, but I did not see it. Do not assert DSO is closed.

DARPA publishes no official submission-to-award month count. The 6-12 month end-to-end figure is my assembly from sourced component durations (30-day abstract cap, X+28 internal review target, 4-6 weeks selection-to-contracting-agent, 180-day cost validity), not a DARPA statement. Labelled as such.

DARPAConnect's specific module/course list could not be enumerated. The public /learning-resources URL 302-redirects to http://pathfinder.theari.us/learning-resources, which returns Page Not Found; the resource library requires free registration. Whether it contains a PM-engagement or abstract-writing module is unknown.
The 90-day notification commitment is documented only for SBIR/STTR. No equivalent published notification-time commitment was found for BAA or RA proposals.

Two different DARPA Extranet inactivity windows appear in DARPA documents (30 days in the Proposer Instructions for BAAT; 45 days deactivation / 90 days deletion in the SBIR SSIP FAQ). These are likely different systems rather than a contradiction, but I did not confirm which applies to a BAAT account. Treat 30 days as the safe assumption.

Whether any DARPA office imposes a limit on how many times the same concept may be resubmitted across annual BAA reissues. No such limit found in any document read; absence of evidence, not evidence of absence.

result.funder_system:
European Molecular Biology Organization (EMBO), Heidelberg, Germany — funded by the EMBC intergovernmental agreement (33 EMBC Member States plus global partners Chile, India, Japan, Singapore, Taiwan). NOT a US funder: eligibility is built on mobility between EMBC/partner countries, so US-based researchers touch EMBO mainly in three ways — (a) as the HOST of an EMBO Postdoctoral Fellow (a US lab can receive a fellow; the fellow must be an EMBC national moving from an EMBC state, capped at 30% of awards), (b) as an EMBC-national postdoc moving TO the US, (c) not at all for YIP/Installation Grants/GIN, which require a group-leader post inside the eligible country lists.

CRITICAL STRUCTURAL FACT for a first-time applicant: EMBO is not one machine. Two separate offices run the mechanisms with materially different rules, and people routinely assume the postdoc rules apply everywhere. They do not.
- EMBO Fellowship Office (fellowships@embo.org; Programme Head Karin Dumstrei) runs Postdoctoral Fellowships and Scientific Exchange Grants. Text-only online forms, WORD limits, rolling/cut-off model, NO feedback ever.
- EMBO Young Investigator Programme Office (yip@embo.org) and Global Activities office (global@embo.org), both under Programme Head Gerlind Wallon, run the Young Investigator Programme, Installation Grants and the Global Investigator Network. Downloadable protected Word "offline forms" uploaded as PDF, PAGE limits, figures allowed, single annual deadline, interviews in November, feedback after an unsuccessful interview.

Mechanisms with live application routes (verified on embo.org sitemap + pages): Postdoctoral Fellowships; Scientific Exchange Grants; Young Investigator Programme; Installation Grants; Global Investigator Network; Maria Leptin | EMBO Science Journalism Fellowships; EMBO Solidarity Grants. Plus conference/training funding and lecture/travel/childcare grants under separate hubs.

Real competitiveness (EMBO Annual Report 2025 Facts & Figures, the funder's own numbers):
- Postdoctoral Fellowships: 2025 = 1,717 applications / 154 awards / 9.0% success. 2024 = 1,350/145/10.7%. 2023 = 1,149/135/11.7%. 2022 = 1,101/227/20.7%. 2021 = 1,166/224/19.2%. The success rate roughly halved over five years — applications rose while awards did not.
- Young Investigator Programme: 2025 = 234 eligible applications / 28 awards / 12.0%; stable ~12-13% across 2021-2025. YIP guidelines state "The success rate of being selected is ~12%".
Both figures matter for advising: EMBO postdoc is now a ~1-in-11 shot, not the ~1-in-5 it was in 2021-22.
result.submission_portal:
ONE portal domain, but NO single account or single front door: **https://applications.embo.org**

Each mechanism has its own registration link with a programme code. These are the actual entry points (scraped from each programme page on embo.org, 2026-09-18):
- Postdoctoral Fellowships: http://applications.embo.org/01/register.php?reg=S019
- Scientific Exchange Grants: https://applications.embo.org/register.php?reg=80DN
- Young Investigator Programme: http://applications.embo.org/01/register.php?reg=P0M8
- Installation Grants: http://applications.embo.org/01/register.php?reg=58UW
- Global Investigator Network: https://applications.embo.org/register.php?reg=M18O
- Solidarity Grants: https://applications.embo.org/register.php?reg=E3PO

THE HIDDEN LONG-LEAD ITEMS (this is the part that catches people out):

1. Account creation is asynchronous. Postdoc guidelines: "Applicants need to register for an EMBO online application account. Once login details for the account have been received by e-mail it is possible to start an application." You register, then WAIT for credentials by email. Do not start this the week of the deadline.

2. Registering does NOT enter you in a round. Stated twice, in caps: "Registration for an EMBO online application account is not sufficient to enter the corresponding evaluation round. An application is only regarded as complete once all the required information is submitted and the candidate confirms completion." There is a "form complete" / "Submit" button that must be clicked. Several FAQ entries exist purely because people forgot to click it.

3. USE REGISTRATION AS RECONNAISSANCE. EMBO explicitly invites this — the guidelines Annex says registration "allows you to see what information is needed in preparing the application." Because the postdoc section limits are NOT published in the guidelines, registering early is the only way to see them. This is the single best first action for a prospective applicant.

4. Third parties submit through their own portal links, and you trigger those links. Referees and the host institute do not email anything to EMBO — the applicant enters their details and "activates" them, which fires an automated email containing a personal form link.
   - YIP/IG/GIN: "We strongly recommend that you complete/activate your referee details at least 4 weeks prior to the deadline to allow referees enough time to submit their letters."
   - There is NO file upload for referees on YIP/IG/GIN: "Referees shall follow the steps explained in the form and paste their letter text in the provided field... Reference letters sent by email are not accepted." Warn your referees, or they will write a PDF and find nowhere to attach it (an actual FAQ entry).
   - You cannot see the letters. You CAN see submission status, on the application system HOME tab.
   - Installation Grants additionally require the Receiving Institute to complete its own online form by the same deadline, again triggered by you activating the contact.

5. ORCID is mandatory for Scientific Exchange Grants ("All applicants must register for ORCID digital identifiers"), Installation Grants and GIN, and requested on others. Register at https://orcid.org/register beforehand.

6. Reference letters can be RECYCLED for YIP/IG re-applicants, via a documented trick: enter the referee's name and postal address but put "yip@embo.org" in the email field, and the office copies the letter from your most recent application. It is a manual process, so status will not update immediately.

7. Planned downtime around cut-offs: "the system may be closed for short periods after each selection deadline for technical and maintenance purposes and occasional downtimes may occur at any time. Candidates must take these potential issues into consideration."

Institutional grants-office involvement is minimal compared with NIH/NSF: there is no Grants.gov/eRA equivalent, no institutional AOR sign-off for fellowships, no DUNS/UEI/SAM registration. The applicant registers as an individual. The only institutional artefacts are letters/forms submitted by the host lab or receiving institute.
result.deadline_structure:
EMBO publishes RULE-BASED RECURRING deadlines, not one-off dates. The rule is the durable fact; the calendar date is the instance. Both are given below, with the rule first — this is the form that survives a year of drift.

**Postdoctoral Fellowships — no deadline, but two hard cut-offs.** Quoting the guidelines (July 2026) verbatim: "There are no application deadlines for EMBO Postdoctoral Fellowships, but there are two cutoff evaluation dates: Fourth Friday of January, 2 PM Central European Time: Applications submitted up to this date will enter the Spring Selection Round... Second Friday of July, 2 PM Central European Summer Time: Applications submitted up to this date will enter the Autumn Selection Round."
- RULE: 4th Friday of January, 14:00 CET (Spring round) and 2nd Friday of July, 14:00 CEST (Autumn round), every year.
- NEXT DATED INSTANCE, from EMBO's own application page: "next cutoff date – hard deadline: Friday 22 January 2027, 14:00 CET."
- Missing the cut-off is not fatal — you roll into the next round: "Applications completed after 14:00 CE(S)T on the day of the evaluation cutoff deadline will enter the next evaluation round. NO EXCEPTIONS WILL BE MADE."
- Subtlety that decides eligibility: the SUBMISSION date, not the cut-off date, is what eligibility is measured against (PhD within 2 years; the 6-months-in-host-country mobility test). Stated twice in the guidelines: "The Spring and Autumn cutoff deadlines... do not play a role in this eligibility check." So submitting early can make you eligible when submitting late would not.

**Annual single deadlines (the group-leader schemes):**
- Young Investigator Programme — RULE: pre-application 1 April, 12:00 midday CEST; full application (invited only) 15 July, 12:00 midday CEST. 2026 instance: 1 April 2026 and 15 July 2026; interviews 17-18 November 2026.
- Installation Grants — RULE: 15 April, 12:00 midday CEST, for the applicant form, the 3 reference letters AND the Receiving Institute Online Application Form. 2026 instance: 15 April 2026; interviews 11-12 November 2026.
- Global Investigator Network — RULE, quoted: "Application deadline: Annually on 1 May, 14:00 CEST." 2026 instance: 1 May 2026; interviews 24-25 November 2026.
Note all three are midday/early-afternoon CET/CEST, not end of day.

**Scientific Exchange Grants — genuinely rolling.** "There are no deadlines for applications and awards are being made throughout the year." But there are two lead-time rules that function as deadlines: "it is strongly recommended that applications be submitted at least three months before the proposed start date of the research visit. At minimum, applications must be submitted 30 days before the start date of the research visit."

**Solidarity Grants — STALE PAGE, flagged not concluded.** The live page (https://www.embo.org/funding/fellowships-grants-and-career-support/embo-solidarity-grants/) displays "Application deadline: 15 February 2023" as of 2026-09-18, while its registration link (reg=E3PO) is still present. Per house rule, a stale published date is not evidence a programme ended. Treat the date as unreliable and confirm with EMBO before advising anyone.

review_stages.stage: POSTDOC — Stage 1, office eligibility pre-screen + Fellowship Committee screen of a condensed form (main scientific achievements, publication list, summary and biological significance of proposed work, justification of host lab choice, reference + acceptance letters)
review_stages.timing: 0-6 weeks after cut-off. Acknowledgement email within max 2 weeks — if nothing arrives in 2 weeks, contact the office, that is EMBO's own instruction

review_stages.stage: POSTDOC — pre-screen outcome emailed to ALL applicants. 'Normally, the top 20-25% ranked applications are selected for the second round'
review_stages.timing: about 6-8 weeks after cut-off (so roughly late March for the January cut-off; early September for the July cut-off)

review_stages.stage: POSTDOC — Stage 2, individual interview by a subject expert drawn from EMBO Members and EMBO Young Investigators. Online video call only. 90 minutes total: 30 min candidate presentation (PhD achievements + proposed postdoc project) then 60 min Q&A. Scheduled 'at the interviewer's convenience'
review_stages.timing: 7-15 weeks after cut-off

review_stages.stage: POSTDOC — Stage 3, full application + interviewer report independently assessed by Fellowship Committee members; biannual Fellowship Committee meeting takes the funding decisions. 'Grey zone' candidates get a second, shorter online interview on the day of the committee meeting (7-min presentation + 10-min Q&A), notified ~2 weeks ahead
review_stages.timing: 15-17 weeks after cut-off

review_stages.stage: POSTDOC — official outcome by email, within two weeks of the committee meeting
review_stages.timing: ~5 months after cut-off. NOTE A SOURCE CONFLICT: the guidelines PDF says results 'announced at the end of June' / 'end of December'; the web application page says 'around the mid of June' / 'around the mid of December'. Plan for mid-to-late June / mid-to-late December

review_stages.stage: POSTDOC — earliest fellowship start. Spring round: must start between 1 July of the award year and 15 February of the following year. Autumn round: between 1 January and 15 August of the following year. Starts are only ever on the 1st or 15th of a month
review_stages.timing: ~5.5 months after the January cut-off; ~6 months after the July cut-off

review_stages.stage: YIP — pre-application (Stage 1) screened by the Young Investigator Committee, each application independently evaluated by four committee members; ~50 invited to full application + interview

review_stages.timing: 17 or 18 November 2026 (~7.5 months after pre-application)

review_stages.stage: YIP — final selection by the whole committee; outcome by email 'within a week of the interview'; results to applicants by 27 November, under embargo until the December press release
review_stages.timing: ~8 months from pre-application deadline

review_stages.stage: INSTALLATION GRANTS — office eligibility screen, committee shortlisting, then confidential review by one EMBO Member (three exclusions permitted)
review_stages.timing: 15 April → 'Pre-application results announced late June' (~2.5 months)

review_stages.stage: INSTALLATION GRANTS — panel interview, same format as YIP: 10-min talk + 10-min Q&A, two parallel sub-panels of 5, hybrid with candidate on Zoom, backup video required. Receiving Institute Confirmation Form (1 page, signed by the head of institute) due by the day of the interview
review_stages.timing: 11-12 November 2026 (~7 months)

'The Board cannot change the ranking order provided by the committee, so Grantees are selected from the top to bottom of the country ranking.' The number of grants per country is not known to EMBO before the meeting
review_stages.timing: SDIG Board meets 23 November 2026; results to applicants December; press release January 2027 (~8 months)

review_stages.stage: INSTALLATION GRANTS — grant start. If already at the Receiving Institute, start is automatically 1 January of the year following selection; if not yet in post, the lab must be set up and the grant started no later than 31 December of the year following selection
