review_stages.timing: 1 May deadline → interview invitations 'By 15 July' → online panel interviews 24 & 25 November → 'Results announced to applicants By 15 December' (~7.5 months)

review_stages.stage: SCIENTIFIC EXCHANGE GRANTS — office eligibility screen (acknowledgement within 2 weeks, with an SEG number assigned), reports from the SEG Advisory Board, final decision by the Head of the EMBO Fellowship Programme. No interview, no panel meeting
review_stages.timing: 'A decision is usually made within two to four months from submission of a complete application.' Rolling

result.months_submission_to_award:
Varies sharply by mechanism; this is one of the places where assuming "EMBO works like X" goes wrong.

- Postdoctoral Fellowships: ~5 months cut-off → decision; ~5.5-6 months cut-off → earliest permitted start. Worked example (Spring): submit by Friday 22 Jan 2027 → pre-screen outcome ~mid-March → interview March-May → decision mid-to-late June 2027 → start any 1st/15th between 1 July 2027 and 15 Feb 2028. Worked example (Autumn): submit by the 2nd Friday of July → decision mid-to-late December → start between 1 January and 15 August of the following year.
- Scientific Exchange Grants: 2-4 months submission → decision. Must be submitted at least 30 days before the visit, recommended 3 months. So realistically budget 3-4 months from application to travelling.
- Young Investigator Programme: ~8 months, pre-application (1 April) → result (by 27 November). Benefits run from the following year.
- Installation Grants: ~8 months deadline (15 April) → result (December), with the SDIG Board on 23 November. Grant starts 1 January of the following year if you are already in post — i.e. ~8.5 months from application to money.
- Global Investigator Network: ~7.5 months, 1 May → by 15 December.

Practical planning consequence: for anyone needing salary continuity, the EMBO postdoc timeline means applying roughly 6-8 months before you need to start, and the group-leader schemes need a ~12-month runway from thinking about it to funds arriving.
result.resubmission_policy:
Different in every mechanism, and the postdoc rule is being ABOLISHED — this is the single most drift-sensitive fact in the whole EMBO system and the thing most likely to be wrong in any advice written before mid-2026.

**Postdoctoral Fellowships — currently once, then never.** Quoting the guidelines (July 2026) verbatim: "Re-application is permitted only once. However, we will only consider a re-application in case of substantial changes to the proposal and/or the CV of the applicant or a change of host lab. The applicant should outline in the 'Other Funding' section under 'application changes' detailed and exact changes made to the proposal and/or the CV."
Then, the change: "Effective from the Autumn 2027 selection round (i.e., for all applications submitted after January 22, 2027, 14:00 CET), re-applications will no longer be permitted. Researchers may submit only one EMBO Fellowship Proposal." The FAQ repeats this independently.
ACTIONABLE CONSEQUENCE: the January 2027 cut-off is the last round from which a second attempt is possible. Anyone who wants two shots must have their FIRST application in by 22 January 2027, 14:00 CET. After that date, EMBO postdoc becomes a one-shot-per-lifetime award. This should change how a postdoc paces their application — it removes the "submit a rough one to get feedback" strategy entirely (and EMBO gives no feedback anyway, see below).
Other postdoc rules: "All eligibility criteria must be met at time of re-submission" — and since eligibility runs off the SUBMISSION date (PhD within 2 years, ≤6 months in the host country in the last 18), a second attempt a year later can simply be time-barred. Candidates may re-apply for the next round while the first is still under decision ONLY if they would no longer be eligible after the decision.
There is NO introduction page in the NIH sense. The changes go in a field called "application changes" inside the "Other Funding" section.
Related new restriction: "Effective from the Autumn 2026 selection round (i.e., all applications submitted after January 23, 2026, 14:00 CET): A host laboratory... can support the submission of maximum one application per selection cycle." If two candidates name the same host lab, EMBO contacts the lab and asks for a withdrawal. So confirm with a prospective host that nobody else is applying to them that round.
Also: an application cannot be edited after submission. Publication updates force the office to re-open it, which RESETS the submission date and can make it ineligible. "Publication updates after the application is submitted are not allowed."

**Young Investigator Programme — one more attempt after an interview.** "If you were rejected after an interview, you may re-apply once more. Previous rejection does not have any impact on the success of the following applications." Re-applicants may recycle reference letters via the yip@embo.org email-field trick. CV dates must be "congruent with the previous application" — the committee checks.

**Installation Grants — unlimited applications, maximum two interviews.** Verbatim: "Candidates can re-apply as many times as they fulfil eligibility criteria, but only once more after having been interviewed (i.e. candidates can only attend two interviews)."

**Global Investigator Network — maximum three interviews.** Eligibility requires that applicants "have not been interviewed by the selection committee more than twice in previous application rounds."

**Scientific Exchange Grants — time-windowed, not counted.** "An applicant who has previously held an EMBO Scientific Exchange Grant or Postdoctoral Fellowship is eligible to re-apply for an EMBO Scientific Exchange Grant if it is for a new project in a different laboratory. Reapplication is possible twelve months after the end of the previous Scientific Exchange Grant or in the case of unsuccessful applicants, the date of application." So: 12 months after your last application if rejected; new project, different lab.
result.page_limits:
EMBO splits cleanly in two: the Fellowship Office schemes use WORD/CHARACTER limits inside a text-only web form (no figures at all); the group-leader schemes use PAGE limits in a downloadable protected Word form (figures allowed and counted).

**Postdoctoral Fellowships — text-only web form; section limits NOT published.** Formatting rule, verbatim: "Applications must be written in English and no special formatting is allowed. Similarly, figures and tables cannot be included in the application." The FAQ describes the system as "text only (no figures or graphs)" and confirms "No document attachments allowed." The per-section character limits are not in the guidelines or the FAQ — they are only visible inside the form. EMBO's own remedy is to register early and look: registration "allows you to see what information is needed in preparing the application." Known sections (from the pre-screen description): summary of main scientific achievements + publication list; summary and biological significance of the proposed work; justification for choice of host lab; plus an "Other Funding" section that carries the "application changes" field for re-applicants. Publication list must carry NO impact factors or citation metrics (EMBO is a DORA signatory), and must exclude papers submitted or in preparation, non-English papers, and conference abstracts.

**Scientific Exchange Grants — the most precisely specified, all word counts:**
- Proposal summary: 200 words (research proposal + biological significance)
- Research proposal: max 1,800 words excluding references, split as background/rationale max 500 + aim and objectives max 300 + detailed workplan at host institute with a timeline per objective max 1,000
- Citations: max 15, Vancouver/numbered style, in-text in brackets; full author list + title + journal/preprint server + year + doi, listed in a separate box
- "No figures or tables may be included"
- Benefit to the home lab: 200 words; justification for choice of host lab: 200 words
- Prior/existing collaboration between host and home lab: 100 words
- Synopsis of present work at home institute: max 500 words; career plans after the grant: max 200 words
- Publication list: last five years only, format authors/title/journal or preprint/year/doi, applicant's name marked with an asterisk, no impact factors
- Referee letters: assessment max 200 words; the home supervisor additionally writes benefit to applicant (200 words) and benefit to home lab (200 words)
- Host supervisor's acceptance form: benefits of the collaboration 200 words, how the project was conceived 200 words, max 5 references to their recent work

**Young Investigator Programme — page limits, offline form:**
- Online: short summary of ongoing research, 2,000 characters including spaces
- Offline form formatting, verbatim: "completed in Helvetica or Arial font, size 10; The margins should not be altered; ...saved in PDF format... colour highlighting, table view or any other formatting is not acceptable"
- Three best papers: summary + why you chose each, max 1,000 characters including spaces each
- Research vision: "no longer than two pages", excluding references. "Any figures are included in the page count." References may go on an additional page
- Tip from EMBO itself: the first two pages of the full-application form are almost identical to the pre-application form, so keep your pre-application file to copy forward

**Installation Grants — page limits, offline form:**
- Two best publications: summary + justification, max 1,000 characters
- Synopsis of recent work (PhD + postdoc): max 1 page
- Research plan: "3 pages maximum, excluding bibliography. Any figures are included within the page count"
- Budget: 5-year timeline; "We do not expect a detailed list of all consumables"; lab member salaries may be included
- Same Helvetica/Arial 10, unaltered margins, PDF, no highlighting or table borders

**Global Investigator Network:**
- Online summary of ongoing research: 100-400 words — and EMBO flags its double duty: "This summary is important in the pre-selection phase and in identifying potential reviewers for your application"
- "Other relevant information" on the CV: max five lines, no extra documentation
- Grants must be listed in euros as "allocated to your group / total", e.g. 60,000 / 180,000
- Authorship symbols specified: * corresponding, # co-first/co-last, § senior author if not listed last
- Same Helvetica/Arial 10 / PDF / no formatting rules

Cross-cutting: EMBO is a DORA signatory and bans journal-based metrics from publication lists in every mechanism. AI disclosure is requested in every mechanism: applicants "are requested to disclose whether AI tools were used in preparing their applications, and for what purpose (e.g., chatGPT was used to improve language style)", with the applicant "fully and solely responsible for the originality and accuracy" of the application.
required_documents: POSTDOC — Completed online application form (text only; no attachments, no figures, no tables) with the candidate clicking to confirm completion

POSTDOC — Exactly TWO reference letters, submitted through the online system. Hard constraints: one MUST be from the PhD supervisor or co-supervisor; NEITHER may come from anyone at the receiving institute; both must be sent from institutional, not private, email addresses
POSTDOC — Acceptance letter from the receiving institute, submitted online, also from an institutional email address. The application cannot be completed until both references and this letter are in

POSTDOC — First (or joint-first) author primary research paper already accepted or published in an international peer-reviewed journal at the time of submission; OR a first-author preprint on a recognised server (arXiv/bioRxiv/medRxiv/Zenodo) carrying publicly available in-depth reviews from an independent service such as Peer Community In or Review Commons. If the paper is 'accepted' but not yet out, the editorial letter must be emailed to fellowships@embo.org BEFORE submitting

POSTDOC — Documentation for any career-break eligibility extension (parental leave, military/civil service, illness, family care), which must be pre-approved by the Fellowship Office before submission

SEG — Online application form; two referees' confidential letters (one must be the current supervisor, neither from the host institute); host supervisor's receiving-institute acceptance form; ORCID iD; publication list (last 5 years). Independent researchers instead supply ONE letter from a Dean/Director and must email fellowships@embo.org to have the form reconfigured

SEG (post-award) — Final report of ~2 pages within six months of the visit, plus a signed English-language letter from the home institution certifying the applicant returned and stayed at least 6 consecutive months. Both go to fellowships@embo.org quoting the SEG number

YIP STAGE 1 — Online pre-application form (basic CV data, 2,000-character research summary, referee details, ORCID) + completed offline Word form uploaded as PDF + THREE reference letters pasted into the referee portal by the referees. Fewer than 3 letters = incomplete and dropped

YIP STAGE 2 (invited only) — Fuller online form adding a list of grants, a list of lab members and a short institute description; plus the full offline form with updated CV and publication list, a summary of each of your three best papers, and a 2-page research vision. An ACCEPTED last-author peer-reviewed paper (or peer-reviewed last-author preprint) is required by the interview date — failure to supply it means exclusion

INSTALLATION GRANTS — Scientist online form + scientist offline form as PDF + THREE reference letters + a Receiving Institute Online Application Form completed by the institute (covering the start-up package offered, institute infrastructure, and how the applicant was selected), ALL by 15 April. Then, if interviewed, a one-page Receiving Institute Confirmation Form signed by the head of institute, due by the day of the interview

GIN — Online form (personal details, ORCID, three referees, host institute description, basic CV, 100-400 word research summary, group members with start/end dates, all current and former grants in euros) + offline form as PDF + three reference letters

ALL MECHANISMS — ORCID iD (mandatory for SEG, IG, GIN); publication list free of impact factors and other journal metrics; AI-use disclosure; research-integrity compliance (EMBO Postdoctoral Fellows must complete an online research integrity course; SEG awardees are strongly encouraged to)
result.program_officer_norms:
EMBO inverts the NIH pattern, and getting this backwards is costly in both directions.

**Contacting the programme OFFICE: expected, and in several cases MANDATORY — skipping it makes you ineligible.** There is no NIH-style "program officer who champions your science", but there is a gatekeeping office that must pre-clear edge cases. The binding language, verbatim from the postdoc guidelines: "The applicant must contact the Fellowship office prior to the submission of the application to obtain an exception, no matter what type. **Applications submitted without prior approval of an exception will be deemed ineligible.**" The FAQ repeats it.

Cases where you MUST write first — these are the real "ask the program officer" moments for EMBO:
- Any career-break extension of the 2-year-post-PhD window (parental leave, military/civil service, illness, caring responsibilities)
- No PhD but claimed equivalent research experience ("should enquire with the EMBO Fellowship office prior to submission")
- A paper that is accepted/accepted-in-principle but not yet published — email the editorial letter to fellowships@embo.org before submitting, and the letter must make clear you are first or co-first author
- Any doubt about whether a publication counts as a primary research paper ("Contact the Fellowship office in case of doubt")
- Eligibility generally: "If in doubt, please write to us... with an updated CV and a summary proposal" — note EMBO asks for a CV and a summary, so send those, not a vague question
- Prior co-publication with the intended host supervisor (this "generally receive[s] lower priority for funding", so it is worth testing before investing months)
- YIP/IG: eligibility extensions, a transition to group leader with no formal change of position, uncertainty about whether you count as an independent group leader, co-corresponding vs last authorship questions
- SEG: if you are an independent researcher, you must email to have the reference structure changed
- If you win another grant while under evaluation, you must tell the office

Office addresses: fellowships@embo.org (Postdoctoral Fellowships, Scientific Exchange Grants; Programme Head Karin Dumstrei); yip@embo.org (Young Investigator Programme AND Installation Grants); global@embo.org (Global Investigator Network). Gerlind Wallon is Programme Head for YIP/IG/GIN; named officers on the 2026 IG guidelines include Roberto Efraín Díaz (Senior Programme Officer) and Grace Denny (Programme Officer); GIN lists Leonor Ruivo (Senior Programme Officer) and Tiffany Myers (Programme Assistant).

EMBO does ask you to do your homework first: "Before contacting the office in case of any questions, please check the above links first."

**Contacting COMMITTEE members: forbidden, and for Installation Grants explicitly disqualifying.** Verbatim from the IG guidelines: "Please do not contact the committee members directly. **Directly contacting Installation Grants committee members for application advice/feedback can be interpreted as attempting to influence selection results and will disqualify your application.**" The YIP guidelines carry the same prohibition without the disqualification clause: "Please do not contact any committee members directly for feedback." This matters because EMBO PUBLISHES the full committee membership in the guidelines PDFs — the names are right there, and using them is the mistake. What you CAN do with those lists is the reverse: YIP, IG and GIN let you EXCLUDE three EMBO Members from reviewing your application for conflict of interest. That is the legitimate way to act on knowing who reviews.

**Feedback after rejection — this is where EMBO differs most from NIH, and it should change strategy.**
- Postdoctoral Fellowships: NONE, ever, at any stage. Verbatim: "No feedback will be provided to applicants at any stage of the application process." EMBO explains the trade-off openly: providing correct, detailed feedback on ">1,400 applications received per year" would require employing several PhD-level staff, and "Instead, the funds are used to support additional fellowships." The FAQ adds: "We cannot provide individual feedback, as we do not have comments from the fellowship committee." There is no summary statement, no score, no percentile, no pink sheet. Combined with re-applications ending after January 2027, the "submit, learn, resubmit" loop that works at NIH does not exist here at all.
- YIP and Installation Grants: no feedback after the pre-selection stage, BUT the committee does give feedback after an unsuccessful INTERVIEW, routed through the programme office. So reaching interview has a consolation value that failing the pre-screen does not.

**What experienced applicants actually use the office for:** binary eligibility rulings before investing effort (the 2-year PhD window, the 6-months-in-country mobility test, whether a paper counts, whether they count as independent); getting an exception formally pre-approved and then summarising it in the "Other relevant information" CV field; re-sending referee invitations that went to spam; re-opening a referee's accidentally-submitted blank form; recycling reference letters for a re-application; and, for postdoc applicants from Autumn 2026 onward, checking with a prospective host lab that no other candidate is naming them that cycle.
result.funded_examples_source:
There is no EMBO equivalent of NIH RePORTER — no searchable award database with abstracts, budgets and no released review documents. But EMBO publishes more than most people realise, in two places, and one of them is genuinely a per-awardee list.

**1. EMBO Annual Report "Facts & Figures" PDFs — the real funded-awards list, and the best single resource.** https://www.embo.org/about-embo/resources/annual-reports/
Direct files: https://www.embo.org/documents/facts_figures/EMBO_annual_report_2025-facts_figures.pdf and .../EMBO_annual_report_2024-facts_figures.pdf; earlier years at https://www.embo.org/documents/news/facts_figures/EMBO_facts_figures_2020.pdf through _2023.pdf.
The 2025 edition is 64 pages and lists EVERY awardee of the year by name:
- Postdoctoral Fellows (pp. 4-16) as a table: Name | Home institute | Group leader | Host institute | Project title. Verified real rows include "Colm Doyle | Cancer Research UK Cambridge Institute | Arnaud Krebs | EMBL Heidelberg | Role of enhancer cooperativity in the control of transcription during development" and "Beau Dronsella | MPI für terrestrische Mikrobiologie Marburg | Michael Jewett | Stanford, United States | A cell-free Calvin cycle as a model system to study enhanced carbon fixation".
- Scientific Exchange Grants (pp. 16-40) in the same five-column format — roughly 24 pages of funded exchange projects.
- Young Investigators (pp. 40-46), Installation Grantees (p. 46) and Global Investigators (p. 47) as Name | Institute | Research interest.
- Plus application/award/success-rate tables by year and by nationality, and a full country-to-country mobility matrix.
This is the closest thing to reading funded applications: a PhD student can see exactly which host labs successfully received EMBO fellows, in which countries, on what kind of project, and phrased in one line — which is also the register EMBO's own summary fields expect. Reading two or three consecutive years is the highest-value hour a prospective applicant can spend.

**2. people.embo.org — searchable directory of EMBO Members, Associate Members, Young Investigators and Global Investigators.** https://people.embo.org (3,149 people listed as of 2026-09-18). Filters: free text, community type (EMBO Member / Associate Member / Young Investigator / Global Investigator), gender, location (all EMBC states plus partners and a long list of other countries including the United States), EMBO subject area, and curated "EMBOwords" keyword sets. Profiles live at people.embo.org/profile/<name-slug> and carry institution, country, award/election year, a research title, a ~60-word plain-language research summary, keywords, subject areas and a link to EMBO's Science Map. Example verified: https://people.embo.org/profile/andrea-ablasser. The hub page for this is https://www.embo.org/the-embo-communities/embo-young-investigator-network/find-a-young-investigator-installation-grantee-or-global-investigator/, which describes it as covering "all current and former EMBO Young Investigators, Installation Grantees and Global Investigators" — though the live filter set on people.embo.org offers Young Investigator and Global Investigator but not a separate Installation Grantee facet. For a YIP or GIN applicant these short summaries are effectively model answers for the 100-400 word / 2,000-character research summary fields.

**Deliberately NOT available — do not promise these:**
- No published sample EMBO applications from EMBO itself.
- No reviewer comments, scores, percentiles or summary statements are released to anyone, ever, for the postdoctoral fellowship — EMBO states it does not even hold committee comments.
- No searchable database of postdoctoral fellows: https://www.embo.org/the-embo-communities/embo-fellows/ is descriptive only, with no roster. The annual-report PDFs are the only per-name postdoc listing.
- EMBO Fellows Network (https://fellowsnetwork.embo.org/) is a members-only platform for awarded fellows, not a public archive.
I could not check whether any university research office publishes a successful EMBO application, because this session's web-search budget was exhausted; direct fetches of embo.org worked throughout, so everything above is from EMBO's own pages and PDFs, not a search index.

result.funder_system: Fulbright Program — U.S. Department of State, Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs (ECA). Not one application system but a federation of mechanisms run by different implementing partners, with final selections approved by the presidentially-appointed J. William Fulbright Foreign Scholarship Board (FFSB). The four doors an early-career researcher meets: (1) FULBRIGHT U.S. STUDENT PROGRAM — administered by IIE, us.fulbrightonline.org; Study/Research, English Teaching Assistantship (ETA), Fulbright-National Geographic, Fulbright-Fogarty; for "graduating college seniors, graduate students, and young professionals". (2) FULBRIGHT U.S. SCHOLAR PROGRAM — administered by IIE (the former CIES), fulbrightscholars.org; "more than 380 awards in more than 120 countries" for 2027-2028; four opportunity types — Scholar Awards, Postdoctoral Awards ("provide recently graduated scholars an opportunity to conduct research and receive professional training abroad"), Distinguished Scholar Awards (7+ years' experience), International Education Administrator (IEA) seminars. (3) FULBRIGHT SPECIALIST PROGRAM — administered by World Learning; a rolling 3-year roster feeding 2-6 week project matches. (4) FULBRIGHT FOREIGN STUDENT / VISITING SCHOLAR PROGRAMS — for non-U.S. citizens, via the binational Fulbright Commission/Foundation or U.S. Embassy in the home country. THE STRUCTURAL FACT THAT DECIDES WHICH DOOR YOU USE IS THE DOCTORATE: the Student Program excludes "Applicants who currently hold or will hold a doctoral degree (Ph.D.) by the national application deadline", so PhD candidates use the Student Program and PhD holders/postdocs use the Scholar Program's Postdoctoral or Scholar Awards. Separately, Fulbright-Hays (DDRA/GPA) is NOT this funder — it is a U.S. Department of Education programme with its own portal and an institutional rather than individual applicant (flagged as a common confusion; my ed.gov fetch 404'd this session, so treat that last point as unverified).
result.submission_portal: All U.S. competitions are INDIVIDUAL applications submitted directly by the applicant to an IIE-hosted portal. There is no Grants.gov, no SAM.gov/UEI, no eRA-style institutional sign-off, and no sponsored-projects office in the path. • U.S. STUDENT: https://apply.iie.org/fulbrightusstudent — "All applicants must complete and submit their applications via the Fulbright Online Application." Enrolled students must additionally be attached to their campus Fulbright Program Adviser (FPA) and mark the application "Ready for Campus Review" by the campus deadline, but the funder is explicit that the FPA does not submit for you: "You are responsible for submitting your own application before the National Deadline; your Fulbright Program Adviser cannot do this on your behalf." Applicants without an FPA apply At-Large and "are at no disadvantage during the selection process". • U.S. SCHOLAR: a year-stamped link — https://apply.iie.org/fusc2027 for the 2027-2028 competition (2026-2027 was https://apply.iie.org/fusc2026); fallback https://apply.iie.org/fulbrightusscholar. THE HIDDEN ACCOUNT TRAP: "If you started an application and/or applied in 2019 or later ... then you already have an application account. Do NOT create a new account." Changed email? Write to Scholars@iie.org rather than opening a second account — and there is an upside to the single account: "by using the same account for your application, some of the fields from your prior application can be filled in automatically in your new application." Applicants from the 2019-20 competition or earlier DO need a new account. • SPECIALIST: World Learning's portal, reached from fulbrightspecialist.worldlearning.org. • NON-U.S. APPLICANTS: no central portal — you "submit ... to the Fulbright Commissions/Foundations or U.S. Embassy in your home country". THE ACTUAL LONG-LEAD ITEMS ARE NOT THE ACCOUNT: (a) the host-institution letter of invitation/affiliation, solicited from a foreign colleague months ahead and, on the Scholar side, fatal if late for awards that require it; (b) recommenders must be REGISTERED in the system before you submit and upload directly — "Letters submitted outside the online system will not be accepted", and on the Scholar side "All applications require two recommendations. Additional letters will not be accepted"; (c) the foreign language evaluator, also registered in-system, who may not be the same person as a recommender or your invitation writer.
result.deadline_structure: Fixed annual dates (except Specialist, which is rolling) — and these ARE genuinely standing dates worth printing, which is why I am giving them rather than hedging to "per-solicitation". • FULBRIGHT U.S. SCHOLAR — SEPTEMBER 15, 5:00 PM EASTERN, EVERY YEAR. Verified across three separate cycles from the funder's own documents: 2024-2025 checklist "Deadline: September 15, 2023"; 2026-2027 instructions "Monday, September 15, 2025, 5:00 PM Eastern (-4:00 UTC)"; 2027-2028 award pages "September 15, 2026, 5:00 PM EDT (UTC -4:00)". The competition and Catalog of Awards open the preceding FEBRUARY (the FY26 administrative roadmap shows the 2027-2028 catalogue and application launching 2/2/2026). Recommendation letters and external language evaluations are due AT THE SAME MOMENT as the application, not later: "This includes Recommendation Letters and External Language Evaluations." The invitation letter has its own, later deadline — September 25, 5:00 PM Eastern for both 2026-2027 and 2027-2028 — but this one HAS drifted (the 2024-2025 checklist said September 30), so read the current instructions. IEA awards are the exception: "*Varying deadlines for IEA programs." • FULBRIGHT U.S. STUDENT — an early-October TUESDAY at 5 pm ET. 2027-2028 cycle: "Tuesday October 6, 2026 at 5 pm Eastern Time"; the cycle opened 31 March 2026. The date is re-announced each spring and has moved by a week or so between cycles, so treat "first-or-second Tuesday of October, 5 pm ET" as the recurring shape and the printed date as the year's fact. THE DEADLINE THAT ACTUALLY BINDS AN ENROLLED STUDENT IS EARLIER AND IS NOT PUBLISHED CENTRALLY: the campus deadline set by your own FPA, "typically 4-6 weeks earlier than the final October deadline" — i.e. late August to mid-September. • FULBRIGHT SPECIALIST — rolling: "Applications are accepted throughout the year", with "Peer review panels evaluate applications to join the Fulbright Specialist Program approximately every eight weeks." • FOREIGN STUDENT / VISITING SCHOLAR (non-U.S.) — per country, no central calendar: applicants "submit their Fulbright application and provide all supporting documents to their respective Fulbright office per established country/award deadlines." • Hard rules attached to every deadline: one award per competition only; no deferral to a future year; and no unsubmitting — "Once you submit, you CANNOT make changes to your application" / "Applications cannot be unsubmitted for any reason." Technical trouble is not grounds for an extension.

review_stages.stage: SCHOLAR — discipline-based Peer Review Committees read independently, then meet virtually; ~20-30 applications per committee, all reviewers read all assigned applications; committees are U.S.-based academics and professionals including Fulbright alumni
review_stages.timing: "Early October: Peer Reviewers access applications and begin reviewing"; "Mid-October through mid-November: Peer Review committee meetings are held virtually" (FY26 actuals: 17 Oct 2025 – 24 Nov 2025) = deadline +1 to +2 months

review_stages.stage: SCHOLAR — peer review decision letter: recommended / not recommended, delivered as a Decision Letter on your application Status page
review_stages.timing: December — FY26 roadmap due date 16 Dec 2025 = deadline +3 months

review_stages.timing: December (FY26 due 19 Dec 2025) = deadline +3 months

review_stages.stage: SCHOLAR — host-country review: Commission/Post make the actual selections; not all recommended applications are selected
review_stages.timing: December–May; FY26 Commission/Post selections due 13 Feb 2026 = deadline +3 to +8 months

review_stages.stage: STUDENT — National Screening Committee panels: "Applications are reviewed by National Screening Committee panels. Reviewers on the NSC are full-time faculty members"

review_stages.timing: Panels approximately every 8 weeks; roster tenure 3 years

result.months_submission_to_award: SCHOLAR: ~3 months to the peer-review yes/no (15 Sept → mid-December decision letter); ~5-9 months to the final select/alternate/non-select letter (February through June); ~12 months to a typical grant start the following academic year, with an outer bound of "no later than June 1" roughly 20 months after submission. STUDENT: ~3.5 months to recommended/non-recommended (6 Oct → end of January); ~5-8 months to the final result (March–June, rolling); grant start usually the following academic year, so ~9-12 months from submission, though "Grant lengths and dates vary by award" and some ETAs start earlier in the summer. SPECIALIST: ~2-3 months to a roster decision (panels every 8 weeks), then an open-ended wait for a project match inside a 3-year roster tenure. PLANNING RULE OF THUMB: about 12 months from submission to departure, and about 18 months from "I should look into this" to departure — because the host-institution invitation, the language evaluation and (for students) the campus committee each need a season of their own before the portal deadline.
result.resubmission_policy: THIS IS WHERE FULBRIGHT DIVERGES MOST SHARPLY FROM NIH: reapplying is allowed and common, but there is NO RESUBMISSION MECHANISM AT ALL — no A1 designation, no Introduction to Resubmission page, no response-to-reviewers, no resubmission-specific deadline, and no page allowance for any of it. Each year's application is a fresh application judged on its own: "Applications are reviewed individually, on their own merit each year." There is no stated cap on how many times you may reapply so long as you remain eligible, and the funder describes both routes as normal — some applicants "choose to revise and strengthen their prior proposal; others opt to propose an entirely new project." A REAPPLICANT IS FLYING BLIND BY DESIGN: "IIE cannot give applicants the specific reasons for selection or non-selection." No reviewer comments, no score, no summary statement. The only substitutes are a conversation with the regional program officer and, for students, your campus adviser and committee. MECHANICAL HELP FOR REAPPLICANTS: log into the same Slate account — prior-year fields can prefill the new application ("just be sure to check them over in case any details have changed"). PRIOR-GRANTEE RULES DIFFER BY PROGRAMME. Scholar: a hard wait — "If I had a prior Fulbright Scholar award, it ended at least two years before the application deadline" — plus a standing thumb on the scale, "Preference will be given to candidates who have not had previous Fulbright Scholar awards." Student: no mandatory wait but an explicit handicap — "there is a program preference for those who have not previously held a Fulbright grant. For the 2027-2028 competition, 2026-2027, 2025-2026, and 2024-2025 participants will be at a competitive disadvantage, but are still eligible to apply, provided they continue to meet all other eligibility requirements." Specialist: the only numeric cap in the system — "you may apply to join the Fulbright Specialist Roster up to two times in a 12 month period", and "If you were not approved following your second application, you will be eligible to reapply 12 months after receiving notification that your second application was not approved." ALSO BINDING WITHIN A CYCLE: "Applicants may apply only for one award per application cycle", applications cannot be deferred to a future year, and submission is irreversible.
result.page_limits: THE TWO PROGRAMMES MEASURE IN DIFFERENT UNITS, AND OLD ADVICE IS THE MAIN HAZARD. SCHOLAR = PAGES (PDF uploads; the portal counts pages and blocks you — "If any files exceed the stated page limit, a warning will only appear on the Review page (at the end of the application). You will not be able to submit your application until a shorter document is uploaded"): Project Statement "no more than 5 pages" (guidance elsewhere describes 3-5 pages, single-spaced, 12-point, 1-inch margins — the 5-page cap is the enforced number); Bibliography/Reference List "no more than 3 pages", required only if your award activity is Research or Teaching/Research and "Not accepted for: Teaching or Professional Project"; Syllabi/Course Outlines "no more than ten pages in total", required only for Teaching or Teaching/Research; CV/Résumé required for all, with a page limit the checklist refers to but does not number ("I tailored my CV/Resume to the award ... and stayed within the page limit") — a search-index snapshot of the application-instructions page reports 6 pages, which I could NOT verify on the funder's page this session (see unresolved); Digital Portfolio for creative/performing arts or journalism "maximum 10 images, 15 pages in length, and/or 30 minutes of audiovisual files". Scholar short essays are character-limited text boxes in the form: Country Selection, Career Trajectory and Cultural Preparation for everyone, plus Teaching Preparation for teaching awards. STUDENT = CHARACTERS, WITH NO PAGE LIMITS ANYWHERE — anyone working from pre-2023 advice about "two single-spaced pages" will write the wrong document: Statement of Grant Purpose "limited to 6,000 characters in length including spaces and punctuation" for Study/Research, "limited to 3,000 characters" for ETA; abstract/summary 1,750 characters; project title 90 characters. THE PERSONAL STATEMENT NO LONGER EXISTS — it was replaced by three short answers: "Flexibility & Adaptability (2,000 character limit)", "Community Engagement (2,000 character limit)", "Impact of Fulbright Award (1,000 character limit)". The Statement of Grant Purpose admits no bibliography, citations, links or personal contact information. Character counts include spaces, punctuation and paragraph breaks; the funder warns against hard returns, which can truncate text in the fixed-space PDF proof even when you are under the limit — preview the proof before submitting.

result.program_officer_norms: EXPECTED AND INVITED — Fulbright sits at the NIH end of this spectrum, not the foundation end, and names the officer for you. SCHOLAR SIDE: the official FAQ states plainly that "The responsible program officer is a good point of contact for discussions of how to shape a competitive application", and the programme offers to "connect with you to help you identify an appropriate Fulbright award and to strengthen your application." Officers are reached through published REGIONAL inboxes rather than named individuals: subsaharanafrica@iie.org, eastasiapacific@iie.org, europeeurasia@iie.org, middleeastnorthafrica@iie.org, southcentralasia@iie.org, westhem@iie.org; specialist tracks at IEA@iie.org, Arctic@iie.org, amazonia@iie.org; general Scholars@iie.org; IIE, 1350 Eye St NW, Washington DC 20005, 202.686.4000. TIMING: the useful window opens when the Catalog of Awards launches in February and effectively closes in mid-August — you contact them while you can still CHANGE AWARD, not while you are polishing prose. WHAT EXPERIENCED APPLICANTS ACTUALLY ASK: is my project coded to the right activity (Research vs Teaching/Research vs Professional Project) and discipline for this award; does this country expect a letter of invitation, forbid one, or merely tolerate one, and how substantive must it be; am I a Scholar, Postdoctoral or Distinguished candidate; how competitive is this specific award and would a neighbouring country be a better bet; can the dates and grant length flex around my teaching term; is the host's appetite this year for teaching or for research. WHAT THEY WILL NOT DO: pre-review your draft, and — after the fact — "IIE cannot give applicants the specific reasons for selection or non-selection." STUDENT SIDE — THE NORM INVERTS: your first call is not the funder. It is your campus Fulbright Program Adviser, whose documented job is to "provide accurate information and guidance to prospective applicants" and to help "preparing their application materials, including essays, securing a language evaluation (if applicable), and determining strong recommendation writers", then to run a campus interview and upload a Campus Committee Evaluation "designed to provide constructive feedback to applicants about their proposal, as well as giving insight to the National Screening Committee (NSC) about the candidate." Find yours at us.fulbrightonline.org/applicants/search-for-a-fulbright-program-adviser. IIE itself takes general questions at FBstudent@iie.org / 1-800-272-6994 (9am-5pm ET) and country questions at FBstudent.EAP@iie.org, .EUR@, .MENA@, .SCA@, .AF@, .WHA@iie.org, plus FBstudent.fogarty@ and FBstudent.natgeo@. No FPA on your campus? Apply At-Large — the funder states At-Large applicants "are at no disadvantage during the selection process and are regularly selected to receive Fulbright grants." A third sanctioned channel on both sides is the alumni network: Alumni Ambassadors exist for "sharing firsthand Fulbright experiences and advice to potential applicants, providing information on creating Fulbright projects", bookable through fbstudent@iie.org.
result.funded_examples_source: FULBRIGHT PUBLISHES GRANTEES, NOT APPLICATIONS — there is no RePORTER-style database of abstracts plus summary statements, and no public archive of funded application texts. What does exist, in descending order of usefulness: (1) FULBRIGHT SCHOLAR DIRECTORY — https://fulbrightscholars.org/fulbright-scholar-directory — more than 50,000 past U.S. Scholar and Visiting Scholar grantees, filterable by name/keyword, home institution, host institution, discipline, program country, academic year and program type (U.S. Scholar, Visiting Scholar, Scholar-in-Residence, Arctic Initiative, Amazonia, Nexus, Public Policy Fellowship). The funder tells you outright to mine it for both models and contacts: "Fulbright U.S. Scholar applicants are encouraged to use the filters below to search for relevant past Fulbright projects and participants to learn more about the in-country experience and solicit contacts for potential host institutions." Titles and short project descriptions only, not full statements, and "Contact information is not provided within the directory, but most contacts are readily searchable online" — which is precisely how people find a prospective host to ask for an invitation letter. (2) FULBRIGHT U.S. STUDENT GRANTEE DIRECTORY — https://us.fulbrightonline.org/alumni/grantee-directory — filterable by U.S. institution, host country, year (1949–2025), field of study and state. (3) Fulbright Scholar List Archive — https://fulbrightscholars.org/fulbright-scholar-list-archive — annual grantee lists (403 to a plain fetch this session; listed in the search index, contents unverified). (4) PRE-2006 SCHOLARS — University of Arkansas Special Collections digitised directories, https://libraries.uark.edu/specialcollections/fulbrightdirectories/ — U.S. Fulbright Scholars 1948-2002 and Visiting Scholars to the U.S. 1950-1987, where "The descriptive information for each scholar is arranged according to academic discipline"; note the caution that OCR "may fail to capture all text". (5) A third-party aggregator, HAPRI's grantee finder at fulbright.hapri.org/find-a-grantee/, surfaced by the search index and not verified this session. (6) FULL SUCCESSFUL ESSAYS: the Scholar site carries a page titled "Project Statement Examples" at https://fulbrightscholars.org/us-scholar-awards/project-statement-examples — it is indexed by search engines but returned 403 to a plain fetch AND "You are not authorized to access this page" in a rendering browser during this session, so I cannot confirm what it holds or whether it is gated. THE RELIABLE ROUTE TO REAL WINNING ESSAYS IS LOCAL, NOT NATIONAL: campus fellowships offices and FPAs typically keep an archive of past winners' Statements of Grant Purpose and project statements and will share them with their own applicants — one of the concrete reasons to go through the campus process even though At-Large carries no penalty. Alumni Ambassadors and directory-identified past grantees in your own subfield are the other route, and the funder endorses contacting them.

result.funder_system:
HOWARD HUGHES MEDICAL INSTITUTE (HHMI) — a private operating foundation, not a grant-making agency in the federal sense. Machinery facts a first-time applicant needs:

(1) HHMI funds PEOPLE, NOT PROJECTS. Applicant Guide, verbatim: "Both programs reflect HHMI's philosophy of supporting 'people, not projects.'" There are no RFAs, no unsolicited proposals, no rolling submissions, and no project budgets to negotiate. FAQ [C4], verbatim: "All Scholars receive the same HHMI lab budget, regardless of their lab size or research program"; salary "is determined by HHMI's salary scale for lab heads, which is non-negotiable."

(2) MOST AWARDS ARE EMPLOYMENT, NOT GRANTS. Investigators and Freeman Hrabowski Scholars become HHMI employees while keeping their faculty appointment and lab at the host institution (a host "collaboration agreement" between HHMI and the university is required). Hanna Gray Fellows are "HHMI-employed postdoctoral scientists or HHMI grantees, depending on the circumstances." Consequence: HHMI's forms are part job application, part grant — accommodations under the ADA are handled by an HR director (metelskiy@hhmi.org), and IP is owned by HHMI as employer ([J1]).

(3) EVERYTHING RUNS THROUGH ONE PORTAL AND ONE MACHINERY. All five current science competitions use the same ARC portal, the same eligibility-questionnaire gate, the same no-journal-names rule, the same "no feedback ever" policy, and the same applicant-submits-personally rule. Learn it once and it transfers across career stages.

(4) THE FIVE CURRENT COMPETITIONS (announced together; hhmi.org/programs, /programs/open-competitions):
 • Cech Fellows — undergraduates (rising juniors/seniors), summer research, up to 200 fellows, up to $15,000 over nine weeks; annual.
 • Gilliam Fellows — 2nd/3rd-year PhD and dual-degree students applying jointly with their PhD advisor; up to 80 fellows; $65,000/yr up to 3 years (+$5,000 discretionary allowance, institutional allowance); annual; postdoc phase (~40/yr) by later internal competition.
 • Hanna H. Gray Fellows — postdocs (≤7 yrs postdoc); up to 2 years postdoc support then conversion to Scholar on landing a qualifying faculty job; biennial.
 • Freeman Hrabowski Scholars — early-career faculty (≤7 yrs as lab head); up to $10M over 10 years, full salary + $500k/yr research budget (then $600k/yr); biennial. From the 2028 cycle, HGF and FHS are ONE combined competition selecting up to 50 scientists.
 • HHMI Investigator — mid-career/senior faculty (≥7 yrs lab head + an active nationally competitive non-training grant of ≥3 yrs); ~$11M over an initial 7-year renewable term; up to 40 selected; "Every 5 years" per hhmi.org/programs/investigators.
 Janelia Research Campus is separate machinery: Group Leader posts are HIRING through janelia.org careers (5-year renewable appointments, advertised deadlines e.g. Nov 4 and Feb 3), not a grant competition.

(5) ELIGIBLE-INSTITUTION GATE (the most common silent disqualifier). Only researchers at institutions on HHMI's published list may apply — 364 institutions listed at hhmi.org/programs/eligible-institutions as counted on 2026-09-18. Institutions can be added on request (scienceprograms@hhmi.org; for the 2028 FHS/HGF cycle the FAQ [B8] says write to FHS@hhmi.org after September 15, 2026 and "We will evaluate your institution for potential inclusion on the list and notify you before the application window opens on November 3, 2026").

(6) SCOPE GATE. HHMI funds basic biological/biomedical mechanism-driven research. FAQ [A1] explicitly excludes: clinical research focused on patient outcomes; purely translational/therapeutic or diagnostic work; epidemiology, health disparities, health services; applied biotech/agriculture; environmental or climate science; observational ecology/animal behavior; and "computational or theoretical research that is not grounded in actual biological data collected experimentally."

(7) AI NOTE (new, from the 2028 Components documents, verbatim): "AI-assisted tools may be used during application review, including to help assess scientific scope and fit with scientific disciplines that HHMI supports. All applications are read by one or more human reviewers, who are responsible for all final decisions."

(8) WHAT HHMI NO LONGER RUNS: the science-education grant line (Inclusive Excellence 3, ~$60M to 104 institutions) was terminated abruptly in February 2025 (reported by Science and STAT). There is currently no open institutional/education grant competition — HHMI's open competitions are all individual-scientist competitions.

DATED DEADLINES ARE SAFE TO PUBLISH FOR THIS FUNDER, with an "as of" marker: HHMI publishes exact dates AND times in its own Applicant Guides, Components documents and program pages, each carrying a "Last Updated" line (2028 FHS/HGF Applicant Guide: "Last Updated September 3, 2026"; 2027 Gilliam FAQ: "Last updated: August 17, 2026"). All dates below are as published on 2026-09-18.
result.submission_portal:
HHMI APPLICATION AND REVIEW CHANNEL ("ARC") — https://arc.hhmi.org/login (register: https://arc.hhmi.org/register). One portal for every HHMI science competition (the 2024 Investigator competition also lived there: arc.hhmi.org/applicant/application/inv2024). There is NO Grants.gov, NO eRA Commons, NO ProposalCentral, and no institutional sponsored-programs routing.

LONG-LEAD ITEMS, in the order they bite:

1. ORCID iD — REQUIRED BEFORE YOU CAN EVEN CREATE AN ACCOUNT. 2028 Components doc, verbatim: "To access the application, you must log in to the HHMI Application and Review Channel (ARC) website: https://arc.hhmi.org/login. If you do not have an account, you may create one by clicking on the Register now link. Prior to creating an account, all users will need to have an ORCID identifier." Verified directly on 2026-09-18 by loading the register form in a browser (plain fetch returns only a JS shell): the fields are First Name, Last Name, ORCID Identifier, Username, Email, New Password. (HHMI staff log in via OKTA; external applicants use the Register route.)

2. ELIGIBILITY QUESTIONNAIRE GATE — you cannot open the application until ARC has deemed you eligible. For the 2028 FHS/HGF cycle the questionnaire went live September 15, 2026, seven weeks before the application itself opened (November 3, 2026). FAQ [B1]: you may not begin "until you have completed this questionnaire and have been deemed eligible." Gilliam works the same way from the day the window opens.

3. INSTITUTION ON THE ELIGIBLE LIST — check https://www.hhmi.org/programs/eligible-institutions (364 institutions on 2026-09-18). If yours is absent, the request must go in BEFORE the window opens (FHS/HGF 2028: write to FHS@hhmi.org after September 15, 2026; general route scienceprograms@hhmi.org).

4. THE APPLICANT SUBMITS PERSONALLY — no grants office, no dean's sign-off, no nomination. FAQ [C3], verbatim: "The application needs to be prepared and submitted by the applicant." FAQ [F1]: "HHMI does not require nominations or evidence of institutional approval at the time you apply." (Institutional delegates cannot prepare or submit.) Gilliam FAQ [C2]: "Institutional grants offices are not involved in preparing or submitting Gilliam applications."

5. THIRD PARTIES GET THEIR OWN ARC LOGINS, TRIGGERED BY YOU. Hanna Gray: you enter your mentor's details and click "Notify"; ARC emails the mentor a login; the mentor must submit questionnaire answers plus a CV or NIH Biosketch by January 5, 2027 (i.e. 3 weeks AFTER the applicant deadline). ARC shows you whether they have submitted. Gilliam: the student is lead applicant and enters the PhD advisor plus one additional reference, who submit through ARC directly; "You are responsible for reminding them to submit by the deadline."

6. FILE MECHANICS — uploads are PDFs; HHMI recommends files not exceed 30 MB each "to avoid errors that may cause your application to show up as incomplete." Technical support: ARCsupport@hhmi.org (this is the address printed in HHMI's own 2028 Components PDFs; a rendered fetch of the HTML FAQ showed a variant "hhmi-arc-support@hhmi.org" that I could not confirm in any HHMI PDF — use the PDF address). Programmatic questions: FHS@hhmi.org / gilliam@hhmi.org / CechFellows@hhmi.org.

7. NOTHING CAN BE CHANGED AFTER THE DEADLINE. FAQ [D1], verbatim: "We do not permit changes to any of the components of the application after the deadline, including the bibliography." Only employment-status changes are reportable.

TOOLING NOTE (not a finding about the programme): www.hhmi.org PDFs and most programme pages fetch fine, but the scientist directory (https://www.hhmi.org/scientists, which redirects to /search/people) sits behind a Cloudflare JS challenge and returned 403 to a plain fetch and a challenge page in a rendering browser; researchfunding.duke.edu is behind bot protection; web.archive.org is unavailable to this tool. Where I could not reach HHMI's own page (the retired 2024 Investigator program announcement PDF now redirects to the programme page), I say so in the relevant field.
result.deadline_structure:
NO STANDARD RECURRING DUE DATES (nothing resembling NIH's Feb 5 / Jun 5 / Oct 5 grid). Each HHMI competition is a fixed, one-shot window announced per cycle, with an exact opening time (9:00 AM ET) and closing time (11:59 PM ET). Between windows there is NO way to apply — HHMI does not accept unsolicited applications. Cadence per hhmi.org/programs: Gilliam annual; Cech Fellows annual; Freeman Hrabowski Scholars + Hanna Gray Fellows biennial (combined into one competition from the 2028 cycle); HHMI Investigator "Every 5 years."

GILLIAM FELLOWS — 2027 competition (PhD students + advisor)
 • Applications open: Tuesday, September 1, 2026, 9:00 AM ET — ALREADY OPEN
 • Applications close: Tuesday, October 27, 2026, 11:59 PM ET
 • Award notification: Summer 2027 | Fellowship term begins: September 1, 2027

FREEMAN HRABOWSKI SCHOLARS + HANNA H. GRAY FELLOWS — combined 2028 competition

CECH FELLOWS — 2027 summer programme (undergraduates)

HHMI INVESTIGATOR — next competition

JANELIA GROUP LEADER (hiring, not a grant): advertised annual calls with fixed deadlines (recent calls closed November 4 and February 3); apply through janelia.org careers.

EXTENSIONS: FAQ [C2], verbatim: "The application window will close on December 15, 2026, at 11:59 pm ET. Deadline extensions will be considered only under exceptional circumstances," with HHMI "strongly" encouraging early submission. Treat the closing time as hard.

PLANNING RULE OF THUMB: because windows are 6–8 weeks long and open on a published date, the real planning trigger is the eligibility-questionnaire date (≈6–8 weeks before the window opens), not the deadline.

result.months_submission_to_award:
Freeman Hrabowski Scholars / Hanna Gray Fellows (2028 cycle): 8 months deadline→first status notification (Dec 15, 2026 → Aug 2027); 14 months deadline→selection (→ Feb 2028); 17–20 months deadline→money/appointment start (May 1–Aug 31, 2028). Add the 2-month questionnaire lead-in and the real span from "decide to apply" to "paid" is ~20–23 months.
Gilliam Fellows (2027 cycle): ~9 months deadline→notification (Oct 27, 2026 → Summer 2027); ~10 months deadline→term start (Sept 1, 2027).
Cech Fellows (2027): ~3 months close→finalist notification; ~6 months close→programme start.
HHMI Investigator (2024 cycle, measured from published dates): ~7.5 months→semifinalist; ~12 months→symposium; ~12.5 months→finalist selection; ~16 months→public announcement; ~17.5 months→appointment start. The window itself is ~5 months long (Sept 28, 2027 – Mar 7, 2028 for the next cycle), so budget roughly 2 years from "competition opens" to "first HHMI salary" for the Investigator route.
Comparison point for planning: an NIH R01 runs ~9–10 months submission→award; every HHMI route is longer, and there is no second submission window inside the same year.
result.resubmission_policy:
REAPPLICATION IS UNLIMITED, BUT THERE IS NO "RESUBMISSION" IN THE NIH SENSE — no A1, no Introduction page, no response-to-reviewers, no marking of the application as a resubmission, and nothing to respond to because HHMI never releases critiques.

• 2028 FHS/HGF FAQ [B9], verbatim: "Yes. There is no limit to the number of times you can apply, and we encourage you to reapply as long as you continue to meet the eligibility requirements for the program you are applying to. A number of current Hanna Gray Fellows and Freeman Hrabowski Scholars applied multiple times before being selected."
• 2027 Gilliam FAQ [B8], verbatim: previous applicants may re-apply "as long as they still meet all other eligibility criteria -- in particular, they must not be beyond their third year of graduate school. Returning applicants are reviewed and evaluated the same as first-time applicants." (Explicitly: no credit, and no penalty, for having applied before.)
• NO FEEDBACK EVER. FAQ [E7], verbatim: "No. Regardless of the outcome, you will not receive any written comments or scores on applications submitted for this competition." Gilliam [D6]: no individual feedback, due to volume. There are no summary statements, no percentile, no scores.
• NO POST-DEADLINE EDITS: [D1] "We do not permit changes to any of the components of the application after the deadline, including the bibliography."

THE REAL LIMIT IS THE ELIGIBILITY CLOCK, NOT A RESUBMISSION RULE:
 – Gilliam: you must still be in year 2 or 3 of the PhD at the application close date, so most students get at most two shots.
 – Hanna Gray: ≤7 years of postdoctoral experience as of the deadline (gaps between research positions count; time between doctorate and first postdoc does not).
 – Freeman Hrabowski: ≤7 years in any independent post-training position as of the deadline (for the 2028 cycle: first independent position started on or after December 15, 2019).
 – Because FHS/HGF are biennial and Investigator is every ~5 years, "reapply next round" means 2 or 5 years later.
 – CLOCK EXTENSIONS EXIST AND ARE THE THING TO ASK ABOUT: FAQ [B14] allows exceptions to the 7-year window for military service, family leave or medical leave that produced an official employment leave or tenure-clock extension DURING the window. Leaves before the first position, and generic COVID extensions, do not qualify. Requests go to Yury Metelski (yury.metelski@hhmi.org — the Components documents give metelskiy@hhmi.org) with official documentation, submitted after September 15, 2026 for the 2028 cycle.
 – Current Hanna Gray Fellows who want the new (2028) terms must reapply, be selected, and forfeit the remainder of their existing fellowship ([B-HGF7]).
 – Multiple applicants from one lab or institution are allowed, with no cap ([B12]).
result.page_limits:
RULES THAT APPLY TO EVERY HHMI APPLICATION:
• NO JOURNAL NAMES ANYWHERE. Verbatim (2028 Components + Guide): "HHMI evaluates scientific merit independently of where work is or will be published. Accordingly, journal names should not appear anywhere in your written materials. This includes references to journals in the context of submission status, revision, or acceptance. Inclusion of journal names is a violation of competition guidelines and will be taken into account in the evaluation of your application." Journal branding visible inside an uploaded article PDF needs no redaction.
• CITATION FORMAT: "Full author list. Title of article. (Year) PMID." Use a DOI for preprints or anything not in PubMed. Preprints (bioRxiv, medRxiv, chemRxiv, arXiv) "count" equally with peer-reviewed papers.
• Reference lists are NOT counted inside the page limit.

FREEMAN HRABOWSKI SCHOLARS + HANNA GRAY FELLOWS, 2028 cycle (from HHMI's own "Components of the Application" PDFs, dated 2026-09):
 • Research Program Description — ONE PDF; "Text, figures, and figure legends must fit within 5 pages in total. The reference list with full citations is not included in this 5-page limit." Figures embedded, each with a legend; figure text ≥10-point; single-spaced; minimum 0.5-inch margins all sides; Arial 11-point text, Arial 10-point legends; cite your significant articles in the body and HIGHLIGHT THOSE CITATIONS IN YELLOW (and in the reference list); file ≤30 MB. Verbatim warning: "If your document does not follow these formatting instructions, your application may not be considered." Structure guidance: not specific aims — "outline the themes, directions, and approaches you will follow," 5–10 year horizon.
 • Research program structured abstract — Background (100 words) + Goals (100 words) + Approach (100 words). Do not repeat it inside the 5-page description.
 • Scientific vision — three questions, 150 words each: what makes the questions compelling/unique; why you are well-suited; how success transforms the field.
 • Hanna Gray adds career-development questions at 150 words each, including "How is your planned research program distinct from that of your postdoctoral mentor?"
 • Leadership/mentoring narratives — 400 words per question (five questions for FHS; equivalents for HGF), covering lessons that shape you as a lab leader, conflict/difficult situations, practices you have established, and the leader you intend to be.
 • Prior research accomplishments — up to 3 records, 250 words each (challenges, significance, your specific contribution); publications not required for a record.
 • Significant articles — FHS: 5 articles if ≥4 years as a lab head at the deadline, 3 if <4 years or lab not yet started; HGF: 1–3 articles. First/co-first/corresponding/co-corresponding authorship only; review articles excluded; each with a 250-word significance statement in your own words, plus author list, the article's abstract copied verbatim, and the article PDF.
 • Optional explanatory notes for gaps in education/training/employment — 100 words each.
 • Bibliography of primary research articles (preprints + peer-reviewed); education/training/employment history; past and current research support; academic/professional service.
 • NO LETTERS OF RECOMMENDATION. FAQ [C8], verbatim: "We are not collecting academic letters of recommendation for this competition." (HGF instead collects a mentor questionnaire + mentor CV/NIH Biosketch, due Jan 5, 2027.)

GILLIAM FELLOWS, 2027 cycle:
 • PhD research overview — 3 pages MAXIMUM including figures; citations uploaded separately and not counted. FAQ [C7], verbatim: "the 3-page limit is intentional… Gilliam applications are reviewed by scientists, but likely not by experts in your specific field."
 • Up to 5 "contributions to science" (may include papers, presentations, and service activities).
 • Leadership responses, career statement, and a JOINT student+advisor conflict-resolution statement.
 • PhD advisor: letter of support limited to 2 pages, plus academic background, relevant articles, current research support, mentoring plan, healthy-research-environment statement.
 • One additional reference letter (not the advisor; a co-advisor may serve).
 • No transcripts required.

HHMI INVESTIGATOR — the 2028 guide is NOT yet published (the competition opens September 28, 2027) and HHMI's 2024 program-announcement PDF now redirects to the programme page. Best available vintage figures, from a 2021-cycle announcement republished by a university research office (research.jhu.edu), so treat as indicative, not current: summary of major research contributions 250 words; abstract of the research programme 300 words; description of ongoing and planned research programme 3,000 words, may include up to one page of figures plus essential references; five selected articles with a significance/impact paragraph each; bibliography, current support, education and training. HHMI's current Investigator page states "Recommendation letters: None required."

result.program_officer_norms:
HHMI HAS NO PROGRAM OFFICERS. There is no NIH-style PO relationship: no one to pitch an idea to, no pre-submission concept review, no scientific advice, no "is this responsive?" conversation, and no advocate inside the review. Contact is with a programme-staff mailbox, and it is for eligibility and process only.

WHO YOU ACTUALLY WRITE TO (addresses taken verbatim from HHMI's own PDFs/pages):
 • FHS@hhmi.org — Freeman Hrabowski Scholars + Hanna Gray Fellows programme staff ("Address any questions to HHMI program staff at FHS@hhmi.org"); also the route for institution-eligibility requests in that cycle.
 • gilliam@hhmi.org — Gilliam Fellows.
 • CechFellows@hhmi.org — Cech Fellows (address obfuscated on the page; decoded from the page's own Cloudflare email-protection data).
 • ARCsupport@hhmi.org — portal/technical problems only.
 • yury.metelski@hhmi.org / metelskiy@hhmi.org (Senior Director, HR Transformation) — ADA accommodations for the application process AND requests to extend the 7-year eligibility window for military/family/medical leave.
 • scienceprograms@hhmi.org — to ask that an institution be added to the eligible list.

WHAT THEY WILL AND WILL NOT ANSWER:
 • WILL: whether your institution can be made eligible (and by when); whether a specific position counts as "post-training" or as a mentored postdoc (FAQ [B-FHS2], verbatim: "If you are unsure if your current or former position meets this definition, contact us at FHS@hhmi.org, and we will answer your questions."); whether a leave qualifies for a clock exception; whether another grant/fellowship is compatible; eligibility questions left open after the questionnaire ([B1]).
 • WILL NOT: pre-screen your science. 2027 Gilliam FAQ [B2], verbatim: "We do not provide specific determinations about research eligibility for potential applicants outside of the application review process." Judge scope yourself against hhmi.org/programs/science-we-support and FAQ [A1].
 • WILL NOT: give feedback, scores or comments, before or after ([E7]).
 • EXPLICIT PROHIBITION for undergraduates — Cech Fellows page, verbatim: "Please do not reach out to desired labs or lab heads about your application" (HHMI matches students to labs).
 • Reviewer identities are not disclosed, and requests to exclude a reviewer are "considered only in extraordinary circumstances" ([E4]).

BEST TIMING, WHICH IS THE PART PEOPLE GET WRONG:
 • Institution-eligibility question: BEFORE the window opens — for the 2028 cycle, after September 15, 2026, with HHMI promising an answer before November 3, 2026.
 • Eligibility-clock exception: from September 15, 2026, with documentation, well before December 15, 2026.
 • Incompatible-award question (e.g. you just won an NIH K or an NSF GRFP): HHMI directs you to write in August 2027, when statuses are announced ([B13a]).
 • Technical/portal problems: days before the deadline, not hours — "HHMI strongly encourages applicants to apply early."

WHAT SUBSTITUTES FOR A PROGRAM OFFICER, AND IS WHERE EXPERIENCED APPLICANTS GET THEIR REAL GUIDANCE:
 1. HHMI's own applicant webinars — "Becoming an HHMI Scientist (for Potential Program Applicants)" (recording on HHMI's YouTube channel, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DUFxec5-YL4; also run through the Genetics Society of America), and competition-specific sessions such as HHMI's virtual information session for the 2024 Investigator competition (recording hosted on HHMI's Panopto).
 2. The FAQ + Applicant Guide + "Components of the Application" PDFs — the Components documents reproduce every field, word limit and tooltip, and are effectively the missing PO conversation; read them before drafting.
 3. YOUR UNIVERSITY'S FOUNDATION RELATIONS / RESEARCH DEVELOPMENT OFFICE — this is the person to actually talk to. Examples on the public record: Johns Hopkins ran an internal HHMI Investigator feedback committee of senior faculty (statement of interest by Jan 22, internal materials by Feb 7, five weeks before HHMI's deadline); Caltech asks applicants to notify Foundation Relations and the Provost's office ("We are here to help ensure that Caltech's proposals are competitive"); Ohio State runs HHMI Investigator Program information sessions.
 4. Current HHMI Investigators, Scholars and Fellows at your institution — HHMI's directory and news releases identify them by name and institution, and HHMI states explicitly that no prior HHMI connection is needed to be competitive ([B10]).
 5. Your mentor/advisor is a formal part of the application (HGF mentor questionnaire; Gilliam advisor materials and mandatory mentorship course), so the "who to talk to" conversation with them must start before you apply, not after.
result.funded_examples_source:
THERE IS NO PUBLIC HHMI EQUIVALENT OF NIH RePORTER: no searchable abstract database of funded applications, no summary statements, no released critiques ([E7]). What does exist, in descending order of usefulness:

1. REDACTED REAL APPLICATIONS INSIDE ARC — the single most valuable resource, and almost nobody outside knows it exists. 2028 FHS/HGF FAQ [C5], verbatim: "Once you begin to complete your application in HHMI's Application and Review Channel (ARC) website, after you verify you are eligible (see question B1), you will also be able to review examples from previous competitions. Note that these examples include redactions and might follow different formatting requirements, so they are shared only for general guidance." The Components document repeats: "You may consult the example applications from prior competitions for general guidance of what we are looking for," while warning that older examples "followed different format specifications and should be consulted only for general guidance and not formatting." ACTION: register in ARC and clear the eligibility questionnaire EARLY (from Sept 15, 2026 for the 2028 cycle) purely to unlock the examples — that is weeks of drafting advantage.

2. HHMI SCIENTIST DIRECTORY AND PROFILES — https://www.hhmi.org/scientists (redirects to https://www.hhmi.org/search/people), browsable by programme (Investigators, Scholars, Fellows), with a research summary on each scientist's profile; plus https://www.hhmi.org/search/investigator-alumni and /search/emeriti. TOOLING NOTE: this directory is behind a Cloudflare bot check — it returned 403 to a plain fetch and a challenge page in a rendering browser on 2026-09-18, so I could not verify profile-level content directly; it opens normally in an ordinary human browser session.

3. COHORT ANNOUNCEMENTS — HHMI news releases name every selectee with institution and research focus (e.g. "HHMI invests over $300 million in 26 new investigators," July 23, 2024, which also gives the base rate: 26 selected from "nearly 1,000 eligible" applicants; "HHMI Names the 2024 Hanna Gray Fellows"; "HHMI Selects 176 Undergraduate Students as Inaugural Cech Fellows"). Use these to build a target list of people at your institution who have actually won, then ask them for their materials — HHMI does not forbid this.

4. PUBLICLY SHARED APPLICANT MATERIALS (found via search, not via HHMI) — a Gilliam Fellow publishes her successful 2020 application with annotations: annotated Career Statement, annotated Scientific Leadership Statement and annotated Research Plan, plus a walkthrough of the 2027 cycle's components and timing (https://www.yaelcourtney.com/resources-and-guides/gilliamguide). This is the only worked example set of real HHMI application text I could find outside ARC.

5. UNIVERSITY RESEARCH-DEVELOPMENT OFFICES — Caltech, Johns Hopkins, Duke, Ohio State and others post HHMI competition pages and run internal feedback committees; some hold sample HHMI applications from their own faculty internally. Ask your foundation relations office directly for prior-year HHMI applications from your institution.

result.funder_system:
International Human Frontier Science Program Organization (HFSPO / "HFSP"), Strasbourg, France (12 quai Saint-Jean, 67080 Strasbourg; +33 3 88 21 51 23). An intergovernmental funder of basic life-science research, financed by ~40 member countries/EU including the USA; US applicants are eligible and US-based PIs are common in the award archive. It is NOT a US agency: no Grants.gov, no eRA Commons, no DUNS/UEI/SAM registration, no budget page at any stage.

CURRENT MECHANISMS (as of 18 Sep 2026): (1) Research Grants - Program (RG-Program), any career stage; (2) Research Grants - Early Career (RG-Early Career; the former "Young Investigator" grants) - all team members within 5 yrs of an independent position and within 10 yrs of the PhD at the LOI deadline; (3) Accelerator Grant (3-yr pilot launched July 2024; open ONLY to PIs of teams awarded in the current March round, to add one member based in India, Japan, New Zealand, Norway, Republic of Korea, Singapore or South Africa; +100,000 USD/yr for years 2-3); (4) Postdoctoral Fellowships - Long-Term (LTF, life-science PhD) and Cross-Disciplinary (CDF, non-biology PhD with little/no life-science experience), 3 years, one competition per year.

TERMINATED: Career Development Award. HFSP's own Triennial Conference Joint Communique: "This award has been terminated. Applications will not be called for the Career Development award in the future. The final funding round for CDAs will have been conducted for the last time in 2018, for funding beginning in 2019." (The CDA description page is still live on hfsp.org in the present tense - a classic stale-page trap.) Short-Term Fellowships survive only as a filter in the historical awards archive.

KEY STRUCTURAL FACTS THAT SHAPE EVERYTHING: grants are team-only (2-4 members, normally one per country, intercontinental preferred; no individual applications, postdocs ineligible; Principal Applicant must be in an HFSPO member country); teams must NOT have collaborated before (">3 co-publications ... strongly reduce the chance of funding"); "preliminary data are not required ... and may indicate that the project is not novel"; award sums are fixed (300k/400k/500k USD per year for 2/3/4-member teams; indirect costs capped at 10%; no PI salary); "A budget is not required at any stage of the application process."

SCALE/ODDS (funder's own FAQ): "Each year, we receive around 700 Letters of Intent (LoIs) ... about 10-15% ... eliminated ... The Selection Committee invites about 80-90 teams ... to submit a full proposal. About one-third of these are funded (thus 4-5% of the original LoIs)." Fellowships 2026 round: "HFSP reviewed proposals from 746 applicants, and 126 were selected to submit full proposals. From there, 55 projects were awarded" (~7% overall; ~44% of invited full proposals). 2025 research grants: "HFSPO received proposals involving more than 2100 researchers in 780 projects" -> 30 Research Grants + 12 Accelerator Grants, 104 scientists.
result.submission_portal:
ProposalCentral (Altum), https://proposalcentral.com/ - the same portal for Research Grants, Accelerator Grants and Fellowships. HFSP migrated to it from its own "HFSP Extranet"; any guidance still naming the Extranet is stale.

HIDDEN LONG-LEAD ITEMS (this is where first-timers lose the cycle):
- Every team member (not just the PI) needs their own ProposalCentral account and completed Professional Profile. Verbatim: "Please make sure that all team members have registered and completed the mandatory fields in their Professional Profile at least 48 hours before this deadline."
- Account activation/password links "expire after 24 hours."
- ORCID is mandatory and must be connected in the Professional Profile, not in the form ("The ORCID is mandatory but it must be completed in the Professional Profile").
- Two-step deadline: the LOI must be INITIATED (open + save the title page to generate a 7-digit LOI ID) about 9 days before the LOI submission deadline for grants, and 7 days before for fellowships. Verbatim (grants): "It is essential to initiate the Letter of Intent as soon as the team has seriously decided to submit a letter of intent, but by 17 March 2026 the latest. Please note that this deadline is not mentioned on the application site."
- No signatures and no budget at LOI stage. At RG full-proposal stage every applicant AND their institutional official must e-sign inside ProposalCentral before submission, and "the institutional officials and the applicants' university or institution must match perfectly, else the application cannot be validated, nor submitted." Institutional officials need "Edit" access; co-PIs need "Administrator" access to complete their parts.
- Fellowships: before the applicant can submit, host supervisor(s) and both referees must have submitted their sections and the host supervisor(s) + host institution official must have e-signed.
- Session times out after 20 minutes of inactivity; HFSP advises drafting all text offline and pasting in. The RG research plan is the only uploaded file (PDF, max 4 MB).
- Portal support: pcsupport@altum.com, +1-800-875-2562 (US/Canada) / +1-703-964-5840, 8:00/8:30 am-5:00 pm ET Mon-Fri. Programme questions: grant@hfsp.org (grants), fellow@hfsp.org (fellowships).

RESEARCH GRANTS (RG-Program + RG-Early Career), award year 2027 cycle:

- LOI initiation (get the 7-digit LOI ID): 17 March 2026, 9:00 AM (Eastern US Time)

- Awards announced: late March 2027. "Awarded teams can start in May 2027 the earliest, and December 2027, the latest."
