review_stages.stage: RG: LOI eligibility + scientific-scope pre-screen by a small committee (three HFSP Scientific Directors/Secretariat scientists + two Review Committee members); out-of-scope LOIs killed here (10-15% of ~700)
review_stages.timing: within ~4 weeks of the late-March LOI deadline; PI "informed as soon as possible"

review_stages.stage: RG: each surviving LOI scored by 2 Review Committee members on novelty/originality, interdisciplinarity, need for collaboration + team integration; ranked into 4 priority groups
review_stages.timing: April-May (RC ratings due mid-May in HFSP's published chronology)

review_stages.stage: RG: top ~1/3 of LOIs go to the Selection Committee, which meets and picks the teams to invite (~80-90 teams)
review_stages.timing: June; SC meets late June

review_stages.stage: RG: LOI outcome notified; Full Proposal guidelines sent to invited teams
review_stages.timing: early-to-mid July = ~3.5 months after the LOI deadline

review_stages.stage: RG: invited Full Proposal submitted (all applicants + institutional officials e-sign)
review_stages.timing: 10 September = ~5.5 months after LOI

review_stages.stage: RG: Secretariat assigns 3 RC members as leads and solicits mail reviewers (applicants name 6 suggestions; HFSP is not bound by them); "at least two (and usually three or more) mail reviews" per application; remote RC briefing meeting
review_stages.timing: within 4 weeks of the deadline; briefing mid-October; mail reviews back November-December

review_stages.stage: RG: RC scores due, then the Review Committee meets in Strasbourg; RG-Program and RG-Early Career discussed in separate sessions; calibration round first; "Scores of 7 and above are considered for funding within the limit of funds available"
review_stages.timing: scores early January; meeting late January (~4.5 months after full proposal)

review_stages.stage: RG: ranking to the Recommendation Committee / a subgroup of the Council of Scientists, then approval by the Board of Trustees
review_stages.timing: early March -> late March

review_stages.stage: RG: awards announced; feedback (summary of RC issues) released to full-proposal applicants
review_stages.timing: end of March = ~12 months after the LOI deadline

review_stages.stage: RG: grant start
review_stages.timing: May at the earliest, 1 December at the latest, in the award year

review_stages.stage: FELLOWSHIPS: formal eligibility check + scope screen by a small review committee; out-of-scope applicants notified
review_stages.timing: May-June

review_stages.stage: FELLOWSHIPS: each eligible LOI scored by 2 Fellowship Review Committee members on an A (highest) to D scale; a third reviewer if the two diverge; "HFSP will then invite the top LOI applicants (usually the top 15-20% of all eligible LOIs) to submit a Full Proposal"
review_stages.timing: June-August; outcome mid-to-end August (~3.5 months after the 12 May LOI)

review_stages.stage: FELLOWSHIPS: Full Proposal re-checked for eligibility (publication rule tightens here), then "2-3 evaluations" from external scientific reviewers, then 2 RC members evaluate in light of those
review_stages.timing: late September -> January

review_stages.stage: FELLOWSHIPS: "The Fellowship Review Committee will meet in early February"; each proposal discussed, leads defend or revise, all members score, average -> ranked funding list
review_stages.timing: early February (~4.5 months after full proposal)

review_stages.stage: FELLOWSHIPS: notification "once internal HFSP formalities are complete (usually towards the end of March)"; then activation window
review_stages.timing: end of March; start 1 April-1 January following

review_stages.stage: ACCELERATOR: evaluated by the Research Grant Review Committee at its regular January meeting; Board of Trustees decides before end of March
review_stages.timing: ~6 months from the late-September deadline

result.months_submission_to_award:
Research Grants: ~12 months from LOI (late March) to award announcement (end of March the following year); ~6.5 months from the invited full proposal (10 Sept) to announcement; money starts May-December of the award year, i.e. 14-20 months after the LOI. Decision point that matters most: ~3.5 months from LOI to the invite/reject letter.
Fellowships: ~10.5 months from LOI (12 May) to notification (end of March); ~6 months from full proposal (24 Sept) to notification; ~3.5 months from LOI to the invite/reject letter; activation 11-20 months after the LOI (1 April-1 January).
Accelerator Grant: ~6 months (late-September deadline -> late-March decision).
result.resubmission_policy:
There is NO NIH-style resubmission track: no A1, no mandatory Introduction page, no response-to-reviewers document, and no second look within a cycle. HFSP is explicit that it cannot re-review: "Given the program structure, it is impossible for us to reconvene the Committee for a second round of assessments each year."

What actually happens: you re-enter the next annual competition as a fresh application, starting again at the Letter of Intent.

FELLOWSHIPS (verbatim FAQ 06): "There is only one application round per year. Should your application be unsuccessful, you may submit an application in a subsequent year, provided you still meet all the eligibility criteria listed in the guidelines. Please note that application guidelines are subject to change each year. If you were successful at the Letter of Intent stage in a previous year but were rejected at the Full Proposal stage, you must submit another Letter of Intent the following year if you wish to apply again. Please note that success at the Letter of Intent stage in one year does not guarantee success in the following year." No cap on attempts is published, but the 3-year post-PhD eligibility window (degree conferred no more than 36 months before the full-proposal deadline) limits most people to 2-3 tries. One LOI per year only - you cannot hedge LTF and CDF in the same round - and "An HFSP postdoctoral fellowship may only be held once."

RESEARCH GRANTS: nothing forbids re-applying, and the site states step 3 (obtaining a new LOI ID) "is mandatory even for those re-applying from previous years". The only formal trace of resubmission is at the full-proposal stage: "Applicants are also asked to complete a resubmission section if applicable (Max. 600 characters)" on the Title Page - i.e. a 600-character note, the nearest thing HFSP has to an introduction page. Constraints that bite instead of a resubmission rule: no individual may appear on more than one LOI in a cycle (all such LOIs are removed); nobody may hold or apply for more than one HFSP award at a time; current awardees are locked out (for AY2027, "Awardees from 2023 and 2024 are not eligible to apply as Principal Applicant or Co-Applicant, this also includes Accelerator Grants awarded in 2024 and 2025"), and 2021/2022 awardees may reapply only with a different team and project - "Applications bearing a strong similarity to previous awards, either in team composition or topic of research, will not be considered eligible." Practical implication: a rejected grant team usually changes something real (team composition, or the project's angle) rather than resubmitting the same LOI.

FEEDBACK you can build a resubmission on: Fellowships - "we cannot provide feedback to unsuccessful applicants at the Letter of Intent stage due to the volume of applications that we receive. However, unsuccessful applicants that were invited to submit a Full Proposal will receive feedback." Research Grants (reviewer handbook, Oct 2023 version) - LOI: "Upon request applicants are informed of the assessment in general terms and the reason(s) that the project was not retained"; Full proposals: all applicants get a Secretariat-written summary of the issues raised by the Review Committee. So a rejected LOI buys you at most a general-terms explanation; a rejected full proposal buys you real reviewer substance.
result.program_officer_norms:
There are no portfolio program officers in the NIH sense - no assigned PO, no pre-submission "concept" call, no relationship to cultivate. Contact is with a central office mailbox staffed by HFSP's own scientists (Secretariat/Scientific Directors): grant@hfsp.org for research grants, fellow@hfsp.org for fellowships. Contact is TOLERATED AND EXPLICITLY INVITED for eligibility and scope, but nobody will read or comment on your draft, and review-committee members are barred from talking to you at all.

What HFSP invites you to ask (verbatim):
- Fellowships, front matter: "If applicants are unsure of their eligibility or the relevance of their proposed research project, they should contact the Fellowships Office at fellow@hfsp.org."
- Fellowships, scope: "In cases of doubt, applicants can contact the HFSP Fellowship Office (fellow@hfsp.org) to request general feedback about the alignment of their proposed project with the objectives and scope of HFSP-funded research." This is the single most valuable pre-submission move for this funder, because 10-15% of grant LOIs and many fellowship LOIs die purely on scope.
- Career-interruption exemptions to the 3-year post-PhD clock MUST be settled first: "Applicants wishing to obtain an exemption must contact fellow@hfsp.org with details of their interruption periods (dates, reasons) to discuss the possibility of an exemption BEFORE initiating their Letter of Intent."
- Other standard asks: which scheme to choose (FAQ 05: "In case of doubt, please email the Fellowships Office (fellow@hfsp.org) for guidance"), degree-equivalency (EURYDICE for European degrees), whether an unusual publication record meets the lead-author rule ("Applicants with queries regarding the eligibility of their publication record should contact fellow@hfsp.org to check"), dual-nationality/host-country edge cases, and for grants, long clinical-service periods that might extend the Early Career window ("applicants should contact the HFSP grant office (grant@hfsp.org)").
- HFSP asks you to read first: "For questions about the HFSP Fellowships, please first read the Application Guidelines (above), then contact the Fellowships Office."

What is DISCOURAGED/IMPOSSIBLE: any contact with reviewers or committee members. Verbatim from the reviewer handbook: "Committee members must not give or discuss with applicants or referees any information relating to the results of the review of a specific application, nor must they offer opinions on the chances of success or failure of a specific application after the Review Committees have met. All requests for information relating to applications or the review process should be referred to the Secretariat." There is no mechanism for HFSP staff to pre-review a draft LOI or full proposal.

THE REAL SUBSTITUTE FOR A PROGRAM OFFICER - staff-run webinars, in the window between the portal opening and the LOI deadline: "We are hosting two Fellowships Webinars on the 25th of March, 2026. Carolyn Johnson (HFSP Senior Scientific Officer) and Guntram Bauer (HFSP Chief Scientific Officer) provide insights into HFSP's expectations for frontier science, application rules and guidelines, and how to develop a compelling Letter of Intent," with two awardees on the panel; free, registration required, two time zones (09:00 and 16:00 CET), recorded on HFSP's YouTube (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E8A-v-tlb-w). An equivalent Research Grants webinar and a LOI-submission video (https://youtu.be/s9In4HSq7OE) exist. Timing norm: ask scope/eligibility questions BEFORE you initiate the LOI (mid-March for grants, before 5 May for fellowships); after submission there is nothing to ask and no negotiation - budgets are fixed and "the financial terms of HFSP funding ... are not negotiable."

One more norm worth knowing: your host/institution must be told early. Grants - "Applicants are advised to alert their institutions on the planned international collaboration", and the institutional official must e-sign in the portal before the full-proposal deadline. Fellowships - "Applicants must keep the host supervisor(s) and host institution aware of their application", and one supervisor may endorse only ONE HFSP fellowship applicant per year, so that conversation is a competitive-slot negotiation, not a formality.
result.funded_examples_source:
No sample applications are published by HFSP - and the old FAQ item "35. Are there examples of successful HFSP fellowship applications?" now 404s (https://www.hfsp.org/node/44336), a dead link that search indexes still serve. What exists instead:

1. THE AWARDS ARCHIVE (the primary source): https://www.hfsp.org/awardees/awards - a filterable database of every award from 1990 to 2026. Filters: Program (Research Grants - Program / Research Grants - Early Career / Long-Term Fellowships - LTF / Cross Disciplinary Fellowships - CDF / Accelerator Grants / plus the discontinued Career Development Awards and Short-Term Fellowships), Award year (1990-2026, "NB: years are award years"), Country and Nationality. Each entry shows the project title, every team member with nationality and institution, and an expandable "Abstract" - i.e. the funded public abstract, which is the closest thing to a model of what HFSP rewards. Searchable by PI name.
2. New awards landing page: https://www.hfsp.org/awardees/newly-awarded, and the annual awardee booklets, e.g. 2025 Research Grant awardees https://www.hfsp.org/bookletRG2025 and the announcement https://www.hfsp.org/hfsp-news/rgawardees2025. Fellowship round results: https://www.hfsp.org/hfsp-news/fellowships-awarded-55-pioneering-postdoctoral-scientists-26-nations.
3. "HFSP Science Digest" on recently awarded projects, linked from the Research Grants overview - short write-ups of funded work.
4. The guidelines themselves point applicants at awarded projects as the scope test: "Examples of funded projects indicating the broad scope of HFSP can be found on our website (2025 HFSP Research Grant Awardees)" and, for fellowships, "Prospective fellowship applicants are encouraged to read about previous HFSP Fellows for examples of the broad scope of projects that have been funded."
5. Nearest substitutes for a sample application, both free and HFSP-published: "The Art of Grantsmanship" by Jacob (Jack) Kraicer, former HFSP Director of Research Grants (https://www.hfsp.org/node/5761; HFSP invites copying and reuse), and the 21-page "Fellowship Primer" written by an HFSP program director for "PhD students who have little experience in dealing with funding organizations and who plan on attempting their first fellowship proposal" (https://www.hfsp.org/sites/default/files/Communications/PRIMER.pdf). Also the reviewer-facing documents, which tell you exactly how you will be scored: fellowship "Assessment Criteria and Reviewer Scoring Guide" (https://www.hfsp.org/sites/default/files/Sciences/fellows/2027/HFSP%20Fellowships%202027%20-%20Assessment%20criteria%20and%20scoring%20guide%20for%20reviewers.pdf) and the research-grant reviewer handbook "The Peer Review Process" (https://www.hfsp.org/sites/default/files/Sciences/Grants/The%20Peer%20Review%20Process.pdf), plus HFSP's own list of recurrent failure modes in the Full Proposal instructions and FAQ 04.
6. Not found: any university research office or public repository hosting a complete funded HFSP LOI or full proposal. Individual awardees sometimes share theirs privately; approaching a named awardee in the archive (or an awardee panellist from the webinars) is the realistic route to seeing a real application.
result.page_limits:
HFSP counts CHARACTERS, not pages - there is essentially one page limit in the whole system. Everything is typed into ProposalCentral text boxes except the research-grant research plan. Limits include spaces and punctuation, and cannot be shifted between boxes.

RESEARCH GRANT - LETTER OF INTENT (same for RG-Program and RG-Early Career): Title 100 characters; up to 10 keywords and up to 10 disciplines (exceeding blocks submission); Abstract of overall project 1,200; one Subproject box per team member, 1,200 each (4 boxes; a 5th member shares box 4); "Frontier Science" (how the work extends the frontier) 1,200; Interdisciplinarity 600; Collaborative aspects / difference from ongoing research 600; up to 5 key references, 1,200 total. Each member also supplies affiliations, degrees, ORCID, a short CV and up to 10 publications from the last 5 years (preprints with DOI allowed; prizes and honours are explicitly not wanted). No figures, no uploads, no budget, no signatures at this stage.

RESEARCH GRANT - FULL PROPOSAL (invited): Scientific abstract 2,400; Public abstract 2,400 (must differ from the scientific one); Overview 8,000; "Difference to ongoing research" 1,500; Interdisciplinarity 1,500; resubmission note (if applicable) 600. Uploaded Proposed Research plan (Word template -> one PDF, named after the PI): "Maximum 30 000 characters including spaces and punctuation in the main text including tables and figure legends but excluding references"; "Type size: Calibri 11-point, text, 1.5 line spacing (references and figure legends can be single spaced)"; "you may include up to 5 figures and/or tables within the text; all combined, these must not exceed two pages"; PDF "should not exceed 4 Mbytes". Also: each member selects up to 10 publications from the last 5 years, and the team names six suggested mail reviewers with up to 5 competence keywords each.

FELLOWSHIPS - LETTER OF INTENT (LTF and CDF identical): summary of the proposed research plan up to 3,000 characters; exactly THREE key references; title, personal data, ORCID, short CV, host institution and supervisor(s) with intended arrival date, disclosure of any prior collaboration with the host, PhD thesis title+abstract and previous postdoc project abstracts, full publication list plus an "Additional Information on Publications" template. "No other documents are required at the Letter of Intent stage" - no letters, no signatures.

FELLOWSHIPS - FULL PROPOSAL (invited): Summary (carried over, do not change); Background and significance 3,000; Specific aims 8,000; Experimental design 6,000; Bibliography up to 15 references; How the project differs from the applicant's previous work 2,500; Why it is at the leading edge of the life sciences 4,000; Why the host lab is a good fit 2,000; Public summary 2,400. Host supervisor recommendation (template, includes up to 10 of the supervisor's publications, a statement that the project is a new direction for the lab, and a mentorship plan) - both supervisors if two. Two additional referee letters, each "no more than 3000 characters (including spaces)", written into the portal template. E-signatures from applicant, host supervisor(s) and host institution official.

ACCELERATOR GRANT: abstract + research plan for the new sub-project, plus the new member's CV and up to 10 publications in the same format as regular team members, signed by the PI, the accelerator member and that member's institutional official.

MECHANISM VARIATION: the machinery is near-identical across RG-Program and RG-Early Career (only eligibility differs: 10 years post-PhD / 5 years independent, exceptions for parental leave, military service or medical absence but not unemployment) and across LTF and CDF (only the applicant's disciplinary background differs). No budget, no biosketch-equivalent, no data-management plan, no facilities section anywhere in the system.
required_documents: ProposalCentral account + completed Professional Profile for EVERY team member/applicant (institution, degrees, publications, position title), done at least 48 hours before the deadline
ORCID iD connected to the ProposalCentral Professional Profile (mandatory; publications can be imported from ORCID)

RG Full Proposal: six suggested mail reviewers with competence keywords (HFSP is not bound by them; you may ask that named competitors be excluded)

Fellowship Full Proposal: recommendation letter from host supervisor(s) via HFSP template (career summary, up to 10 publications, why this is a new direction for the lab, mentorship plan)

Fellowship Full Proposal: e-signatures from applicant, host supervisor(s) and host institution official
Accelerator Grant: sub-project abstract and research plan, accelerator member's CV and up to 10 publications, signatures from PI, new member and the new member's institutional official
NOT required anywhere: a budget, letters of institutional commitment beyond the signature, biosketches in a fixed format, data-management or facilities sections

result.funder_system:
JDRF / Breakthrough T1D (JDRF rebranded to Breakthrough T1D in 2024; the legal entity and grant machinery are continuous — old jdrf.org grant URLs redirect to breakthrought1d.org). Private nonprofit, US-headquartered (200 Vesey St, 28th Floor, New York, NY 10281), funding globally in 20+ countries. One centralized "Grant Center" in the US reviews and awards nearly all grants; national affiliates (UK, Canada, Australia, Israel, Netherlands) run a small number of country-specific or co-funded calls with their own portals and dates — the UK page states: "All Breakthrough T1D grants are reviewed and awarded through our centralised Grant Centre in the US, except for our UK-specific research funding opportunities and those we fund in partnership with other organisations."

Mechanism set (Grant Handbook 2026, §2): Strategic Research Agreement (SRA — single-project, multi-project, clinical; LOI required; budget/duration "as approved"); Innovative Grants ($200k, 1 yr, no LOI, not renewable); training awards — Postdoctoral Fellowship (3 yr, stipend by years of experience), Advanced Postdoctoral Fellowship ($95k/yr, 3 yr), Career Development Award ($200k/yr, 5 yr), Kellogg Family Early-Career Patient-Oriented Diabetes Research Award ($200k/yr, 5 yr); Conference Grants; Industry Discovery & Development Partnership (IDDP, for-profit, LOI by invitation). Indirect costs capped at 10% of direct costs everywhere (0% on fellowships and IDDP). Breakthrough T1D follows NIH salary guidelines for PIs and postdocs.

Method note: nearly everything below was read directly from breakthrought1d.org's own PDFs and pages (curl + PDF text extraction). Two exceptions, flagged: (a) the funded-research portfolio page returns a Cloudflare 403 to a plain fetch and was read through a rendering fetch; (b) archived snapshots of the funding-opportunities page (web.archive.org) were used to establish that the training-award and Project Concept deadlines recur on the same dates year to year.
result.submission_portal:
**RMS360**, a SmartSimple Cloud instance: https://breakthrought1d.smartsimple.us/ (login page https://breakthrought1d.smartsimple.us/s_Login.jsp). There is no Grants.gov / proposalCENTRAL route for the US organisation. (Some *partner* competitions run elsewhere — e.g. the Canadian JDRF–Stem Cell Network fellowship uses ProposalCentral, and US Conference Awards use a monday.com form, https://forms.monday.com/forms/2b9e293552179e96015222acccb5516b?r=use1 — but every Breakthrough T1D research mechanism proper goes through RMS360.)

THE HIDDEN LONG-LEAD ITEM — it is not the PI account, it is the institutional accounts. The login page splits registration two ways: "Researchers: (PIs and Co-PIs) **Register Here**" vs "Institutional Officials: (Research/Finance/Tech Transfer Office) **Contact Support**." Concretely, from the RMS360 Pre/Post-Award FAQ:
- The PI self-registers (orange REGISTER button). If your organisation is not in the dropdown, you must submit a new-organisation registration to Breakthrough T1D and wait for it to be created.
- A proposal cannot be submitted without an **RO (Research Office contact)** and **FO (Finance Officer)** selected on the Contacts tab. If yours are not in the dropdown, you create the RO/FO account — and then "a list of previously registered research officer's from your institution will appear. Please contact one of the listed research office contacts and ask them to log into their RMS360 account to approve the newly registered RO or FO." If no one at your institution is registered, or you cannot reach them, preawardsupport@BreakthroughT1D.org must approve it. Until that approval happens the RO/FO does not appear and you cannot proceed.
- **Co-PIs must themselves be registered in RMS360** and must have an up-to-date biosketch in their RMS360 profile; the biosketch is pulled from the profile and auto-appended, it is not an attachment. The PI must tick "My Biosketch is up to date" on the Contacts tab to submit. (Key Personnel do *not* need accounts — their biosketches are uploaded as attachments.)
- Submission is two-step and the second step is not yours: "The PI submits an application to their Research Office (RO)" then "The RO approves the budget, and formally submits the proposal to Breakthrough T1D from the Pending RO Approval tab." Handbook: "Please work directly with your RO to ensure this process is completed prior to the submission deadline." A PI who clicks Validate & Submit at 4:55pm has not submitted.
- For training awards, **three confidential recommendation references must be submitted directly in RMS360 by the referees**, and "proposals cannot be successfully validated until all references are submitted" — i.e. your referees are on the critical path, not a courtesy.
- Practical: use Chrome or Firefox; attachments must be unlocked, non-password-protected PDFs, 3–4 MB each.

Realistic advance time for a first-time applicant with no institutional history at Breakthrough T1D: start the RMS360/RO/FO setup 4–6 weeks out, and brief referees at the same time.
result.deadline_structure:
There are NO NIH-style standard due dates across the whole funder. The structure is three-layered, and two of the three layers do recur on stable dates that are worth printing:

**1. Annual, dated, recurring — Training Awards (all four: PDF, Advanced PDF, CDA, Kellogg ECPODRA).** One full-proposal deadline a year, no LOI, first business day of July:
- FY26 Training Awards: "Full Proposals due 1 July 2025"
- FY27 Training Awards: "Full Proposals due 2 July 2026"
RFAs are posted to the site ~April–May (FY27 RFA PDFs are dated 2026/04). So: expect FY28 training awards to open ~April–May 2027 with a deadline on/about 1 July 2027 — treat as pattern, not promise, and confirm on the page.

**2. Semi-annual, dated, recurring — Project Concepts** (the investigator-initiated route into a Strategic Research Agreement). "A semi-annual submission for Strategic Research Agreement Letters of Intent." Two rounds a year, early November and early May, with notification ~6 weeks later. Verbatim from the current page:
- "Round 1 — Letters of Intent due 5 Nov 2026 … Notification by 17 Dec 2026"
- "Round 2 — Letters of Intent due 6 May 2027 … Notification by 17 Jun 2027"
The 2024–25 cycle was 6 Nov 2024 → notification 20 Dec 2024, and 6 May 2025 → 17 Jun 2025. The dates are stable to within a day or two across years.

**3. Per-solicitation — everything else.** Topic RFAs (islet vascularization, ketone monitoring, CGM–pump devices, organ-on-a-chip, immune tolerance, C-peptide monitoring, CVD trials…) each carry their own dated timeline table inside the call PDF, and several say "no extensions will be given" / "no extensions will be considered". Innovative Grants and Common Mechanisms in Autoimmunity Insight Awards are single-stage with one dated deadline per round (Common Mechanisms: 9 Jan 2025, then 8 Jan 2026 — an early-January annual pattern). Conference Awards are rolling. IDDP inquiries are accepted year-round and LOIs are by invitation.

**Time of day, stated twice and drift-sensitive** — funding page: "Letters of Intent and Full Proposals are due by **5:00pm Eastern Time** on the deadline date, unless otherwise noted." Handbook §2: "Applications are due at 5pm eastern on the deadline date, unless otherwise noted."

**A trap worth naming.** As of 18 Sep 2026 the live "Open opportunities" list still displays calls whose LOI dates ran in Oct–Dec 2025 and Jan 2026 alongside genuinely open ones. Items are not reliably removed once closed. A listed date in the past means the page is stale, not that a second round is open — and conversely a closed listing is not evidence the programme ended. Always open the call PDF and read its own timeline table.

review_stages.stage: Letter of Intent (LOI) submitted in RMS360 — required for Strategic Research Agreements and IDDP, and for most topic RFAs; not used for training awards, Innovative Grants, or Common Mechanisms Insight Awards. Typically 2 pages on the RMS360 template (one 2025 RFA, the organ-on-a-chip call, used 4 pages)
review_stages.timing: Day 0

review_stages.stage: LOI review (internal Breakthrough T1D scientific staff and/or external) and triage; approved LOIs are invited to a full proposal. 'An approved LOI is required prior to the submission of a full proposal.'
review_stages.timing: 2–4 weeks. CGM–pump: LOI 2 Sep 2026 → LOI outcome 17 Sep 2026 (2 wks). Vascularization and organ-on-a-chip: LOI 28 Jan 2026 → outcome 11 Feb 2026 (2 wks). Ketone monitoring: LOI 12 Nov 2025 → outcome 10 Dec 2025 (4 wks). Project Concepts: LOI 5 Nov 2026 → notification by 17 Dec 2026 (6 wks)

review_stages.stage: Full proposal prepared and submitted — PI validates and submits to the institutional RO, RO approves the budget and submits to Breakthrough T1D. For SRAs, 'Breakthrough T1D scientific personnel works collaboratively with the investigator or investigator team to develop a full application'
review_stages.timing: 4–7 weeks after the LOI invitation. Vascularization/organ-on-a-chip: outcome 11 Feb → full proposal 11 Mar 2026 (4 wks). Ketones: outcome 10 Dec → full proposal 21 Jan 2026 (6 wks). CGM–pump: outcome 17 Sep → full proposal 4 Nov 2026 (7 wks)

review_stages.stage: Administrative triage — incomplete applications, missing budget/biosketch, over-length research plans, formatting violations, or poor fit to the Research Strategy are eliminated before review. This is a real and frequently-invoked gate, named repeatedly in the handbook
review_stages.timing: Immediately after submission, before scientific review

review_stages.stage: Scientific review — 'either conducted internally by Breakthrough T1D Scientific Staff or externally by a Scientific Review Panel at the discretion of Breakthrough T1D Scientific Staff and Breakthrough T1D Senior Management.' Reviewers 'provide qualitative critiques and quantitative scores.' Criteria: scientific validity/merit, technical feasibility, significance, innovation, ability to complete in the funding period; RFAs add their own list (e.g. relevance, approach, translational plan, environment). There is no standing named study section and no published roster
review_stages.timing: The bulk of the ~4–5 months between full-proposal deadline and award notification

review_stages.stage: Rebuttal window (SRA and IDDP, not guaranteed) — 'The reviewers' written critiques will be shared with the applicant. Breakthrough T1D Staff may request a rebuttal from the applicant to address concerns raised by the reviewers.' For IDDP: 'This process may include the opportunity for the applicant to view anonymized critiques and provide a rebuttal.' This is a mid-review right of reply, not a post-rejection appeal
review_stages.timing: Within the review period; timing not published

review_stages.stage: Clinical review (human-subjects applications only) — 'All applications that receive a funding recommendation after scientific review will undergo clinical review where a subsequent review of the study protocol and supporting documents will be performed.' Reviewed by the Breakthrough T1D Grant Review Committee with an expert clinician on the panel; additional ethics and/or statistical review possible. 'Funding for these grants will not be awarded until the review process is completed'
review_stages.timing: After scientific review, before award; adds unquantified time

review_stages.stage: Funding recommendation and final decision — Breakthrough T1D Scientific Staff recommend to Senior Management; 'Final approval for applications is determined by either Breakthrough T1D Senior Management or by a committee of the Breakthrough T1D International Board of Directors.' Board committee sign-off is the analogue of NIH Council and is the step applicants most often forget exists
review_stages.timing: Folded into the notification date

review_stages.stage: Award notification in writing (email 'Award Notification' + 'Award/Activation Instructions' to PI and RO). 'Applicants will be notified in writing regarding the status of their application. Note that status of an application will not be given by phone'
review_stages.timing: ~4–5 months after the full-proposal deadline. Vascularization/organ-on-a-chip: full proposal 11 Mar 2026 → award notification July 2026. Ketones: 21 Jan 2026 → May 2026. CGM–pump: 4 Nov 2026 → 31 Mar 2027. Single-stage Innovative FY25: proposal 24 Oct 2024 → response Jan 2025 (~2.5 mo). Common Mechanisms: proposal 8 Jan 2026 → 'Response to applicants: June 2026' (~5 mo)

review_stages.stage: Activation and earliest anticipated start — PI and RO log into RMS360, accept the non-negotiable Terms and Conditions, and complete activation materials ('customarily due 1 month prior to the anticipated grant start date'). Funding does not flow until activation is complete
review_stages.timing: 1–3 months after notification. CGM–pump: notification 31 Mar 2027 → earliest start 1 May 2027. Ketones: May 2026 → July 2026. Vascularization/organ-on-a-chip: July 2026 → October 2026. Common Mechanisms: June 2026 → August 2026. Innovative FY25: Jan 2025 → 1 Mar 2025

result.months_submission_to_award:
Measured from the four current RFAs plus the FY25 Innovative call, not estimated:

- **Two-stage RFA / SRA (LOI → start): ~8 months, very consistent.** CGM–pump 2 Sep 2026 → 1 May 2027 = 8 months. Vascularization 28 Jan 2026 → Oct 2026 = 8 months. Organ-on-a-chip 28 Jan 2026 → Oct 2026 = 8 months. Ketone monitoring 12 Nov 2025 → Jul 2026 = 8 months.
- **Full proposal → award notification: 4–5 months.** Full proposal → earliest start: **~6–7 months**.
- **Single-stage, no LOI: 4–7 months submission → start.** Innovative FY25: 24 Oct 2024 → 1 Mar 2025 = ~4 months (fastest mechanism at this funder). Common Mechanisms Insight Awards: 8 Jan 2026 → Aug 2026 = ~7 months.
- **Project Concept LOI → notification: ~6 weeks** (5 Nov 2026 → 17 Dec 2026). If the concept is invited forward, add the full-proposal arc above.
- **Training awards: NOT PUBLISHED.** The four FY27 training RFAs contain no timeline table at all — no notification date, no start date. The only anchor is the "FY27" label on a 2 July 2026 deadline. Do not quote a number for these; ask the Program Administrator.

Headline for a planner: **assume 8 months from first submission to first dollar, and about 9–10 months from "I should apply" to money if you include RMS360/RO/FO setup and proposal writing.** That is roughly one NIH cycle faster than NIH's ~9–10 months submission-to-start, but the two-stage LOI gate means the *decision to compete* has to be made ~10 months before funds arrive.
result.resubmission_policy:
Allowed, and the policy is short. Grant Handbook 2026, §3, verbatim:

"Breakthrough T1D accepts applications resubmitted after rejection by the Breakthrough T1D review committee(s) discussed above. All resubmitted applications must include:
A copy of the summary statement for the original application if provided for rejected submission.
An introduction (limited to two pages) addressing each of the reviewer's concerns if provided for the rejected submission.
These documents must be included in the Resubmission section of the Research Plan."

Mechanics in RMS360: the Application Type page asks "Is the application a resubmission? Select YES or NO", and if yes requires "Summary Statement from the previous application" plus, in the checklists' words, "Rebuttal Letter (included in the research plan and does not exceed 2 pages)". The fellowship and CDA checklists name the same item "Introduction to Revised Application (2 pages maximum)" as a Research Plan component. So the 2-page document travels under three names — introduction / rebuttal letter / Introduction to Revised Application — and they are the same thing.

Note the conditionals: both required items are qualified "if provided for the rejected submission." Breakthrough T1D does not always release critiques — the handbook says "Generally, applications undergo a pre-review process. For applications receiving a full review, critiques containing the reviewers' comments **may** be provided." An application killed at administrative triage or at LOI triage generates no summary statement, so there is nothing to attach and nothing to respond to; you are effectively submitting fresh.

**Number of resubmissions: no published cap — not found.** Nothing in the handbook, the RFAs, or the site states a one-resubmission (NIH A1) rule.
**Time window: none published — not found.** But there is a practical window: a resubmission still needs an open call to go into. Training awards recur once a year (early July), Project Concepts twice (Nov/May), topic RFAs may never recur on the same topic. So the effective resubmission clock is set by the calendar of calls, not by a policy.
**What must change: not specified beyond "addressing each of the reviewer's concerns."** There is no stated requirement to mark changes, no italics/bold convention, no percentage-changed rule.
**No appeal of a funding decision.** The handbook's "Grant Appeals Procedure/Rebuttal" (§5.9) is post-award only — it governs a Grantee Institution's 15-day response to a probation or corrective-action notice. The reviewer rebuttal (SRA/IDDP) is a *mid-review* right of reply, before the decision, and is offered at staff discretion. A first-time applicant should not read "appeals procedure" in the table of contents and expect a route to contest a rejection.
result.page_limits:
Single-spaced, **10-point font only** ("Type size limitations must be observed throughout the application. Use 10-point size font only"), margins **at least 1/2 inch in all directions**, no text boxes, figures inserted as .jpg or .gif (not .tif), each uploaded attachment 3–4 MB, unlocked PDFs. Violations are grounds for administrative triage: "Proposals with research plans exceeding the page limit will not be considered."

RESEARCH PLAN — varies by mechanism, this is the number people get wrong:
- Strategic Research Agreement: **12 pages** "maximum unless noted otherwise on RFA call document" (several RFAs override it — the vascularization call sets **10 pages**)
- Career Development Award: **12 pages** including figures and tables
- Kellogg Family Early-Career Patient-Oriented Diabetes Research Award: **12 pages**
- Postdoctoral Fellowship: **7 pages** including figures and tables
- Advanced Postdoctoral Fellowship: **7 pages**
- Innovative Grant: **3 pages** including figures and tables, not including references
- Literature Cited / references: **no page limit** in every mechanism

REQUIRED STRUCTURE of the research plan (fixed headings, not free-form): a) Specific Aims; b) Background and Significance of this work to type 1 diabetes; c) Preliminary Studies/Results (if applicable); d) Research Design and Methods; e) Literature Cited. Fellowships add e) other aspects of the training environment and f) planned coursework *inside* the 7 pages.

OTHER COMPONENTS:
- Letter of Intent: **2 pages** on the RMS360 template (typical across RFAs; the organ-on-a-chip call used 4)
- Future Career Plans Statement: **2 pages** (PDF, APF, CDA, Kellogg)
- Training Plan Statement, written by the sponsor, includes biosketch + list of previous trainees: **2 pages** (PDF, APF) / **4 pages** (Kellogg ECPODRA)
- Introduction to Revised Application / rebuttal letter (resubmissions only): **2 pages**
- Abstracts: two abstracts, one scientific and one lay; the lay abstract is broken into 6 named categories (General Audience Summary, Technical Abstract, Objective, Background/Rationale, Anticipated Outcome, Relevance to type 1 diabetes) and **each category has a 600-word limit**
- Biosketch: **Breakthrough T1D or NIH format both accepted**, uploaded to the RMS360 *profile* (auto-appended), not to the application

AMBIGUITY WORTH FLAGGING: the handbook says the resubmission introduction and prior summary statement "must be included in the Resubmission section of the Research Plan," while the SRA checklist calls the rebuttal "included in the research plan and does not exceed 2 pages," and the fellowship checklists list "Introduction to Revised Application" as a separate Research Plan line item alongside "Research Plan (7 pages maximum)." Whether the 2 pages count against the 7/12-page limit is not stated unambiguously. Since over-length means automatic triage, this is exactly the question to email preawardsupport@BreakthroughT1D.org about before you write.
required_documents: RMS360 account for the PI, plus RMS360 accounts for all Co-PIs (each with an up-to-date biosketch in their profile) — registration, not a document, but a submission blocker

result.program_officer_norms:
**Expected — closer to NIH than to a typical private foundation, and for two mechanisms it is mandatory.** This funder is unusual: staff scientists are co-developers of the proposal, not gatekeepers you route around. Four distinct levels, all in the funder's own words:

1. **Mandatory (IDDP / for-profit).** "Whether via an RFA or ad hoc, IDDP applicants should contact Breakthrough T1D staff before submitting an LOI" and "Potential applicants **must** contact Breakthrough T1D Research staff prior to submitting an LOI. Discussions are facilitated with a non-confidential pitch deck and ideas for a potential research project." Named scientific contacts appear in each RFA for exactly this.

2. **Structurally mandatory (Strategic Research Agreement).** "Submission of an application **requires permission from Breakthrough T1D** and is initiated with an LOI submitted to Project Concept Call in RMS360, an open Breakthrough T1D Funding Opportunity, or by direct invitation from Breakthrough T1D Staff." And once invited: "The Breakthrough T1D scientific personnel works collaboratively with the investigator or investigator team to develop a full application in accordance with Breakthrough T1D strategic objectives." You cannot submit an unsolicited SRA.

3. **Strongly recommended (clinical / human-subjects work).** "It is strongly recommended that the principal investigator [PI] speaks with the Breakthrough T1D scientific manager prior to submitting the study documents."

4. **Encouraged (topic RFAs, budget/scope exceptions, eligibility edge cases).** CGM–pump RFA: "Applicants are encouraged to consult with the Breakthrough T1D scientific staff below to discuss the alignment of their proposal to this RFA and to develop the projected study concept." Vascularization RFA: "If your project budget and/or timeline exceeds $900,000 and/or 3 years, please discuss with Breakthrough T1D staff." Innovative RFA: if you need more than $200k or more than a year, "please contact the administrative contact listed below to discuss possible options for submission." Training RFAs: applicants whose career gaps (parenting, caregiving, personal health, COVID shutdowns) push them outside the eligibility window "should reach out to Breakthrough T1D staff ahead of their application submission. Breakthrough T1D aims to be flexible and adjust these time frames if necessary and appropriate" — that is a written invitation to ask for an eligibility waiver, and asking is the only way to get one.

**WHEN in the cycle.** Before the LOI, not after. For two-stage RFAs the LOI-to-outcome window is only 2–4 weeks and the useful conversation is in the weeks *before* the LOI deadline; RFAs often pair with an informational webinar ~2 weeks before the LOI date (e.g. "Informational Webinar and Q&A 13 January 2026 (12PM–12:45PM EST)", register by 12 Jan) — attend it, it is the cheapest access to the programme scientist. For training awards, contact in May–June for a 1–2 July deadline. Once a full proposal is submitted, contact is over: "status of an application will not be given by phone."

**WHO to contact — the roles are split and mixing them up wastes a week.**
- *Scientific fit, scope, budget size, whether your idea belongs in this RFA* → the named **Scientist / Senior Scientist / Associate Director of Research** printed in each RFA (e.g. aghavami@breakthrought1d.org for devices; abashore@BT1D.org for cell therapy/vascularization; aguzman@BreakthroughT1D.org for in-vitro modelling; jvieth@BreakthroughT1D.org for autoimmunity).
- *RMS360 mechanics, eligibility, forms, attachments, "does my 2-page introduction count against the page limit"* → the named **Program Administrator** in the RFA (e.g. smukerjee@breakthrought1d.org for all four training awards; mmeyer@BreakthroughT1D.org; mprakash@BT1D.org) or the general **preawardsupport@BreakthroughT1D.org**.
- *Active-award questions after you win* → postawardsupport@BreakthroughT1D.org.
- *Human-subjects design* → your assigned Breakthrough T1D scientific manager / Clinical Trial Management group.

**What experienced applicants actually ask.** Is this project inside the current Research Strategy and which priority area does it map to (alignment "will be given priority consideration in the review process"). Is the idea already covered in the existing portfolio — staff explicitly weigh "relevance of the proposed research in complementing the existing Breakthrough T1D project portfolio", so they will tell you if you are duplicating a funded grant. Is my budget/duration plausible for this call, and should I ask for the exception. Am I eligible given my career gap or my faculty-appointment date. Should this be an SRA, an Innovative Grant, or an IDDP. For clinical work: will this trigger clinical review and what will the committee want to see. What they do *not* ask: for a preview of the score, or for feedback on draft text — staff co-develop invited SRA full proposals, but do not pre-review unsolicited drafts.
result.funded_examples_source:
**Primary: the Breakthrough T1D Global Research Portfolio / research abstracts database — https://www.breakthrought1d.org/explore-research/funded-research/**. A searchable, filterable, exportable database of the funder's own grants. Filters: Funding Mechanism (Strategic Research Agreement, Career Development Award, Industry Development, etc.), Research Priority Area (Beta Cell Replacement, Immunotherapies, Prevention, etc.), Grant Status (Active or Complete), plus geography and institution. Each record shows Principal Investigator, Project Title, Grant Duration, Institution, Award Amount and **Lay Abstract**. The site's stated search conventions: "Geographic (US-based): State abbreviation followed by country (no commas); Geographic (non-US): Country (no abbreviations); Institution: Keyword only." There is also a map view — click a state or country for institutions, current funding and abstracts. Roughly 500 active grants. (This page 403s a plain fetch behind Cloudflare; it was read through a rendering browser fetch. It renders fine in a normal browser.)

**What is public and what is not — this is the honest limit.** Handbook §5.3.2: "Most grant materials submitted to Breakthrough T1D are for internal Breakthrough T1D use only. Exceptions include the Lay Abstract submitted at the time of Application and the Web Progress Reports, submitted on an annual basis with the Annual and Final Progress Report." So: **lay abstracts and annual/final lay progress reports are public; full applications, research plans, budgets, reviewer critiques and summary statements are not.** There is no NIH-RePORTER equivalent exposing specific aims pages, and no published "sample funded application" library from Breakthrough T1D or, as far as I could establish, from university research offices for this funder. Do not promise a reader they can read a funded Breakthrough T1D proposal.

**How to work around that, in descending order of usefulness:**
1. Read 10–20 lay abstracts in your priority area from the portfolio, filtered to your target mechanism — this is the single best proxy for "what wins here", because the lay abstract is written by the funded PI to the funder's own six-category template that you will also have to fill in.
2. Read the annual Web Progress Reports on completed grants in the same area — they show what milestones the funder actually accepted, which matters because SRAs are milestone-driven.
3. Affiliate results pages publish named awardees per competition, e.g. https://breakthrought1d.ca/research/grant-opportunities/ carries a "Results" link for each past round.
4. Find the resulting papers: grantees must acknowledge Breakthrough T1D with the grant number, so a literature search on the acknowledgement string surfaces the science a given grant produced.
5. Ask a current or former awardee at your institution — the portfolio's institution filter tells you exactly who they are, which is the intended use of that filter for an early-career applicant.
6. For co-funded work, The Leona M. and Harry B. Helmsley Charitable Trust's own grants listing overlaps the Breakthrough T1D portfolio (the application asks permission to share with Helmsley).

unresolved: US TRAINING AWARD REVIEW ARC — not found. The four FY27 training RFAs (PDF, APF, CDA, Kellogg) contain no timeline table: no review date, no notification date, no earliest start date. The handbook adds nothing. Only the deadline (2 July 2026) and the 'FY27' label are published. The 8-month LOI-to-start figure comes from topic RFAs and must not be transferred to training awards. Ask smukerjee@breakthrought1d.org.
NUMBER OF PERMITTED RESUBMISSIONS — not found. No published cap anywhere (no NIH-style A1 rule stated). Absence of a stated limit is not the same as unlimited; confirm with preawardsupport.
RESUBMISSION TIME WINDOW — not found. No stated expiry on how long a summary statement stays usable for a resubmission.

WHETHER THE 2-PAGE RESUBMISSION INTRODUCTION COUNTS AGAINST THE RESEARCH-PLAN PAGE LIMIT — ambiguous in the source. Handbook §3 places it 'in the Resubmission section of the Research Plan'; the SRA checklist says the rebuttal is 'included in the research plan'; the fellowship/CDA checklists list it as a separate Research Plan item beside 'Research Plan (7/12 pages maximum)'. Over-length triggers automatic triage, so this must be confirmed in writing before drafting.

REVIEWER IDENTITY AND PANEL STRUCTURE — not published. No standing study sections, no published reviewer rosters, no published scoring scale or score ranges, no published success rates or paylines for any mechanism. Review is 'internal Breakthrough T1D Scientific Staff or externally by a Scientific Review Panel at the discretion of Breakthrough T1D Scientific Staff and Senior Management' — the choice between the two is discretionary and not disclosed to applicants in advance.

WHETHER CRITIQUES ARE RELEASED TO UNSUCCESSFUL APPLICANTS — conditional and unquantified. 'For applications receiving a full review, critiques containing the reviewers' comments MAY be provided.' No stated entitlement.

WHETHER A REJECTED APPLICATION CAN BE APPEALED — no published route. The handbook's 'Grant Appeals Procedure/Rebuttal' (§5.9) governs only a grantee institution's 15-day response to post-award probation or corrective action. Do not present it as a route to contest a funding decision.

PROJECT CONCEPT LOI PAGE LIMIT AND TEMPLATE — not found on the public site; the template lives inside RMS360 behind login. Topic RFAs typically specify 2 pages (one specified 4), so 2 pages is a reasonable working assumption but is not established for the Project Concept call specifically.

The last call document I could retrieve is FY25 (deadline 24 Oct 2024). A closed listing is not evidence the mechanism was discontinued; the handbook still carries it.

The 1 July 2025 / 2 July 2026 training-award pattern and the 5–6 Nov / 5–6 May Project Concept pattern are inferred from two and three observed cycles respectively, not from a funder statement that these dates recur. Present them as an observed pattern with a 'verify on the page' instruction, never as a guarantee.

result.funder_system:
Leukemia & Lymphoma Society, rebranded **Blood Cancer United (BCU)** in 2025. Both domains are live and interlinked: lls.org redirects/mirrors to bloodcancerunited.org, and the legacy portal host lls.fluxx.io still appears as a sign-in link on current program pages. All 2026-2027 guideline PDFs are branded "Blood Cancer United" and the contact address is researchprograms@bloodcancerunited.org.

ROUTE NOTE (house rule): plain WebFetch returned HTTP 403 on every bloodcancerunited.org page, and the guideline PDFs sit behind a Widen pdf.js viewer that returns only the viewer shell to a plain fetch. Everything below was read from the funder's own pages and its own PDFs via a rendering browser (page text + pdf.js text extraction), not from a search index. Read 2026-09-18.

ONE CENTRAL MACHINE, MANY MECHANISMS. The machinery genuinely is identical across mechanisms:
- one portal (Fluxx), one account, one email address for all questions
- one cross-programme rulebook: "Research Grant Programs Policies & Procedures, Revised March 2026" (https://llsorg.widen.net/s/lhgrqln9lz/en-policies-and-procedures.pdf)
- one annual rhythm: every 2026-2027 mechanism notifies in July 2027 and starts 1 October 2027
- per-mechanism Guidelines & Instructions PDF that is re-issued every cycle ("Download the most up to date ... template each time you apply ... these are updated annually")

MECHANISMS AND WHO THEY ARE FOR (2026-2027 cycle; status as of 2026-09-18):
- CDP Fellow — postdoc with <=3 yrs postdoc experience as of 1 July of award-start year. 3 yrs, max $70k/yr, min $65k to salary, +$3,600/yr childcare. Salary only, not a project grant. OPEN.
- CDP Special Fellow — 3-5 yrs postdoc/instructor. 2 or 3 yrs, max $75k/yr, min $70k salary, +childcare. OPEN.
- CDP Scholar — independent tenure-track faculty, first independent position started >=4 and <=8 yrs before 1 January of the award-start year, NOT a full professor by the start date, must already hold >=$200k/yr blood-cancer funding for >=3 yrs. 5 yrs, max $120k/yr. Review is programme-based, not project-based. OPEN.
- CDP Scholar in Clinical Research — MD, independent clinical researcher whose work "must directly involve patients". 5 yrs, max $125k/yr. OPEN.
- TRP (Translational Research Program) — established independent investigator (>3 yrs independent). 3 yrs, max $250k/yr / $750k total, IDC capped at 10%, <=40% of direct costs on post-doctoral-degree salaries. 2027 cycle requires in vivo proof of concept for small molecules (in vitro with patient samples may pass for some MoAs; in vitro acceptable for some cell/immunotherapies). OPEN.
- DGP (Discovery Grant Program) — basic/discovery mechanism, >3 yrs in an independent faculty appointment at LOI. Same $250k/yr / $750k / 10% IDC ceiling. CLOSED for 2026-2027 (LOI passed 12 Aug 2026).
- ACT (Academic Clinical Trials) — investigator-initiated Phase 1/2 trials able to enrol within 3-6 months of 1 Oct 2027. Up to $1M over up to 3 yrs ($200k yr 1, $400k yrs 2-3), IDC capped at 15%. Co-funded with Rising Tide Foundation. OPEN.
- SMART — US-citizen/PR medical students (ideally 3rd/4th yr, 2nd yr considered) at schools NOT affiliated with an NCI-Designated Cancer Center or with limited malignant-haematology research. One year full-time lab research; $75,000 living + $5,000 relocation + $6,000 conference. OPEN.
- Periodic RFP initiatives: Equity in Access, SCOR, HCL2030, IMPACT, MCL2, RAFL-I, CMML initiative. All currently closed; they open as dated RFPs on the same portal.
- TAP (Therapy Acceleration Program) is a venture/partnership arm, not a grant application route.

INTERNATIONAL: CDP and TRP both state "The program welcomes applications worldwide from appropriate non-profit academic institutions and investigators of any nationality." TRP has a ring-fenced Snowdome Foundation slot for one meritorious Australian-linked application. SMART is US-only.
result.submission_portal:
**Blood Cancer United Research Portal, a Fluxx instance at https://bloodcancerunited.fluxx.io** (legacy link https://lls.fluxx.io/user_sessions/new is still published on the CDP page and appears to reach the same system). Not ProposalCentral, not Grants.gov — a search index will tell you ProposalCentral; the funder's own guidelines do not.

THE HIDDEN LONG-LEAD ITEM — you cannot self-register. Policies & Procedures (rev. March 2026): "Applicants must have an account to submit a letter of intent and/or a full application. To request an account, please complete the intake form located at this link: Account Creation Request; the Research Administration team will send an email with account details once created." TRP guidelines are blunter: "Only Blood Cancer United staff members have administrative permission to create new accounts." The intake form currently resolves to https://www.llsform.org/ho0999SER/qm43km6adu/index.html (linked as "create a new account" from every programme page). Returning applicants reuse their old login; password reset is self-service.

ALSO LONG-LEAD, AND ROUTINELY MISSED:
1. Your INSTITUTION must be registered too, with named officials in Fluxx: Institutional Signing Official, Financial Officer, Technology Transfer Official, admin/research administrator, optional post-award contact. "If your institution is not listed, contact researchprograms@bloodcancerunited.org for assistance." Start this weeks out.
2. **ORCiD iD is mandatory** for CDP and must be supplied at the LOI phase (https://orcid.org/).
3. Reference-letter writers upload directly and blind through the portal via a unique emailed link; the applicant registers them in the portal during the LOI phase and can never see the letters.
4. Administrators/assistants can be given their own portal accounts to help you.

MECHANICS THAT BITE: clicking "Submit" locks that phase; you must self-identify your status from two indicators in the portal ("It is the applicant's responsibility to determine their status"); confirmation emails arrive within 2 business days and often land in spam; the final upload is ONE combined PDF in the template's exact order.

SMART IS THE EXCEPTION: it is not submitted through Fluxx. You "apply for consideration" through an interest form linked from the SMART page, after reading the SMART RFA (https://llsorg.widen.net/s/rcmz9qrkln/en-smart-rfp).
result.deadline_structure:
DATED, PUBLISHED, PER-MECHANISM, AND ANNUALLY RECURRING — not rolling, not per-solicitation-only. Every deadline is a calendar date at **3:00 PM Eastern Time**. Funder's own words: "The submission deadlines will be enforced. Please note that all times are Eastern Time (ET). If any date falls on a weekend or US holiday, the deadline becomes the next business day." And: "Do not ask for exceptions to these policies, including but not limited to exceptions to deadlines or making corrections to your document past the deadline."

2026-2027 CYCLE, AS PUBLISHED (checked 2026-09-18):

CDP (all four subcategories share one date set) — three gates, not one:
- Eligibility phase opens July 2026; **closes 15 October 2026, 3:00 PM ET**
- Eligibility determination: rolling, "typically within 2 business days of submission" (may take up to 10)
- LOI phase opens immediately after eligibility approval; **closes 1 November 2026, 3:00 PM ET**
- Blind letters of reference due **15 November 2026, 3:00 PM ET**
- Full application **closes 15 November 2026, 3:00 PM ET**
- Award Notification **July 2027**; Award Start **1 October 2027**

TRP — Call for Proposals 27 July 2026; **LOI 16 October 2026, 3:00 PM ET**; invite/decline notice by ~20 November 2026 ("If you have not received an email regarding your LOI approval by November 20, 2026, contact researchprograms@..."); **full application 22 January 2027, 3:00 PM ET**; Panel Review Meeting **March 2027**; Award Notification **July 2027**; start **1 October 2027** (end 30 September 2030).

ACT — **LOI 29 September 2026, 3:00 PM ET**; notification of full-application invite **late November 2026**; **full application 8 January 2027, 3:00 PM ET**; notification of awards **July 2027**; start **1 October 2027**.

DGP — **LOI 12 August 2026** (passed); invite notice early September 2026; **full application 3 November 2026, 3:00 PM ET**; awards July 2027; start 1 October 2027.

SMART — opened 1 June 2026; **applications due 15 December 2026, 3:00 PM ET**; acceptance notified February 2027; lab placement March 2027; contract signed by 1 May 2027; research runs 1 July 2027 - 30 June 2028.

Equity in Access (RFP initiative) — **LOI was 10 September 2026, 3:00 PM ET**, up to $750,000 per study, funding expected to begin October 2027. Page now reads closed.

THE PATTERN TO PLAN AGAINST: LOIs cluster August-October, full applications November-January, everyone hears in July, everyone starts 1 October. So the planning horizon for a 2027 start is roughly 11-13 months from the first gate. If you are reading this after a cycle's LOI has passed, the same programme reopens at approximately the same point the following year — the dates shift by days, not months.

TWO OPERATIONAL WARNINGS IN THE FUNDER'S OWN WORDS: "It is highly recommended that submissions are done the day prior to the deadline"; and, for TRP, "Late submissions due to last-minute activity (e.g., starting less than 24 hours before the deadline or resuming an application less than 3 hours before the deadline) will not be accommodated."

review_stages.stage: CDP only — Eligibility phase review by BCU scientific staff (a hard gate before you may write anything). "In prior award cycles, ~20-30% of eligibility requests were rejected." An eligibility submission rejected for administrative reasons (missing/unclear info) may be revised once before the eligibility deadline; "Submissions rejected based on eligibility criteria may not be resubmitted."
review_stages.timing: Rolling, typically within 2 business days of submission, up to 10 business days. Contact staff if nothing after 10 business days. Window: July 2026 to 15 Oct 2026.

review_stages.stage: LOI submission (CDP: after eligibility approval, fields lock and auto-populate the full application). TRP/ACT/DGP/EIA: the LOI is a triage gate — "We will only be inviting full applications that will be competitive."
review_stages.timing: CDP: 1 Nov 2026 (no triage; all eligible applicants proceed). TRP: 16 Oct 2026, invite/decline by ~20 Nov 2026 (~5 weeks). ACT: 29 Sep 2026, invite late Nov 2026 (~8 weeks). DGP: 12 Aug 2026, invite early Sep 2026 (~3 weeks).

review_stages.stage: Full application submitted as a single combined PDF plus web form
review_stages.timing: CDP 15 Nov 2026; DGP 3 Nov 2026; ACT 8 Jan 2027; TRP 22 Jan 2027

review_stages.stage: Peer review panel. CDP: "an independent, voluntary panel of experts"; application receives a Priority Score "based on the NIH scoring system", plus a separate Mission Score (1-5) for blood-cancer relevance. TRP: the TRP Subcommittee of the Medical & Scientific Affairs Committee; primary and secondary reviewers assign initial scores and "Only applications that fall above a scoring level determined by the committee chair will be discussed in detail" — i.e. NIH-style triage/streamlining; Overall Priority Score 1-9.
review_stages.timing: TRP panel meets March 2027 — about 2 months after the full-application deadline. CDP does not publish a panel month in the 2026-27 guidelines (the stale website FAQ implies a January review); treat the CDP panel month as unconfirmed.

review_stages.stage: Oversight/board approval — the equivalent of NIH Council. CDP: applications "within or near the payline will be presented to Blood Cancer United's oversight committees for approval." TRP: "priority scores and funding recommendations of the TRP Subcommittee will be presented to the Medical & Scientific Affairs Committee and Blood Cancer United's National Board of Directors for final determination of awardees. The Board of Directors will determine the number of awards funded based on scientific merit and the budget approved." Policies & Procedures: "After each review meeting, Blood Cancer United's Medical & Scientific Affairs Committee and Mission Oversight Committee meet to endorse and approve proposals for funding."
review_stages.timing: Between the panel (March 2027 for TRP) and notification (July 2027) — roughly March-June 2027

review_stages.stage: Notification. "Funding status is relayed by email only and is not available by phone." Portal status moves from "Under Review" to "Awarded", "Waitlist" or "Not Funded". Note the waitlist state — a near-miss is not always a no.
review_stages.timing: July 2027 for every 2026-27 mechanism (SMART: February 2027 acceptance, March 2027 lab placement)
