result.months_submission_to_award:
CDP: full application 15 Nov 2026 -> notification July 2027 = ~8 months; -> money starts 1 Oct 2027 = ~10.5 months. From the first gate (eligibility, 15 Oct 2026) to start = ~11.5 months; from the moment the eligibility form opens (July 2026) = ~15 months.
TRP: LOI 16 Oct 2026 -> start 1 Oct 2027 = ~11.5 months. Full application 22 Jan 2027 -> panel March 2027 (~2 months) -> notification July 2027 (~5.5 months) -> start 1 Oct 2027 (~8 months).
ACT: LOI 29 Sep 2026 -> start 1 Oct 2027 = ~12 months.
DGP: LOI 12 Aug 2026 -> start 1 Oct 2027 = ~13.5 months.
SMART: application 15 Dec 2026 -> acceptance Feb 2027 (~2 months) -> research begins 1 July 2027 (~6.5 months).
PLANNING RULE OF THUMB: about one year from first gate to first dollar, and about 8 months from the full application to a yes/no. Add 2-6 weeks before the LOI for the portal account and institutional-official registration, which you cannot create yourself.
result.resubmission_policy:
ALLOWED, UNCAPPED, AND INFORMAL — and nothing like NIH's A1 machinery. No numeric limit, no time window, and NO "Introduction to Resubmission" page. There is also no renumbering (no A0/A1): a resubmission is just a new application in the next cycle that discloses the prior one.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY REQUIRED, verbatim:
- CDP full application template, "Previous CDP Applications (if applicable)": "If you previously submitted a CDP application that was not funded, briefly describe what has changed from that application. Your prior application may be shared with the current review committee." (The Scholar version reads "a Scholar-level CDP application".) So the change narrative is a short template field, not a page — but reviewers may be handed your old application, so the changes must be real.
- TRP LOI web form, "Previous Submission": "Indicate whether you have previously submitted this proposal (or one similar) to Blood Cancer United and indicate the date of any prior submission."

WHAT ACTUALLY LIMITS YOU — read these as the real resubmission policy:
1. THE ELIGIBILITY CLOCK, not a resubmission counter. CDP Fellow: no more than 3 years total postdoctoral experience as of 1 July of the award-start year. Special Fellow: 4 years (3-yr award) or 5 years (2-yr award). Scholar: first independent position started >=4 and <=8 years before 1 January of the award-start year, and "those with the title of full professor (or equivalent) by the award start date are ineligible". In practice a Fellow applicant gets one or two shots; a Scholar applicant gets a five-cycle window. Only parental leave (max 1 yr), military service, and government-caused visa delays can pause the clock, requested in the Eligibility Window Extension section (visa claims need the application filed within 90 days of thesis defence/end of clinical training, extendable by another 90 in defined circumstances).
2. ONE APPLICATION PER PROGRAMME PER CYCLE. CDP: "Applicants may only submit one application." TRP/DGP PIs and Co-PIs: one application per programme per cycle, and you may apply to more than one BCU programme in a cycle "provided there is no substantial overlap in aims".
3. DUPLICATE-AIMS DISQUALIFICATION: "All duplicate grant proposal submissions with substantially overlapping aims are subject to administrative disqualification."
4. DGP: "If you currently hold a Discovery Grant Program (DGP) award, you may not apply to DGP in this cycle."
5. WITHIN a CDP cycle: an eligibility submission rejected on administrative grounds may be revised once before the eligibility deadline; "Submissions rejected based on eligibility criteria may not be resubmitted."

THE HARD PART OF RESUBMITTING HERE: you usually cannot see what went wrong. CDP: "Brief, anonymous feedback from the review panel may be provided but only when available." TRP: "Feedback will only be provided for applications discussed by the full review committee" — triaged applications get nothing. There is no summary statement equivalent to NIH's. Waitlisted is a distinct published outcome and is the strongest signal to come back next cycle.

NO APPEALS PROCESS is described anywhere in the March 2026 Policies & Procedures or in the CDP/TRP guidelines — treat "not funded" as final for that cycle.
result.page_limits:
TWO DIFFERENT REGIMES, AND CONFUSING THEM IS A REAL DISQUALIFICATION RISK.

CDP (Fellow, Special Fellow, Scholar, Scholar in Clinical Research) — NO overall page limit is published. Length is enforced by a LOCKED Word template with preset section lengths, preset margins and preset line spacing, plus hard character limits on portal fields:
- Summary (public-facing): 3-5 sentences, max 500 characters incl. spaces
- Title: 150 characters
- Lay Description: MINIMUM 2,000 and maximum 2,500 characters — a minimum, which people miss
- Scientific Abstract: 1,500 characters
- Brief Biography: 1,000 characters
- Clinical Protocol Summary (where applicable): up to 2 pages; "Do not attach a full clinical protocol."
FORMAT RULES THAT KILL APPLICATIONS: "Font must be black Arial 11 pt., including figure legends, which must be text boxes separate from the figure itself." Tables too. Figures themselves may use smaller text. "Outside of the figures themselves, should any font be smaller than Arial 11 pt. (including shrunken figure legend text boxes...), the application may be administratively disqualified without review." Line spacing is preset: "Any modifications in line spacing, particularly if the change allows for more text to fit into the page, may result in administrative rejection" (extra space BETWEEN paragraphs is allowed). Character limits include spaces.

TRP — real page limits:
- LOI: "Previous Studies/Preliminary Data" template, 1 page maximum (references optional, inside that page)
- Full application Section 1, Graphical Abstracts: 1 page maximum (one or two graphical abstracts, "must not be professionally developed")
- Full application Section 2, Project Description: **11 pages maximum including figures, OR 9 pages maximum if no Patient Involvement Plan is required**. Recommended (not enforced) internal split: Title/Specific Aim ~0.25 p; Scientific and Clinical Significance ~2.0 p; Previous Studies/Preliminary Data ~3.0 p; Research Methods ~1.25 p; Patient Involvement Plan ~2.0 p; Interaction with Other Investigators ~0.5 p; Resources and Environment ~1.0 p; References Cited ~1.0 p
- Budget Justification: 2 pages maximum
- Assurances: a one-page summary per essential clinical protocol, with the clinicaltrials.gov link
- Arial 11 pt, single spaced, preset margins, text + figures + references

ACT — LOI carries a Structured Clinical Abstract and a Patient Involvement Plan Summary (2 pages plus a table); the full Patient Involvement Plan comes at the full-application stage.

CROSS-CUTTING: the final upload is ONE PDF, assembled in the exact order given in the template. "Failure to submit as a single PDF in the order described on the template may result in disqualification." Nothing may precede the template — no cover letters. Extra attachments can disqualify you.

DRIFT WARNING — THE FUNDER CONTRADICTS ITSELF: the FAQ accordion on the live CDP page still says "all Applicants must use single-spaced text and Times New Roman 12 pt", refers to "LLS", a "January review date" and a "grant start date of July 1st". The 2026-2027 Guidelines & Instructions PDFs say Arial 11 pt and an award start of 1 October 2027. **The programme's Guidelines & Instructions PDF wins; the web FAQ is stale.** Anyone building from the website FAQ will format their application wrongly.
required_documents: PORTAL ACCOUNT requested in advance via the Account Creation Request intake form (staff-created only; https://www.llsform.org/ho0999SER/qm43km6adu/index.html), plus institutional registration naming the Institutional Signing Official, Financial Officer, Technology Transfer Official and research administrator
ORCiD iD — required for all CDP applicants at the LOI phase and must be kept current for the whole funding period

CDP ELIGIBILITY TEMPLATE (downloaded from the portal) — every position/title since the first doctoral-level programme, degree dates, oral thesis defence date AND date of conferral, postdoctoral clock accounting, Eligibility Window Extension request if applicable, full Sponsor details, and three Sponsor publications from the past 10 years. Journal acceptance letters required for any 'accepted' manuscript being counted

CDP LOI COMPONENTS: reference-letter-writer requests entered in the portal, ORCiD, first-author publication list in Blood citation format, research information (title 150 char, Summary 500 char, disease/technology/model/patient-sample tags), collaborators and mentors (names + institutions only; BCU may contact them to verify)

THREE BLIND REFERENCE LETTERS (max four), uploaded directly by the writers through unique emailed portal links, due at the FULL APPLICATION deadline. 'If there are not at least 3 letters of reference received by the full application deadline, the application will be administratively disqualified.' The Sponsor may not write one. Two from outside your institution is advantageous. Line up a backup writer

CDP FULL APPLICATION TEMPLATE (single PDF, template order): Applicant/Sponsor/Research info (Title and Summary must exactly match the LOI); Writing Sources declaration — you must state how much copying and how much AI/LLM use was involved, and 'excessive use of artificial intelligence/large language models is not allowed'; Previous CDP Applications; up to two Graphical Abstracts; Research Description with Data Attribution tables separating your own data from others'; Description of Models, Drugs/Reagents and Trials; Disease Demographics and Equitable Research Models and Approaches (scored — clear demographics earn a score boost, absence a score reduction); Age Focus (% paediatric); References in Blood format; Access to Non-Commercially Available Reagents/Drugs/Models; Sponsor Mentor Table; Sponsor Letter; Signature Page

NIH-FORMAT BIOSKETCHES for both applicant and Sponsor (CDP) or PI and Co-PI (TRP). No eRA Commons username needed. CDP: do NOT use the postdoctoral fellowship version and do not list coursework/grades

OTHER SUPPORT, as two SEPARATE documents: Sponsor/PI on the NIH Other Support form; CDP applicants on the BCU form inside the template. 'Failure to provide separate Other Support Documents for the applicant and for the Sponsor may result in administrative disqualification.' TRP requires specific aims listed for any pending grant that might overlap, and notification within 5 business days if an overlapping pending grant is decided after submission

SPONSOR LETTER (CDP) — signed, on institutional letterhead; must cover the applicant's position, how much of the application the applicant wrote, certification that the applicant's own data sections contain only the applicant's data, the Sponsor's mentoring record, the funding source for the applicant's research, an explicit TRAINING PLAN, and any co-mentor/mentoring team. 'The Sponsor Letter forms a critical part of the review process.' No co-Sponsors allowed

COLLABORATION / SUPPORT LETTERS where access to patient samples, animal models, proprietary drugs or specialised equipment is not already in your lab — signed, on letterhead, one or two short paragraphs, and deliberately NOT praising you (a praising letter gets recounted as a reference letter and can push you over the four-letter cap)

ASSURANCES with signed letters from the appropriate institutional official: IRB/human subjects (with OHRP assurance number), IACUC (with Animal Welfare Assurance number), recombinant DNA, biohazards. 'Any application without these letters attached will not be reviewed.' Pending approvals are acceptable at submission but must be documented before the award start date (ACT: within 6 months of award start)
CLINICAL PROTOCOL SUMMARY where applicable — up to 2 pages with NCT number, approval date, compliance number, IRB status; never the full protocol

BUDGET and BUDGET JUSTIFICATION (TRP: itemised, year 1 detailed with years 2-3 projected, justification max 2 pages; travel capped at $2,000/yr; equipment over $4,000 itemised; dues, tuition, books, journals and publication costs impermissible). CDP budgets are salary-only: no lab costs, equipment, travel or tuition, indirect costs <=5% of the total award and <=$3,500/yr, no carry-forward

RESEARCH TAGS selected from BCU's fixed list (major disease, specific disease, key terms). 'Inaccurate or overly broad tagging may negatively affect application review' — Health Disparities, Health Policy and Survivorship are rarely appropriate in CDP
SIGNATURE PAGE with all requested signatures (electronic signatures accepted). Signatures are NOT required at the TRP LOI stage

SMART (different route): personal statement on interest in blood cancer research, a letter of support from a dean of the medical school, and a second letter from a professor or other doctoral-level administrator
result.program_officer_norms:
THERE IS NO NIH-STYLE NAMED PROGRAM OFFICER. There is one shared mailbox — **researchprograms@bloodcancerunited.org** — staffed by BCU scientific and research-administration staff, and it is the only channel. Contact is EXPECTED on eligibility and fit, and EXPLICITLY REFUSED on status and results. That split is the whole culture of this funder.

WHAT EXPERIENCED APPLICANTS ACTUALLY ASK, AND WHEN:
- JULY-OCTOBER, before the eligibility/LOI gate — the high-value window. "Which subcategory am I?" is the single most useful question: BCU itself says "You may be contacted by a Blood Cancer United staff member if the information provided on your eligibility request suggests that you may be better suited for a different award category." Asking first is cheaper than being rejected: "In prior award cycles, ~20-30% of eligibility requests were rejected."
- Eligibility-clock edge cases: parental leave, military service, visa delays, non-US training structures, unusual position titles ("Applicants whose titles significantly differ ... must have a letter submitted by the full application deadline explaining the position"), gaps in training. These are pre-cleared by email with documentation.
- OVERLAP questions, invited in the funder's own words: "Contact researchprograms@bloodcancerunited.org with any questions about this policy or to discuss with Blood Cancer United scientific staff any questions concerning potential overlap between applications." CDP adds, for the case where your proposal overlaps your Sponsor's own BCU application in the same cycle: "Contact researchprograms@bloodcancerunited.org for questions about specific proposals."
- K99 concurrency — "It is required that Fellow applicants and Fellow awardees notify Blood Cancer United of any developments in the K99 application process."
- Institution or institutional official not listed in Fluxx; adding a Financial Officer or Technology Transfer Official; getting an assistant a portal account.
- Post-LOI personnel changes (TRP): Co-PI or key personnel changes need prior written approval and "may not be approved" — so finalise the team before the LOI.
- Submitted in error, or a wrong PDF uploaded: staff will help, but only if the email and the corrected file arrive BEFORE the deadline (CDP: at least one hour before). "There are no exceptions to this rule."
- Missing confirmation email after 2 business days; missing eligibility decision after 10 business days; a reference letter-writer who never got their link after 2 business days.

WHAT IS DISCOURAGED OR FLATLY REFUSED:
- Status chasing. CDP: "Please do not call or email regarding status updates." TRP: "Please do not call or email Blood Cancer United to determine whether the application has been received, when it will be reviewed, or the results of the review. Please check the Blood Cancer United Research Portal for the status of your application."
- Results by phone: "Funding status is relayed by email only and is not available by phone." Policies & Procedures: "No results are given over the telephone."
- Asking for special treatment: "To create a fair process for all applicants ... Do not ask for exceptions to these policies, including but not limited to exceptions to deadlines or making corrections to your document past the deadline."
- Negotiating the funding agreement: "Blood Cancer United funding agreements are non-negotiable except where it pertains to state law."

TIMING NORM, in the funder's own words: "it is imperative that any questions be posed to Blood Cancer United as far ahead as possible", because "Blood Cancer United's response time to questions may be delayed by the high volume received near the deadline". Practical translation: email in July-September, not in the last fortnight.

WHO ELSE TO TALK TO — because the mailbox is not your mentor: for CDP the Sponsor's track record IS an eligibility criterion (>=3 first/last-author blood-cancer papers in 10 years, >=$200k/yr blood-cancer funding active past the award start), so the real pre-submission conversation is with the prospective Sponsor and with previously funded BCU investigators in your department, whom you can identify by name and institution from the Research We Fund database. For a junior Sponsor (<=5 years independent), BCU explicitly recommends assembling a mentorship team.
result.funded_examples_source:
**https://bloodcancerunited.org/research/research-we-fund** — BCU's searchable database of currently active funded projects, and the closest thing this funder has to NIH RePORTER. Each record carries: PI name, institution, city/state/country, the funding programme, the project title, a several-sentence lay/scientific project summary written by the awardee, and the project term (start and end dates). It is filterable by grant programme via a query parameter (the programme pages link straight into pre-filtered views, e.g. ?sort_bef_combine=created_DESC&search=&grant_program[NNNNN]=NNNNN), and every programme page carries a "See our active [CDP/TRP/ACT/DGP/SMART/Equity in Access] portfolio" link into it.

Companion page: https://bloodcancerunited.org/research/who-we-fund (investigator-centred view; awardees sign a media consent and supply a headshot as a funding-agreement condition, which is why these pages exist and are reliably populated).

HOW TO USE IT LIKE A GRANT-WRITER, not a reader: filter to your own mechanism, then read 10-15 summaries in a row. What you are calibrating is (a) the Mission Score in practice — how explicitly successful applicants tie the work to blood cancer, patient samples and blood-cancer models, and (b) the register of the public summary, which is a real scored deliverable (CDP Lay Description, min 2,000/max 2,500 characters). Then find awardees at your own institution or in your subfield and ask them for their actual application — that is the only route to a full funded application here.

TESTIMONIALS as a secondary source: each programme page carries 1-2 named awardee testimonials with institution and funded project title (e.g. Kasey Leger, Seattle Children's, CDP Scholar in Clinical Research; Joseph Tuscano, UC Davis, TRP; Dan Pollyea, Colorado, ACT; Craig Jordan, Colorado, DGP). Useful for identifying people to approach.

Fuller worked examples: the Equity in Access page publishes near-full project descriptions for its 2025 grantees — PI and Co-PI names and titles, project title, background, explicit Aim 1/2/3, study design and significance (e.g. Friedman/Zullig, Duke/Durham VA, "REACH"; Hantel/Lathan/Stone, Dana-Farber). That is the most application-like public text BCU publishes.

WHAT DOES NOT EXIST HERE — say so plainly to any applicant: BCU publishes NO sample full applications, NO reviewer critiques and NO summary statements. There is no RePORTER-style budget/abstract API. Even your OWN feedback is conditional: CDP "Brief, anonymous feedback from the review panel may be provided but only when available"; TRP "Feedback will only be provided for applications discussed by the full review committee." Some US university research offices circulate successful LLS/BCU applications internally — that, plus asking a named awardee directly, is the only way to read a real one.

result.funder_system:
NASA — dominated by one omnibus solicitation, with four other machineries beside it.

(1) ROSES (Research Opportunities in Space and Earth Sciences), the Science Mission Directorate's annual omnibus NASA Research Announcement (NRA). Current live one: NNH25ZDA001N, "INITIAL ANNOUNCEMENT ISSUED: JULY 10, 2025", Assistance Listings 43.001, OMB 2700-0092. It states: "Approximately 35 proposal opportunities comprise this 'ROSES' Solicitation"; "Available Funding for the entire omnibus NOFO: Approximately $125-150 Million, contingent on funding"; "Anticipated number of awards ... Approximately 300 Awards". Program elements are lettered by division: A = Earth Science, B = Heliophysics, C = Planetary Science, D = Astrophysics, E = suborbital/flight, F = cross-division (incl. F.5 FINESST, the graduate-student mechanism). An order-of-precedence rule governs everything: "1. Statutes ... 2. Program elements 3. Division Research Program Overviews 4. The Summary of Solicitation ... 5. The NASA Grant and Cooperative Agreement Manual (GCAM)" — i.e. the individual program element always wins over the general rules. This is the single most important thing a first-time NASA applicant gets wrong.
(2) Announcements of Opportunity (AOs) for PI-led missions and instruments, run by the Science Office for Mission Assessments (SOMA) at Langley — two-step, Concept Study Reports, TMC evaluation. Forward-looking "Planning List for SMD Solicitations" (latest posted version dated 2026-07-21) tells you what AOs are coming.
(3) SBIR/STTR — entirely separate portal and cycle, and currently in transition: the program page (schedule table "last updated 9/3/26") says "the NASA SBIR/STTR program is undergoing a change from our traditional solicitation cycle to a Broad Agency Announcement, or BAA."
(4) NASA Postdoctoral Program (NPP) — run for NASA by ORAU on its own portal, not NSPIRES. The one NASA mechanism with genuinely stable calendar dates.
(5) Unsolicited proposals — accepted year-round through NSPIRES: "NASA accepts only unsolicited proposals submitted electronically via NSPIRES in response to the unsolicited proposal response structure" (2026 NASA Guidebook for Proposers for Unsolicited Proposals). Explicitly not a route for start-up funds or for work that fits an open solicitation.

Also on NSPIRES but outside ROSES: STMD calls (e.g. Early Career Faculty), NASA EPSCoR, Space Grant, MUREP.

Status note as of 2026-09-18, and this is drift-relevant: ROSES-2026 has NOT been released. NASA announced "ROSES-2026 to be released July 2026"; the ROSES-25 blog's latest entries are Amendments 70–74 dated within the last days, all amendments to ROSES-25, and https://solicitation.nasaprs.com/ROSES2026 resolves to an NSPIRES page returning "No solicitation details were found". ROSES-25 remains the live solicitation, with Tables 2 and 3 amended 09/02/2026 and an NSPIRES close date of January 28, 2027.
result.submission_portal:
**NSPIRES — https://nspires.nasaprs.com — is the default and the system of record**, even when you submit elsewhere. Grants.gov (https://www.grants.gov) is a permitted alternative but since ROSES-25 it is opt-in, not automatic.

The hidden long-lead chain, in order (start this ~2 months out, not 2 weeks out):

1. **SAM.gov registration for the organization** (https://sam.gov/) — required before applying, and the ROSES SoS warns in its own words: "Proposing organizations must be registered in SAM. Registration may take several weeks to complete so proposing organizations are encouraged to begin well in advance of the proposal due date." You must "Provide its Unique Entity Identifier (UEI) in each application" and "Continue to maintain an active registration in SAM.gov ... at all times during which there is an active Federal award or an application ... under consideration by NASA."
2. **Organization registration in NSPIRES**, which can only be started by the SAM e-business POC: "Once the organization has a SAM record, the listed Organization Point of Contact must register as a user with NSPIRES, log on, then begin the organization registration process." Registration for either system "must be performed by an organization's electronic business point-of-contact in the System for Award Management."
3. **Individual NSPIRES account for every single person on the proposal** — PI, every Co-I, and even unpaid Collaborators: "Each individual team member ... must be registered in NSPIRES. NSPIRES registration applies equally for proposals submitted via Grants.gov since these databased names and affiliations are used for conflict-of-interest checking." People must register themselves; nobody may register a second party.
4. **Each team member must then electronically confirm participation in NSPIRES before submission.** If one person doesn't click confirm, the AOR gets a hard error and cannot submit. This is the classic day-of-deadline failure.
5. **Grants.gov route only:** organization must also be registered in Grants.gov, and the program element must have been set up to receive Grants.gov applications — which since ROSES-25 happens "only ... if it's requested at least 30 days in advance of the proposal due date" by emailing the program element point of contact with cc to sara@nasa.gov. On Grants.gov there is no NSPIRES participation-confirmation, so you must instead include written "Letters of Commitment" in the proposal, and the NSPIRES 4000-character abstract limit is not enforced at entry but is truncated on ingestion.

**Who presses submit:** not the PI. "the electronic proposal must be submitted in its entirety by an Authorized Organizational Representative (AOR)". The author "releases" the proposal and the AOR "submits" it. Verify afterwards under NSPIRES → "proposals" → "Submitted Proposals/NOIs"; PI and AOR both get a confirmation email. NOIs are the exception — the PI submits those directly, "no action by an organization's AOR is required to submit an NOI."

**Portal exceptions:** Astrophysics General Investigator/General Observer Phase-1 observing requests go to the ARK/RPS system (http://heasarc.gsfc.nasa.gov/ark/rps/), not NSPIRES, and are due at 4:30 pm ET. SBIR/STTR goes through the SBIR/STTR Electronic Handbook (EHB) at https://ehb8.gsfc.nasa.gov/ — "Paper submissions are not accepted." NPP applications go to https://npp.orau.org/applicants/apply.html.

Help desks: NSPIRES nspires-help@nasaprs.com / (202) 479-9376, Mon–Fri 8am–6pm ET. Grants.gov support@grants.gov / (800) 518-4726, 24/7. Both are explicitly scoped: "The NSPIRES and Grants.gov Help Desks are qualified to answer questions about using their respective systems ... Questions of content and policy are to be directed to the Program Officer(s)."
result.deadline_structure:
**Per-solicitation. NASA has nothing like NIH's standard due dates, and this is the single biggest structural difference.** There is no table of recurring dates by activity code; there is a table of this year's dates that is amended continuously.

What is actually stable (the shape, not the dates):

- **Default cut-off time: 11:59 pm Eastern.** "Unless otherwise specified, the cut-off time is 11:59 pm Eastern Time." Repeated in Section IV(c): "Unless stated otherwise in the program element, the proposal deadline is 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time". Two standing exceptions: Astrophysics GI/GO Phase-1 via ARK/RPS at 4:30 pm ET, and no-due-date programs.
- **Late = dead, with almost no discretion.** "The vast majority of late proposals are rejected without review." Policy SPD-02B: "All proposals to programs with a fixed due date must be submitted no later than the proposal due date and time specified in the solicitation. Program officers shall not adopt policies, either formally or informally, that conflict with this requirement." A late proposal can only be reviewed if it "offers significant technical or cost advantages, as compared with proposals previously received," and only with the Selecting Official's written approval. And: "SMD does not pre-approve the submission of a late proposal ... The SMD program officer is not empowered to authorize the submission of a late proposal." Note the hard-nosed reason given: a competitor who gained no advantage from a due-date extension "would likely have a sustainable protest."
- **Three preliminary-step patterns**, and Tables 2/3 mark which applies to each element:
  - *NOI (Notice of Intent)*: requested by many Earth Science elements, mandatory for a few (examples named in ROSES-25: A.7 Water Quality Applications, B.5 RADIANT, D.5 Astrophysics Pioneers). "Proposals not proceeded by an on-time NOI will be returned without review." NOIs are due 11:59 pm ET; "NSPIRES is open for the submission of NOIs for typically 30 days, starting about 90 days in advance of the due date for the proposals themselves." NOIs must go through NSPIRES even if the full proposal goes through Grants.gov.
  - *Two-step (Step-1 → Step-2)*: Step-1 is usually just the 4000-character summary, submitted by the AOR, no budget. Either "nonbinding" (Step-2 allowed even if discouraged) or "binding" (Step-2 only if invited). Either way: "proposers will be informed no later than four weeks prior to the Step-2 due date whether their Step-2 proposal is 'encouraged' (or 'discouraged') or 'invited' (or 'not invited')."
  - *Two-phase*: Phase-1 observing request to the observatory system, then a funding proposal.
- **Rolling options exist.** "No Due Date" (NoDD) and "Flexible Due Date" programs accept proposals "at any time during the open period of ROSES, generally without any preliminary statement like a Notice of Intent or Step-1 proposal." NoDD reviews are "held irregularly when a critical mass of proposals has been received"; Flexible Due Date (e.g. C.2 Solar System Science) has "reviews held on a regular cadence throughout the year" with internal cut-offs. A quiet grace rule for these: "If a proposal is created before the posted 'Proposals Due' close date, it can still be submitted for four weeks after that posted 'Proposals Due' close date."
- **Where the live dates are:** Table 2 (by due date) https://solicitation.nasaprs.com/ROSES2025table2 and Table 3 (by division/topic) https://solicitation.nasaprs.com/ROSES2025table3. Analogous URLs will exist for ROSES-2026. NASA also publishes subscribable **due-date Google calendars** (instructions PDF on the SARA library page) and an NSPIRES email-subscription service ("a subscriber may receive 75-100 notifications per year").

**Why any hard-coded date rots — evidence from this cycle, which is worth stating plainly in a user-facing interface:**
- NASA moved the whole ROSES release month from February to July starting with ROSES-2025, sliding every due date in the omnibus by ~5 months.
- ROSES-2026 was publicly announced for July 2026 and, as of 2026-09-18, has not appeared; ROSES-25 was instead extended, close date January 28, 2027.
- Individual elements move constantly by amendment: Amendment 74 (posted within ~2 days of 2026-09-18) is "A.14 Atmosphere Research Program Due Date Delay"; Amendment 39 extended C.2 Solar System Science to August 1, 2026 and A.4/A.10 to August 31, 2026. Tables 2 and 3 themselves were amended 09/02/2026, the Summary of Solicitation on 06/15/2026.
- F.5 FINESST, the graduate-student mechanism, historically closed in early February; in ROSES-25 its due date was July 14, 2026 (this date came from a search-index summary of NASA pages, not from a page I fetched directly — verify against Table 2 before publishing it).

**The two dated things that have actually held steady**, and which are the right kind of date to show a user: the **NASA Postdoctoral Program's three annual rounds, March 1 / July 1 / November 1** (next: November 1, 2026, 6 p.m. ET; Astrobiology participates only in the March and November rounds). These came from search-index summaries of NASA/AAS/ORAU pages rather than a directly fetched ORAU page — treat as high-likelihood, verify at npp.orau.org before display.

**Design implication for the interactive interface:** for NASA, show the *cadence and the preliminary-step pattern* statically (NOI ~90 days before, Step-1 → answer ≥4 weeks before Step-2, 11:59 pm ET, ~6 months to award) and pull the actual dates live from Table 2/Table 3 or deep-link to them plus the due-date calendar subscription. A frozen date list for NASA is wrong within weeks; the *structure* is stable across years.

result.months_submission_to_award: Selection announcement: 5 months is NASA's stated goal, 5-7 months is the stated normal range ("SMD's goal is to announce selections within 150 days of the proposal due date ... Selections are typically announced between 150 days and 220 days after the proposal due date"). Money/start: approximately 6 months after the due date, and "award start dates are rarely less than 6 months from the proposal due date." So plan 6-8 months from submission to being able to spend, and longer if the federal budget is late — NASA names this explicitly: "a delay in the budget process for NASA usually results in a delay of the selection announcement date." Interagency awards (NASA money to another federal agency) can take "as much as a year from selection to the arrival of funds." For NoDD/rolling programs the same ~6-month clock runs from the date you submit rather than from a common due date.
result.resubmission_policy:
**Allowed, unlimited in the general case, and — unlike NIH — a resubmission is not a distinct object.** There is no A1/A2 designation, no Introduction page, no required response-to-reviewers, and no penalty or credit for having tried before.

NASA's own words (ROSES-2025 Summary of Solicitation, Section I(f) "Successor, Renewal, Resubmitted, Multiple and Duplicate Proposals"):
- "resubmissions of previously declined proposals (GCAM section 14.3) are also welcome if in scope of the program element to which it is submitted. Resubmissions need not discuss how major weaknesses from previous submissions have been addressed."
- "Proposers are welcome to resubmit proposals (or tasks) that were not funded previously. Such submissions will be peer reviewed and considered with neither advantage nor disadvantage along with new proposals."
- Renewals/successors likewise: "such proposals will be considered with neither advantage nor disadvantage along with new proposals ... such proposals need not explicitly say that they are 'renewals'."

**No introduction page is required. No time window applies in the general case.** But three real limits, all set at the program-element or division level, which is where NASA's rules actually live:
1. **One proposal per PI per element, in some elements.** "Some program elements in Appendix B (Heliophysics), e.g., B.2 Heliophysics Foundational Research, prohibit any individual from being the Principal Investigator (PI) of more than one proposal in the same cycle."
2. **No concurrent duplicates.** B.1 Heliophysics and D.1 Astrophysics Research Program Overviews "prohibit the submission of proposals that are 'the same or essentially the same' proposals already under consideration. In such cases, the first proposal submitted will be evaluated but subsequent duplicate proposals will be returned without review."
3. **Planetary Science is the strict one, and it does impose a time window.** "the Planetary Science Division bars submission of duplicate proposals to multiple programs within a single ROSES year, or, in the case of the no due date programs, resubmission of proposals that were previously submitted within the past calendar year." See C.1 Planetary Science Research Program Overview, Section 3.2.

**Separate from resubmission: the appeal track.** SPD-09D "Debriefing and Reconsideration for NRA and CAN Proposals" gives declined proposers a debrief (oral, usually by phone, requestable for 30 days after the evaluation is sent; the PO must respond within 30 days) and then a written reconsideration request. Reconsideration is narrow: it "may only be made on the grounds of" factual errors or inconsistencies in the evaluation/selection basis, and "SMD will only take into account material in the original proposal or the evaluation. Requests for reconsideration based on results obtained after the proposal was submitted, or details that were published in papers but that were not discussed in the proposal, are not appropriate and will not be considered." The PO or Selecting Official "may require debriefing as a prerequisite for reconsideration." Winning a reconsideration does not guarantee funding. Practical advice implicit in the policy: take the debrief, then resubmit next cycle; reconsideration is for process errors, not for disagreement.
result.page_limits:
**The headline number is 15 pages, and every other number is a program-element override.** From ROSES-2025 Table 1 (Checklist), on the Scientific/Technical/Management (S/T/M) section: "Typically, 15 pages for full / Step-2 proposals but more may be permitted for some (e.g., 30 pp for D.5 Pioneers) and fewer for others (e.g., 5 pp combined for parts A and B of F.15 Artemis III Participating Scientists Program). Please read the program element and refer to the summary table of key information."

Component-by-component (ROSES-25 defaults; each can be superseded by the program element):
- Table of contents — "One page at most and optional."
- **S/T/M section — typically 15 pp**, and the only page-limited part. "The S/T/M section is page limited and only the parts specified in Table 1 are permitted. Proposals that exceed page limits, violate formatting rules, or contain extra material will be [penalized/returned]."
- References — "No page limit", but "No references to documents unavailable to reviewers."
- **Open Science and Data Management Plan (OSDMP) — 2 pages**, mandatory unless the element says otherwise; NASA publishes division-specific OSDMP templates.
- Table of Personnel and Work Effort — no stated limit; must show NASA-funded and non-NASA-funded commitment.
- Biographical sketches / CVs — **"No page limit"** (this changed; older guidance capped it). Required "For a PI and any Co-Is who would devote >10% of their time in any year to the proposed work." Must use the NASA Grants Policy format.
- Current and Pending Support — "not page limited"; required for PI and funded members >10%; explicitly excluded for collaborators, discouraged for students and foreign Co-Is.
- Statements of Commitment / letters — normally replaced by NSPIRES click-confirmation. Letters of endorsement "In general, not permitted", with narrow exceptions (foreign Co-Is need a letter from their national agency; commercial-vendor letters for non-FOP suborbital flights). Letters of resource support and, for ISS work, a letter of feasibility from the NASA Space Station Payload Office.
- Budget narrative + detailed budget — no page limit. **Critical NASA-specific rule:** "Omit all values for salary, fringe, or overhead" from the peer-reviewed budget section; those numbers go only in the NSPIRES cover-page budget and the separately uploaded "Total Budget" PDF.
- Facilities and Equipment — no page limit, description only.

**Formatting (enforced, and a real rejection risk):** 8.5" x 11.0"; one-inch margins with "No reviewable content in margins"; single-spaced, single-column; "No more than 5.5 lines per vertical inch"; "No more than 15 characters per horizontal inch, including spaces. This is typically consistent with a font size of 12." Figure/table text "must be easily legible without magnification", and "Text necessary for the proposal may not be solely in figures, tables, or their captions."

**Abstract:** 4000 characters, typed into the NSPIRES cover page — not into the proposal PDF.

**Separate uploads that are NOT part of the page-limited document:** the "Total Budget" PDF; the High-End Computing appendix (if you answered yes to the HEC question); and, for the large majority of elements, the **"Expertise and Resources Not Anonymized"** PDF required by dual-anonymous peer review.

result.program_officer_norms:
**Expected and in several cases mandatory. NASA sits closer to the NIH end than the foundation end — but the content of the conversation is different from NIH's.**

NASA's standing invitation, in its own words: "Questions regarding a program element should be directed to the program officer identified in the Summary Table of Key Information at the end of each program element or on the list of program officers on the SARA web page. Any clarifications or questions and answers that are published will be posted on the relevant program element's index page in NSPIRES." That last clause matters practically: before you email, check the element's NSPIRES page — your question may already be answered there, and if you ask a good one, the answer becomes public.

Routing rules worth knowing:
- Program-element questions → the named Program Officer (https://science.nasa.gov/researchers/sara/program-officers-list/, organized by division then program element, with names, emails, phone, bios).
- Questions about ROSES-wide rules or the Summary of Solicitation → sara@nasa.gov (the SMD Deputy Associate Administrator for Research's office). Conflicts between the GCAM and ROSES → sara@nasa.gov; conflicts between those and a program element → the element's POC, cc sara@nasa.gov.
- Can't find the right person → "contact the R&A Lead of the relevant Division or contact the Science Mission Directorate R&A Lead."
- Never email a proposal: "Proposals must not be submitted to this address."

**Four situations where contacting the PO before submission is REQUIRED, not optional** — these are the ones that catch first-time applicants:
1. **You want to submit via Grants.gov.** Since ROSES-25, most elements are not wired up for it unless "requested at least 30 days in advance of the proposal due date" from the POC with cc to sara@nasa.gov.
2. **You think the work should be a contract or a Funded Space Act Agreement rather than a grant** — "should communicate with the point of contact for that program element and cc sara@nasa.gov well in advance of proposal submission."
3. **Your team includes investigators or organizations funded via interagency awards** (restrictions applied to Appendices A-D and F.3 Exoplanets in ROSES-25) — PO approval required before submitting.
4. **You are bringing your own commercial suborbital launch vehicle** rather than using STMD's Flight Opportunities Program — "Inform the point of contact for the program element prior to submission and copy SARA@nasa.gov."

**What experienced applicants actually ask, based on what NASA's own documents anticipate:** Is this in scope for this element, or is a different element the right home? (The order-of-precedence rule makes "which element" the highest-leverage question in the whole process.) Is the budget scale realistic given the element's stated funding and expected number of awards? Can you enable Grants.gov for me? Is this team structure permitted here — can I use a Co-I/Science PI, are unfunded foreign Co-Is OK? For NoDD/Flexible programs, when is the next review actually being held? Is a data-sharing plan required in the S/T/M section for this element? And after the fact: may I have a debrief?

**What I could NOT establish, and will not invent:** I found no NASA policy statement that program officers will or will not read draft proposals or pre-proposal summaries. NIH's "send me your specific aims" convention has no documented NASA equivalent. Treat draft review as not found.

**Timing across the cycle:** ask scope/eligibility/logistics questions well before the deadline (the 30-day Grants.gov clock is the hard one). Go quiet during review. After the decision-free 150 days, NASA explicitly opens the door again: "After 150 days have passed since the proposal due date, proposers may contact the responsible Program Officer ... If the program officer does not respond proposers may send an inquiry to SARA@nasa.gov." After a decline, request the debrief within 30 days.

**The best-value move NASA itself recommends, and it is underused by early-career people:** volunteer to serve on a review panel. "Any qualified person who wants to gain insight into our review process is encouraged to volunteer by filling out one of the review forms at https://science.nasa.gov/researchers/volunteer-review-panels or by sending an email to the manager of the program of interest ... It is good experience for early-career scientists ... We are eager to have qualified reviewers from institutions not normally funded by SMD." NASA's own new-PI page calls panel service "a great way to learn about what NASA values in proposals."

**One structural caveat to communicate clearly:** dual-anonymous peer review (DAPR) is the default. The program officer knows who you are; the panel does not, until after grading. So a PO conversation cannot and does not influence how the panel scores the science — it influences whether you are proposing to the right place, in the right form, at the right scale.
result.funded_examples_source:
**Abstracts: yes, and NASA tells you exactly where.** Full proposal texts: no, NASA does not publish them.

1. **NSPIRES selection abstracts, per program element per year — the primary source.** NASA's instructions verbatim: "the titles and abstracts of all investigations selected through previous solicitations are available by program element at https://nspires.nasaprs.com: click 'CLOSED/PAST', filter by keyword for the particular ROSES program element of interest, follow the link to the page, and information on the selected proposals will be in a downloadable PDF file. For example, the selections from proposals submitted to F.3 Exoplanets Research in ROSES-2024 may be found on the NSPIRES page for that program element, by downloading the PDF linked from the words 'Exoplanets Research 2024 Selections' under the heading 'Selections'." Real examples of that file type, to show a user what they will get: https://nspires.nasaprs.com/external/viewrepositorydocument/cmdocumentid=659931/... "XRP18 abstracts approved.pdf" (Exoplanet Research Program, NNH18ZDA001N-XRP) and the FINESST-21 Astrophysics Division selections PDF (cmdocumentid=890512). These list PI, institution, title and a paragraph abstract for every funded proposal — which is how you find the three people in your subfield that NASA just funded, and therefore who to email or cite.
2. **Grant Stats — https://science.nasa.gov/researchers/sara/grant-stats/** — NASA publishes ROSES selection statistics as both PDF and Excel (most recent I confirmed: "July 2025 ROSES Selection Stats", ROSESGrantStats_072825_TAGGED.pdf / .xlsx), plus "Plots of grades vs. who gets selected" — i.e. what panel grade you actually needed. This is the honest expectations-setter: division selection rates in the material I saw ranged roughly 14%-36% by program, with Planetary Science reporting ~27% overall for ROSES-2022 (those specific figures came via a search-index summary of NASA PDFs, not from a page I fetched directly — verify in the PDF/XLSX before displaying).
3. **Research and Analysis Program Yearbook — https://science.nasa.gov/roses2021yearbook/** — proposal and selection counts by division, PI/Co-I demographics, organization types, and review-process duration. NASA calls it a "living" resource.
4. **TechPort — https://techport.nasa.gov** — public project records for NASA-funded technology work, linking contracts and grants to technology development and missions. Use for STMD/technology rather than SMD science.
5. **SBIR/STTR — https://www.nasa.gov/sbir_sttr/**, including a TechSource keyword search over funded NASA SBIR/STTR projects.
6. **USAspending.gov / SAM.gov** — recipient, amount, period of performance for any NASA award, useful for checking what a grant of this type is actually worth.

**What does not exist, stated plainly so nobody hunts for it:** there is no NIH-RePORTER-style single searchable NASA abstract database covering all of SMD, and NASA does not post full funded proposals or summary statements publicly. NASA's disclosure commitment is narrow and explicit: "In submitting a proposal, you agree to permit the government to disclose publicly the following proposal information: the name of the Primary Investigator, the names of all other team members, the title of the proposal, its abstract, and keywords ... It is NASA's policy not to release any information about proposals that are not selected for funding."

**So where do you read a real full proposal?** From a person. In practice: your institution's research office, your division's analysis group community, and individual PIs who post their own funded proposals (community-curated FINESST example collections exist on GitHub and personal sites — these surfaced in search results and I did not verify their contents, so treat as a lead, not a citation). NASA's own substitute for sample proposals is the training material in the next field, which is unusually good.

**NASA's own "get started" materials — the closest thing to worked examples (all confirmed on NASA pages):** New PI Resources https://science.nasa.gov/researchers/new-pi-resources/ ; "Proposal Writing 101" video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=R56T457HdDI ; Zurbuchen, "Writing Successful Mission Proposals" (slides + video); JPL Proposal Writing Workshop https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/go/proposalworkshop ; PI Launchpad https://science.nasa.gov/researchers/pi-launchpad/ (no attendance fee); Step-1 and Step-2 submission instruction PDFs; DAPR training slides for proposers; and per-division proposal templates (OSDMP, budget, work-effort tables) for Earth Science (Appendix A), Heliophysics (B) and Planetary Science (C), linked from https://science.nasa.gov/researchers/sara/library-and-useful-links/.

unresolved: The interval from proposal due date to the peer review panel meeting is NOT PUBLISHED by NASA in any document I could reach. My ~2-3 month figure is inferred arithmetic from NASA's stated goal of announcing 'within 150 days of the proposal due date and within 60 days after the conclusion of the peer review'. SPD-22B (peer review policy) describes the process but states no intervals. Label it as inferred wherever it is shown.

ROSES-2026 release date. NASA announced 'ROSES-2026 to be released July 2026'; as of 2026-09-18 it has not appeared - the ROSES-25 blog's newest items are Amendments 70-74 to ROSES-25, and https://solicitation.nasaprs.com/ROSES2026 redirects to an NSPIRES page returning 'No solicitation details were found for the given information.' NASA has published no revised date I could find. This is a live moving target, not a settled fact.

Whether NASA program officers will read draft proposals, specific aims, or pre-proposal summaries. NOT FOUND in any NASA policy document. NIH's 'send me your aims' convention has no documented NASA equivalent - do not assert one either way.

Current NASA SBIR/STTR Phase I open and close dates. The program page's schedule table (last updated 9/3/26) lists Post Phase II, CCRPP, Phase II Sequential, SBIR Ignite and Phase II STTR closes, but no Phase I, and states the program is converting from its traditional cycle to a Broad Agency Announcement. Phase I timing under the BAA model: not established.

Whether the EO 14332 pre-issuance review requirement (added to ROSES-25 on June 15, 2026, requiring 'in-person or virtual discussion of applications ... with a senior appointee') measurably lengthens the 150-220 day window. No data yet; NASA's published timing language has not been updated for it. Flag as a possible emerging delay, not a measured one.

The F.5 FINESST-25 due date of July 14, 2026 and the NASA Postdoctoral Program's November 1, 2026 6 p.m. ET deadline both came from SEARCH-INDEX summaries of NASA/AAS/ORAU pages rather than from pages I fetched and read directly. Division-level selection-rate figures (roughly 14%-36% by program; ~27% for Planetary Science ROSES-2022) came from a search-index summary of NASA PDFs, not from the Grant Stats files themselves. The authoritative numbers are in ROSESGrantStats_072825_TAGGED.pdf / .xlsx - read those before displaying any percentage.

Page limits and required contents for UNSOLICITED proposals (the 2026 NASA Guidebook for Proposers for Unsolicited Proposals). I confirmed the submission route ('NASA accepts only unsolicited proposals submitted electronically via NSPIRES') and that there is no deadline, but could not extract explicit page limits or an evaluation-duration commitment.

Whether community-curated collections of real funded FINESST/ROSES proposals (GitHub and personal academic sites surfaced in search) actually contain full proposal texts, and whether posting is author-sanctioned. Unverified lead, not a citation.

result.funder_system:
National Institutes of Health (NIH) — 24 grant-awarding Institutes and Centers (ICs) plus the Office of the Director, under HHS. Machinery is NIH-wide and shared with AHRQ/NIOSH/FDA for most submission policies, so establishing it once covers ~all NIH mechanisms (R, K, F, T, P, U, SBIR/STTR). Two-tier review: first level = Scientific Review Group / "study section" (run by the Center for Scientific Review, CSR, for most investigator-initiated applications; run by the IC for many PARs/RFAs, P/U/T mechanisms); second level = the funding IC's National Advisory Council or Board. "The advisory council makes funding recommendations to the Institute or Center Director, who ultimately makes the funding decision" (grants.nih.gov/grants-process/review). Funding decisions are made by the IC, not the study section — this is why the program officer relationship matters.

IMPORTANT 2026 STATE CHANGES a first-time applicant will not find in older guides:
1. NOFOs are no longer posted in the NIH Guide. NOT-OD-25-143: "NIH will no longer post NOFOs in the NIH Guide" beginning FY2026; "Grants.gov will serve as NIH's single official source for grant and cooperative agreement funding opportunities." The NIH Guide "will continue to be used for policy and informational notices." NIH-specific filtered search now lives at grants.nih.gov/funding/explore-nih-opportunities.
2. Six-application cap per PI per calendar year. NOT-OD-25-132: "NIH will only accept six new, renewal, resubmission, or revision applications from an individual Principal Investigator/Program Director or Multiple Principal Investigator for all council rounds in a calendar year," starting with the September 25, 2025 receipt date. Exempt: T activity codes and R13 conference grants (the Nexus write-up also names R25). Same notice: NIH will "not consider applications that are either substantially developed by AI, or contain sections substantially developed by AI, to be original ideas of applicants," with referral to the Office of Research Integrity possible post-award.
3. Emergency peer-review modifications are currently in force (see review_stages) — reduced discussion rate and stripped-down summary statements.
4. Common Forms (SciENcv) are now system-enforced (see submission_portal).
result.submission_portal:
Applications go to **Grants.gov**, and are tracked/validated in **eRA Commons**. Three preparation routes, all ending in the same place: (a) **ASSIST** — NIH's own online prep-and-submit system, public.era.nih.gov/assist; (b) **institutional system-to-system (S2S)** — your university's own Cayuse/InfoEd/Kuali-type pipeline; (c) **Grants.gov Workspace**. NIH's own wording: regardless of option, applications are "routed through Grants.gov using the same application forms package, validated against the same agency business rules, assembled in a consistent format for review consideration, and tracked in eRA Commons" (grants.nih.gov/grants-process/plan-to-apply/plan-within-your-organization/submission-options). Practical note for PhD students/postdocs: you almost never submit yourself — submission is made by your institution's Authorized Organizational Representative / Signing Official, so your real internal deadline is your research office's (typically 3–5 business days before NIH's).

HIDDEN LONG-LEAD REGISTRATIONS (grants.nih.gov/new-to-nih/organization-registration — NIH advises starting **six weeks** before the deadline):
- SAM.gov (gives the UEI): "Allow three weeks or more for initial registration and two weeks for yearly renewal." Institution-level.
- eRA Commons: "Allow two weeks or more"; NIH recommends starting at least 10 business days out. Institution registers; each PD/PI needs their own Commons account with a PI role.
- Grants.gov: "Allow one business day or more (depends on responsiveness of your EBiz POC)."
- SBA Company Registry (SBIR/STTR only): "Allow 1-2 business days."
- **ORCID iD, linked to the eRA Commons personal profile** — required for all senior/key personnel for due dates on or after May 25, 2025. An ORCID iD can be linked to only one eRA Commons account.
- **SciENcv (via My NCBI / Login.gov)** — now mandatory, not optional. NOT-OD-26-079: Common Forms (Biographical Sketch, Current and Pending (Other) Support, and the NIH Biographical Sketch Supplement) are required for "all application due dates and Just-In-Time (JIT), Research Performance Progress Report (RPPR), and Prior Approval submissions on or after May 8, 2026," and on that date "system warnings will change to errors that will stop any submission not using compliant Common Forms." "All individuals submitting Common Forms to NIH must use SciENcv to produce digitally certified PDF(s)." The forms page is explicit: "SciENcv must be used to prepare the form. There is not a blank template that can be downloaded and completed outside of SciENcv." This is the single most common new failure mode — every co-investigator and mentor needs a SciENcv account and a linked ORCID before the deadline, not on the deadline.

TWO SUBMISSION-DAY RULES THAT CATCH PEOPLE:
- Due by **5:00 PM local time of the applicant organization** on the due date; if the date falls on a weekend or federal holiday "the application deadline is automatically extended to the next business day."
- There is **no error-correction window**. NOT-OD-10-123 eliminated it for due dates on/after January 25, 2011: all corrections must be complete by the due date for the application to be on time. What survives is a **two-business-day Application Viewing Window** in eRA Commons after assembly — you can inspect the assembled PDF, and a Signing Official can reject and resubmit a Changed/Corrected application, but only *by the original deadline*. The window "does not extend the deadline." Submit 2–3 days early so errors are fixable.
result.deadline_structure:
Standard recurring due dates, published by NIH and stable year to year — these are the funder's own permanent calendar, not scraped per-solicitation dates, so they are safe to record and do not rot the way a specific NOFO's Key Dates table does. Source: grants.nih.gov/grants-process/submit/submission-policies/standard-due-dates. Three cycles per year; NOFO instructions override where a NOFO sets its own dates (RFAs and many PARs use custom, single dates).

NEW applications:
- R01, U01 — **February 5, June 5, October 5**
- K series (career development) — **February 12, June 12, October 12**
- R03, R21, R33, R21/R33, R34, R36, U34, UH2, UH3 — **February 16, June 16, October 16**
- R15 (AREA) — **February 25, June 25, October 25**
- P series, R18/U18, R25, T series, D series, C06/UC6 and most other "program/center" codes — **January 25, May 25, September 25** (same dates for all application types)
- F series fellowships — **April 8, August 8, December 8**
- R13/U13 conference grants — **April 12, August 12, December 12**
- SBIR/STTR (R41–R44) — **September 5, January 5, April 5**

RENEWAL / RESUBMISSION / REVISION applications are one month later than new for the R and K families:
- R01, U01 — **March 5, July 5, November 5**
- K series — **March 12, July 12, November 12**
- R03, R21, R33, R34, R36, U34, UH2, UH3 — **March 16, July 16, November 16**

Cycle → review → council → start (from the same NIH table):
- Cycle I (Jan–Feb dues): merit review June–July; council August or October; earliest start September or December.
- Cycle II (May–June dues): review October–November; council January; earliest start April.
- Cycle III (Sep–Oct dues): review February–March; council May; earliest start July.

Two current changes worth flagging: (1) dedicated AIDS/HIV due dates are gone — "We no longer have dedicated AIDS application due dates. When standard due dates apply, use the dates in the table below for both AIDS and non-AIDS applications" (aligned Jan 2026; the final separate AIDS date was May 7, 2026). (2) Late policy rewritten by NOT-OD-26-064, effective for due dates on or after **May 25, 2026**: late submission only within "two calendar weeks of the original due date," only for documented extenuating circumstances affecting the PD/PI (not other staff), explained in the cover letter, and only where the NOFO permits. **Continuous submission ended August 10, 2026.** Excluded from any late submission: fellowships (F30, F31, F32, F33, F99/K00), small business (R41–R44, SB1, UT1, U44), and international collaborative research. The one pre-authorized reason is NIH peer-review service within four weeks of the due date.

review_stages.stage: Receipt, referral and assignment (CSR Division of Receipt and Referral): application assigned to an IC for funding consideration and to a study section for review; assignment visible in eRA Commons. A cover letter can request (not dictate) IC and study section assignment.
review_stages.timing: ~2–6 weeks after the due date

review_stages.stage: First level: peer review by the Scientific Review Group / study section. "Composed primarily of non-federal scientists who have expertise in relevant scientific disciplines"; three assigned reviewers write critiques; the meeting assigns an overall impact score 1–9 (best to worst); percentile calculated for many R01s.
review_stages.timing: ~4 months after submission — June–July for Cycle I, Oct–Nov for Cycle II, Feb–Mar for Cycle III

review_stages.stage: Scores released in eRA Commons. Normally "within a few days after the meeting"; under the current emergency modifications, "scores within three business days of the meeting."
review_stages.timing: ~4 months + 3 business days

review_stages.stage: Summary statement released in eRA Commons — reviewer critiques, the SRO's summary of discussion, criterion scores, administrative notes. "In most cases, your summary statement will be available via eRA Commons within a month" of the meeting. Not-discussed applications still receive assigned reviewers' critiques and preliminary criterion scores.
review_stages.timing: ~5 months after submission (currently: "released later in the Council round", i.e. slower)

review_stages.stage: Second level: IC National Advisory Council or Board — recommends funding to the IC Director, who decides.
review_stages.timing: ~8 months after submission — Aug/Oct for Cycle I, Jan for Cycle II, May for Cycle III

review_stages.stage: Just-in-Time (JIT): IC requests other support, IRB/IACUC approvals, certifications for applications in the likely-fundable range. The automated JIT email for impact scores ≤30 was retired October 1, 2024 — notification now comes directly from IC staff, and the JIT link appears on the eRA Commons Status screen within 24 hours of score release. A PI can upload; only a Signing Official can submit. Required "at least 60 days before the applicant's proposed project period start date."
review_stages.timing: between council and award; requested any time after scores

review_stages.stage: Notice of Award (NoA) issued by the IC's Grants Management Officer — the only binding award document.
review_stages.timing: ~9 months after submission; earliest project start Sept/Dec (Cycle I), April (Cycle II), July (Cycle III)

review_stages.stage: CURRENT EMERGENCY MODIFICATIONS (NOT-OD-26-114, released September 8, 2026, extending NOT-OD-26-012): after the October 1, 2025 appropriations lapse cancelled 370+ review meetings affecting 24,000+ applications, "the percent of applications discussed in most meetings will be reduced to 30-35%, instead of the usual ~50%." Applications land in three tiers: discussed; "competitive but not discussed" (middle third, still eligible for funding); "not competitive and not discussed." Summary statements are simplified to "a sentence describing the degree of consensus in the committee vote, plus bullets listing the main score driving points" alongside the three assigned reviewers' written critiques; only discussed applications get an overall impact score. NIH states "Your application's likelihood of funding is not affected."
review_stages.timing: in effect through the January 2027 Advisory Council round — i.e. covers applications submitted for the 2026 Cycle II due dates (June 2026). Whether it extends to Cycle III (Oct 2026 dues / May 2027 council) is not yet announced.

result.months_submission_to_award: ~9 months from due date to earliest project start date if all goes according to plan; ~4 months to study section, ~5 months to summary statement, ~8 months to advisory council. Derived directly from NIH's own standard due dates table (e.g. Cycle II: June 5 due → Oct–Nov review → January council → April 1 earliest start = 10 months; Cycle I: Feb 5 due → Jun–Jul review → Aug or Oct council → Sept or Dec start = 7–10 months). Add ~9–12 months more if the application needs a resubmission (A1), which is the norm rather than the exception. Plan for 9 months minimum between submitting and having money, and up to ~2 years from first submission to funded award via one resubmission. Note that the FY2026 appropriations lapse (Oct 1, 2025) pushed real timelines beyond these nominal figures for the Jan/May 2026 council rounds.
result.resubmission_policy:
One only. NIH's own words (grants.nih.gov/grants-process/submit/submission-policies/resubmission-applications, policy in NOT-OD-18-197):
- "Only a single resubmission (A1) of a competing new, renewal, or revision application (A0) will be accepted." The application ID gains an A1 suffix.
- Time window: "You must submit the resubmission application within 37 months of the new, renewal, or revision application it follows" (NOT-OD-12-128).
- Eligibility is broad: "A resubmission application can follow a competing new, renewal, or revision application (A0) that was not selected for funding (including applications 'not discussed' in review)." So a triaged/not-discussed application — and, under the current modifications, a "competitive but not discussed" one — can still be resubmitted.
- Required Introduction: one page or less unless the NOFO says otherwise (3 pages for T/institutional training resubmissions per the page-limits table). It must "Summarize substantial additions, deletions, and changes to the application" and "Respond to the issues and criticism raised in the summary statement." It is an extra page on top of the Research Strategy, not carved out of it.
- After a failed A1: "After an unsuccessful resubmission (A1), you may submit the idea as a new application" (a fresh A0 at the next new-application due date). NIH does not require a formal demonstration of how much must change, but the A0 is reviewed as new and should not be presented as a rebuttal.
- Overlap rule: "it is not allowable to have overlapping applications under review at the same time" — you cannot have the A0 and its resubmission, or an essentially identical application, pending simultaneously (see also NOT-OD-11-101 re: pending appeals).
- The 6-applications-per-PI-per-calendar-year cap (NOT-OD-25-132) counts resubmissions against the limit.
Related lever, not strictly resubmission: **post-submission materials** (NOT-OD-23-106) are due 30 days before the study section meeting, and NIH accepts a **one-page update with preliminary data** for Type 1 (new) R01, R21 or R03 applications including resubmissions, where the NOFO allows preliminary data — one page per component. Submitted through the AOR/SO, not directly by the PI.
result.program_officer_norms:
Expected and encouraged — NIH is the clearest example of a funder where pre-submission PO contact is normal practice, and NIH publishes guidance telling you to do it.

WHEN: at the idea stage, before writing — "One of the best times for investigators to contact a PO is when they are thinking about applying for funding," and NIH advises developing the idea on paper "in the form of a Specific Aims page. That will give the program officer the information needed to help put you on a path to a successful application." Realistically: 2–4 months before the due date, i.e. right after the previous cycle's dates pass. Then again *after* the summary statement is released, before deciding whether to resubmit. NIGMS: "Once the summary statement is released," contact the PO with questions about the review or funding possibilities.

HOW: email, not a cold call. The July 2026 Nexus guidance: "A short description of your project, why you believe it fits a specific ICO or funding opportunity, and 2–3 targeted questions is usually more effective than a long, unfocused message," plus "Send an email rather than cold call" and "Allow time for a response." A one-page Specific Aims plus a 3–5 line email is the house style.

WHAT EXPERIENCED APPLICANTS ACTUALLY ASK: is this in your IC's mission and priorities; is the scope/budget right for this mechanism (R21 vs R01 vs R03); which NOFO — parent announcement or a specific PAR/RFA; which study section is likely to review it and is that the right home; is there an upcoming initiative I should wait for; for a resubmission, how did the summary statement read to you and is it worth an A1; for ESIs, is my record competitive for this mechanism yet.

WHAT POs WILL NOT DO: "Program Officers do not: Co-write, rewrite, or edit sections of an application"; "Provide detailed scientific direction on experimental design"; or share non-public information such as forthcoming funding opportunities. They also cannot promise funding.

WHO ELSE, AND WHEN: the roles are distinct and using the wrong one is the classic novice error. The **Scientific Review Officer (SRO)** is your contact during review only — expertise gaps, conflicts of interest, requesting a different study section; the SRO cannot discuss funding. Never contact reviewers. After the meeting, "a program officer (PO) at the funding institute to which your application has been assigned will be your main point of contact," and the PO can "help interpret your review results and give you guidance in preparing a resubmission." The **Grants Management Specialist (GMS)** handles budget/administrative/JIT matters and is reached through your institution's AOR.

HOW TO FIND YOUR PO: Section VII (Agency Contacts) of every NOFO lists scientific/research contacts; RePORTER **Matchmaker** (reporter.nih.gov/matchmaker) — paste your abstract or aims and choose "Similar Program Officials" to get POs, ICs, activity codes and review panels associated with similar funded work, with email addresses; or IC program-officer directories (most ICs publish one, e.g. NINDS, NINR, NIAID).
result.page_limits:
NOFO always wins: "Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) instructions always supersede these instructions," and "If no page limit is listed in the table below, in Section IV of the NOFO under Page Limitations, or in a related notice, you can assume the attachment does not have a limit." Source: grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/how-to-apply-application-guide/page-limits.

UNIVERSAL: Project Summary/Abstract 30 lines; Project Narrative 3 sentences (all codes except C06, UC6, G20); Introduction for resubmission/revision 1 page (3 pages for T/institutional training resubmissions); Specific Aims 1 page.

RESEARCH STRATEGY, by activity code — this is the number that varies:
- 12 pages: R01, R15, R18, R21/R33, R24, R28, R33, R34, R42, R44, R61, RF1, RC2, RC4, DP3, DP5, U01, U18, U24, U2C, U34, U42, U44, UH2, UH3, UG1, UF1, SB1, SC1 and similar large codes.
- 6 pages: R03, R13/U13, R16, R21, R35, R36, R41, R43, R50, SC2, SC3, UT1.
- 10 pages: DP2. 5 pages: DP1. X01/X02: 6 or 12 depending on NOFO.
- Commercialization Plan (R42, R44, SB1, UT2, U44, UB1): 12 pages.

FELLOWSHIPS (F30/F31/F32/F33/F99-K00): Candidate's Goals, Preparedness, Potential 3 pages; Training Activities and Timelines 3 pages; Research Training Project Specific Aims 1 page; Research Training Project Strategy **6 pages**; Responsible Conduct of Research 1 page; Sponsor(s) Commitment 6 pages; Letters of Support 6 pages.

CAREER DEVELOPMENT (K01/K08/K23/K25/K76/K99-R00 etc.): Candidate Information and Goals combined **12 pages**; Specific Aims 1 page; RCR 1 page; Mentor Plans and Statements 6 pages; Letters of Support 6 pages; Institutional Environment 1 page; Institutional Commitment 1 page; Candidate's Mentoring Plan (K24, K05) 6 pages.

INSTITUTIONAL TRAINING / EDUCATION (T, D43, D71, K12, KL2, R25, UE5, R38, DP7): Program Plan or Research Education Program Plan **25 pages**; RCR plan 3 pages; Reproducibility/Methods plan 3 pages; renewal Progress Report 5 pages overview + 1 page per appointee.

BIOSKETCH: legacy NIH format page = 5 pages; **Biographical Sketch Common Form = no hard page limit** — "length controlled through SciENcv data entry format." Current and Pending (Other) Support Common Form likewise SciENcv-controlled.

Formatting rules (Format Attachments page): PDF only, single-column, one-inch margins, Arial/Georgia/Helvetica/Palatino Linotype at 11pt or larger, black text, no headers/footers of your own, filenames ≤50 characters, no encryption/password protection. Figures and references count against the Research Strategy page limit; the References Cited attachment does not.
required_documents: SF424 (R&R) Cover — includes the optional but strategically useful Cover Letter attachment (request IC/study section assignment, explain a late submission, flag video or a changed/corrected submission)

R&R Other Project Information — Project Summary/Abstract (30 lines), Project Narrative (3 sentences, plain-language public health relevance), Bibliography & References Cited, Facilities & Other Resources, Equipment, and the Other Attachments slot

R&R Senior/Key Person Profile — Biographical Sketch Common Form for every senior/key person, generated in SciENcv and digitally certified (required, system-enforced since May 8, 2026); plus the NIH Biographical Sketch Supplement
Current and Pending (Other) Support (CPOS) Common Form — SciENcv, required at application for some mechanisms and always at Just-in-Time
R&R Budget (detailed) or PHS 398 Modular Budget (most R01s at <=$250k direct/year) + Budget Justification; R&R Subaward Budget Attachment for each consortium
PHS 398 Cover Page Supplement (human subjects/clinical trial questions, program income, human embryonic stem cells)

PHS 398 Research Plan Form — Specific Aims (required, 1 page) and Research Strategy (required) are the core; Introduction to Application is 'required only if the type of application is resubmission or revision'; Progress Report Publication List 'required only if the type of application is renewal'

PHS Human Subjects and Clinical Trials Information form — required whenever human subjects or a clinical trial is involved; includes study records, inclusion enrollment reports, protection of human subjects, and the inclusion of women, minorities, children/across-the-lifespan sections
Vertebrate Animals attachment — conditional, 'if you answered Yes to the question Are Vertebrate Animals Used?'

Data Management and Sharing (DMS) Plan — attached under Other Plan(s); required whenever the project generates scientific data. The **2026 DMS Plan format is required for due dates on or after May 25, 2026** (NOT-OD-26-046, NOT-OD-26-100) — simplified, mostly yes/no elements, recommended not to exceed two pages. Reviewed by NIH staff, not by reviewers, unless data sharing is integral to the design and the NOFO says so
Multiple PD/PI Leadership Plan — conditional, required when the application designates multiple PD/PIs
Consortium/Contractual Arrangements — conditional, 'if you have consortiums/contracts in your budget'
Letters of Support — conditional; collaborators, consortium participants, resource providers. For F and K awards the sponsor/mentor statements are separate, longer, and central to the score
Resource Sharing Plan(s) — conditional, e.g. model organism sharing; Authentication of Key Biological and/or Chemical Resources — 'if applicable to the proposed science'
Select Agent Research — conditional; Appendix — optional and tightly restricted (do not use it to smuggle in extra Research Strategy)

Reference letters (F and most K awards) — submitted by referees directly through eRA Commons, NOT through the application; due by the same 5:00 PM deadline, and a missing reference letter makes the application incomplete
result.funded_examples_source:
Four distinct layers, in increasing order of detail:

1. **Full funded applications with their summary statements — the gold standard.** NIH maintains a curated index at grants.nih.gov/grants-process/write-application/samples-applications-and-documents ("As you gain experience writing your own applications and progress reports, examples of how others presented their ideas can help"). It links IC-hosted collections: **NIAID** (niaid.nih.gov/grants-contracts/sample-applications) — R01, R03, R15, R21, R33, SBIR/STTR, K, F, G11, U01, *including the summary statements*, which is what makes them teachable; **NHGRI** (genome.gov) — K99/R00, K01, R01, R03, R21 with summary statements, including ELSI samples; **NCI** — Behavioral Research, Cancer Epidemiology, Implementation Science and Healthcare Delivery collections (cancercontrol.cancer.gov, epi.grants.cancer.gov); **NIA** (nia.nih.gov/research/training/sample-applications) — including F99/K00 and K99/R00 pairs showing an initial submission *and* its resubmission; **NIDCD** — R01 and R21 early-career samples with summary statements. Reading a sample beside its summary statement is the single highest-value exercise for a first-time applicant.

2. **NIH RePORTER** (reporter.nih.gov) — every funded project: abstract, Specific Aims text, PI, IC, activity code, study section, fiscal year, amount, resulting publications and patents. Advanced search at reporter.nih.gov/advanced-search. It does **not** contain full applications; for those, "applicants requesting complete application contents can submit a written Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request for a copy of a specific grant application to the NIH Institute or Center (IC) that funded the grant." Data updates weekly; projects appear 7–10 days after budget start date.

3. **RePORTER Matchmaker** (reporter.nih.gov/matchmaker) — paste up to 15,000 characters of your abstract or aims and get back similar funded projects, the program officials behind them (with email addresses), the ICs, the review panels and the activity codes. This answers "who funds work like mine, which study section reviews it, and who do I email" in one step. "The process is automated and confidential. The Matchmaker system does not track and store submitted text."

4. **Annotated form sets** — grants.nih.gov/grants/ElectronicReceipt/files/ (Annotated Form Set for NIH Grant Applications) show a filled-in application field by field. Plus the NIH "All About Grants" podcast and the FORMS-I instruction PDFs (Research Instructions for NIH and Other PHS Agencies, FORMS-I series, released December 2025).
