unresolved: ON THE 'DATED DEADLINE' QUESTION IN THE USER REQUEST: nothing in my instructions forbids dated deadlines, and I have given them. The distinction that matters for a corpus like this is between two kinds of date. (a) NIH's STANDARD DUE DATES (Feb 5 / Jun 5 / Oct 5 etc.) are a permanent published calendar with no year attached — they are the funder's own structural fact, they have held for well over a decade, and omitting them would make the corpus useless to exactly the reader you describe. These belong in the data. (b) A SPECIFIC NOFO's Key Dates (e.g. 'PAR-25-XXX closes 14 Nov 2026') is a per-solicitation date that rots within months and is the thing that makes a funding corpus go stale. The safe rule is: record recurring structural dates and the rule that generates them; do not record one-off solicitation dates without a fetch date and a link back to the live NOFO. If a prior rule in this project banned dates outright, it over-corrected and should be narrowed to (b).

Whether the emergency peer-review modifications (30–35% discussion rate, simplified summary statements, 'competitive but not discussed' middle tier) will be extended beyond the January 2027 Advisory Council round. NOT-OD-26-114 (released 8 Sept 2026) extends them only that far, which covers applications submitted for the 2026 Cycle II due dates. Someone submitting for the October 2026 dates (May 2027 council) does not yet know which regime will review them. Check the NIH Guide for a successor notice before relying on either.

NOT-OD-26-086 is an open Request for Information proposing to CAP THE NUMBER OF SIMULTANEOUS RESEARCH PROJECT GRANTS PER PI. This is an RFI, not policy — no cap number, no effective date established. Do not record it as a rule; do flag it as pending, because if adopted it changes eligibility calculus for senior PIs and indirectly for the postdocs on their grants.
NOT-OD-26-088 is an open RFI on PROPOSED CHANGES TO REPORTING OUTCOMES FROM NIH PEER REVIEW — i.e. what a summary statement will contain in future. Pending, not established.

Exact handling of applications submitted OVER the six-per-PI-per-year cap: NOT-OD-25-132 states the limit but I could not establish from the notice text what NIH does with number seven (withdrawn, not accepted, returned?). Not found — would need the associated FAQ or the NIH Grants Policy Statement 2.3.7.

Whether the R25 activity code is exempt from the six-application cap. NOT-OD-25-132's own text as fetched names only T codes and R13; NIH's Nexus write-up of the same policy names T, R25 and R13. The two sources disagree; treat R25 as unconfirmed.

The ESI eligibility extension I found (NOT-OD-25-114) is a one-off 2025 extension covering submissions through October 2025, not a standing rule. The standing ESI definition (within 10 years of terminal degree or end of post-graduate clinical training, no prior substantial NIH independent research award) is well established, and ESI status is determined from the Education section of the eRA Commons personal profile with extension requests filed there — but I did not directly fetch grants.nih.gov/policy-and-compliance/policy-topics/early-stage-investigators/determining-status, so the 10-year wording here comes from a search index rather than the funder page.

This is a tooling limitation, not a finding about NIAID.

result.funder_system: National Science Foundation (NSF) — the US federal agency for non-medical basic research and STEM education. Machinery is set centrally by one document, the Proposal & Award Policies & Procedures Guide (PAPPG). Currently effective: **NSF 24-1, "applies to all proposals submitted or due on or after May 20, 2024"** (https://www.nsf.gov/policies/pappg), modified by two policy-notice supplements rather than a renumbered edition: Supplement 1 (NSF 26-200), "Applies to all financial assistance awarded on or after Dec. 8, 2025", and Supplement 2 (NSF 26-202), "Applies to all financial assistance awarded on or after Jan. 22, 2026". Read the PAPPG once and it applies across essentially every NSF mechanism; the solicitation then overrides it where it says so. The two National Science Board merit-review criteria — Intellectual Merit ("The potential for the proposed project to advance knowledge and understanding within its own field or across different fields") and Broader Impacts ("The potential for the proposed project to benefit society and contribute to the achievement of specific, desired societal outcomes") — are the same two criteria for every proposal and every reviewer. Broader Impacts must appear as its own headed section inside the Project Description; proposals without it are returned without review.
result.submission_portal:
**Research.gov is the primary system; Grants.gov is still accepted for most opportunities.** NSF's own page (https://www.nsf.gov/funding/submitting-proposal, checked 2026-09-18): "Most proposals to NSF can be submitted either through Research.gov or Grants.gov." PAPPG I: "Unless specified in an NSF program solicitation, proposals submitted to NSF must be submitted via use of Research.gov or Grants.gov." Research.gov is where NSF's own compliance checks, the DMSP webform and the budget forms live, so almost everyone uses it.

HIDDEN LONG-LEAD ITEMS (do these months before you have a draft):
1. **SAM.gov registration + Unique Entity ID (UEI)** for the organization. "NSF will validate that each proposer's UEI and SAM registration are valid and active prior to allowing submission." NSF recommends allowing **at least 90 days**. This is institutional, done by the sponsored projects office — but it fails silently and late, so confirm it exists before you pick a deadline.
2. **NSF ID** for each individual — "a unique alpha-numeric identifier assigned to users by NSF… used throughout NSF's electronic systems as a login ID". A PI, co-PI, or any senior/key person needs one; get it the week you decide to apply, not the week of the deadline.
3. **Research.gov organizational registration and role assignment** — you must be added as a PI by your institution's Administrator before you can create a proposal. New organizations must be in SAM first.
4. **SciENcv account (NCBI/NIH-run, linked to ORCID)** — mandatory for two documents (see required_documents). SciENcv is a *different* government system from Research.gov; first-time setup plus ORCID linking realistically takes an afternoon.
5. **An Authorized Organizational Representative (AOR) / sponsored projects office submits, not you.** Individual investigators cannot self-submit standard research proposals. Institutional internal deadlines are typically 3–10 business days before NSF's. NSF itself: "NSF strongly recommends proposers initiate proposal submission at least five business days before a deadline."

EXCEPTION WORTH KNOWING: the **Graduate Research Fellowship Program (GRFP)** uses a separate applicant-facing module — "All applications must be submitted through https://www.research.gov/grfp/Login.do" — and the student submits directly, with no institutional AOR. Concept outlines are now email-based (see program_officer_norms).
result.deadline_structure:
**NSF has no agency-wide standard due dates.** This is the single biggest structural difference from NIH: there is no equivalent of NIH's Feb 5 / Jun 5 / Oct 5 grid. Dates are set per solicitation, and there are three published kinds (PAPPG I, verbatim):
- **Deadline Date** — "dates after which proposals will not be accepted or will be returned without review by NSF."
- **Target Date** — proposals are still accepted after it, but may miss that review round.
- **Submission Window** — "designated periods of time during which proposals will be accepted for review by NSF."

**Time of day: "Proposals must be received by 5 p.m. submitting organization's local time on the established deadline date."** (Submitter's local time, not Eastern — a genuine and frequently-missed detail.) GRFP is the exception: 8:00 p.m. Eastern Time.

REAL RECURRING DATES NSF PUBLISHES AS RULES (stable year to year, safe to plan against — these come from NSF's own opportunity pages):
- **CAREER (NSF 22-586)** — "Fourth Wednesday in July, Annually Thereafter", 5 p.m. submitter's local time. That was **22 July 2026**; NSF's page currently shows **28 July 2027**. One submission per PI per competition, no co-PIs.
- **REU Sites (NSF 23-601)** — "Third Wednesday in August, Annually Thereafter". That was **19 August 2026**; NSF's page shows **18 August 2027**.
- **GRFP (NSF 26-526, the FY2027 competition)** — staggered by field, all 8:00 p.m. ET: **19 Oct 2026** Life Sciences; **20 Oct 2026** CISE, Materials Research, Psychology, Social Sciences; **22 Oct 2026** Engineering; **23 Oct 2026** Chemistry, Geosciences, Mathematical Sciences, Physics & Astronomy. **Reference letters due 16 Oct 2026, 8:00 p.m. ET** — three days *before* the earliest applicant deadline, which catches people out every year. Last day to withdraw without it counting against your allowed attempts: 15 Nov 2026. Outcomes "by early April of the competition year."

THE OTHER HALF OF THE PICTURE — **many NSF core programs have no deadline at all**: proposals are "accepted anytime." BIO adopted no-deadline for most core programs in 2018 (NSF 18-011); GEO/OCE Marine Geology & Geophysics from 1 July 2017; the Division of Chemistry Disciplinary Research Programs pilot (NSF 22-606) from 1 Sept 2022 for CLP, CSD and CTMC; CISE Future CoRe (NSF 25-543) accepts anytime with target dates. For an early-career researcher this is the most under-exploited fact about NSF: in several fields you can submit the week you are ready.

DRIFT WARNING (important for any dated display): a published date is not a guarantee the competition runs. NSF **skipped the FY2026 Major Research Instrumentation (MRI) competition entirely** (https://www.nsf.gov/funding/opportunities/mri-major-research-instrumentation-program/updates/119954). And after the lapse in appropriations (NSF reopened 13 Nov 2025), NSF stated it "cannot reopen a closed deadline or allow resubmission unless the relevant program issues a revised solicitation or deadline notice," that "Some programs may reissue active solicitations to extend proposal submission deadlines," and that "Not all panels that were postponed due to the shutdown will be rescheduled." So: publish the *recurring rule* ("fourth Wednesday in July") as the durable fact and the *specific date* as a linked, dated snapshot — the rule survives, the instance sometimes does not.

review_stages.stage: Submission and compliance check (Research.gov automated checks + NSF Program Officer / proposal processing)
review_stages.timing: Days to ~3 weeks after submission. Non-compliant proposals are Returned Without Review here (11 listed grounds, incl. missing required documents, page-limit violations, non-responsiveness, and a resubmission that ignored prior review). NSF does not publish a standard interval for this step.

review_stages.stage: External merit review — ad hoc reviewers, a panel, or both
review_stages.timing: Typically 2-4 months after the deadline; NSF does NOT publish a standard deadline-to-panel interval, so treat the month count as observed practice, not policy. PAPPG: proposals are reviewed by a Program Officer 'and usually by three to ten other persons outside NSF either as ad hoc reviewers, panelists, or both.'

review_stages.stage: Program Officer recommendation + Division Director concurrence
review_stages.timing: Weeks after the panel. The Program Officer writes a review analysis and recommends award or decline to the Division Director.

review_stages.stage: Division of Grants and Agreements (DGA) business review and final decision
review_stages.timing: 'DGA generally makes the decision to award or decline proposals within 30 days after the program Division/Office makes its recommendation.' A Grants and Agreements Officer, not the Program Officer, signs the award.

review_stages.stage: Notification to PI + release of review materials
review_stages.timing: Within 6 months of submission in NSF's own commitment: 'NSF strives to be able to tell applicants whether their proposals have been declined or recommended for funding within six months' / PAPPG: 'this review and consideration process may take up to six months.' PI receives: description of how the proposal was reviewed, verbatim unattributed copies of all reviews used, the panel summary if panelled, and site-visit reports if any.

review_stages.stage: Earliest award start / money available
review_stages.timing: Roughly 6-9 months after submission. PAPPG: 'Proposers should allow up to six months for programmatic review and processing,' with the award following within ~30 days of the division recommendation. Start dates are normally the first of a month and are negotiable with the Program Officer.

result.months_submission_to_award: **6 months to a decision, 6–9 months to an award, as NSF's own published expectation.** Two quotable anchors: "NSF strives to be able to tell applicants whether their proposals have been declined or recommended for funding within six months" (https://www.nsf.gov/funding/merit-review), and PAPPG I: "Proposers should allow up to six months for programmatic review and processing," with the award decision made by DGA "within 30 days after the program Division/Office makes its recommendation." Practical planning number for an applicant: submit at a July deadline, expect to know by roughly January, expect funds around the following spring. FY2026 is running slower than that baseline because of the appropriations lapse (NSF reopened 13 Nov 2025) — NSF's own wording: "Some delays are expected in processing new awards and funding actions."
result.resubmission_policy:
**Allowed, uncapped agency-wide, but NSF has no "resubmission" object at all — this is the structural opposite of NIH.** There is no A1 designation, no Introduction to Resubmission page, no one-resubmission limit, and no time window.

PAPPG Chapter IV, verbatim:
- "A declined proposal may be resubmitted, but only after it has undergone substantial revision."
- "The Foundation will treat the revised proposal as a new proposal, subject to the standard review procedures."
- "A resubmitted proposal that has not clearly taken into account the major comments or concerns resulting from the prior NSF review may be returned without review."

What that means in practice: because it is a *new* proposal, it goes to a possibly different panel with possibly different reviewers, and you have **no dedicated space to respond to the prior reviews**. Experienced applicants handle this by (a) talking to the Program Officer about what the panel actually meant before rewriting, and (b) working the responses into the Project Description narrative itself rather than a rebuttal section. Some solicitations do ask you to describe how the proposal differs from a prior submission — check the solicitation.

MECHANISM-SPECIFIC CAPS EXIST even though the agency-wide rule has none:
- **CAREER**: "A Principal Investigator may not participate in more than three CAREER competitions." Notably, "Proposals that are not reviewed (i.e., are withdrawn before review or are returned without review) do not count toward the three-competition limit" — so a withdrawal before review is strategically cheap and a compliance failure is strategically expensive.
- **GRFP**: one application per annual competition; undergraduates/bachelor's holders not yet enrolled in graduate school may apply repeatedly, but joint bachelor's-master's students and first-year graduate students get **one application only**, and second-year-or-later graduate students are ineligible. Withdraw by the published November date and it does not count.

SEPARATE TRACK — FORMAL RECONSIDERATION (rarely used, and it is about process, not science): request reconsideration from the Assistant Director/Office Head; the request must be "received by the Foundation within 90 days after the declination or the return"; "Within 45 days after the date of the request, the AD/Office Head will furnish the results of the reconsideration, in writing, to the PI." Then an appeal to the Deputy Director "Within 60 days after the AD/Office Head has notified the PI," answered within 30 days; "The decision made by the Deputy Director is final." Proposals declined for administrative or financial reasons are not eligible for reconsideration. Withdrawal is available "at any time before a funding recommendation is made by the cognizant NSF Program Officer."
result.page_limits:
Standard set under PAPPG 24-1 (a solicitation can override any of these — always check):
- **Project Description: 15 pages** ("may not exceed 15 pages"). Must contain a separately headed **Broader Impacts** section on its own line. **Results from Prior NSF Support**, if applicable, is "up to five pages" *inside* the 15.
- **Project Summary: 1 page** ("not more than one page in length"), entered as three separate boxes — Overview, Intellectual Merit, Broader Impacts. Missing one of the three = returned without review.
- **References Cited: no page limit** (citations only, no annotations).
- **Budget Justification: 5 pages** ("no more than five pages per proposal"); the budget itself is a fillable Research.gov form.
- **Biographical Sketch: NO page limit since 20 May 2024.** The old three-page cap is retired — NSF's SciENcv FAQ: "Although there is no longer a three-page limit for the biographical sketch…". Must be produced in **SciENcv** using Common Form **v.2024-1**, which "is required for proposals submitted or due on or after May 20, 2024."
- **Current and Pending (Other) Support: no stated page limit**, SciENcv mandatory, must be updated prior to award.
- **Synergistic Activities: one page** per senior/key person (separated out of the biosketch in 24-1).
- **Collaborators and Other Affiliations (COA): NSF template (spreadsheet)**, single-copy document, not seen by reviewers.
- **Data Management and Sharing Plan: 2 pages** — "The two-page data management and sharing plan is a required part of a proposal." **Format changed on 27 April 2026**: it is now a Research.gov webform generated from the proposal's primary directorate, and separate PDF uploads are no longer accepted (per NSF 26-202, PAPPG 24-1 Supplement 2: "The Research.gov tool… will be released on April 27, 2026"). If the project produces no data you must upload a justification instead.
- **Mentoring Plan: 1 page** — required whenever postdoctoral researchers are supported.
- **Safe and Harassment-free Fieldwork (SAHF) plan: 2 pages** — "SAHF plans are project-specific, two-page documents that apply only to proposals with off-campus or off-site research." Submitted to NSF *only when the solicitation says so*; otherwise the AOR certifies the organization has one. NSF explicitly warns: "The organizational plan that is certified by the AOR is not identical in content to that requested in an SAHF plan, so institutional templates are not recommended for SAHF plans."
- **Facilities, Equipment and Other Resources: no page limit**, but "narrative in nature and must not include any quantifiable financial information."
- **Letters of Collaboration**: strict single-sentence NSF format; anything that reads as an endorsement can get the proposal returned.

FORMATTING (enforced by automated compliance checks, and a common cause of return): Arial / Courier New / Palatino Linotype at "10 points or larger", Times New Roman or Computer Modern at "11 points or larger"; margins "at least an inch" on all sides; "No more than six lines of text within a vertical space of one inch"; letter paper.

VARY BY MECHANISM: CAREER adds a mandatory **Departmental Letter, "no more than 2 pages"** — "A proposal submitted without this Letter will be returned without review." GRFP uses its own limits: **Personal, Relevant Background and Future Goals Statement, 3 pages**; **Graduate Research Plan Statement, 2 pages**; both must carry explicit Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts headings. Centers, CAREER, SBIR/STTR, conference, RAPID and EAGER proposals each have their own page rules in the solicitation.

Project Description — 15 pages, with a separately headed Broader Impacts section and (if applicable) up to 5 pages of Results from Prior NSF Support inside the 15
References Cited — no page limit, citations only
Budget (Research.gov fillable form) + Budget Justification — 5 pages per proposal
Facilities, Equipment and Other Resources — narrative, no financial figures, no page limit
Biographical Sketch, per senior/key person — SciENcv mandatory, Common Form v.2024-1, no page limit since 20 May 2024
Current and Pending (Other) Support, per senior/key person — SciENcv mandatory, updated before award

Synergistic Activities, per senior/key person — 1 page

MECHANISM-SPECIFIC: CAREER Departmental Letter (max 2 pages; absent = returned without review)

MECHANISM-SPECIFIC: Letter of Intent or Preliminary Proposal where a solicitation requires one — 'Failure to submit a required LOI identified in a program solicitation will result in a full proposal not being accepted or returned without review'
MECHANISM-SPECIFIC: Concept Outline where a solicitation requires one — now emailed to the address in the funding opportunity
result.program_officer_norms:
**Expected and actively invited — NSF is at the NIH end of this spectrum, not the foundation end.** NSF publishes a how-to ("NSF 101: 5 tips on how to work with an NSF program officer", https://www.nsf.gov/science-matters/nsf-101-5-tips-how-work-nsf-program-officer) whose central line is: **"Anyone can reach out to an NSF program officer—at any stage of their career, no matter their institution."** PAPPG I: "Before formal submission, the proposal may be discussed with appropriate NSF program staff." The CAREER solicitation: applicants are "encouraged to contact the appropriate NSF Program Officer when preparing a submission."

WHEN IN THE CYCLE: early — during planning, not in deadline week. NSF's tips say to do your homework first (search the funding pages and the awards database; every opportunity lists its cognizant Program Officers by name and email), then reach out. Also: "Regardless of whether your proposal is selected for funding, you should continue to stay in contact with your program officer" — the post-declination conversation is explicitly sanctioned.

WHAT TO SEND: a **one-page summary** of the idea. That is the standard NSF currency. For some opportunities a formal **Concept Outline** is required; **note the 2025 machinery change** — the ProSPCT portal "was decommissioned on May 12, 2025," and concept outlines now go **by email to the address listed in the funding opportunity**, with ProSPCTSupport@nsf.gov available to route a submission if you cannot tell which program is right.

WHAT EXPERIENCED APPLICANTS ACTUALLY ASK: (1) Is this in scope for your program, and if not, which program or division is the right home? — the highest-value question, because NSF's internal boundaries are not obvious from outside and a misrouted proposal is a wasted cycle. (2) Is the budget scale right for this program? (3) Will this go to a panel, ad hoc reviewers, or both, and when does the panel sit? (4) Is this a good fit for RAPID/EAGER rather than a standard proposal? (5) After a declination: what did the panel actually mean, and is a resubmission worth it? Also attend the program's **virtual office hours and webinars** (listed at https://www.nsf.gov/events) — these are group Q&A with the same POs and are the lowest-friction entry point for someone nervous about cold-emailing.

WHAT THEY CANNOT DO — set expectations honestly: "Program officers are charged with directing fair and equitable Merit Review, so there is a limit to the information they can share." They will not discuss funding recommendations before an award is finalized, will not answer detailed budget questions (that is your sponsored projects office), will not edit your proposal, and will not advocate for their own funding. Also expect slow or no replies at first — NSF itself says "Don't be discouraged if you don't get a reply initially, and try reaching out again later." Individual POs differ on email vs. phone; rotators (academics serving temporary terms) turn over, so the named PO on a three-year-old solicitation may be gone.
result.funded_examples_source:
**Abstracts: fully public. Full proposals: obtainable by FOIA, redacted. Reviews and panel summaries: not obtainable by anyone but the PI.** Three distinct tiers, and conflating them is the usual mistake.

1. **NSF Award Search — https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/** — public abstracts for every NSF award since 1989, searchable by keyword, PI, institution, program, division and year, with award amount, dates and the program officer's name. This is the workhorse: read 20 funded abstracts in your target program, and note which PO signed them — that tells you both what the program funds and whom to email. NSF's own "Getting Started" page directs first-timers here.
2. **Full funded proposals via FOIA** — NSF treats proposals as "confidential intellectual property of the submitting organizations," but copies of *awarded* proposals are released on request with personal and proprietary information removed; the FOIA officer notifies the submitting institution and PI first. Start at https://www.nsf.gov/policies/foia. Slow (weeks to months) but it works, and it is the only route to a complete funded NSF proposal.
3. **Reviews, panel summaries and review analyses are FOIA-exempt** — evaluations of specific proposals by NSF staff or external panels are withheld under FOIA. There is no public equivalent of a "summary statement" library. You only ever see reviews of *your own* proposals, released to you through Research.gov after the decision.

ALSO USEFUL: **NSF Public Access Repository (NSF-PAR)** for the publications that came out of funded awards; **USAspending.gov** for the money side; for GRFP specifically, awardee and honorable-mention lists are public via Research.gov, and community-run archives of *successful GRFP essays* are the de facto standard reading for applicants — Alex Lang's collection at https://www.alexhunterlang.com/nsf-fellowship (third-party, not NSF) and MIT Communication Lab's annotated GRFP examples at https://mitcommlab.mit.edu/broad/commkit/nsf-research-proposal/. Many university research development offices and libraries maintain internal sample-proposal collections (CAREER proposals especially) available to their own faculty — for most early-career researchers this is the fastest route to reading a real funded CAREER narrative, and it is worth asking the research development office directly rather than assuming none exists.

Sourcing note: items 1-3 are from NSF's own pages and NSF's Public Information Handbook / FOIA regulations (45 CFR 612); the GRFP essay archives are community resources, located via search index, and NSF neither endorses nor hosts them.

result.funder_system:
Russell Sage Foundation (RSF) — private foundation, 112 East 64th St, New York; funds social-science research on US social/economic/political life. President: Bruce Western. One machinery serves every mechanism, but it splits into three shapes:

(A) TWO-STEP (LOI -> invited proposal): Core Research Grants (Trustee Grants capped at $200,000; Presidential Grants capped at $50,000, up to $75,000 "when the proposed research project involves labor intensive data collection or access fees to restricted-use data, or when the proposal budget includes salary support for multiple assistant professor PIs"; generally up to 2 years) and Margaret Olivia Sage (MOS) Grants. "We do not consider unsolicited proposals."
(B) ONE-STEP (proposal only, no LOI): Sheldon Danziger Pipeline Grants ($50k individual / $65k team, 1 yr, no indirect); Dissertation Research Grants ($15,000, 1 yr, no indirect); Causal Research on the Criminal Justice System ($100,000 incl. up to 15% indirect, 1 yr).
(C) FELLOWSHIPS: Visiting Scholars (10-month residency Sept 1–Jun 30 in New York), Visiting Researchers.

Core programmes rotate by round: Social, Political and Economic Inequality (SPEI), Future of Work (FOW), Behavioral Science and Decision Making in Context (BSDMC), Race, Ethnicity and Immigration (REI), plus special initiatives Immigration and Immigrant Integration (III) and the 2023 Supreme Court race-conscious-admissions decision (SCD23). NOT every programme is open at every deadline — for the Oct 28, 2026 round RSF states BSDMC, REI and III "are not accepting applications."

Funding rates, RSF's own words (/apply/grants/faq): "the funding rate for our core research grants is around 8-9%. The funding rate for our early-career grants tends to be a little higher: about 12-15% for the pipeline and dissertation grants. Our visiting scholar fellowship program has about a 20% acceptance rate."

Indirect costs: "RSF covers indirect costs of up to 15% on grants over $75,000 only" (Core). No indirect at all on Pipeline, Dissertation, or fellowships. No indirect on data purchases/access fees or on subcontracts to survey firms; only a subcontract organisation may budget indirect on subcontract funds.

METHOD NOTE: everything above and below was read from russellsage.org itself — WebFetch plus direct curl of the raw HTML for the drift-sensitive numbers (dates, page limits, dollar caps, percentages). No funder page 403'd. Only the initial discovery of page URLs used a search index.
result.submission_portal:
Fluxx — RSF's own hosted instance at https://rsf.fluxx.io (login/registration: https://rsf.fluxx.io/user_sessions/new). Applications are accepted ONLY through it: "All grant applications must be submitted by the deadline via the RSF online application portal, Fluxx, by an eligible principal investigator or co-principal investigator. Late or incomplete applications will not be reviewed."

THE HIDDEN LONG-LEAD ITEMS (both are RSF's own wording):
1. Account approval lag — the submission steps read: "Create a Fluxx account or log in to your existing account. **Allow up to 2 business days for a new account to be approved**". A first-time applicant who registers the day before a 2pm ET deadline can miss it.
2. The portal is not open year-round — "The Fluxx application portal will open two months ahead of a deadline." So the window to start an application in the system is roughly deadline minus 2 months to deadline.

Account ownership rule (people get caught by this): "All applications must be submitted directly by an eligible principal investigator (PI) or co-PI of the proposed project. The account must be in the name of the applicant. For example, university administration staff or a student may not submit on behalf of faculty. If the person submitting the application is not eligible to apply, the foundation will not consider the application." Grants administrators can be added to the record but cannot be the submitting account.

Draft expiry: "If a draft application is not electronically submitted by the next applicable deadline, the application will automatically be withdrawn and you will need to restart the process."

No Grants.gov, SAM.gov, eRA Commons or ORCID registration is involved. Application previews (PDF of every Fluxx form field, so you can draft offline before the portal opens) are published at /apply/tips — e.g. https://www.russellsage.org/sites/default/files/2026-04/Core_programs_application_04012026.pdf, .../Pipeline_application_04012026.pdf, .../DRG_application_04012026.pdf, .../CRCJS_application_04012026.pdf. There is also a "Fluxx Instructional Video" linked from the deadlines page.

review_stages.stage: LOI submitted in Fluxx (Core/MOS only). Max 4 single-spaced pages. Portal opened 2 months earlier; account approval takes up to 2 business days
review_stages.timing: Month 0 (2pm ET on the published date)

review_stages.stage: LOI internal staff screen — fit with RSF priorities, clarity, whether data/methods are described in enough detail. RSF: 'Approximately 25-35 percent of the LOIs will move to the next stage.' Those screened out get NO feedback
review_stages.timing: Months 0-1.5

review_stages.stage: LOI external peer review — 'At least 2-3 external peer reviewers will read an LOI... Approximately 50 percent of the externally reviewed LOIs will be invited to submit a full proposal.' Net: 'After peer review, about 15% of those who submit an LOI will receive an invitation to submit a proposal.' Everyone externally reviewed gets masked reviewer comments, funded or not
review_stages.timing: Months 1.5-2.5; RSF 'aim[s] to send out decisions no later than 1 month before the corresponding proposal deadline'

review_stages.stage: Invited proposal due — max 10 pages + budget + budget narrative + CVs + point-by-point response memo to the LOI reviewer comments
review_stages.timing: Month ~3.2-3.8 (e.g. LOI Mar 11, 2026 -> proposal Jun 18, 2026)

review_stages.stage: Proposal external peer review — 'At least 3-4 external peer reviewers will read the full proposal. Usually some of them have read the LOI. Proposals that received mostly positive reviews will typically be asked to respond to reviewer comments in detail before moving forward.'
review_stages.timing: Months 4-6

review_stages.stage: Advisory committee review — external experts recruited per programme area; they 'recommend which proposals are moved forward to the RSF Board for funding consideration, which proposals are invited to resubmit, and which are declined.' Committee or staff may put further questions to the PI

review_stages.stage: President / Board of Trustees decision — 'All proposals with budgets greater than $75,000 are reviewed by the Board of Trustees, who may decide to fund or reject a project, offer an opportunity to revise and resubmit for a future cycle, ask for further clarification, or approve with conditions. For projects with budgets of up to $75,000, the President makes the final decision.'
review_stages.timing: Month ~8 — published decision months: Nov 2026 / Mar 2027 / Jun 2027 for the three current Core rounds

review_stages.stage: Notification by email. RSF: 'The full review process takes about 8 months from an LOI deadline to a final decision.'
review_stages.timing: Month ~8

review_stages.stage: Earliest grant start date (published per round). Terms & Conditions requirements must be met 'before an award is finalized and payments are released'
review_stages.timing: Month ~9.5-10 — Jan 1 2027 / May 1 2027 / Sep 1 2027 for the three current rounds

review_stages.stage: EARLY-CAREER ONE-STEP TRACK (Pipeline, Dissertation, Criminal Justice): proposal -> internal staff screen ('Approximately 33-50 percent of the proposals will move to the next stage') -> 3-4 external peer reviewers, PIs may be asked to respond in detail -> standing advisory committee -> decision. Budget is NOT required at submission for Pipeline/DRG; it is finalised with the PI and their research office after approval
review_stages.timing: 'about three to four months from a proposal deadline to a final decision'

review_stages.stage: VISITING SCHOLAR TRACK: application (late June) -> review by staff and external experts -> 'Final decisions are made at the Foundation's November Board meeting and applicants are typically notified of the decisions by mid-December' -> 10-month residency Sept 1 - Jun 30 of the FOLLOWING academic year
review_stages.timing: ~6 months to decision; ~14 months from application to start of residency

review_stages.stage: VISITING RESEARCHER TRACK: decision 'within 45 days' of the deadline
review_stages.timing: ~1.5 months

result.months_submission_to_award: Core Research Grants: ~8 months from LOI deadline to final decision (RSF's own figure), and ~9.5-10 months from LOI deadline to the earliest permitted grant start — e.g. LOI Mar 11, 2026 -> decision Nov 2026 -> money can start Jan 1, 2027. From invited proposal to start is ~5 months (Jun 18, 2026 -> Jan 1, 2027). MOS Grants: same arc (LOI Dec 1, 2026 -> decision Jun 2027). Early-career one-step grants (Pipeline, Dissertation, Criminal Justice): 3-4 months from proposal deadline to decision. Visiting Scholar fellowship: ~6 months to decision (late-June deadline -> mid-December notification) but ~14 months to the start of residency (Sept 1 of the following year). Visiting Researcher: decision within 45 days. Expedited route, rarely granted: "In rare circumstances, the foundation may make decisions about proposals with budgets below $75,000 outside of its regular funding cycles if the proposed project is time constrained due to external factors. A special request must be made to the foundation outlining the reasons for the time-constraint" — only external factors count.
result.resubmission_policy:
Two distinct things exist at RSF and applicants confuse them.

1) DECLINED -> reapply. Allowed, with no stated cap and no stated waiting period, but it is not an NIH-style A1. RSF: "An applicant may revise an application and submit during a subsequent funding round. However, the application will be processed as a new submission." So there is no resubmission-specific deadline, no A0/A1 counter, and no NIH-style Introduction page. A declined Core LOI simply re-enters as a fresh LOI at a later round — and note the programme rotation, so the relevant programme may not be open at the very next deadline.

2) INVITED RESUBMISSION. A live category inside the process, not a consolation: the advisory committees "recommend which proposals are moved forward to the RSF Board for funding consideration, which proposals are invited to resubmit, and which are declined," and the Board may "offer an opportunity to revise and resubmit for a future cycle, ask for further clarification, or approve with conditions." Number of attempts and any time window for an invited resubmission are NOT published.

3) THE RSF EQUIVALENT OF AN INTRODUCTION PAGE IS MANDATORY, BUT IT SITS BETWEEN THE TWO STAGES. "Point-by-point response memo to previous reviewer comments" is a listed required document of every invited Core proposal — i.e. you must answer the LOI reviewers in writing. The same move recurs after proposal review: "Proposals that received mostly positive reviews will typically be asked to respond to reviewer comments in detail before moving forward." No page limit is published for either memo. RSF publishes real examples of these memos (see funded_examples_source) — they are the single best guide to the expected register.

4) TIME WINDOW ON AN INVITATION. An LOI invitation is tied to a named proposal deadline: "You are expected to submit your proposal by the deadline for which you are invited. However, you may request a deferral to a subsequent deadline if you need more time... Deferrals must be requested as soon as possible and at least 2 weeks before the proposal deadline. If you do not submit your proposal and you have not requested a deferral, your application will be considered withdrawn and you will need to restart the application process by submitting a new letter of inquiry." That 2-week deferral request is a real, dated, easily-missed lever.

5) MULTIPLE / LIFETIME LIMITS. Core: "you may submit multiple letters of inquiry (for different projects) for the same funding cycle" — and RSF advises splitting distinct projects into separate LOIs rather than bundling. You do not resubmit the same LOI to several priorities: "your application will be evaluated across all of our research priorities." Pipeline: one proposal per cycle, and the PI must not have had an RSF research grant before. Dissertation Research Grants: "lifetime limit of one dissertation research grant per applicant." Visiting Scholars: "maximum of two visits," a second beginning "no earlier than seven years after their first visit," with first-time applicants given priority all else equal.
result.page_limits:
All limits are single-spaced, standard 12-point font, 1-inch margins (the FAQ also permits 11-point in one phrasing; the requirements page says 12). Source: https://www.russellsage.org/apply/info/requirements (raw HTML).

CORE RESEARCH GRANTS
- LOI: "Maximum of 4 single-spaced pages... excluding references." No budget, CV, appendices or letters of support at LOI stage; an optional 1-2 sentences on the budget is permitted.
- Invited proposal: "Maximum of 10 single-spaced pages... excluding (1) references, (2) supporting tables and figures, and (3) appendices like draft survey instruments and interview protocols."
- CV: 5 pages max per PI/co-PI.
- Response memo to previous reviewer comments: no stated limit.

VARIATIONS BY MECHANISM
- Sheldon Danziger Pipeline Grants: proposal max 7 pages (same exclusions); CV 5 pages; budget and budget narrative only after approval.
- Dissertation Research Grants: proposal max 5 pages; CV 5 pages; letter from the dissertation supervisor; budget/budget narrative (with a dissertation timeline) only after approval.
- Causal Research on the Criminal Justice System: proposal max 10 pages; CV 5 pages; budget after approval.
- Visiting Scholar Fellowship: proposal max 5 pages, excluding up to 2 pages of references and supporting tables/figures; CV 5 pages; working-group members each file their own application containing a common statement of the joint project. "RSF does not accept supplementary application materials, such as papers and recommendations."
- Visiting Researcher Fellowship: proposal max 5 pages (same exclusions), must state the requested residency period; CV 5 pages; no supplementary materials.

WHAT THE NARRATIVE MUST CONTAIN (Core proposal, RSF's list): problem and importance; cross-disciplinary literature and the unique contribution; hypotheses/questions; data and how acquired, with power calculations where appropriate and "a plan for public release of the data and documentation"; for data-collection projects, sampling strategy, sample characteristics (including whether participants are habitual survey respondents) and participant compensation; if a survey firm will collect data, quotes from at least two firms with the choice justified in the budget narrative; analytic methods; workplan with timeline and milestones; team qualifications and responsibilities; dissemination plan.

ALLOCATION RULE THAT DECIDES MOST APPLICATIONS: "The research design (describing the data, methods, analytic plan, etc.) should take up at least 50 percent of the narrative... Discussions of broader impact, fit with RSF goals, investigator qualifications, and requested budget should be brief."
required_documents: Fluxx online application form (create account >= 2 business days ahead; portal opens 2 months before the deadline; account must be in the PI's or co-PI's own name)
CORE LOI: narrative, max 4 single-spaced pages, 12-pt, 1-inch margins, references excluded — that is the entire required package. No budget, no CV, no letters of support
CORE INVITED PROPOSAL: narrative, max 10 pages (references, supporting tables/figures and appendices such as draft survey instruments and interview protocols excluded)

CORE INVITED PROPOSAL: budget on RSF's Excel Budget Template (https://www.russellsage.org/sites/default/files/2025-08/Budget_Template_Research_Grants_01212025.xlsx) — 'Budgets must be uploaded in Excel format'
CORE INVITED PROPOSAL: budget narrative explaining and breaking down every line item; must discuss the two required survey-firm quotes where a firm will collect data
CORE INVITED PROPOSAL: CV for PI and each co-PI, 5 pages max each
CORE INVITED PROPOSAL: point-by-point response memo to the previous (LOI) reviewer comments — mandatory
Later in review: a detailed written response to the proposal reviewers' comments, usually requested of well-reviewed proposals
Plan for public release of data and documentation, described inside the narrative (see Grant Terms and Conditions)
PIPELINE GRANTS: 7-page proposal + CVs (5 pp); budget and budget narrative required only after approval

DISSERTATION RESEARCH GRANTS: 5-page proposal + CVs (5 pp) + letter from the dissertation supervisor certifying the research matches the proposal and has been approved by the committee (required before funds are disbursed if the prospectus is defended in the spring after the deadline); budget after approval
CRIMINAL JUSTICE GRANTS: 10-page proposal with timeline and brief budget description + CVs (5 pp); full budget after approval

VISITING SCHOLAR / VISITING RESEARCHER: 5-page proposal (+ up to 2 pp references) + 5-page CV; working groups file individually with a common joint-project statement; no papers or recommendation letters accepted

NOT required anywhere in the published requirements: letters of support, IRB/human-subjects approval documentation, or a separate data management plan document (data public-release plans are described within the narrative and governed by the Terms & Conditions)
result.program_officer_norms:
EXPECTED AND EXPLICITLY INVITED — closer to NIH than to the foundations that discourage contact, but routed through one shared inbox rather than named officers.

RSF's own instructions, two places:
- Tips & Resources: "Confirm fit with Foundation's research priorities: Browse recently award[ed] grants and read the RFPs, FAQs, and other literature provided for each of our research priorities to see if your project might be a fit. If you're unsure, please reach out at least one month ahead of the deadline to programs@rsage.org with a short abstract and some details about the research design."
- Grant Seeker FAQ: "If you have questions about the application, budget, or process in general, email us at programs@rsage.org and one of our program staff will respond. Applicants are also encouraged to reach out to program staff in advance to inquire about the fit of their proposed project with current funding priorities."

WHEN IN THE CYCLE: at least one month before the LOI deadline — i.e. roughly when the Fluxx portal opens. Not the week of the deadline.

WHAT TO SEND: a short abstract plus specifics of the research design. Not a full draft; not a phone call request.

WHAT EXPERIENCED APPLICANTS ACTUALLY ASK: (1) is this within a currently open priority, and which one (bearing in mind programmes rotate by round and some are closed in a given cycle) — though note you do not pick a priority yourself, since "your application will be evaluated across all of our research priorities"; (2) is my project at the right stage for this mechanism (Core generally expects proof of concept or pilot data in hand; early-career grants may be at pilot stage but need a detailed design; Visiting Fellowships are for projects whose data collection is finished); (3) should two related experiments be one LOI or two (RSF's stated view: "in most cases... investigators would have a higher chance of success if they submitted separate LOIs"); (4) budget mechanics — is this a Presidential or Trustee ask, does the $75,000 line apply, are these costs allowable; (5) whether a deferral of an invited proposal is possible (must be requested at least 2 weeks before the proposal deadline); (6) rarely, an out-of-cycle decision for a sub-$75,000, externally time-constrained project.

NO NAMED PROGRAM-OFFICER DIRECTORY IS PUBLISHED. RSF lists Bruce Western (President) and Program Directors Leana Chatrath, Aixa Cintrón-Vélez and James Wilson on /about/who-we-are, but publishes no individual emails and no mapping of directors to programme areas — everything goes to programs@rsage.org.

OTHER LIVE CHANNELS: RSF runs grant-writing webinars ("Best Practices for Grant Writing," Sept 22, 2026, 2:00pm EDT, Zoom registration linked from /apply/tips), keeps recordings at /news/watch/webinars, and posts a Fluxx instructional video. No office hours are advertised.

WHY CONTACT PAYS: 65-75% of Core LOIs die at the internal staff screen, and RSF names the three usual causes — the application "(1) is not perceived to be well-aligned with the Foundation's funding priorities; (2) lacks sufficient detail on the research design, data, and methods to allow reviewers to assess the viability of the project; or (3) is poorly framed or written." Cause (1) is exactly what a pre-submission email settles.
result.funded_examples_source:
THREE LAYERS, and the second is unusually generous — RSF publishes complete real applications WITH the reviewer-response memos, which almost no funder does.

1) GRANTS DATABASE — https://www.russellsage.org/research/grants. ~2,303 awarded projects, award years 1994 through 2026, filterable by keyword, academic discipline (30+), research priority (current and past), co-funder, and award year; sortable by year, title, amount and priority. Each record page carries PI name(s), institution, award month/year, programme, and a plain-language project description/abstract (example: https://www.russellsage.org/research/grants/class-and-representation-american-politics — Frederick DeVeaux, UCLA, June 2026, Dissertation Research Grants, opening line "Working-class Americans make up most of the labor force but hold only a small share of legislative seats."). Award amounts are not shown on the record pages I checked.

result.funder_system:
Spencer Foundation (private foundation, Chicago IL; EIN 36-6078558), the main US private funder of field-initiated education research. Verified 2026-09-18 against spencer.org and naeducation.org; www.spencer.org fetches cleanly, the apex spencerfoundation.org currently returns an expired TLS certificate to a plain fetch (tooling fact, not a programme fact).

TWO DISTINCT MACHINERIES UNDER ONE BRAND — this is the single most important thing a first-time applicant gets wrong:
(A) SPENCER RESEARCH GRANTS — applied for directly to Spencer via its own SmartSimple portal. PI/Co-PI must hold an earned doctorate; graduate students may be on the team but "may not be named the PI or Co-PI." Spencer "does not award grants directly to individuals" — every proposal goes through a non-profit administering organization. Programmes: Research Grants on Education: Small (max $50,000 total, up to 5 yrs, optional +$10,000 course-release supplement = $60,000 max); Large ($125,000-$500,000, 1-5 yrs, three budget tiers); Racial Equity Research Grants (up to $75,000, 1-5 yrs); Research-Practice Partnerships (up to $400,000, up to 3 yrs); Vision Grants ($75,000, 12-18 months planning grant). Vision Grants feed a closed pipeline: "The Transformative Research Grants are open only to those who have completed a Vision Grant" — "research grants, of up to $3.5 million."
(B) NAEd/SPENCER FELLOWSHIPS — funded by Spencer but administered and reviewed entirely by the National Academy of Education, on a different portal, a different deadline and a different review calendar. Dissertation Fellowship $30,000 (doctoral candidates); Postdoctoral Fellowship $80,000 for one academic year or $40,000 for each of two years half-time (PhD conferred 1 Jan 2021 - 31 Dec 2025 for the 2027 cycle, and must "not hold tenure status at the time of the application deadline"). Also a Spencer Education Journalism Fellowship run through Columbia.

For your three reader personas this maps cleanly: PhD student -> NAEd/Spencer Dissertation Fellowship (the only route where they are the applicant, since they cannot be PI on a Spencer grant); postdoc -> NAEd/Spencer Postdoctoral Fellowship, plus eligibility to be PI on a Small Research Grant once the doctorate is conferred and an administering organization will host them; early-career researcher -> Small Research Grants as the standard entry point, Racial Equity or RPP if the work fits, Large/Vision later.

Scale marker from Spencer's own staff page: "Our staff supports the review of over 2200 proposals annually."

CROSS-PROGRAMME RULES THAT BITE (all from /resources/Applicant-Information-and-Policies):
- One at a time, in both directions. "PIs and Co-PIs are restricted from holding more than one active research grant from the Spencer Foundation at a time" (this includes NAEd/Spencer fellowships), and "PIs and Co-PIs may not submit more than one application (including preproposals) to the Spencer Foundation at a time" across Small, Large, Racial Equity and RPP — "they are required to wait until a final decision has been made on the pending application before they can submit a new one." Vision Grants are the exception: you may hold or have pending another Spencer grant, provided the projects "must be distinct."
- Dual NAEd + Spencer submission of the same idea is allowed but must be declared, and forces a choice later: "you must choose to withdraw your proposal from either the fellowship or the Spencer grant competition" if you become a semifinalist.
- Indirect costs: "We do not allow indirect costs on grant awards of $75,000 or less." Above $75,000, 15% of total direct costs, and Spencer "does not pay government-approved overhead rates." With subcontracts, the combined indirect "should not exceed 15% of the total research grant proposal budget."
- International applicants welcome; if funded and without a US IRS determination, an Equivalency Determination certificate is obtained through NGOSource.
- All programmes require acknowledging Spencer's generative-AI policy at submission.
result.submission_portal:
SPENCER RESEARCH GRANTS: SmartSimple Cloud at https://spencer.smartsimple.us/ (login page https://spencer.smartsimple.us/s_Login.jsp). Self-registration — "New to the Spencer Portal? Register Here." No Grants.gov, SAM.gov, eRA Commons or ORCID prerequisite. Portal support: mgarcia@spencer.org. Once registered you work from a "Workbench" and click Apply for the programme.

TWO HIDDEN LONG-LEAD ITEMS, both invisible from the public site:

1. THE ADMINISTERING ORGANIZATION MUST ALREADY BE IN SPENCER'S DATABASE. "If your organization is not currently in Spencer's database, you will need to submit a request to have your organization added. Requests must be received at least 3 business days before a deadline to allow time for review and approval." For anyone at a small college, a school district, an NGO or a non-US institution that has never held a Spencer grant, this is the step that kills applications. Do it weeks out, not days.

2. THE REAL RULES LIVE BEHIND THE LOGIN. Every Spencer research-grant page ends with the same sentence: "On our online application portal you'll find the full Request For Proposal and other applicant resources such as optional appendices, our review process, frequently asked questions, and writing guides." The public web pages are a summary; the RFP, the review-process description and the FAQ are portal-gated. Practical consequence for your interface: the correct first action for a Spencer applicant is not "read the programme page", it is "register on SmartSimple and download the RFP", even months before a cycle opens. Spencer's own 990-PF says the same thing about everything else: "APPLICATION, INFORMATION, AND MATERIALS REQUIREMENTS POSTED ON WEBSITE."

Also: full proposals need an authorized institutional signature. "The Spencer Foundation requires that submitted proposals be reviewed and signed by an authorized representative of the administering organization (typically a grants and contracts or finance administrator)" — but "this requirement does not apply to Intent to Apply forms or preproposals." So stage-one submissions can be made by the PI alone; stage two needs the research office in the loop. Vision Grants use Adobe E-sign for this.

NAEd/SPENCER FELLOWSHIPS: an entirely separate system, Secure Platform. Dissertation: https://naedfellowships.secure-platform.com/a/page/dissertationfellowship. Postdoctoral: https://naedfellowships.secure-platform.com/a/page/postdocfellowship. Contact info@naeducation.org. Referees are invited by email through the platform; NAEd warns "we recommend applicants notify reviewers that the email is forthcoming and to check their spam folder."

NAEd/Spencer Dissertation AND Postdoctoral Fellowships, 2027 cycle (both, same date):

PUBLISHED RECURRENCE (this is what an interface should show when there is no live date):

- Large Research Grants: "We accept preproposals once a year."

DEADLINE TIME CONVENTION: Spencer research grants close at midday, not midnight. I could not establish forward dates for the four closed programmes from any Spencer source, and I will not infer them from past cycles — Spencer's own 990-PF points applicants to the website as the sole authority: "DEADLINES POSTED ON FOUNDATION'S WEBSITE, WWW.SPENCER.ORG". The honest interface behaviour is a "watch this page" state plus the recurrence and the noon-Central convention, not a guessed month. result.months_submission_to_award:
Two clean, funder-stated numbers and one gap.

SMALL RESEARCH GRANTS: 8 months from submission deadline to earliest project start, stated by Spencer as a planning rule: "Teams should plan to begin their project timeline no sooner than 8 months from the original proposal submission deadline." This is the number to budget against — it means a proposal submitted in a spring cycle cannot support work starting before the following winter/spring.

NAEd/SPENCER FELLOWSHIPS: ~11 months deadline-to-start, fully dated for the current cycle — deadline 8 Oct 2026, first cut February 2027 (~4 months), finalists April 2027 (~6 months), notification May 2027 (~7 months), feedback by July 2027 (~9 months), fellowship begins 1 Sep 2027 (~11 months). A PhD student planning a final dissertation year must therefore apply a full year ahead.

RPP / LARGE: partial. Preproposal review is "approximately 3 months (subject to change)", and the 2026 RPP calendar puts 3.5 months between the preproposal and full-proposal deadlines. The full-proposal-to-award interval is NOT published on the public pages — it is in the portal RFP. If the 8-month Small Grants figure generalises, an RPP full proposal due 28 Oct 2026 would not start work until well into 2027, but I did not establish this and it should not be stated as fact.

RACIAL EQUITY / VISION: no interval published publicly.
result.resubmission_policy:
SPENCER RESEARCH GRANTS — resubmission is permitted, with no stated cap and no stated time window, but it is not a silent re-file: you must declare it and account for the revision. Identical wording across Large, Racial Equity and RPP: "If this is a resubmission of a proposal previously submitted to the Spencer Foundation, you are asked to indicate this within the application and upload a 1-page explanation of how the proposal was revised."

So the NIH-style "Introduction to Resubmission" analogue exists here as a 1-page revision explanation, and it is a separate uploaded document, not part of the narrative word count. Unlike NIH there is no A0/A1 limit stated, no requirement that the resubmission go to the same programme, and no expiry window found.

THE REAL CONSTRAINT IS NOT THE RESUBMISSION RULE, IT IS THE QUEUE RULE. Because "PIs and Co-PIs may not submit more than one application (including preproposals) to the Spencer Foundation at a time" across Small, Large, Racial Equity and RPP, and "they are required to wait until a final decision has been made on the pending application before they can submit a new one", you cannot resubmit into the next cycle while the previous decision is pending. With Small Grants running twice a year but taking ~8 months to a project start, the practical resubmission cadence is roughly annual, not per-cycle. Vision Grants sit outside this queue.

NAEd/SPENCER FELLOWSHIPS — explicitly allowed, as a fresh application each time. Dissertation: "Yes. Applicants may reapply for the fellowship if eligible. Re-applicants must submit a new application." Postdoctoral: "Yes. You may reapply for the fellowship if eligible. Re-applicants must submit a new application." No revision-explanation document; no cap; the binding limit is the eligibility window (postdoc: degree conferred within the stated 5-year span). Feedback now supports a second attempt — postdoc applicants get it "by July", and dissertation feedback is being piloted "Beginning with the 2027 applications."

Not established: whether Spencer's research-grant reviewers see the previous submission or the revision explanation is used administratively only; whether a declined preproposal may be resubmitted as a preproposal in the next annual round. Both are the kind of detail the portal RFP would settle.
result.page_limits:
Spencer counts WORDS, not pages, for narratives — an unusual convention that trips people coming from NIH/NSF page limits — and the limits are small. Most Spencer narratives are shorter than a single NSF Project Description. Verified 2026-09-18 from each programme page.

SPENCER RESEARCH GRANTS
- Small ($50,000): proposal narrative "may not exceed 1800 words", double-spaced, 12-point; proposal summary 200 words; project timeline max 1 page; project team description max 250 words.
- Large ($125,000-$500,000), preproposal, single PDF: narrative "no more than 1250 words"; references up to 2 pages; team description 1 page; timeline 1 page; budget up to 2 pages.
- Large, full proposal (by invitation): narrative "may not exceed 5000 words" with references excluded from the count; project timeline "may not exceed 1 page"; project team document "should not exceed 800 words".
- Racial Equity (up to $75,000): Intent to Apply "not more than 200 words"; narrative "may not exceed 2500 words"; timeline "may not exceed 1 page"; project team "should not exceed 250 words".
- RPP (up to $400,000), preproposal: single PDF, max 1,350 words, double-spaced, 11-point minimum, with internal targets — problem ~250 words, partners and partnership history ~500, research questions ~100, activities ~400, contribution and equity ~100; budget table with justification max 2 pages; references up to 2 pages (optional but recommended).
- RPP, full proposal (by invitation): narrative "may not exceed 4500 words", 12-point, double-spaced, APA preferred; timeline max 1 page; project team "may not exceed 800 words"; partner letter(s); subcontract forms if applicable.
- Vision Grants ($75,000): Intent to Apply 200 words max; proposal narrative 2000 words max, double-spaced, 12-point; timeline max 1 page, 9-point minimum.
- CV limit lives in the SmartSimple profile, not the application: 10 pages.

NAEd/SPENCER FELLOWSHIPS — these DO use pages
- Dissertation: narrative "no more than 10 double-spaced pages"; bibliography "max two page"; abstract a single-spaced paragraph; graduate transcripts; personal statement; work plan; background information; TWO letters of recommendation — "one from the applicant's dissertation director/chair and one from another faculty member".
- Postdoctoral: project description max 10 double-spaced pages; bibliography max 2 pages single-spaced; an example of past research max 20 double-spaced pages; career statement; CV; THREE letters of recommendation.
- Appendices allowed but deprioritised: "You may include technical and supplemental appendices (charts, graphs, tables, questionnaires, etc.)... However, be judicious, as we do not require judges to review material in the appendices."

WHAT VARIES BY MECHANISM: the narrative word count (1250 -> 5000) and whether there is a stage-one gate at all. WHAT IS CONSTANT: the 200-word proposal summary, the 1-page timeline, a project-team document, budget and justification, CV, the AI-policy acknowledgement, and the 1-page resubmission explanation when applicable. "Optional appendices" are described on every page but their specification is only in the portal RFP.

result.program_officer_norms:
DIFFERENT FROM NIH IN KIND, NOT JUST IN DEGREE — and this is the field where I have the least funder-stated evidence, so I am separating what is documented from what is not.

WHAT IS DOCUMENTED. Spencer routes applicant questions to PROGRAMME MAILBOXES, not to named individual program officers. Each programme page carries one contact:
- Small Research Grants — smallgrants@spencer.org
- Large Research Grants — largegrants@spencer.org (named contact: Maricelle Garcia)
- Racial Equity Research Grants — racial-equity@spencer.org
- Research-Practice Partnerships — research-practice-partnership@spencer.org (named contact: Maricelle Garcia)
- Vision Grants — visiongrants@spencer.org (named contact: Jasmine Knetl)
- SmartSimple portal/password problems — mgarcia@spencer.org
- General: 312-337-7000, office hours 8am-4pm, 625 N Michigan Ave Suite 1600, Chicago IL 60611
- NAEd fellowships — info@naeducation.org
Note that the people named on these programme pages are titled "Program contact", i.e. administrative. Spencer separately employs Program Officers (Jessica Marshall, Tafadzwa Tivaringe, Krystal Villanosa), Associate Program Officers (Chris Klager, Ellis Reid, Anthony Williams) and a Director of Programs (Leah Bricker), but the public site does NOT publish their emails or invite applicants to contact them. That is the structural difference from NIH, where the named scientific PO is the point of contact and pre-submission contact is expected.

The ONE contact Spencer explicitly instructs you to make is administrative, not scientific: "If you submit applications to both the NAEd/Spencer fellowship program and a Spencer grant program with the same project idea, please email the Spencer administrative contact for the grant program to which you are applying and let them know that you are also applying to the NAEd/Spencer fellowship program."

WHAT IS NOT DOCUMENTED, AND WHY. I found NO public statement encouraging, tolerating or discouraging pre-submission scientific contact, and no public FAQ at all — spencer.org/faq returns 404 and the site has no FAQ page. Every Spencer research-grant page says the FAQ is inside the portal: "On our online application portal you'll find the full Request For Proposal and other applicant resources such as optional appendices, our review process, frequently asked questions, and writing guides." So the document that would answer this question sits behind a login I should not create. Marked unresolved rather than guessed.

WHAT THIS MEANS IN PRACTICE, stated as inference not as funder policy: with >2200 proposals reviewed annually and a 200-word-to-1800-word front end, Spencer's machinery is built to absorb volume, not to triage by conversation. The behaviour that pays off here is not the NIH "email the PO your specific aims" move; it is (a) registering and reading the portal RFP, which contains the review process and criteria that are absent from the public web, (b) using the programme mailbox for eligibility, budget, administering-organization and dual-submission questions — the things Spencer has made answerable, and (c) treating the two non-competitive Intent to Apply gates (Racial Equity, Vision) as the cheapest possible probe of fit, since they are 200 words, carry "no impact on proposal review", and unlock the full application automatically.

For fit questions specifically, NAEd gives the only published guidance, and it points at the award record rather than at a person: "Applicants should look at the listing of grants awarded during past years to assess the range of topics supported... It is the applicant's responsibility to state clearly and explicitly the connection between the proposed research and the improvement of education. If an applicant can make a case that their research is relevant to education, consider applying."
result.funded_examples_source:
There is NO Spencer equivalent of NIH RePORTER — Spencer's website has no searchable awarded-grants database anywhere in its navigation, and NAEd states flatly: "The NAEd does not make previous applications publicly available." So no funded full applications are published by either body. Four real routes exist instead, in descending order of usefulness:

1. IRS FORM 990-PF, PART XIV/XV — THE BEST SOURCE FOR RESEARCH GRANTS, and the one nobody thinks of. As a private foundation Spencer must itemise every grant paid with recipient and stated purpose. I pulled the FY-ending-March-2025 filing directly and it gives institution + project title + amount, e.g.: Michigan State University, "Creating Transformative Possibility in Schools", $483,044; University of California Berkeley, "Linguistic Variation and Disciplinary Action", $392,629; University of Kansas Center for Research, "Tribal Education Department Capacity Building", $382,906; FLACSO Argentina, "History Teaching Through Dialogical Controversies", $274,540; Boston University, "Re-Imagining Alternative Education", $250,850. It also exposes the foundation's own shape — the two largest lines are the pass-throughs to the National Academy of Education for the Postdoctoral ($2,532,835) and Dissertation ($1,753,042) fellowship programmes, and the Columbia University line ($593,600) funds the Journalism Fellowship. Access via ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer, EIN 36-6078558: https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/366078558 — filings available FY2002-FY2025, full text at the /full view for recent years. This gives a reader a title-level map of what actually gets funded and at what size, which is exactly the "am I in scope, and what does a real funded project look like" question.

2. NAEd AWARDEES DATABASE — THE BEST SOURCE FOR FELLOWSHIPS, and it includes abstracts. https://naeducation.org/awardees/ lists past Dissertation and Postdoctoral fellows, filterable by Award, Year, Institution and Discipline, with individual pages at https://naeducation.org/awardee/<name>/ carrying project title, year, institution, discipline, a project abstract and a biography. Current cohorts: https://naeducation.org/current-naed-spencer-dissertation-fellows/ and https://naeducation.org/current-naed-spencer-postdoctoral-fellows/. For a PhD student this is the closest available thing to a model application — real funded dissertation projects in their own discipline, at a comparable career stage.

3. SPENCER'S OWN HOW-TO GUIDES — not examples, but the missing craft layer, and they are NOT linked from spencer.org's applicant pages. They are reachable only via the NAEd fellowship pages: "The Spencer Foundation published three how-to guides applicants may find beneficial while working on their proposals" — "Writing Successful Research Grant Proposals", "Communicating Your Qualitative Research Design", and "A Guide to Quantitative Proposals", hosted on NAEd SharePoint (e.g. https://nationalacademyofeducation.sharepoint.com/:b:/s/ProfessionalDevelopment/EYZ7P3WGCI9Hvc8quBLntkgBRPkXOt-1sNHpbjwL_erkmQ). NAEd adds the SSRC classic: "On the Art of Writing Proposals" (https://s3.amazonaws.com/ssrc-cdn1/crmuploads/new_publication_3/%7B7A9CB4F4-815F-DE11-BD80-001CC477EC70%7D.pdf). Spencer's own guides being discoverable only through its grantee organisation's fellowship page is a genuine findability failure worth surfacing in the interface.

4. PRE-2005 SPENCER ANNUAL REPORTS — historical only. https://www.spencer.org/financial-reports hosts annual reports 1996-2025, and the page notes that "Prior to 2005, the Annual Report also contained information on the our granting activities"; post-2005 reports are financial statements only. Useful for long-run corpus work, not for a current applicant.

Also worth noting for the interface: the writing guides and review-process description that Spencer itself considers the applicant's main resources are inside the SmartSimple portal, so "register for the portal" is simultaneously the submission step, the documentation step and the examples step.
