unresolved: ASCR and IRP project-narrative page limits: NOT STATED in the FY2026 Open Call NOFO. BES, BER, FES, HEP and NP all state one; ASCR and IRP do not. An applicant to those two must ask the named subprogram contact. Not found — do not invent a number.

Actual (as opposed to target) time from submission to award for the Open Call: DOE publishes only the 6-month target and the 12-month regulatory ceiling. No observed median or distribution is published. Not found.

Whether there is any waiting period before resubmitting a declined Open Call application: no waiting period is stated anywhere in the NOFO. The only stated constraint is substantive (must be 'substantially revised in light of merit reviewer comments'). Absence of a rule, not a rule of absence — but I could not find any time bar.

Whether ASCR, NP and IRP carry the same 'previously declined applications ... may be declined without additional merit review' rule that BER and HEP state explicitly. It appears only in the BER and HEP sections of the FY2026 NOFO. Not established for the other four offices.

Date discrepancy in DOE's own materials: the FY2026 Open Call NOFO cover and Section V say the NOFO closes 'September 30, 2026, 11:59 PM Eastern Time', while the science.osti.gov Open FOAs listing renders it as 'September 30, 2026, 7:59 PM Eastern'. Treat the NOFO PDF as authoritative and submit well before either.

Further internal inconsistency in the same NOFO: the issue date is given as 30 September 2025 on the PDF cover and as Monday, 29 September 2025 on the web page; the predecessor DE-FOA-0003432 is described as published 'September 30, 2024' on page 1 and 'September 29, 2024' on page 142. Immaterial to applicants but a caution that even the funder's own dates drift.

ECRP FY2026 selection announcement date: the NOFO says selection 'will be completed by July 2026' and the FAQ suggests a 1 September 2026 start, but no public announcement date is given, and the ECRP page does not state when selectees are named. FY2025 selectees appear to have been announced around February 2026 based on a laboratory press release, which would be far later than the FY2026 stated schedule — I could not reconcile this against a DOE primary source and am not treating it as established.

Whether PAMS institutional registration requires approval by an institutional administrator (and therefore has its own lead time beyond the stated 'at least a week'): the NOFO describes self-service association with an institution, but the 'Submit to DOE' privilege that a pre-application requires is granted by the institution, and I found no published statement of how long that takes. Not found — ask your sponsored research office early.

The FY2027 Open Call: expected to be issued around 29-30 September 2026 as a successor NOFO, by the annual pattern, but it was not published as of this research and its topic-level target dates are therefore unknown. All FY2026 target dates above will be superseded.

result.funder_system: U.S. Department of Justice → Office of Justice Programs (OJP) → National Institute of Justice (NIJ). NIJ is DOJ's research, development and evaluation agency; its machinery is OJP's machinery, so almost everything below is identical across NIJ's research mechanisms (Research & Evaluation topic solicitations, forensic science R&D, Graduate Research Fellowship, concept-paper solicitations) and is shared with sister OJP agencies (BJA, OJJDP, OVC, BJS). Assistance Listing Number for NIJ research is 16.560. Final award decisions are made by the Director of NIJ (statutory carve-out from OJP's default, where the Assistant Attorney General decides). Peer review ratings are explicitly advisory only: "Peer review ratings...are strictly advisory" (nij.ojp.gov/funding/proposal-review). Key structural point for an early-career applicant: the *institution* is always the applicant, never the individual — this is true even for the Graduate Research Fellowship, where NIJ states "The official applicant is the sponsoring academic institution. Students must contact and seek the assistance of the university's Office of Sponsored Programs, or equivalent office." Non-U.S. entities are not eligible; all awards go to U.S. institutions.
result.submission_portal:
Two-step, two-system, two-deadline submission. Nothing goes to a single NIJ portal.

STEP 1 — Grants.gov: submit the SF-424 (Application for Federal Assistance) only. For concept-paper solicitations, the concept paper is ALSO uploaded here in Step 1. Signed by the organization's Authorized Organizational Representative (AOR). SF-424 Section 8F must name the person who will complete the JustGrants application — JustGrants assigns the application to that email address.

STEP 2 — JustGrants (DOJ's Justice Grants System, justicegrants.usdoj.gov): the full application — web forms plus uploaded attachments. Grants.gov transmits the SF-424 to JustGrants, which emails the Section 8F contact with instructions.

HIDDEN LONG-LEAD REGISTRATIONS (the item that sinks first-time applicants):
1. SAM.gov registration, which issues the Unique Entity Identifier (UEI). "This process may take several weeks." OJP: "Applicants are encouraged to start the SAM.gov registration or renewal process at least 30 days prior to the application's Grants.gov deadline" and warns that those who fail to begin "at least 10 business days prior to the Grants.gov deadline may not be able to complete the process in time and will not be considered for a technical waiver that allows for late submission." SAM.gov must be RENEWED every 12 months — an expired registration blocks submission. NOFOs now print an explicit "begin SAM.gov by" date in the Key Dates table.
2. Grants.gov account + AOR role, confirmed by the entity's E-Business Point of Contact (E-Biz POC), who is designated during SAM.gov registration. NIJ: "it can take several weeks for first-time registrants to receive confirmation of registration and a user password."
3. JustGrants Entity Administrator must exist and must grant roles (Application Submitter, Authorized Representative) to the right people. This is a separate onboarding from Grants.gov and is where university research offices most often stall.

Practical: OJP recommends submitting the SF-424 at least 48 hours before the Grants.gov deadline and the full JustGrants package at least 48 hours before the JustGrants deadline. Expect four Grants.gov confirmation emails within 48 hours (submission receipt, validation receipt, grantor retrieval receipt, tracking number) and a JustGrants login email within 24 hours after those.

Late submission: not automatic. "OJP does not automatically approve requests to submit a late application even in the event of technological difficulties." A technical waiver requires contacting the NOFO's named contact within 24 hours of the missed deadline with support-desk tracking numbers and screenshots. Explicitly insufficient grounds: failing to register in time, not following Grants.gov instructions, and "Technical issues with the applicant's computer or information technology environment, such as issues with firewalls or browser incompatibility."

Help desks: OJP Response Center 800-851-3420, OJP.ResponseCenter@usdoj.gov (9am–5pm ET M–F); Grants.gov 800-518-4726 (24/7); JustGrants Service Desk 833-872-5175, JustGrants.Support@usdoj.gov (7am–9pm ET M–F, 9am–5pm weekends/holidays); SAM.gov Federal Service Desk.
result.deadline_structure:
PER-SOLICITATION. NIJ publishes NO standard recurring due dates — there is no NIJ equivalent of NIH's standard due dates by activity code, and no new-vs-resubmission date split. Every date lives in the individual NOFO's "Key Dates and Times" table. What IS stable is the SHAPE, not the dates:

STABLE SHAPE (safe to publish):
- Each NOFO carries two deadlines about 7–8 days apart: a Grants.gov Step-1 deadline at 11:59 p.m. ET, then a JustGrants Step-2 deadline at 8:59 p.m. ET. The 8:59 p.m. JustGrants cutoff is a recurring trap — it is not midnight.
- Each NOFO prints a "begin SAM.gov registration by" date roughly 5–6 weeks before the Grants.gov deadline.
- Most NOFOs schedule a pre-application webinar roughly 2–4 weeks after release.
- Typical window from NOFO release to Grants.gov deadline: ~5–8 weeks. (FY25 GRF: released 25 Mar 2026, Grants.gov 19 May 2026 = ~8 weeks. FY25 AI: released 14 May 2026, deadline 15 Jun 2026 = ~4.5 weeks. FY26 Victims: released 22 Jul 2026, deadline 14 Aug 2026 = ~3.5 weeks.) Three to eight weeks is the real planning window — you cannot start drafting when the NOFO drops if your SAM.gov is stale.
- The one genuinely recurring calendar anchor is the federal fiscal year end: NIJ must obligate the year's funds by 30 September. The GRF FAQ states "All notices of award are anticipated to be made no later than September 30." Every NIJ cycle is ultimately pulled toward that date.

WHY A DATED DEADLINE WOULD ROT (documented, not inferred): NIJ's cycle slipped a full fiscal year. FY24 NOFOs closed June–December 2024 (normal). FY25 NOFOs did not close until May–June 2026 — GRF closed 27 May 2026, the June cluster (Corrections, Forensic Science Systems, Forensic Science Innovations, School Safety, Drugs & Crime, Human Trafficking, AI, Emerging Technology, Policing, Youth Justice) closed 9–17 June 2026. FY26 NOFOs were then released July 2026 and closed 31 Jul – 4 Sep 2026. Two fiscal years' solicitations ran inside one calendar year. Anyone who had memorised "NIJ closes in June" from the FY24 pattern would have been wrong twice. Source: nij.ojp.gov/funding/expired.

SITE STATE AS OF 2026-09-18 (tooling fact, NOT a finding): both nij.ojp.gov/funding/current and nij.ojp.gov/funding/forthcoming returned "There are no results for your filter settings" — zero open and zero forthcoming opportunities listed. This is consistent with the FY26 cycle having just closed in early September; it is NOT evidence that NIJ stopped funding. The correct instruction to a user is "check /funding/current and /funding/forthcoming, and set a Grants.gov saved search on Assistance Listing 16.560," never a date.

review_stages.stage: Step 1 — Grants.gov SF-424 submitted (plus concept paper, for two-stage NOFOs)
review_stages.timing: Deadline set per NOFO, 11:59 p.m. ET; submit 48h early

review_stages.stage: Step 2 — Full application submitted in JustGrants
review_stages.timing: 7–8 days after the Grants.gov deadline, 8:59 p.m. ET

review_stages.stage: Responsiveness / Basic Minimum Requirements (BMR) screen — eligible applicant, in scope, and the asterisked required attachments present. Failures 'will neither proceed to peer review nor receive further consideration' (appealable)
review_stages.timing: Notice to failures 'within a few weeks after the submission due date'

review_stages.stage: Peer review by independent panel — usually external non-DOJ reviewers (also internal or hybrid). Ad hoc panel: 3+ reviewers score each criterion 1–10 for a total of 100, then discuss toward consensus. Standing panel: 15–30 members on up to 3-year terms, ~25% replaced annually; pairs screen first, top applications go to a full-panel 0–10 vote
review_stages.timing: The dominant block of the ~6-month arc; NIJ does not publish a panel-meeting date

review_stages.stage: Programmatic and financial review by NIJ staff — staff may contact applicants only about incomplete forms. 'NIJ staff are not authorized to provide information on peer review scores or comment on programmatic, risk, or budget/financial reviews while the merit review is in progress'
review_stages.timing: After peer review

review_stages.stage: Risk review under 2 C.F.R. 200.206 — SAM.gov exclusions, past performance, audit findings; for awards over $250,000 also the non-public integrity/performance (ex-FAPIIS) segment of SAM.gov
review_stages.timing: Before award decisions

review_stages.stage: Selection — 'All final award decisions will be made by the Director of the National Institute of Justice (NIJ)', weighing peer review ratings, staff recommendations, geographic coverage, strategic priorities, past performance and available funding
review_stages.timing: Pulled toward 30 September (fiscal year end)

review_stages.stage: Award notice via JustGrants to Application Submitter, Authorized Representative and Entity Administrator; Authorized Representative must accept or decline within 45 days. Unsuccessful applicants are notified after all awards are announced and 'OJP also provides unsuccessful applicants with a summary of peer reviewer comments'
review_stages.timing: ~6 months after the closing date, historically; by 30 Sept in compressed years

review_stages.stage: Award clearing before research may begin — 'Award clearing takes roughly three months, during which research maybe prohibited or significantly constrained' (FY26 Victims NOFO)
review_stages.timing: ~3 months after the award date

review_stages.stage: Optional applicant debriefing on request (online form; you supply the specific questions you want discussed) — feedback keyed to peer review panel comments
review_stages.timing: After the non-selection notification; no request deadline published

result.months_submission_to_award:
NIJ's own published figure: "The application review process (including peer review, decisionmaking, and other considerations) may take 6 months or longer. Notices of award and nonaward are sent about 6 months after the closing date of a notice of funding opportunity." NIJ instructs applicants to budget accordingly: "your start date should be at least 6 months after the closing date of the notice of funding opportunity to allow for NIJ's decision- and award-making processes." The GRF FAQ repeats "may take up to six months."

Measured against actual FY25 NOFOs, 6–7 months holds: FY25 Graduate Research Fellowship, JustGrants deadline 27 May 2026 → "Anticipated Period of Performance Start Date: January 1, 2027" = ~7 months. FY25 AI, concept paper due 15 June 2026 → start 1 January 2027 = ~6.5 months.

The FY26 cycle was compressed and broke the pattern: FY26 Research and Evaluation of Services for Victims of Crime, JustGrants deadline 21 Aug 2026 → "Anticipated Notification Date: By September 30, 2026" = ~6 weeks. Treat that as a symptom of a late-released cycle racing fiscal year end, not as the new norm.

REAL PLANNING NUMBER: add the ~3-month award clearing period on top. From the day you submit to the day you can actually run research is realistically ~9 months (6 to notification + 3 to clearance), and up to ~12 months from the day the NOFO drops. Period of performance is typically up to 60 months (GRF: 12–60 months).
result.resubmission_policy:
Allowed, and structurally encouraged — but much looser than NIH. No cap on the number of resubmissions was found anywhere in NIJ or OJP guidance, and no time window or expiry was found. There is no A0/A1 concept and no "substantial revision" test.

An introduction-equivalent IS required and it is called the "Resubmit Response." From the FY26 Victims NOFO, verbatim: "Resubmit Response (if applicable) (not counted against the proposal narrative page limit.): If an applicant is resubmitting an application presented previously to NIJ but not funded, the applicant should indicate that this is a resubmission. A statement should be provided, no more than two pages, containing: (1) the proposal title, submission date, and NIJ assigned application number of the previous application, and (2) a brief summary of revisions to the application, including responses to previous feedback received from NIJ." The FY25 GRF NOFO carries the same requirement in identical terms. It sits as section 2 of the proposal narrative, after the title page, and does NOT count against the page limit.

Cross-NOFO resubmission is explicitly permitted — this is a meaningful difference from NIH. NIJ FAQ: "If you are resubmitting a proposal that was originally submitted under a different Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO), follow the instructions in the Resubmit Response section of your current NOFO's Proposal Narrative." So a proposal declined under, say, Policing Practices can be re-aimed at Youth Justice in the next cycle.

What you have to respond to: every unsuccessful applicant automatically receives feedback — "OJP also provides unsuccessful applicants with a summary of peer reviewer comments." That summary is the raw material for the Resubmit Response. You can additionally request a formal debriefing (nij.ojp.gov/funding/nij-applicant-request-debriefing) via an online form on which you supply the specific questions you want discussed; the debrief is keyed to the peer review panel comments.

Adjacent but distinct: NIJ also runs phased re-application, where a funded formative/process evaluation can lead to "a subsequent application for funding of further evaluation research," and NIJ "may give applications for subsequent funding a higher priority consideration, but funding is not guaranteed." That is a follow-on, not a resubmission.
result.page_limits:
FORMAT (standard across research NOFOs, stated in the NOFO itself): "Be double-spaced, using a standard 12-point size font / Have no less than 1-inch margins / Have numbered pages." Consequence of breaking it: "If the Proposal Narrative does not follow this format, NIJ may reduce the score/ranking of the application."

PROPOSAL NARRATIVE LIMIT VARIES BY MECHANISM — this is the single most mechanism-dependent number:
- Standard Research & Evaluation topic solicitations: 30 pages (FY26 Research and Evaluation of Services for Victims of Crime: "Not exceeding 30 pages").
- Graduate Research Fellowship: 8 pages, and the GRF inverts the usual exclusion rule — "If included in the main body of the proposal narrative, any tables, charts, figures, and other illustrations do count toward the 8-page limit." The GRF FAQ also says "There are no line spacing, font, or formatting requirements other than the page limit specified in the notice of funding opportunity," so the 12pt/double-space/1-inch rule does not bind GRF.
- Concept-paper (two-stage) solicitations — FY25 AI for Criminal Justice Purposes and FY25 Emerging Technology: cover page + narrative "up to four pages" + "One page outlining the applicant's capabilities" + "One additional page for a budget sketch," double-spaced 12pt, 1-inch margins, numbered. Enforcement is absolute: "Any content submitted that exceeds the four-page limit will not be reviewed."

WHAT IS EXCLUDED FROM THE NARRATIVE LIMIT (standard R&E): "The page limit does not include the bibliography/references or appendixes, list of key personnel, resumes of key personnel, list of previous and current NIJ awards and products, charts, tables, or other necessary appendixes." Plus, per the NOFO's own section list: title page, Resubmit Response, table of contents and figures, and appendices.

OTHER FIXED LIMITS:
- Proposal Abstract: 2,000 characters, entered as a JustGrants web form, third person, no bullets or tables, no personally identifying information (funded abstracts are published on OJP.gov and USASpending.gov). CAUTION — NIJ's FAQ page still says the abstract "should not exceed 600 words"; that conflicts with the 2,000-character limit in the FY25/FY26 NOFOs and the OJP Application Resource Guide. Follow the NOFO.
- Resubmit Response: no more than 2 pages.
- Data Management, Sharing and Archiving Plan (DMSAP): maximum 2 pages.
- Biosketches: NSPM-33 Common Forms (Biographical Sketch and Current and Pending (Other) Support) are now the required format; forensic science NOFOs allow up to 5 pages per person; SciENcv is encouraged.

SCORING WEIGHTS (identical across the FY25 GRF, FY25 AI and FY26 Victims NOFOs — treat as NIJ's standard rubric): Statement of the Problem 5%, Project Design and Implementation 40%, Capabilities and Competencies 15%, Potential Impact 25%, Budget 15%. Project Design plus Potential Impact = 65% of the score. The "Potential Impact" 25% is where NIJ differs most from NSF/NIH: it asks for actionable knowledge for practitioners and policymakers and an explicit dissemination strategy, and NIJ expects "equal effort" on practitioner-facing dissemination products as on scholarly products.

Concept-paper scoring is different: an INTERNAL NIJ panel of subject matter experts scores narrative, budget sketch and personnel sketch each as EXCEPTIONAL (4) / EXCELLENT (3) / GOOD (2) / FAIR (1) / UNACCEPTABLE (0); a paper "must receive a GOOD, EXCELLENT, or EXCEPTIONAL score in all three components" to be invited to a full proposal. External peer review only happens at the full-application stage.

Tribal Authorizing Resolution (tribal applicants)

Disclosures and assurances in JustGrants: Disclosure of Lobbying Activities / SF-LLL, Disclosure of Duplication in Cost Items, DOJ Certified Standard Assurances, DOJ Certifications (lobbying; debarment/suspension; drug-free workplace; coordination with affected agencies), Applicant Disclosure and Justification for DOJ High-Risk Grantees

GRF-ONLY additions, all BMR-required: Verification of Current Enrollment; Undergraduate AND Graduate Transcripts; Statement of Support (from the advisor/institution); plus an optional Personal Statement. Funds are released only once a dissertation committee is formed and the topic approved.
result.program_officer_norms:
DISCOURAGED — in fact prohibited during an open competition. This is the sharpest possible contrast with NIH, and it is the single most important thing to tell someone whose grant instincts were formed at NIH or NSF.

NIJ, verbatim: "Because notices of funding opportunity are competitive, NIJ staff cannot have individual conversations concerning the notice of funding opportunity with prospective applicants." There is no NIJ program-officer pre-submission call, no "send me your specific aims," no informal read of fit. Emailing an NIJ scientist to pitch your idea will get you redirected, not coached.

WHAT REPLACES IT — three legitimate channels, in cycle order:
1. PRE-APPLICATION WEBINAR (the real substitute). Most NIJ NOFOs schedule one, printed in the Key Dates table, typically 2–4 weeks after release and 3–5 weeks before the deadline; e.g. FY25 AI: "A webinar for this NOFO will be held May 26, 2026, 1 p.m. - 2 p.m. ET. Register for the webinar." FY25 GRF: 15 April 2026. NIJ posts recordings and full transcripts afterwards (nij.ojp.gov/events, and per-NOFO transcript pages such as nij.ojp.gov/funding/fy25-research-evaluation-technology-ai-webinar-transcript). Attending live and asking in the Q&A is the closest NIJ has to a program-officer conversation, and the answers are on the record for every competitor. Reading past transcripts for a recurring solicitation is the highest-value, lowest-cost preparation move available — it is where NIJ staff say things like how page limits are enforced ("we would stop reading after one page for the budget sketch and four pages for the narrative") and that level of effort in the budget must match what the narrative promises.
2. OJP RESPONSE CENTER — the only sanctioned individual channel while a NOFO is open: 800-851-3420 / 202-353-5556 TTY, OJP.ResponseCenter@usdoj.gov, 9am–5pm ET M–F. Experienced applicants use it for answerable, factual questions: is my entity type eligible; is this activity in scope; is this cost allowable; can I submit to two categories; does an entity that is a subrecipient on another application have a conflict. They do not use it for "is my idea good." Budget-policy interpretation goes instead to the OCFO Customer Service Center, 800-458-0786.
3. AFTER THE DECISION — a formal debriefing. Every unsuccessful applicant automatically gets "a summary of peer reviewer comments"; you may additionally request a debriefing via NIJ's online form, on which you list the "Specific questions to be discussed during the debrief," the PI and primary contact, and who else will attend. This is where the real conversation happens with NIJ, and it is the input to the next cycle's Resubmit Response. Treat the debrief as the pre-submission meeting you were not allowed to have — held a year early for the next attempt.

DURING REVIEW, silence is policy: "NIJ staff are not authorized to provide information on peer review scores or comment on programmatic, risk, or budget/financial reviews while the merit review is in progress." Staff will contact YOU only if a submitted form is incomplete.

AFTER AWARD, the relationship flips and becomes personal: you are assigned both an NIJ Grant Manager (administrative) and an NIJ Scientist/science officer (substantive), with roles documented at nij.ojp.gov/funding/grants-nij-grant-manager-and-scientist-roles-and-responsibilities. Early-career researchers routinely build the relationship from that side, or by serving as an NIJ peer reviewer (nij.ojp.gov/funding/becoming-peer-reviewer-nij) — which is the most reliable way to learn what a competitive NIJ application looks like, since panels bring in roughly 25% new reviewers each year.

Early-career-specific: NIJ gives enhanced review consideration to New Investigator/Early Career PIs, but you must self-designate on the proposal title page. Eligibility is (i) assistant professor or equivalent full-time staff scientist at a U.S. institution, (ii) terminal degree or post-graduate clinical training completed within six years of the submission deadline, and (iii) no prior NIJ funding as PI or co-PI, with Graduate Research Fellowships excepted. Nobody will apply this for you.
result.funded_examples_source:
You can read abstracts, final reports and data from NIJ-funded work, but NOT full funded applications — NIJ publishes no counterpart to NIAID's sample-applications page, and I found no university research office hosting successful NIJ proposals either. Four real routes, in descending usefulness:

1. NIJ AWARDS DATABASE — https://nij.ojp.gov/funding/awards/list. "This page includes all awards funded by the National Institute of Justice since 2003"; ~7,493 awards totalling ~$3.98 billion. Filter by fiscal year, topic (corrections, courts, forensic sciences, crime prevention, drugs, law enforcement...), state, award status, funding category, keyword, award ID, awardee name, and the originating solicitation. Each row gives project title, original solicitation, recipient institution, state, award number, award amount and status; each award's detail page carries the project description and "a list of products (e.g., publications, reports, peer-reviewed articles) generated by the awardee." THIS IS THE HIGHEST-VALUE MOVE for a new applicant: filter to the solicitation you are about to answer, read the last two cohorts of funded abstracts, and you have NIJ's revealed preferences — typical award size, typical team, typical design, and which institutions win. NIJ explicitly asks applicants to do this: "Applicants are encouraged to refer to previously and currently funded studies to inform the development of complementary, novel areas of research."

2. FINAL RESEARCH REPORTS — every NIJ research award must deliver a Final Research Report, and grantee reports are posted publicly. Search the NCJRS Virtual Library (https://www.ojp.gov/ncjrs-virtual-library/search, 235,000+ items, "all known OJP works and sponsored research") or NIJ's own publications list (https://nij.ojp.gov/library/publications/list, which includes "reports submitted by grantees"). A funded project's abstract plus its final report together let you reverse-engineer roughly what the application promised.

3. DATA — archiving is mandatory. NIJ's principal repository is the National Archive of Criminal Justice Data at ICPSR (https://www.icpsr.umich.edu/web/pages/NACJD/), with NIJ's own index at https://nij.ojp.gov/library/datasets-nij-funded-research. Many deidentified datasets download freely; restricted files need a Restricted Data Use Agreement, IRB letter, confidentiality security plan and an NIJ Privacy Certificate. Useful both as example deliverables and as free data for a proposal that avoids new collection.

4. USASPENDING.GOV — funded proposal abstracts are republished there and on OJP.gov ("The text from abstracts will be made publicly available on the OJP.gov and USASpending.gov websites if the project is awarded"), searchable across all DOJ awards if you want cross-agency comparison.

5. YOUR OWN REVIEWS — every unsuccessful applicant receives a summary of peer reviewer comments automatically, and can request a debriefing. Combined with the published scoring weights (5/40/15/25/15), that is the most specific feedback NIJ gives anyone.

NOT FOUND: any repository of complete funded NIJ applications, and any NIJ-published example or model proposal. Recorded as a genuine gap, not a failed search.

unresolved: Number of resubmissions permitted: NOT FOUND. Neither NIJ nor OJP states a cap, and none of the three NOFOs read imposes one. Absence of a stated limit is not the same as an explicit 'unlimited' — do not publish 'unlimited' as a quoted rule.

Time window for resubmission: NOT FOUND. No expiry on how old a declined application may be when resubmitted, and no rule that it must go back to the same NOFO (cross-NOFO resubmission is explicitly allowed).

Debriefing request deadline: NOT FOUND on nij.ojp.gov/funding/nij-applicant-request-debriefing. Whether numeric peer review scores are disclosed at a debrief is also unstated — the page implies panel comments only.

Stage-2 dates for the concept-paper mechanisms: the FY25 AI and Emerging Technology NOFOs give only 'Approximately by July 15, 2026, selected applicants will receive invitation to submit a full application'; the full-application deadline is set individually in the invitation email ('a new submission deadline'), and no anticipated notification date is printed. Cannot be published as a general rule.

Conflict left unresolved in NIJ's own sources: the NIJ FAQ page says the proposal abstract 'should not exceed 600 words', while the FY25/FY26 NOFOs and the OJP Application Resource Guide say 2,000 characters (~300 words). The FAQ page appears stale. Applicants should follow the NOFO; flag this as an example of NIJ's own guidance pages drifting out of sync with live NOFOs.

Whether NIJ will return to its pre-2025 seasonal calendar: UNKNOWN. FY25 solicitations closed a full fiscal year late (May–June 2026) and FY26 closed July–September 2026. No NIJ statement explaining or projecting the schedule was found — I found no announcement of a delay, only the dated evidence on the expired-opportunities page.

nij.ojp.gov/funding/current and /funding/forthcoming both returned 'There are no results for your filter settings' on 2026-09-18. This is a page-state observation. It does NOT mean NIJ has stopped issuing solicitations and must not be recorded as a programme status.

Method note: the NIJ FY26 Victims, FY25 GRF and FY25 AI NOFO PDFs would not parse through the plain fetch tool (binary/compressed streams returned as garbage). result.funder_system: USDA National Institute of Food and Agriculture (NIFA) — the competitive-grants arm of USDA REE. Its flagship is AFRI (Agriculture and Food Research Initiative, Assistance Listing 10.310, ~$300M/yr anticipated), issued as three annual NOFOs/RFAs: Foundational and Applied Science (FAS), Education and Workforce Development (EWD), and Strengthening Agricultural Systems (SAS, formerly Sustainable Agricultural Systems). Machinery below is NIFA-wide where stated, AFRI-specific where marked. Two governing documents sit above every mechanism: the NIFA Grants Application Guide (agency-wide, April 2026 version) and the individual NOFO/RFA — and the RFA wins: "The RFA overrides the NIFA Grants Application Guide if there is a discrepancy between the two documents." Note a structural quirk: NIFA guidance pages on nifa.usda.gov have been progressively migrated to the USDA Guidance Portal (usda.gov/guidance) under EO 13891, so many NIFA pages now show only a "Guidance Resources Moved to USDA.gov" stub with a Download button — the substance is in the linked PDF, not the webpage.
result.submission_portal:
Grants.gov, using Grants.gov Workspace. The RFA is categorical: "Applicants must apply to this RFA electronically; no other method or response is accepted." AFRI FY26 FAS funding opportunity number is USDA-NIFA-AFRI-011134.

THREE REGISTRATIONS, in order, and they are the hidden long-lead item (verbatim lead times from the NIFA Grants Application Guide, April 2026):
1. SAM.gov — entity registration, which generates the UEI. "Important: Allow 4-6 weeks to complete SAM.gov registration." "SAM.gov registration must be renewed annually" (an expired SAM registration silently blocks submission — check it months out, not the week of).
2. Grants.gov — organizational registration plus an Authorized Organization Representative (AOR). Guide's own estimates: organizations with an EIN "should allow 7 business days to complete all registration steps, but additional time may be required for AOR Authorization depending upon the responsiveness of your E-Biz POC"; organizations applying for an EIN "should plan on a minimum of 2 full weeks"; "Individual applicants can potentially register in as little as 1 business day."
3. eRA Commons — ONLY for programs that have migrated. "Some NIFA funding opportunities are managed through the eRA Commons grants management system. Applicants responding to NOFOs or RFPs from programs that have transitioned to eRA Commons must be registered with this system prior to application submission. The NOFO or RFP will outline whether registration in eRA Commons is required." Organizations must designate at least one Signing Official (SO) and one Project Director (PD) in eRA Commons. "Important Note: Creating an eRA Commons account can take up to two weeks." IMPORTANT FINDING: the FY26 AFRI FAS NOFO (MOD6, Aug 2026) contains NO occurrence of "eRA", "Commons" (as a system) or "SciENcv" — AFRI FAS FY26 goes through Grants.gov, not eRA. NIFA is mid-migration; which programme you are applying to decides.

A fourth system matters post-award, and surprises people: REEport, inside the NIFA Reporting Portal (portal.nifa.usda.gov). Nothing is awarded until it is used — "Submitting a Project Initiation Form is required to begin award processing at NIFA." Land-grant universities go through a two-step REEport site-administrator assignment first; all other institutions are one-step.

An older FAQ line in the Guide says "NIFA requires no separate registration beyond the Grants.gov registration" — that predates the eRA migration and conflicts with the Guide's own Step 6; treat the NOFO as authoritative.

Practical note for a first-time PI: none of these registrations are yours to do. SAM.gov and Grants.gov are institutional, held by your sponsored-programs office, and only the AOR can press submit. Your first action is an email to your research office, not to Grants.gov.
result.deadline_structure:
Per-solicitation AND dated AND recurring — all three at once, which is why this one is easy to get wrong.

There is no NIH-style agency-wide standard due-date calendar. Each AFRI program area priority carries its own deadline (and its own LOI deadline where one applies), published in Part I-C of the NOFO and consolidated on one canonical page: https://www.nifa.usda.gov/grants/programs/agriculture-food-research-initiative/afri-deadlines. Every deadline is 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time.

ACTUAL FY2026 DATES, as NIFA published them (these are the real dates, and they show the recurring shape of the year):

THE RECURRING RHYTHM (this is what to plan against, since the year number changes): FAS NOFO posts late summer/early autumn, deadlines in the first three weeks of December; EWD and SAS NOFOs post in winter, deadlines mid-March to end of April; predoc and postdoc fellowships are the latest of the spring set. Awards must all land by 30 September.

THE DRIFT WARNING, and the reason a date alone is not enough: NIFA amends deadlines mid-cycle. The FY26 FAS NOFO carries "MODIFICATIONS: 11/14/25 — The APPLICATION DEADLINE has been extended for various AFRI Program Area Priorities," with Table 2 on page 5 summarising the changes and edits on ~40 pages; later mods (7/30/26, 8/18/26, 8/24/26) withdrew individual commodity-board topics outright. So: use the dated deadline to plan, and re-check the AFRI Deadlines page and the current NOFO MOD number before you rely on it. Workshop/conference grants run on their own clock entirely — LOI at least 195 days before the workshop, full application at least 150 days before.

review_stages.stage: Submission closes, 5:00 p.m. ET. Grants.gov validation, then NIFA administrative screening for compliance with the RFA. Applications that miss margins, font size, page limits, or omit Project Summary / Project Narrative / Bibliography "will be returned without review" — the screen is mechanical and unforgiving.
review_stages.timing: Day 0 to ~30 days. Hard checkpoint the funder itself publishes: "If the AR has not received correspondence from NIFA regarding a submitted application within 30 days of the established deadline, contact the Program Contact identified in Part I – C and request the proposal number assigned to the application. Failure to do so may result in the application not being considered for funding by the peer review panel." This is the single highest-value 30-day diary entry in the whole process.

review_stages.stage: Panel manager selected by the National Program Leader (an outside established scientist, hired as a part-time temporary USDA employee for 1–2 years); panel assembled with the NPL. Balance targets: expertise coverage, geography, institution size/type, rank; ≥30% returning panelists; "No more than one individual, including the panel manager, can serve from a single institution or, with very few exceptions, from a single state."
review_stages.timing: Weeks after close (NIFA publishes no month count for this step)

review_stages.stage: Written reviews. "Typically, three to four panelists review each proposal. If needed for additional expertise, up to three ad hoc reviewers may also evaluate a proposal. Each panelist is assigned 12 to 20 proposals, for which they provide written reviews." Scores for AFRI and most programs: excellent / very good / good / fair / poor. AFRI criteria: scientific merit; qualifications of project personnel and adequacy of facilities; relevance to program priorities including importance of the topic for agriculture.
review_stages.timing: Before the panel meeting

review_stages.stage: Panel meeting. Panelists seated at a single table; oral evaluation from each assigned reviewer, then whole-panel discussion; conflicted panelists leave the room. Research, integrated and strengthening applications are discussed and ranked SEPARATELY. Consensus ranking in five bands: outstanding / high priority / medium priority / low priority / do not fund — "Only proposals ranked in the first three categories may be considered for funding." A "panel summary" is written by a panel member reflecting the consensus, including a synthesis section with suggestions for improvement. Rankings are reassessed on the final day.
review_stages.timing: Reported at roughly 3–5 months after the deadline. CAUTION: this month count comes from a search-index summary of NIFA pages, NOT from a NIFA page I could read. NIFA's own "Wait for Notification" page gives no timeline at all, and the RFA gives none.

review_stages.stage: Funding recommendation. NPL and panel manager work down the panel ranking until funds are exhausted, checking budgets for appropriateness and screening for duplicate funding from other agencies. AFRI then applies FASE strengthening funds to lift eligible below-the-line applications from small/mid-sized institutions, MSIs and EPSCoR states, and New Investigator applications get "special consideration ... that fall below the funding line." Centers of Excellence status acts as an explicit tie-breaker between equally meritorious applications.
review_stages.timing: Immediately after panel

review_stages.stage: Notification — everyone, funded or not. "After the review process has been completed, NIFA sends copies of reviews, not including the identity of reviewers, and a summary (if applicable) of the review panel comments to the PD." Declined applicants get the written reviews, the panel summary AND "information on the relative ranking of their proposal" — i.e. you learn which of the five bands you landed in, which is the single most useful input to a resubmission decision. Sent by email only.
review_stages.timing: After funding decisions

review_stages.stage: Award phase, step 1 — Response. "When a funding recommendation is finalized, the national program leader managing the program notifies each potential awardee. This is an informal notification," followed by email from REEportNotifications@usda.gov. The PI must then submit a Project Initiation Form in REEport (objectives and expected outcomes, in both technical and non-technical terms). Nothing advances until this is filed.
review_stages.timing: Weeks before the Notice of Award

review_stages.stage: Award phase, step 2 — Processing. NIFA program team collects updated documents, then NIFA's Awards Management Division does the final administrative review, then the Notice of Award / Award Face Sheet issues and funds can be drawn via ASAP.
review_stages.timing: Weeks

review_stages.stage: Award effective date — the one hard statutory anchor. "The date specified by the NIFA awarding official as the effective date of the grant must be no later than September 30 of the federal fiscal year in which the project is approved for support and funds are appropriated for such purpose."
review_stages.timing: No later than 30 September of the fiscal year

result.months_submission_to_award:
Roughly 4 to 10 months, and the ceiling is the reliable number.

The only month count NIFA itself guarantees is the end-stop: awards must be effective no later than 30 September of the federal fiscal year. Working from the real FY26 FAS dates, that gives the outer bound precisely:
- 4 Dec 2025 deadline → 30 Sep 2026 = 9.9 months maximum
- 11 Dec 2025 → 9.6 months maximum
- 18 Dec 2025 → 9.4 months maximum
- 2 Oct 2025 (Commodity Board A1811) → 12.0 months maximum
- 19 Mar 2026 (EWD) → 6.4 months maximum
- 30 Apr 2026 (EWD Postdoctoral) → 5.0 months maximum
Note what that implies and what applicants routinely miss: the spring EWD and SAS deadlines have a SHORTER runway to the same 30 September wall than the December FAS deadlines, not a longer one. A postdoctoral fellowship applicant submitting 30 April has at most five months to award.

Peer review itself is reported at 3–5 months from the deadline, which would put FAS panel outcomes around March–May and EWD around June–August. FLAG: I could not verify the 3–5 month figure on any NIFA page I successfully read — it comes from a search-index summary. NIFA's "Wait for Notification" page states how you will be notified but gives no timeline, and neither RFA states one. Treat 3–5 months as indicative, and the 30 September ceiling as firm.

Two genuinely fixed intermediate checkpoints you can diary: proposal number / correspondence by 30 days after the deadline (chase it if silent), and Project Initiation Form in REEport immediately on informal notification from the NPL.

Practical consequence for anyone with a contract, visa or student start date riding on this: assume money does not move until late summer for a December submission, and budget a start date accordingly. Rapid Response (A1712/A1713) is the only expedited route — "Application review and processing will be expedited to ensure timely project start-up," with deliverables required within 90 days of award.
result.resubmission_policy:
Allowed, with no stated numeric cap and no time window — but a one-page response document is mandatory and there is no separate resubmission deadline.

AFRI recognises exactly three application types (FY25 and FY26 RFA wording is identical): New, Resubmitted, and Renewal.

RESUBMITTED, verbatim: "Resubmitted applications must include the one-page 'Response to Previous Review' (see Part IV – C), regardless of whether they are resubmitted in sequential years or to the same program area priority as submitted previously, and are subject to the same criteria and due dates herein. Resubmitted applicants must enter the NIFA-assigned proposal number of the previously submitted application in the Federal Field (Field 4) on the application form."

Read the clause carefully, because it settles the three questions applicants actually ask:
- Can I move to a different program area priority? Yes — the requirement follows you "regardless of whether they are resubmitted ... to the same program area priority as submitted previously." Changing priority does not make it a new application.
- Is there a special deadline? No — "subject to the same criteria and due dates herein." You compete in the ordinary cycle, against new applications, with no separate track and no handicap or bonus.
- How many times? Neither the FY25 nor FY26 FAS RFA states a limit, and neither states a time window in which you must resubmit. UNRESOLVED as an explicit numeric cap — I found no "no more than N resubmissions" language anywhere in either RFA.

THE INTRODUCTION PAGE — mechanics, verbatim from the FY2026 FAS "Additional Information for Part IV, C": "The Project Narrative attachment should include two components: (1) a maximum 1-page response to the previous review (containing the previous proposal number in the first line) titled 'Response to Previous Review' as the first page of the attachment and (2) the 7- or 18-page Project Narrative, as required. The one-page 'Response to Previous Review' does not count against the 7- or 18-page limit of the Project Narrative."
So: same PDF, first page, titled exactly "Response to Previous Review", previous proposal number on line one, free of the page count. It is not a separate attachment — filing it as one is a common error.

What must change: NIFA does not prescribe content. The leverage comes from what you were sent — the written reviews, the panel summary with its synthesis-and-suggestions section, and your relative ranking band. If you were ranked "low priority" or "do not fund", those two bands are ineligible for award, which is a materially different signal from falling just below the funding line in "medium priority".

RENEWAL is a distinct type, not a resubmission: "Renewal applications must contain the same information as required for new applications and must contain a progress report. The progress report must include the implementation of the data management plan (DMP) of the previously funded project." The progress report sits INSIDE the narrative page limit (unlike the Response to Previous Review, which sits outside it). Enter the prior proposal number in Field 4. Note many AFRI program area priorities state "Unless otherwise stated, grants are not renewable" — check your priority. Seed Grants are explicitly not renewable, and "Seed grant awardees may receive no more than two seed grants (for different projects) within any five-year period." New Investigators "may only receive one New Investigator Seed Grant as PD during their career."
result.page_limits:
FORMATTING, applied mechanically and fatally (NIFA Grants Application Guide + AFRI Part IV-C): 12-point font minimum "regardless of line spacing"; single line spacing, "no more than six lines per vertical inch"; 1-inch margins all sides; "Do not use a condensed or narrow font (e.g., Arial Narrow)"; PDF only, not password protected; filenames ≤50 characters, no spaces, no special characters, all unique; pages numbered sequentially (except in eRA). The sanction, verbatim: "To ensure fair competition, applications exceeding the respective page limitation or violating the limitations on margins or font size will be returned without review." Also: "Reviewers will not be expected to access and evaluate information provided in the Project Narrative as URLs or hyperlinks" — no smuggling content out to a website.

PROJECT NARRATIVE — AFRI FAS (FY2026, verbatim):
- 18 pages: Standard, New Investigator Standard, Workshop, Strengthening Standard, Strengthening Workshop. Also CAP and Strengthening CAP (18 pages).
- 7 pages: Sabbatical, Equipment, Seed (Strengthening or New Investigator), and Rapid Response A1712/A1713.
- Program-area exceptions exist and override: e.g. CARE (A1701) — "The Project Narrative must not exceed a total of 7 pages."
- Centers of Excellence justification goes at the END of the narrative, INSIDE the page limit.

PROJECT NARRATIVE — AFRI EWD (verbatim): "The Education and Workforce Development RFA project narrative page limit is 10 for all programs, except for the Predoctoral Fellowship program which has a 6-page limit." Postdoctoral Fellowship: 10 pages. (A predoc fellowship at 6 pages is the tightest document in the AFRI portfolio.)

EVERY OTHER ATTACHMENT (AFRI FAS, verbatim limits):
- Project Summary/Abstract: "maximum 1-page and approximately 250 words". Must include relevance to the Program Area Priority. For A1811 Commodity Board, the last sentence must name the commodity board topic.
- Response to Previous Review: max 1 page, outside the narrative limit (resubmissions only)
- Key Personnel Roles: 2-page limit
- Logic Model: 2-page limit — REQUIRED for all Integrated Project applications, encouraged otherwise
- Management Plan: 3-page limit — REQUIRED for all Integrated Project applications, encouraged otherwise. Must include org chart, administrative timeline, governance, sustainability beyond the award, and an advisory group of stakeholders
- Data Management Plan: 2-page limit, "Required for all applications". Agency-wide rule, verbatim: "The DMP is limited to two pages. These two pages do not count toward the page limits for the project narrative and should not be used to circumvent the project page limit." If genuinely no data: the statement "No data will be produced" plus an explanation is acceptable
- Mentoring Plan: 2-page limit for seed and standard grants. Required for all grant types (except workshop, equipment, sabbatical) that involve student or participant training; predoc and postdoc fellowships have their own separate mentoring requirements. NEWLY ADDED — "December 20, 2024: Mentoring Plan (MP) added for all program areas"
- Facilities & Other Resources: NO page limit
- Equipment: NO page limit
- Documentation of Collaboration: NO page limit (letters of support, subcontract commitment letters)
- Bibliography & References Cited: no stated limit, but complete references with titles and all co-authors, consistent journal format, alphabetical or numbered by citation order
- Preprints: allowed only if "directly germane", single-spaced, each labelled with submitting organization, PD name(s) and application title. Explicitly NOT a route around the page limit: "Information may not be appended to an application to circumvent page limitations."
- Conflict of Interest list: one per Senior/Key Person, collated into a SINGLE PDF, using NIFA's required template. Categories: all thesis/postdoctoral advisees and advisors; all co-authors within the past 3 years including pending and submitted; all collaborators
- Current and Pending Support: one per key person; this application must itself be listed as "Pending" even if nothing else is active

BIOSKETCH — a live divergence worth checking before you write one. The NIFA Grants Application Guide (April 2026) says: "The Project Director/Principal Investigator (PD/PI) and all senior/key personnel must complete a USDA Biographical Sketch using SciENcv ... SciENcv controls the format and content of the Biographical Sketch Common Form. Do not submit custom biosketches or narrative versions. Documents marked Draft will not be accepted." SciENcv requires an eRA Commons or other federal login and certification before download. BUT the FY26 AFRI FAS NOFO's own required-items list says "Curriculum Vitae", not Biographical Sketch, and contains no mention of SciENcv — and the RFA overrides the Guide. If you are applying to AFRI, follow the NOFO; if to a NIFA programme that has moved to eRA, budget time for SciENcv (it is a real long-lead item).

NARRATIVE STRUCTURE (AFRI expects these headings): Introduction (long-term goal and supporting objectives, prior work, preliminary data, stakeholder role, why this institution); Rationale and Significance (must state the specific relationship to a Program Area Priority — "Applications that do not address at least one Program Area Priority will not be reviewed"); Approach (objectives/specific aims, methods, techniques and feasibility, expected results, evaluation, data analysis, communication plan, pitfalls, limitations); and a year-by-year Project Timetable covering the entire project "including periods beyond the grant funding period."

SF-424 (R&R) Project/Performance Site Location(s)
R&R Other Project Information Form (carries the narrative attachments)
Project Summary/Abstract — max 1 page, ~250 words, must state relevance to the Program Area Priority. CRITICAL: omitting this means no review
Project Narrative — 7 or 18 pages (FAS) / 10 or 6 pages (EWD) by grant type. CRITICAL: omitting this means no review

Bibliography & References Cited. CRITICAL: omitting this means no review — "Failure to include any of the three critical required documents of Project Summary/Abstract, Project Narrative, or Bibliography & References Cited sections as PDF attachment will result in the application not being reviewed or considered for funding by NIFA"
Data Management Plan — 2 pages, required for ALL applications
Mentoring Plan — 2 pages; required for all grant types except workshop, equipment and sabbatical where students or participants are trained or mentored (added Dec 2024)
Facilities & Other Resources — no page limit
Equipment — no page limit

Budget Justification

Management Plan — 3 pages, REQUIRED for Integrated Projects, encouraged otherwise
Response to Previous Review — 1 page, first page of the Project Narrative attachment, RESUBMISSIONS ONLY

Letter of Intent — where the program area priority requires one; mandatory for ALL Workshop Grants, at least 195 days before the workshop. "Proposals submitted without prior approval of the letter of intent by the program leader are returned without review"

result.program_officer_norms:
EXPECTED AND EXPLICITLY ENCOURAGED — closer to NIH than to a private foundation, and NIFA says so in writing in at least four places. This is the opposite of the "discouraged" pattern.

NIFA's own peer-review document describes contact as the normal, observed behaviour rather than a grudging allowance: "After reading the RFA, applicants often will contact the program staff to discuss the applicability of a topic to the program goals and suitability for prospective submission as a proposal."

The Application Guide instructs it twice: "Questions about applicant eligibility or the specific funding program that you are interested in should be directed to the NIFA program staff listed in the NOFO or RFP." And: "NOFOs and RFPs will contain contact information of NIFA program staff working on a particular funding opportunity. All specific questions regarding that funding opportunity should be directed to NIFA program staff."

The AFRI Grant Types document goes further and makes it near-obligatory for three grant types: "Investigators are encouraged to contact the appropriate Program Area Priority Contact, regarding suitability of project topics to verify that their submission is appropriate to the program area priority. For Equipment Grants, investigators are encouraged to contact the appropriate Program Area Priority Contact regarding appropriateness of requested equipment for topics within program area priority requirements." For Workshop Grants: "For all requests of $25,000 or more, applicants should consult with the program contact listed in the request for applications (RFA) regarding suitability of the application for submission to the relevant program area priority." And in program area text: "Applicants who have questions about the fit of their projects are welcome to contact program staff."

WHO, exactly. Every AFRI RFA publishes a named contact list in Appendix I: the AFRI Program Office (AFRI@usda.gov), the Associate Director for Programs and the four Institute Deputy Directors, then Program Area Contacts with individual names, direct phone numbers and usda.gov emails for each of the six program areas — e.g. Plant Health lists nine named NPLs with phone numbers; Animal Health lists seven. You are not emailing a generic inbox; you are emailing a named National Program Leader who is a scientist in your field. Each individual program area priority description in Part I-C also lists its own "Program Area Priority Contact(s)" by name.

WHEN in the cycle. Right after the NOFO posts and before you write — i.e. September–October for a December FAS deadline, January–February for a March/April EWD or SAS deadline. Two windows are effectively closed: nothing useful can be said once the panel is convened, and during review NPLs are bound by confidentiality. The one contact that is not optional is the 30-day post-deadline chase if you have had no correspondence and no proposal number.

WHAT EXPERIENCED APPLICANTS ACTUALLY ASK (all of these are answerable, and grounded in what NIFA says NPLs decide):
- "Does this idea fit priority A1141 or A1143?" — the highest-value question, because "Applications that do not address at least one Program Area Priority will not be reviewed", and the NPL is the person who makes that call.
- "Which grant type should this be — Standard, Seed, or New Investigator Standard?" — affects page limit (18 vs 7), budget ceiling, and which pool you compete in.
- "Do I qualify as a New Investigator?" — the criteria are unusually mechanical (fewer than 75 total publications, fewer than 25 as first or senior author, under 5 years post-graduate career-track experience, not more than 12 years past the terminal degree, no competitively awarded federal research funds as PD except pre/postdoc, equipment and AFRI Seed grants). There is an AFRI New Investigator Decision Tree PDF, and NPLs confirm edge cases.
- "Is my institution eligible for Strengthening funds?" — turns on EPSCoR state, enrollment ≤17,500, MSI status >50%, and the published "Most/Least Successful Institutions" tables. Worth confirming, because strengthening funds rescue below-the-line applications.
- "Is my LOI likely to be invited?" — for LOI priorities and all Workshop Grants this is decisive: the program leader approves or the full application is returned without review.
- "What was last year's success rate for this priority?" — NIFA directs applicants to do exactly this: "Applicants should refer to the Funding Opportunity web page for programs of interest to see the previous year's success rate and gauge the level of competition."
- "Is the equipment I want appropriate here?" / "Is a $40k workshop suitable for this priority?" — both explicitly invited.
- For Rapid Response: email afri-rapidresponse@usda.gov after submitting, as the NOFO instructs.

Also free and underused: "NIFA program staff also conduct various grantsmanship webinars throughout the year, covering various NIFA competitive programs, to educate applicants regarding NIFA funding opportunities." NIFA ran a dedicated AFRI New Investigator webinar series (recorded, on YouTube, with a handout) aimed at early-career applicants and the research administrators supporting them.

What NPLs will NOT do: read a draft narrative, predict a score, or comment during review. Confidentiality is enforced hard — reviewer identities are never released, and a conflicted NPL or panel manager is excluded from every aspect of a given application's review.
result.funded_examples_source:
Strong and unusually rich — because NIFA requires every awardee to file a public-facing project description before money moves, funded abstracts are systematically available, including in non-technical language.

1. NIFA DATA GATEWAY — the primary route. https://www.nifa.usda.gov/data/data-gateway. "The Data Gateway enables users to find funding data, metrics, and information about research, education, and extension projects that have received grant awards from NIFA." Its NIFA Enterprise Search gives project detail, financial detail and advanced search; you can filter, choose which data elements to display, and export results. Six pre-built modules: Recent Awards (FY2002 to present, sortable by title, state, amount), Congressional District map, Knowledge Area, Subject of Investigation, Field of Science, and Award Trends. There is an "Introduction to NIFA Data Gateway" video tutorial.

2. WHY THE ABSTRACTS ARE GOOD, and this is the part worth knowing: the content comes from the mandatory Project Initiation Form every awardee files in REEport. It "requires a description of objectives and expected outcomes of the funded work, in both technical and non-technical terms. Technical data submitted in the Project Initiation Form is made publicly available in the NIFA Data Gateway." So for any funded project you get the objectives and expected outcomes as the PI wrote them — and a plain-language version alongside, which is a better model for writing your own Project Summary than most funded-abstract databases offer.

3. REEIS — https://reeis.usda.gov (redirects into NIFA's site). "The Research, Education, and Economics Information System (REEIS) provides information on NIFA's research, education, and extension programs as well as those of other USDA partner organizations," with data marts, tabular and graphical reports, text searches and data downloads. "REEIS is accessible to the public with no registration required." This is where the historical CRIS project record lives; REEport replaced the old CRIS web forms for reporting, and progress reports use the standard federal RPPR format.

4. NIFA REPORTING PORTAL — https://portal.nifa.usda.gov (hosts REEport, Plan of Work, and links to REEIS, Data Gateway and PRS). Login is for awardees; the public routes are Data Gateway and REEIS.

WHAT YOU CANNOT GET, and should not expect: full funded applications are not published, and reviews are not published. NIFA's confidentiality rule is explicit — written reviews and evaluations are "shared only with the respective applicant", reviewer identities are never released, and unfunded applications are retained for three years and "released only with the consent of the applicant or to the extent required by law." There is no NIH-style public sample-application library from NIFA itself. The practical substitutes are (a) asking a funded PI in your department for their narrative — routine and usually granted, and the Data Gateway lets you find the ones near you by state or congressional district; (b) university research-office AFRI toolkits, which do circulate annotated examples; and (c) reading your own panel summary after a first attempt, which is the closest thing to a summary statement NIFA produces and which every applicant receives.

TWO MORE THINGS WORTH READING BEFORE WRITING: the published success rate for your specific priority on its Funding Opportunity page (NIFA explicitly tells applicants to check it), and the "AFRI Review Criteria" PDF on the NOFO Resources page — the actual scoring rubric your panel will use.

SOURCING NOTE, per house rules: everything above was read from NIFA's own pages and PDFs. I could not reach nifa.usda.gov PDFs through a plain fetch (consistent 60-second timeouts) or via curl (connection reset), and usda.gov's guidance portal returns 403 to a plain fetch; I retrieved the authoritative PDFs by fetching them same-origin inside a rendering browser and decoding them locally. One figure — "3–5 months" for the peer review phase — rests on a search-index summary only and is flagged as unverified.

unresolved: Peer-review duration in months. The "3-5 months from deadline to panel outcome" figure comes from a SEARCH-INDEX summary, not from a NIFA page I could read. NIFA's own "Wait for Notification" page publishes notification mechanics but no timeline, and neither the FY25 nor FY26 AFRI FAS RFA states one. The only funder-stated time anchor is the 30 September award-effective-date ceiling. Treat any month count between deadline and notification as indicative.

Numeric cap on resubmissions. Neither the FY25 nor FY26 AFRI FAS RFA states a maximum number of resubmissions or a deadline by which you must resubmit. NOT FOUND — I am reporting absence of a stated limit, not permission without limit.

Which NIFA programmes have migrated to eRA Commons. The Application Guide says only "programs that have transitioned" and defers to each NOFO. AFRI FAS FY26 is clearly NOT on eRA (no occurrence of eRA/Commons/SciENcv anywhere in the 126-page NOFO), but I could not obtain a list of which NIFA programmes ARE. Anyone outside AFRI must check their own NOFO, and budget two weeks for eRA Commons if it applies.

Biosketch format for AFRI specifically. The April 2026 Application Guide mandates a SciENcv-certified USDA Biographical Sketch and forbids custom biosketches; the FY26 AFRI FAS NOFO's required-items list says "Curriculum Vitae" and never mentions SciENcv. The RFA overrides the Guide, so AFRI FY26 appears to take a CV — but whether SciENcv becomes mandatory for AFRI in FY27 is UNRESOLVED and is a genuine long-lead risk (SciENcv needs a federal login and a certification step).

Whether the FY2027 AFRI NOFOs have posted. As of 18 Sep 2026 the AFRI Deadlines page still showed the FY26 table (Dec 2025 FAS, Mar/Apr 2026 EWD and SAS) and I found no FY27 AFRI NOFO on the NIFA funding-opportunities listing. The recurring pattern predicts an FY27 FAS NOFO in late summer/early autumn 2026 with December 2026 deadlines, but I could not confirm it had posted. NOT FOUND, not "not happening".

Page limits for the EWD and SAS NOFOs at attachment level. I read the FY2026 FAS "Additional Information for Part IV, C" in full; the equivalent EWD and SAS documents exist on the same resources page but I did not open them. EWD narrative limits (10 pages general, 6 predoctoral, 10 postdoctoral) come from the FY2026 AFRI Grant Types document and are solid; the per-attachment limits for EWD/SAS may differ from FAS.
Current typical success rates per program area priority. NIFA directs applicants to each Funding Opportunity page for the previous year's success rate; I did not extract these figures per priority.

Tooling note, not a finding: nifa.usda.gov PDFs time out on plain fetch (60s) and curl was reset; usda.gov's guidance portal returns 403 to plain fetch and serves PDFs as forced downloads. Every authoritative document above was retrieved by fetching it same-origin inside a rendering browser and decoding it locally. No failed fetch was treated as evidence that anything ended.
